->THIRD OBJECTIONS<-

### NINTH OBJECTION.

For indeed, the ideas that represent <term>substances</term> <note>In 17th-century philosophy, a "substance" is a thing that can exist on its own, such as a tree, a person, or God, rather than a quality like "red" or "fast."</note> to me are undoubtedly something more, and possess, so to speak, more <term>objective reality</term> <note>Descartes uses "objective reality" to mean the amount of "being" or perfection represented by a mental concept, not "objectivity" in the modern sense of being unbiased.</note> than those that represent only <term>modes or accidents</term> <note>These are properties or qualities that cannot exist without a substance, such as color, shape, or motion.</note> to me. Just as the idea by which I conceive of a God—supreme, eternal, infinite, all-knowing, all-powerful, and the universal creator of all things outside of himself—undoubtedly has more objective reality in itself than those ideas by which finite substances are represented to me.

I have already remarked several times before that we have no idea of God, nor of the soul; I now add, nor of substance. For I fully admit that substance—insofar as it is matter capable of receiving various accidents and subject to their changes—is perceived and proven through reasoning; nevertheless, it is not conceived, nor do we have any idea of it. If this is true, how can it be said that the ideas representing substances are "something more" and have "more objective reality" than those representing accidents? Furthermore, it seems that Mr. Descartes has not sufficiently considered what he means by these words *have more reality*. Does reality admit of "more" and "less"? Or, if he thinks one thing is "more" of a thing than another, let him consider how it is possible for this to be made clear to the mind, and explained with all the clarity and evidence required in a demonstration, and with which he has handled other matters several times before.

### RESPONSE.

I have said several times that I apply the name "idea" to that which reason itself makes known to us, as well as to all other things we conceive, in whatever way we conceive them. And I have sufficiently explained how reality admits of "more" and "less" by saying that a substance is something more than a mode; and if there are <term>real qualities</term> <note>A Scholastic term referring to properties that were thought to have a sort of independent existence.</note> or incomplete substances, they are also something more than modes, but something less than complete substances; and finally, that if there is an infinite, independent substance, that substance has more being, or more reality, than a finite and dependent substance. This is so manifest in itself that there is no need to provide a more ample explanation.

<summary>Thomas Hobbes argues that we cannot have a true "idea" of substance or God, only a reasoned inference, and questions the hierarchy of reality; Descartes responds that "idea" covers all mental concepts and maintains that an infinite being inherently possesses more reality than a finite property.</summary>
<keywords>Descartes, God, substance, mode, accident, objective reality, being, infinite, finite, demonstration, Thomas Hobbes</keywords>

### TENTH OBJECTION.

There remains then only the idea of God, in which *it* must be considered if there is anything that could not have come from myself. By the name of God, I mean an *infinite, independent, supremely intelligent, supremely* powerful <term>substance</term> <note>In 17th-century philosophy, a "substance" is something that exists in itself and does not depend on anything else for its existence.</note>, and by which not only myself, but all other things that exist (if there are others that exist) were created. All of which things, to tell the truth, are such that the more I think about them, the less they seem able to come from me alone. And consequently, it must be concluded from all that has gone before, that God necessarily exists.

Considering the attributes of God, so that from them we may have an idea of Him and see if there is anything *in* that idea which could not have come from ourselves, I find, if I am not mistaken, that neither the things we conceive by the name of God come from us, nor is it necessary that they come from anywhere other than external objects. For by the name of God, I mean a substance—that is to say, I understand that God exists (not by an idea, but by reasoning)—I understand that this substance is *infinite* (that is to say, that I can neither conceive nor imagine its boundaries, or its final parts, without being able to imagine others beyond them) <note>Hobbes is arguing that "infinite" is a negative term; it describes our inability to find an end, rather than a positive quality of God.</note> from which it follows that the name "infinite" does not provide us with the idea of divine infinity, but rather that of our own boundaries and limits; I also understand that this substance is *independent*, that is to say, I do not conceive of any cause from which God could come. From this, it appears that I have no other idea that corresponds to this name "independent," except for the memory of my own ideas which all have their beginning at various times, and which consequently are dependent.

This is why, to say that God is *independent* is to say nothing else than that God is among the number of things whose origin I cannot imagine; just as saying that God is *infinite* is the same as if we said He is among the number of things whose limits we do not conceive. And thus this whole idea of God is refuted; for, what is this idea which is without end and without origin?

*Supremely intelligent*. I also ask by what idea Monsieur Descartes conceives the intelligence of God.

*Supremely powerful*. I also ask by what idea His power regarding future things—that is to say, non-existent things—is understood.

Certainly, for my part, I conceive of power through the image or memory of past things, reasoning in this way: He has done thus, therefore He was able to do thus; therefore, as long as He exists, He

<summary>This page presents a critique of Descartes’ proof of God's existence, arguing that terms like "infinite" and "independent" do not describe God’s nature but rather the limitations of human imagination and memory.</summary>

### THIRD OBJECTIONS

Now when it is said here that whether we wish it or not, we give our belief to the things that we clearly conceive, it is the same as if one said that whether we wish it or not, we will and desire good things when they are clearly known to us. For this way of speaking—"whether we do not wish it"—has no place on such occasions, because it is a contradiction <note>Hobbes is pointing out a logical flaw in the phrasing: if the mind is compelled by clarity, "will" or "lack of will" becomes irrelevant.</note> to will and not to will the same thing.

## FOURTEENTH OBJECTION ON THE FIFTH MEDITATION.

*On the essence of corporeal <note>In this context, "corporeal" simply means physical or having a body.</note> things.*

As, for example, when I imagine a triangle, even if there perhaps exists no such figure anywhere in the world outside of my thought, and there never has been, there nevertheless remains a certain nature, or form, or determined essence of this figure, which is immutable and eternal, which I have not invented, and which does not depend in any way on my mind, as is apparent from the fact that one can demonstrate various properties of this triangle. <note>This italicized paragraph is a quote from Descartes' Fifth Meditation, which Hobbes is about to critique.</note>

If there is no triangle anywhere in the world, I cannot understand how it has a "nature," for that which is nowhere is nothing at all, and therefore has no being or nature. The idea that our mind conceives of a triangle comes from another triangle that we have seen, or one invented based on things we have seen. But once we have called the thing from which we think the idea of a triangle originates by the name "triangle," even if that thing perishes, the name remains. Similarly, if we have once conceived in our thought that all the angles of a triangle taken together are equal to two right <term>right angles: an angle of 90 degrees, forming a square corner</term> angles, and we have given this other name to the triangle: "it is a thing that has three angles equal to two right angles"—even if there were no triangle in the world, the name would nevertheless remain. And thus the truth of this proposition will be eternal: that a triangle is a thing that has three angles equal to two right angles. But the *nature* of the triangle will not be eternal because of this; for if it happened by chance that every triangle generally perished, that nature would also cease to be.

Likewise, this proposition *man is an animal* will be eternally true because of the names; but supposing the human race were annihilated, there would no longer be a human nature. <note>Hobbes is arguing for "Nominalism"—the idea that universal truths are simply about how we use language and names, rather than about spiritual or eternal blueprints existing in reality.</note>

From which it is evident that essence, insofar as it is distin— <margin>The text cuts off mid-sentence at the bottom of the page.</margin>

<summary>In this passage, Thomas Hobbes challenges Descartes' claim that mathematical shapes like triangles have an "eternal nature" independent of the mind, arguing instead that such truths are merely based on how we define names and words.</summary>

# BIOGRAPHICAL NOTE ON RENÉ DESCARTES

---

*René Descartes*, known in Latin as *Cartesius* <note>original: "Cartesius"</note>, was born in 1596 at *La Haye* <note>Now known as Descartes, Indre-et-Loire, in honor of the philosopher.</note>, near *Loches* (*Indre-et-Loire*); the son of a counselor to the parliament of *Rennes*, he completed his studies at the Jesuit college of *La Flèche*, where he distinguished himself through a precocious talent for philosophy and the exact sciences. In 1617, after a somewhat stormy youth, yielding to the requests of his father, he took up the profession of arms and served for four years in the army of the Duke of Nassau and that of the Duke of Bavaria.

*Descartes* subsequently traveled through *Germany*, *Sweden*, *Holland*, *Switzerland*, and *Italy*; he then went to *Rome* and returned to *Paris* in 1626. After assisting at the siege of *La Rochelle* <note>A major military engagement between French royal forces and the Huguenots.</note>, he renounced his military career and, resolved to devote himself entirely to meditation, he withdrew to *Holland*. There he lived in seclusion, residing by turns in *Amsterdam*, *The Hague*, *Leiden*, and the "delightful solitude" of *Egmont*.

In 1637, he published in *Leiden* his immortal *Discourse on the Method*, in which he established the foundations of a new philosophy based upon methodical doubt. In 1641, his book of *Meditations* appeared, which was followed, in 1644, by the *Principles of Philosophy*. He had worked on a treatise on light, based on the system of *Copernicus* <note>The heliocentric model placing the sun at the center of the universe.</note>, which he abandoned upon hearing news of the condemnation of *Galileo*—not out of a conviction that he was in error, but out of considerations of prudence. His orthodoxy, however, was not beyond reproach; for in 1666, at the time of the transfer of his remains to the Church of *Sainte-Geneviève* <note>The site of the current Panthéon in Paris.</note>, a superior order forbade *Father Lallemand* from delivering his funeral oration. The *Discourse on the Method*, published alongside the *Geometry*, the *Dioptrics*, and the *Meteors*, drew upon its author the opposition of Catholic and Protestant theologians; the latter proved themselves no less relent- <note>The text breaks off here; the catchword "achar-" refers to "acharnés," meaning "relentless" or "fierce."</note>

<summary>This page provides a concise biography of René Descartes, detailing his transition from a soldier to a philosopher and highlighting his major works and the religious controversy they sparked.</summary>
<keywords>René Descartes, biography, Discourse on the Method, Meditations, Jesuit education, military service, Galileo, scientific revolution</keywords>

### BIOGRAPHICAL NOTE ON RENÉ DESCARTES

...born; he was accused of atheism and his books were nearly burned by the hand of the executioner.

Descartes, weary of all these struggles which took up a great part of his time, having resisted the advances of King Louis XIII and Cardinal de Richelieu, yielded to the urgings of Queen Christina of Sweden and went to settle in Stockholm in 1649; he was welcomed there with marks of the liveliest enthusiasm; the queen wished to take philosophy lessons from him; every day, at five o'clock in the morning, Descartes went to the court and lectured on philosophy before an elite audience. One day he caught a cold, and he died on February 11, 1650, in his fifty-fourth year.

The philosophy of Descartes, or *Cartesianism*, spread rapidly throughout all of Europe, and it can be said that Descartes has been the father of French philosophy since the 17th century. His honor lies in having substituted a new idealism for the decaying doctrines of scholastic philosophy <note>A medieval school of thought that attempted to reconcile Christian theology with Aristotelian logic; it had become rigid and formulaic by Descartes' time.</note>, founded on the certainty that the very thought we have of our existence and of God's must give us. A great number of Descartes' ideas, especially in physics, have had to be abandoned. Since the last century, his philosophy has declined among us; but even the systems furthest removed from his still owe much to his method, and it is, one might say, to Descartes as to Bacon <note>Francis Bacon (1561–1626), an English philosopher who championed the inductive method and the scientific revolution.</note>, that all the masters of modern thought are indebted, for various reasons.

# ON METHOD 1

### FIRST PART

Good sense is the best distributed thing in the world: for everyone thinks they are so well provided with it that even those who are the most difficult to satisfy in all other matters are not in the habit of desiring more of it than they already have. In this, it is unlikely that everyone is mistaken; rather, it testifies

1. The *Discourse on Method*, written in French by Descartes, appeared for the <unclear>first</unclear> time with the *Dioptrics*, the *Meteorology*, and the *Geometry*, in a quarto volume <note>original: "in-4°"; a book size where each sheet is folded twice to form four leaves.</note> published in Leiden in 1637. It is the text of this edition that we have followed, though we have guided ourselves, for spelling, by the French edition of 1668, which is more correct and regular.
2. If this discourse seems too long to be read all at once, it can be divided into six parts. And in the first, one will find various considerations regarding the sciences. In the second, the principal rules of the Method that the author has sought. In the third, some of the rules of morality that he has derived from this Method. In the fourth, the reasons by which he proves the existence of God and of the human soul, which are the foundations of his metaphysics. In the fifth, the order of the questions of physics that he has investigated, and particularly the explanation of the movement of the heart and some other difficulties belonging to medicine, as well as the difference between our soul and that of the beasts. And in the last part, what things he believes are required to go further in the investigation of nature than he has, and what reasons led him to write. — (*Note placed by Descartes at the beginning of the* DISCOURSE ON METHOD).

<meta>This page continues the opening argument of Part One of the Discourse on Method. It completes the thought initiated on the previous page regarding "good sense" and introduces Descartes' personal humility alongside his confidence in his newly developed method.</meta>

### DISCOURSE ON METHOD

that the power of judging well and distinguishing the true from the false, which is properly what we call good sense or reason, is naturally equal in all men; and thus that the diversity of our opinions does not arise from some being more reasonable than others, but only from the fact that we conduct our thoughts by different paths and do not consider the same things. For it is not enough to have a good mind, but the main thing is to apply it well. The greatest souls are capable of the greatest vices as well as the greatest virtues; and those who walk only very slowly can advance much further, if they always follow the right path, than those who run and wander from it.

For my part, I have never presumed my mind to be in any way more perfect than those of the common people; indeed, I have often wished I had a thought as quick, or an imagination as clear and distinct, or a memory as ample or as present as some others. And I know of no other qualities than these that serve the perfection of the mind; for, as for reason or sense, insofar as it is the only thing that makes us human and distinguishes us from the beasts, <margin>*</margin> I am inclined to believe that it is whole and complete in each person, and to follow in this the common opinion of the Philosophers who say that there is "more" or "less" only among the *<term>accidents</term>* <note>In traditional philosophy, "accidents" are non-essential qualities like height or hair color that can change without changing the essence of the person.</note>, and not at all among the *<term>forms</term>* <note>The "form" refers to the essential nature or "blueprint" of a species; in this case, the human capacity for reason.</note> or natures of *individuals* of the same *species*.

<margin>X</margin> But I will not fear to say that I think I have had the great fortune to have encountered, since my youth, certain paths which have led me to considerations and maxims from which I have formed a method by which it seems to me that I have the means to increase my knowledge by degrees, and to raise it little by little to the highest point that the mediocrity of my mind and the short duration of my life can permit it to reach. For I have already gathered such fruits from it that, although in the judgments I make of myself I always try to lean toward the side of distrust rather than toward that of presumption, and although, looking with a philosopher’s eye at the various actions and enterprises of all men, there are almost none that do not seem to me vain and useless, I do not fail to receive extreme satisfaction from the progress I think I have already made in the search for truth, and to conceive such hopes for the future that if, among the occupations of men, purely as men, there is any one that is solidly good and important, I dare believe it is the one I have chosen.

<summary>Descartes argues that reason is equal in all humans and that intellectual differences arise from how one applies that reason. He introduces his "Method" as a personal discovery that has allowed him to seek truth systematically despite his own perceived intellectual limitations.</summary>

### DISCOURSE ON THE METHOD

perhaps it is only a bit of copper and glass that I take for gold and diamonds. Thus my purpose here is not to teach the method that everyone must follow to lead their reason well, but only to show in what way I have tried to lead my own. # PART TWO

I was then in Germany, where the occasion of the wars which are not yet finished <note>This refers to the Thirty Years' War (1618–1648), which was ongoing when Descartes published this work in 1637.</note> had called me; and, as I was returning from the coronation of the Emperor <note>Ferdinand II, crowned in Frankfurt in 1619.</note> toward the army, the beginning of winter detained me in a quarter where, finding no conversation to divert me, and having, moreover, fortunately, no cares or passions to trouble me, I remained all day long shut up alone in a <term>stove-heated room</term> <note>original: "poêle." ...not that I would advise anyone to imitate me. Those whom God has more generously gifted with His grace will perhaps have loftier designs, but I fear that this project is already too daring for many. The mere resolution to strip oneself of all opinions previously accepted as true is not an example that everyone should follow. Indeed, the world is almost entirely composed of two types of minds for whom such a path is not at all suitable. First, there are those who, believing themselves more capable than they actually are, cannot help but rush their judgments, nor do they have enough patience to organize <gloss>in an orderly fashion</gloss> all their thoughts. Consequently, if they once took the liberty of doubting the principles they received and straying from the common path, they would never be able to keep to the path one must take to go more directly, and they would remain lost all their lives. Second, there are those who have enough reason or modesty to judge that they are less capable of distinguishing truth from falsehood than others by whom they could be instructed; these people should be content to follow the opinions of those others rather than search for better ones themselves.

But, like a man who walks alone and in the darkness, I resolved to go so slowly and to use such caution in all things that, even if I advanced only a very little, I would at least be sure not to fall. I did not even wish to begin by entirely rejecting any of the opinions that might have slipped into my beliefs without being introduced by reason, until I had first spent enough time planning the work I was undertaking and seeking the true method for arriving at the knowledge of all things of which my mind was capable.

In my younger years, I had studied—among the branches of philosophy—logic, and—among the mathematical sciences—the analysis of the geometers and algebra: three arts or sciences that seemed likely to contribute something to my design. But, in examining them, I noticed that, as for logic, its syllogisms <note>A syllogism is a form of logical argument where a conclusion is drawn from two premises (e.g., All men are mortal; Socrates is a man; therefore Socrates is mortal).</note> and most of its other instructions serve more to explain to others the things one already knows—or even, like the art of Lully <note>Ramon Llull (1232–1315) was a philosopher who devised a system of revolving wheels with symbols to "automatically" generate arguments, which Descartes critiques here as being hollow.</note>, to speak without judgment about things one does not know—rather than to actually learn them. And although logic does indeed contain many very true and very good precepts, there are nonetheless so many others mixed in that are either harmful or superfluous, that it is almost as difficult to separate them as it is to draw a statue of Diana or Minerva out of a block of marble that has not yet been roughed out.

---

Then, regarding the analysis of the ancients and the algebra of the moderns, besides the fact that they extend only to very abstract matters that seem to have no practical use, the former is always so restricted to the consideration of figures <note>In this context, "figures" refers to geometric shapes like triangles and circles.</note> that it cannot exercise the understanding without greatly fatiguing the imagination; and in the latter, one has so subjected oneself to certain rules and certain numbers that it has been turned into a confused and obscure art that embarrasses the mind, instead of a science that <gloss>cultivates it</gloss>. This was why I thought I had to look for some other method which, comprising the advantages of these three, would be free from their defects. And, just as a multitude of laws often provides excuses for vices, so that a State is much better governed when, having only a very few, they are very strictly observed; so, instead of that great number of precepts of which logic is composed, I believed I would find the <margin>method</margin> four following rules to be sufficient, provided I made a firm and constant resolution never to fail to observe them even once.

The first was never to accept anything as true that I did not evidently know to be such; that is, to carefully avoid haste and prejudice...

The third, to conduct my thoughts in an orderly manner, beginning with the simplest objects and those most <insert>easy to know,</insert> in order to climb little by little, as if by steps, to the knowledge of the most complex, and even assuming an order among those that do not naturally precede one another;

And the last, to make everywhere such complete enumerations <note>An "enumeration" is a thorough, step-by-step listing of all elements in an argument to ensure no part of the problem has been overlooked.</note> and such general reviews that I would be certain of omitting nothing.

These long chains of simple and easy reasons, which geometers <note>Descartes is referring to mathematicians who use deductive logic to move from simple axioms to complex theorems.</note> are accustomed to using to reach their most difficult demonstrations, had given me cause to imagine that all things that can fall under human knowledge follow one another in the same way, and that, provided only that one refrains from accepting anything as true which is not, and that one always maintains the order necessary to deduce one from the other, there can be none so remote that they are not eventually reached, nor so hidden that they are not discovered. And I was not much troubled to seek which ones it was necessary to begin with, for I already knew it was with the simplest and easiest to know; and, considering that among all those who have previously sought truth in the sciences, only the mathematicians were able to find any demonstrations—that is to say, certain and evident reasons—I did not doubt that it was through these same things they examined, although I expected no other utility from them except that they would accustom my mind to nourish itself on truths and not be satisfied with false reasons. But I did not intend, for that reason, to try to learn all those particular sciences commonly called mathematics; and, seeing that although their objects are different, they do not fail to agree in that they consider nothing other than the various relations or proportions found therein, I thought it better that I should examine only these proportions in general, without assuming them to be in anything but subjects that would serve to make my knowledge of them easier, yet also without restricting them to those subjects in any way, so as to be better able to apply them afterward to

Indeed, I dare say that the exact observation of these few precepts I had chosen gave me such ease in disentangling all the questions to which these two sciences extend, that in the two or three months I spent examining them—having begun with the simplest and most general, and each truth I found being a rule that served me afterward to find others—not only did I succeed in solving several that I had formerly judged very difficult, but it also seemed to me toward the end that I could determine, even in those areas I was ignorant of, by what means and to what extent it was possible to resolve them. In this, I will perhaps not appear too vain to you if you consider that, there being only one truth for each thing, whoever finds it knows as much about it as can be known; and that, for example, a child instructed in arithmetic, having performed an addition according to its rules, can be certain of having found, regarding the sum he was examining, all that the human mind could find. For, after all, the method that teaches one to follow *the true order and to enumerate exactly all the circumstances* of what one seeks, contains everything that gives certainty to the rules of arithmetic.

But what satisfied me most about this method was that through it I was assured of using my reason in everything, if not perfectly, at least as best as was in my power; moreover, I felt that by practicing it, my mind was gradually becoming accustomed to conceiving its objects more clearly and more distinctly; and that, not having restricted the method to any particular subject matter, I promised myself to apply it as usefully to the difficulties of other sciences as I had done to those of algebra. Not that I would therefore dare to undertake at once to examine all those that might present themselves, for that itself would have been contrary to *the order it prescribes*;

### 16

...was not yet certain of any [philosophical truths], I thought that I must, above all, try to establish some there. Since this was the most important thing in the world, and a task where haste and prejudice were most to be feared, I decided I should not attempt to accomplish it until I had reached a much more mature age than the twenty-three years I then was. I felt I needed to spend a long time preparing myself, both by uprooting from my mind all the wrong opinions I had accepted before that time, and by gathering many experiences to serve as the raw material for my reasonings, while constantly practicing the method I had prescribed for myself so as to strengthen my hold on it more and more.

# PART THREE

And finally, just as it is not enough, before beginning to rebuild the house where one lives, to pull it down and provide materials and architects (or to practice architecture oneself), and to have carefully drawn up the blueprint; but one must also have provided oneself with some other house where one can be comfortably lodged during the time the work is in progress; so, in order that I should not remain indecisive in my actions while reason obliged me to be so in my judgments, and that I might continue to live as happily as I could from then on, I formed for myself a <term>provisional moral code</term> <note>original: "morale par provision." For, beginning from that time to count my own opinions as nothing (because I wanted to submit them all to examination), I was certain I could do no better than to follow those of the most sensible people. And finally, I could not have limited my desires nor been content if I had not followed a path by which, thinking I was assured of acquiring all the knowledge of which I was capable, I thought I was also assured, by the same means, of acquiring all the true goods that would ever be in my power; especially since, as our <term>will</term> <note>will: The faculty of choice or desire.</note> is inclined to follow or flee from nothing except as our <term>understanding</term> <note>understanding (entendement): The intellectual capacity to grasp and analyze ideas.</note> represents it to the will as good or bad, <margin>|</margin>it is enough to judge well in order to do well, and to judge as best as one can in order to also do one's best—that is to say, to acquire all the virtues and along with them all the other goods that can be acquired; and when one is certain that this is the case, one cannot fail to be content.

# DISCOURSE ON THE METHOD

After having thus assured myself of these maxims and having set them apart with the truths of faith, which have always been foremost in my belief, I judged that, for all the rest of my opinions, I could freely undertake to rid myself of them; and, inasmuch as I hoped to better achieve this by conversing with men than by staying any longer shut up in the <term>stove-heated room</term> <note>original: "poêle." And in all the nine years that followed, I did nothing else but roam here and there in the world, trying to be a spectator rather than an actor in all the <term>comedies</term> <note>Descartes uses the theatrical metaphor of the "world as a stage" (theatrum mundi), common in the 17th century, to describe his detached observation of human affairs.</note> played there; and, reflecting particularly on each matter regarding what might make it suspect and give us cause for error, I meanwhile uprooted from my mind all the errors that might have previously crept in. 

Not that I imitated the <term>skeptics</term> <note>skeptics: A school of philosophy (like Pyrrhonism) that argued certain knowledge is impossible. And just as, in tearing down an old house, one usually sets aside the debris to serve in building a new one, so, in destroying all those of my opinions that I judged to be ill-founded, I made various observations and acquired several experiences which have since served me to establish more certain ones; and, furthermore, I continued to practice the method I had prescribed for myself. ### DISCOURS DE LA MÉTHODE

the foundations I have taken are firm enough, I find myself in some way forced to speak of them. I had long noticed that, for the sake of morals, it is sometimes necessary to follow opinions that one knows to be very uncertain, just as if they were indubitable, as has been said above; but, because I then desired to devote myself only to the search for truth, I thought it necessary for me to do the exact opposite, and to reject as absolutely false everything in which I could imagine the slightest doubt, in order to see if anything would remain in my belief after that which was entirely indubitable. Thus, because our senses deceive us sometimes, I wanted to suppose that there was no thing that was such as they make us imagine it; and, because there are men who make mistakes in reasoning, even concerning the simplest matters of geometry, and commit <term>paralogisms</term> <note>A paralogism is a piece of illogical or faulty reasoning, specifically one the reasoner believes to be true.</note>, judging that I was as subject to error as any other, I rejected as false all the reasons I had previously taken for demonstrations; and finally, considering that all the same thoughts we have while awake can also come to us when we sleep, without any of them being true at that time, I resolved to pretend that all the things that had ever entered my mind were no more true than the illusions of my dreams. But immediately after, I noticed that, while I wanted thus to think that everything was false, it was necessarily the case that I, who was thinking this, was something; and noticing that this truth: *I think, therefore I am* <note>original: "je pense, donc je suis." This is the famous "Cogito," the first certainty Descartes finds that cannot be doubted.</note>, was so firm and so assured that all the most extravagant suppositions of the <term>skeptics</term> <note>Skeptics were philosophers who argued that true knowledge is impossible to attain.</note> were not capable of shaking it, I judged that I could receive it without any scruple as the first principle of the philosophy I was seeking.

Then, examining with attention what I was, and seeing that I could pretend that I had no body and that there was no world nor any place where I was, but that I could not pretend for all that that I did not exist, and that on the contrary, from the very fact that I thought of doubting the truth of other things, it followed very evidently and very certainly that I existed; whereas, if I had only ceased to think, even if all the rest of what I had ever imagined had been true, I had no reason to believe that I had existed; I knew from this that I was a <term>substance</term> <note>In 17th-century philosophy, a "substance" is something that can exist on its own, without needing anything else to support its existence.</note> whose whole essence or nature is only to think, and which, in order to exist, has no need of any place nor depends on any material thing; so that this "me"—that is to say, the soul, by which I am what I am—is entirely

He concludes that his essence is that of a thinking soul, independent of the physical body.</summary>

After this, I considered in general what is required for a proposition to be true and certain; for, since I had just found one that I knew to be so, I thought I ought also to know in what this certainty consists. And having noticed that there is nothing at all in this—*I think, therefore I am*—which assures me that I am speaking the truth, except that I see very clearly that in order to think, one must exist, I judged that I could take as a general rule that the things we conceive very clearly and very distinctly are all true, but that there is only some difficulty in noticing well which ones those are that we conceive distinctly.

</margin>

Following this, reflecting on the fact that I doubted, and that consequently my being was not entirely perfect (for I saw clearly that it was a greater perfection to know than to doubt), I took it into my head to search for where I had learned to think of something more perfect than I was; and I clearly recognized that it must be from some nature that was in fact more perfect. As for the thoughts I had of many other things outside of myself, such as the sky, the earth, light, heat, and a thousand others, I was not so troubled to know where they came from, because, noticing nothing in them that seemed to make them superior to me, I could believe that, if they were true, they were dependencies of my nature, insofar as it had some perfection; and if they were not true, that I held them from nothingness, that is to say, that they were in me because I had some defect. But it could not be the same for the idea of a being more perfect than my own; for to hold it from nothingness was manifestly impossible; and because it is no less contradictory that the more perfect should be a consequence and a dependency of the less perfect than it is that something should proceed from nothing, I could not hold it from myself either. So that there remained only the possibility that it had been put into me by a nature that was truly more perfect than I was, and even which had in itself all the perfections of which I could have any idea, that is to say—to explain myself in a word—which was God. Finally, if there are still men who are not sufficiently persuaded of the existence of God and of their soul by the reasons I have brought forward, I want them to know that all the other things of which they think themselves perhaps more assured—such as having a body, and that there are stars and an earth, and similar things—are less certain. From this it follows that our ideas or notions, being real things and coming from God in all that is clear and distinct about them, cannot be anything but true. Consequently, if we quite often have ideas that contain falsehood, these can only be the ones that are somewhat confused and obscure, because in that respect they participate in nothingness <note>Descartes suggests that error is not a "thing" created by God, but rather a "lack" or "nothingness" that occurs because humans are finite and imperfect.</note>; that is to say, they are only thus confused in us because we are not entirely perfect. But, if we did not know that all that is real and true in us comes from a perfect and infinite being, however clear and distinct our ideas were, we would have no reason to be certain that they had the perfection of being true.

And so that there is less difficulty in understanding what I will say about it, I would like those who are not well-versed in anatomy to take the trouble, before reading this, to have the heart of some large animal that has lungs cut open before them—for it is in every way quite similar to that of a man—and to have shown to them the two chambers or cavities that are there.

Furthermore, I would like people to consider that the great artery and the arterial vein <note>original: "veine artérieuse," the pulmonary artery</note> are of a much harder and firmer composition than the venous artery and the vena cava; and that these last two widen before entering the heart, forming two pouches there, called the auricles <note>original: "oreilles du cœur," literally "the ears of the heart," now called the atria</note>, which are composed of a flesh similar to the heart’s own; and that there is always more heat in the heart than in any other place in the body; and finally, that this heat is capable of causing any drops of blood that enter its cavities to promptly swell and dilate, just as all liquids generally do when they are dropped drop by drop into a very hot vessel.

For, after that, I need say nothing else to explain the movement of the heart, except that when its cavities are not full of blood, it necessarily flows from the vena cava into the right cavity and from the venous artery into the left, since these two vessels are always full and their openings facing the heart cannot then be blocked; but as soon as two drops of blood have entered in this way, one in each of its cavities—drops which must be quite large, because the openings through which they enter are very wide and the vessels from which they come are very full of blood—they rarefy <note>In 17th-century science, "rarefaction" refers to a substance becoming less dense and expanding in volume</note> and dilate because of the heat they find there. By this means, causing the whole heart to swell, they push and close the five little doors <note>Descartes refers to the tricuspid and mitral valves</note> which are at the entrances of the two vessels from which they come, thus preventing any more blood from descending into the heart; and, continuing to rarefy more and more, they push and open the six other little doors <note>The pulmonary and aortic valves</note> which are at the entrances of the two other vessels through which they exit, causing by this means all the branches of the arterial vein and the great artery to swell at almost the same instant as the heart. The heart then immediately afterward deflates, as do these arteries, because the blood that has entered them cools down; and their six little doors close—

<summary>Descartes explains the mechanical function of the heart's valves and proposes that the heartbeat is caused by the rapid heating and expansion (rarefaction) of blood rather than muscular contraction.</summary>

But, if it is asked how the blood in the veins is not exhausted by flowing thus continually into the heart, and how the arteries do not become overfilled since all the blood passing through the heart goes into them, I need offer no other answer than that which has already been written by a physician from England ¹, who deserves praise for having broken the ice in this area, and for being the first to teach that there are many small passages at the ends of the arteries through which the blood they receive from the heart enters the small branches of the veins, from where it returns again toward the heart; so that its course is nothing other than a **perpetual circulation**. He proves this very well by the common experience of surgeons who, having tied the arm moderately tight above the place where they open the vein, cause the blood to come out more abundantly than if they had not tied it at all; and the exact opposite would happen if they tied it below, between the hand and the opening, or if they tied it very tightly above. And what else is needed to explain nutrition and the production of the various <term>humors</term> <note>The "four humors" (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) were traditional medical categories, though Descartes provides a mechanical explanation for them here.</note> in the body, except to say that the force with which the blood, while expanding, passes from the heart toward the ends of the arteries, causes some of its parts to stop among those of the limbs where they are located? And finally, what is most remarkable in all of this is the generation of the <term>animal spirits</term> <note>Despite the name, these were not "spiritual" in a modern sense; Descartes imagined them as the thinnest, most agitated particles of blood that acted like a hydraulic fluid to move the muscles.</note>, which are like a very subtle wind, or rather like a very pure and very vivid flame. Rising continually in great abundance from the heart into the brain, these spirits go from there through the nerves into the muscles and give movement to all the limbs. This will not seem strange at all to those who, knowing how many different <term>automata</term> <note>Self-operating machines or robots.</note> or moving machines the industry of men can make using only very few pieces, in comparison to the great multitude of bones, muscles, nerves, arteries, veins, and all the other parts in the body of each animal, consider this body as a machine which, having been made by the hands of God, is incomparably better ordered and has in itself more admirable movements than any of those that can be invented by men. And I had paused here particularly to show that, if there were such machines that had the organs and the external shape of a monkey or some other animal without reason, we would have no way of recognizing that they were not of the same nature as these animals; whereas, if there were any that resembled our bodies and imitated our actions as much as was morally possible, we would always have two very certain means to recognize that they were not, for all that, true men. [...which we] do to declare our thoughts to others (for one can certainly conceive of a machine being so made that it utters words, and even that it utters some in relation to physical actions that cause some change in its organs—as, if it is touched in a certain place, it asks what one wants to say to it; if in another, it cries out that it is being hurt, and similar things; but not that it arranges them differently to respond to the sense of all that is said in its presence, as even the most <term>dull-witted</term> <note>original: "hébétés" — referring to those with significantly diminished mental capacity or "slow" intellect.</note> of men can do); and the second is that, although they might do several things as well or perhaps better than any of us, they would inevitably fail in some others, through which it would be discovered that they were acting not by knowledge, but only by the arrangement of their organs: for, while reason is a <term>universal instrument</term> <note>Descartes defines reason as a single tool that can be applied to any problem, unlike physical mechanisms which must be custom-built for one specific task.</note> that can serve in all sorts of situations, these organs need a particular arrangement for each particular action; hence it is <term>practically impossible</term> <note>original: "moralement impossible" — in 17th-century philosophy, this means "impossible for all practical purposes," or beyond any reasonable doubt, rather than a matter of ethics.</note> for there to be enough different arrangements in a machine to make it act in all the occurrences of life in the same way that our reason makes us act.

This does not happen because they lack organs, for we see that magpies and parrots can utter words just as we do, and yet cannot speak as we do—that is, by testifying that they think what they say; whereas men who, being born deaf and mute, are deprived of the organs that others use for speaking, as much as or more than the beasts, are accustomed to invent for themselves certain signs by which they make themselves understood to those who, being usually with them, have the leisure to learn their language. It is also quite remarkable that, although there are many animals that show more <term>ingenuity</term> <note>original: "industrie" — meaning skill, cleverness, or instinctive ability.</note> than we do in some of their actions, we see that they show none at all in many others; so that what they do better than us does not prove that they have a mind—for by that logic they would have more than any of us and would do better in everything else—but rather that they have none at all, and that it is nature which acts in them according to the arrangement of their organs. This is much like a **clock**, which is composed only of wheels and springs, yet can count the hours and measure time more accurately than we can with all our <term>prudence</term> <note>original: "prudence" — here meaning practical wisdom or human judgment.</note>.

After that, I had described the **rational soul** and shown that it can in no way be derived from the power of matter, as were the other things I had spoken of, but that it must be expressly created. I showed how it is not enough for it to be lodged in the human body like a **pilot in his ship** <note>A classic philosophical metaphor used to describe the soul's relationship to the body; Descartes argues here for a much more intimate union than just a driver directing a vehicle.</note>, except perhaps to move its limbs; rather, it needs to be joined and united more closely with the body in order to experience feelings and appetites similar to ours, and thus compose a true man. For the rest, I have dwelled a little on the subject of the soul because it is of the greatest importance. For, after the error of those who deny God (which I believe I have sufficiently refuted above), there is none that leads weak minds further from the right path of virtue than imagining that the soul of beasts is of the same nature as ours, and that consequently we have nothing to fear or to hope for after this life, any more than flies and ants. Whereas, when one knows how much they differ, one understands much better the reasons which prove that ours is of a nature entirely independent of the body, and consequently that it is not subject to dying with it; then, since we see no other causes that might destroy it, we are naturally led to judge that it is **immortal**.

## PART SIX

It has now been three years since I reached the end of the <term>treatise</term> <note>original: "traité" — This refers to his work *The World* (*Le Monde*), which presented a comprehensive scientific system.</note> that contains all these things, and I was beginning to revise it in order to place it in the hands of a printer, when I learned that persons to whom I defer, and whose authority carries hardly less weight over my actions than my own reason does over my thoughts, had disapproved of an <term>opinion on physics</term> <note>original: "opinion de physique" — A reference to the heliocentric theory (that the Earth revolves around the Sun). Galileo Galilei had been condemned by the Roman Inquisition for this view in 1633.</note> published a short time before by someone else. I will not say that I held that same opinion, but rather that I had noticed nothing in it, before their censure, that I could imagine being prejudicial either to religion or to the State, nor consequently anything that would have prevented me from writing it if reason had persuaded me of it. This made me fear that there might likewise be found among my own opinions some in which I had been mistaken, notwithstanding the great care I have always taken never to accept any new beliefs for which I did not have very certain demonstrations, and never to write anything that could turn to anyone’s disadvantage. This was sufficient to oblige me to change the resolution I had made to publish them. For, although the reasons for which I had previously taken that resolution were very strong, my inclination, which has always made me hate the profession of making books, immediately made me find enough other reasons to excuse myself from it. And these reasons, on both sides, are such that not only do I have some interest in stating them here, but perhaps the public also has an interest in knowing them.

I have never placed much value on the things that came from my own mind; and as long as I gathered no other fruits from the **method** I use—except for satisfying myself regarding some difficulties belonging to the <term>speculative sciences</term> <note>original: "sciences spéculatives" — Theoretical branches of knowledge, such as metaphysics or pure mathematics, which seek understanding rather than practical application.</note>, or attempting to regulate my <term>morals</term> <note>original: "mœurs" — This term encompasses one's conduct, habits, and ethical behavior in society.</note> by the reasons it taught me—I did not feel obliged to write anything about it. For as far as morals are concerned, everyone is so full of their own perspective that one might find as many reformers as there are heads, were it permitted for anyone other than those whom God has established as sovereigns over his peoples, or those to whom he has given enough grace and zeal to be prophets, to undertake to change anything therein. And although my speculations pleased me greatly, I believed that others also had theirs which perhaps pleased them...

But as soon as I had acquired some general notions regarding **physics**, and beginning to test them in various particular difficulties, I noticed how far they can lead, and how much they differ from the principles that have been used until now, I believed that I could not keep them hidden without sinning greatly against the law that obliges us to procure, as much as is in us, the general good of all men. For they showed me that it is possible to arrive at knowledge that is very useful to life, and that instead of that <term>speculative philosophy</term> <note>original: "philosophie spéculative" — This refers to Scholasticism, the traditional, highly theoretical philosophy taught in medieval universities, which Descartes viewed as being of little use for practical problem-solving.</note> taught in the schools, we can find a practical one, by which, knowing the power and actions of fire, water, air, the stars, the heavens, and all the other bodies that surround us, as distinctly as we know the various trades of our artisans, we could employ them in the same way for all the uses for which they are fit, and thus make ourselves like <term>masters and possessors of nature</term> <note>original: "maîtres et possesseurs de la nature" — This is one of Descartes' most famous phrases, signaling a shift from a passive observation of nature to an active, technological control over it.</note>. This is not only to be desired for the invention of an infinity of devices that would allow us to enjoy the fruits of the earth and all the comforts found there without any pain, but also principally for the preservation of **health**, which is undoubtedly the first good and the foundation of all other goods of this life; for even the mind depends so much on the temperament and the disposition of the organs of the body that, if it is possible to find some means that commonly makes men wiser and more capable than they have been until now, I believe it is in **medicine** that one must seek it. It is true that the medicine currently in use contains few things whose utility is so remarkable; but, without having any intention of despising it, I am sure there is no one, even among those who make it their profession, who would not admit that everything known is almost nothing compared to what remains to be known, and that we could rid ourselves of an infinity of diseases, both of the body and of the mind, and perhaps even of the weakening of old age, if we had enough knowledge of their causes and of all the remedies with which nature has provided us.

Now, having the intention to devote my entire life to the search for such a necessary **science**, and having found a path that seems to me such that one must infallibly find it by following it, unless prevented either by the brevity of life or by the lack of **experiments** <note>original: "expériences" — In the 17th century, this word encompassed both the subjective "experience" and the controlled scientific "experiment."</note>, I judged there was no better remedy against these two obstacles than to faithfully communicate to the public everything little I had found and to invite fine minds to try to go further,

...by contributing, each according to his inclination and power, to the experiments <note>original: "expériences" — In the 17th century, this term referred to both sensory "experiences" and controlled scientific "experiments." Descartes is arguing for an empirical approach where data is gathered to test theories.</note> that would need to be conducted, and also by communicating to the public all the things they might learn, so that, the last starting where the previous ones had finished, and thus joining the lives and works of many, we might all together go much further than each individual could do alone.

I even noticed, concerning experiments, that they are all the more necessary as one is more advanced in knowledge. For, in the beginning, it is better to make use only of those which present themselves of their own accord to our senses, and which we cannot ignore provided we reflect on them even a little, rather than searching for more rare and elaborate ones. The reason for this is that these more rare experiments often deceive when one does not yet know the causes of the most common ones, and the circumstances upon which they depend are almost always so particular and so small that it is very difficult to notice them. But the order I have followed in this was as follows. First, I tried to find in general the principles or <term>first causes</term> <note>original: "premières causes" — Foundational truths that serve as the starting point for all other knowledge, which Descartes believed could be found through pure reason.</note> of everything that is or can be in the world, without considering anything for this purpose but God alone, who created it, nor deriving them from anywhere else but from certain <term>seeds of truths</term> <note>original: "semences de vérités" — Also known as innate ideas; these are concepts that Descartes believes are naturally imprinted on the human mind by God, such as the laws of geometry or the idea of existence.</note> which are naturally in our souls. After that, I examined what were the first and most ordinary effects that could be deduced from these causes; and it seems to me that by this means I have found the heavens, the stars, an earth, and even on the earth, water, air, fire, minerals, and some other such things, which are the most common of all and the simplest, and consequently the easiest to know. Then, when I wished to descend to those that were more particular, so many diverse ones presented themselves to me that I did not believe it possible for the human mind to distinguish the forms or species of bodies that are on the earth from an infinity of others that could be there if it had been the will of God to put them there, nor consequently to make them useful to us, unless we encounter the causes through their effects, and make use of many particular experiments. Following which, casting my mind back over all the objects that had ever presented themselves to my senses, I dare to say that I have not noticed anything there that I could not explain conveniently enough by the principles I had found. But I must also confess that the power of nature is so ample and so vast, and these principles are so simple and so general, that I notice almost no particular effect that I do not immediately recognize can be deduced from them in several different ways...

But since that time, I have had other reasons that have made me change my opinion and think that I should truly continue to write down all the things I judge to be of some importance, as I discover their truth, and to take the same care as if I intended to have them printed. This is both so that I may have all the more opportunity to examine them well—as, without doubt, one always looks more closely at what one believes will be seen by many than at what one does only for oneself (and often things that seemed true to me when I began to conceive them appeared false when I tried to put them on paper)—and so as not to lose any opportunity to benefit the public, if I am capable of it, and so that, if my writings are worth anything, those who possess them after my death may use them as will be most appropriate. And since many eyes can see more than one man alone, I hoped that by starting to use it now, they might also assist me with their own discoveries. However, although I recognize how extremely prone I am to error, and I almost never trust the first thoughts that come to me, the experience I have with the objections that can be raised against me prevents me from hoping for any profit from them. I have often experienced the judgments of both those I considered friends and those I thought were indifferent, as well as some whose malice and envy would surely try to uncover what friendship might hide from my friends. Yet, it has rarely happened that anyone raised an objection I had not already foreseen—unless it was very far removed from my subject. Thus, I have almost never encountered a critic of my opinions who did not seem to me either less rigorous or less fair than I am to myself. Nor have I ever noticed that the debates practiced in the Schools <note>The "Schools" refers to the traditional 17th-century universities where Scholastic philosophy and formal debate were the standard methods of instruction.</note> have led to the discovery of any truth previously unknown. For while everyone tries to win, they practice making a case for what is probable <note>original: "vraisemblance" — refers to things that seem likely or plausible but lack certain proof.</note> rather than weighing the reasons on both sides. Those who have been good advocates for a long time do not necessarily become better judges afterward.

As for the benefit others might receive from the communication of my thoughts, it could not be very great yet, because I have not yet taken them far enough to avoid the need for many additions before they can be put to practical use. And I believe I can say without vanity that if there is anyone capable of this, it must be me rather than anyone else—not because there are not many minds in the world incomparably better than mine, but because one cannot grasp a thing so well, or make it one's own when learning it from someone else, as when one discovers it for oneself. This is so true in this matter that although I have often explained some of my opinions to very intelligent people who seemed to understand them quite clearly while I spoke, I noticed when they repeated them that they almost always changed them in such a way that I could no longer claim them as mine. On this occasion, I am glad to ask here that future generations <note>original: "nos neveux" (literally "our nephews"); a common 17th-century term for descendants or posterity.</note> never believe that the things told to them come from me unless I have published them myself; and I do not...

I am not at all surprised by the extravagances attributed to all those ancient philosophers whose writings we no longer possess; nor do I judge, for that reason, that their thoughts were very unreasonable, given that they were the finest minds of their times, but only that they have been poorly reported to us. We also see that it has almost never happened that any of their followers has surpassed them; and I am certain that the most passionate of those who now follow Aristotle <note>Aristotle (384–322 BC) was the central authority for "Scholastic" university education in Descartes’ time. Descartes is critiquing those who treat Aristotle’s word as final.</note> would consider themselves fortunate if they had as much knowledge of nature as he had, even on the condition that they would never have more. They are like ivy, which does not tend to climb higher than the trees that support it, and even often grows back down after it has reached their tops; for it seems to me that these people also "grow back down"—that is, they make themselves in some way less learned than if they refrained from studying—who, not content with knowing all that is clearly explained in their author, wish besides that to find in him the solution to many difficulties of which he says nothing and about which he perhaps never thought. 

However, their way of philosophizing is very convenient for those who have only very mediocre minds; for the obscurity of the distinctions and principles they use is the reason they can speak of all things as boldly as if they knew them, and maintain everything they say against the most subtle and skillful, without anyone having the means to convince them of error. In this, they seem to me like a blind man who, in order to fight without disadvantage against one who sees, had made him come into the depths of some very dark cellar; and I can say that these people have an interest in my refraining from publishing the principles of the philosophy I use; for, being very simple and very evident as they are, I would do almost the same by publishing them as if I opened some windows and let daylight into this cellar where they have gone down to fight. 

But even the best minds have no reason to wish to know them; for if they wish to know how to speak of all things and acquire the reputation of being learned, they will achieve it more easily by contenting themselves with probability <term>vraisemblance: claims that appear likely or plausible but lack the absolute certainty Descartes seeks</term>, which can be found without much trouble in all sorts of matters, than by seeking the truth, which is only discovered little by little in some areas, and which, when it is a matter of speaking of others, obliges one to confess frankly that they are unknown. If they prefer the knowledge of some small truth to the vanity of appearing to be ignorant of nothing, as it is undoubtedly much preferable, and if they wish to follow a plan similar to mine, they have no need for...

### FIFTH OBJECTIONS

It seemed to me, you say, that I felt several things while sleeping which I have since recognized I did not feel at all. But even if you were mistaken—in that, without using the eye, it seems to you that you felt what cannot be felt without it—you have nonetheless not always experienced the same falsehood. Furthermore, you have used the eye in the past, and it is through it that you felt and received the images that you can now make use of without it.

Finally, you observe that you think: certainly, that cannot be denied. But it still remains for you to prove that the faculty of thinking is so far above corporeal nature that neither these <term>animal spirits</term><note>In 17th-century physiology, "animal spirits" were thought to be extremely subtle fluids that traveled through the nerves to produce sensation and movement; they were not "spirits" in a supernatural sense, but the most refined part of the blood.</note>, nor any other body, however slender, subtle, pure, and agile it may be, could be so well prepared or receive such dispositions as to be rendered capable of thought. You must also prove at the same time that the souls of beasts are not corporeal; for they think, or if you prefer, beyond the functions of the external senses, they know something internally, not only while awake, but also while they sleep. Finally, you must prove that this coarse and heavy body contributes nothing to your thought (even though you have never been without it, and you have never thought anything while being separated from it), and therefore, that you think independently of it: in such a way that you cannot be hindered by the vapors or by those <note>Original: "fumées noires et épaisses" (black and thick smokes). This refers to the medical theory of the time that physical illness or "melancholy" produced literal vapors that clouded the brain.</note> black and thick fumes which nonetheless sometimes cause so much trouble to the brain.

4. For I see that you have not only stripped yourself of the body, but also of a part of the soul. Are you following in this the example of those ancients who, believing that the soul was diffused throughout the whole body, nonetheless estimated that its principal part—which the Greeks call <term>the ruling part</term><note>original: "τὸ ἡγεμονικὸν" (to hegemonikon). Not that they believed the soul itself was not found in that part, but because they believed the mind was as if added and united in that place to the soul, and that it informed that part along with the soul. And truly, I should have remembered this after what you said in your *Treatise on Method* <note>Referring to Descartes' famous 1637 work, "Discourse on the Method."</note>: for you show therein that your thought is that all those offices which one ordinarily attributes to the <term>vegetative and sensitive souls</term><note>Aristotelian philosophy divided the soul into three levels: the "vegetative" (basic life/growth), the "sensitive" (sensation/movement, shared with animals), and the "rational" (unique to humans). # TO THE DEANS

## AND DOCTORS OF THE SACRED FACULTY OF THEOLOGY

### OF PARIS .

->GENTLEMEN,<-

The reason that leads me to present this work to you is so just, and when you learn of its design, I am certain you will also have a reason so just to take it under your protection, that I think I can do no better to make it recommendable to you than to tell you in a few words what I have proposed for myself within it. I have always held that the two questions of God and the Soul were the principal ones among those that ought to be demonstrated by the arguments of <term>Philosophy</term><note>In the 17th century, "Philosophy" included what we now call science and logic, as well as ethics and metaphysics.</note> rather than <term>Theology</term><note>Theology relies on divine revelation and scripture, whereas Descartes sought to prove these points using logic alone.</note>. For although it is enough for us who are faithful to believe through Faith that there is a God, and that the human soul does not die with the body; certainly, it does not seem possible to ever persuade <term>Unbelievers</term><note>Original: "Infideles." Descartes is referring to those who do not accept the authority of the Church or Scripture.</note> of any Religion, nor perhaps even any Moral virtue, if one does not first prove these two things to them by <term>natural reason</term><note>The human capacity to discover truth through logic and observation without the aid of supernatural revelation.</note>. And since in this life greater rewards are often offered for vices than for virtues, few people would prefer the just to the useful if they were restrained neither by the fear of God nor by the expectation of another life. And although it is absolutely true that one must believe there is a God because it is so taught in the <term>Holy Scriptures</term><note>The Bible.</note>, and on the other hand that one must believe the Holy Scriptures because they come from God—the reason for this being that Faith is a gift from God, and the very one who gives the grace to make us believe other things can also give it to make us believe He exists—one could not, nonetheless, propose this to Unbelievers, who might imagine that one was committing here the error that Logicians call a <term>Circle</term><note>Original: "un Cercle." A logical fallacy, often called "circular reasoning," where the proof of a statement assumes the statement is already true. Descartes is aware of the criticism that he proves God's existence using clear ideas, while claiming clear ideas are only reliable because God exists.</note>.

And in truth, I have noticed that you Gentlemen, along with all Theologians, do not only assert that the existence of God can be proven by natural reason, but also that one infers from the Holy Scripture that the knowledge of Him is much clearer than that which one has of several things—

Furthermore, knowing that the principal reason why many impious people do not want to believe that there is a God, and that the human Soul is distinct from the body, is that they say no one until now has been able to demonstrate these two things: although I am not of their opinion, but on the contrary hold that most of the reasons brought forward by so many great figures concerning these two questions are just as many demonstrations when they are well understood, and that it is almost impossible to invent new ones: nonetheless, I believe that nothing more useful could be done in **Philosophy** than to carefully seek out the best ones once and for all, and to arrange them in an order so clear and so exact that it will be certain from now on to everyone that they are true demonstrations. And finally, insofar as several persons have desired this of me—those who know that I have cultivated a certain **method** for resolving all sorts of difficulties in the sciences; a method which is truly not new, as there is nothing older than truth, but which they know I have used successfully enough on other occasions—I thought it was my duty to also test it on such an important matter.

Now, I have worked with all my might to include in this Treatise everything I have been able to discover by its means. It is not that I have collected here all the various reasons that could be alleged to serve as proof for such a great subject; for I never believed that this was necessary, except when there were none...

# PREFACE

I have already touched upon these two questions of **God** and the **Human Soul** in the French discourse that I published in the year 1637, concerning the method for rightly conducting one’s reason and seeking truth in the sciences. I did not intend to treat them exhaustively at that time, but only in passing, in order to learn from the judgments passed on them how I should treat them afterward. For they have always seemed to me to be of such importance that I judged it appropriate to speak of them more than once; and the path I follow to explain them is so little traveled, and so far from the ordinary route, that I did not think it useful to show it in French, or in a discourse that could be read by everyone, for fear that <term>feeble minds</term><note>Descartes often worried that his radical doubt, if read by those without proper training, might lead to permanent skepticism or moral confusion rather than a firmer foundation for knowledge.</note> might believe they were permitted to attempt this path.

Now, having requested in that *Discourse on Method* that all those who found something worthy of criticism in my writings do me the favor of alerting me to it, nothing remarkable was objected to me except two things regarding what I had said touching these two questions, to which I wish to respond here in a few words before undertaking their more exact explanation.

The first is that, from the fact that the human mind, reflecting upon itself, knows itself to be nothing other than a **thinking thing**, it does not follow that its nature or its <term>essence</term><note>The "essence" is the fundamental quality that makes a thing what it is; without it, the thing would cease to exist.</note> consists *only* in thinking; in such a way that this word *only* excludes all other things that one might perhaps also say belong to the Nature of the Soul.

To which objection I respond that it was not at all my intention to exclude them according to the order of the truth of the matter (which I was not treating then) but only according to the order of my thought; so that my meaning was that I knew nothing that I recognized as belonging to my essence, except that I was a thinking thing, or a thing that has in itself the faculty of thinking. Now, I will show hereafter how, from the fact that I know nothing else that belongs to my essence, it follows that there is indeed nothing else that in effect belongs to it.

The second is that it does not follow, from the fact that I have within me the idea of a thing more perfect than I am, that this **Idea** is more perfect than I, and much less that what is represented by this Idea exists.

But I respond that in this word *Idea*, there is an ambiguity here; for it can either be taken **materially**, as an operation of my <term>Understanding</term><note>In 17th-century philosophy, the "Understanding" (or Intellect) is the faculty of the mind that perceives ideas and grasps truths, distinct from the imagination or the senses.</note>, and in this sense it cannot be said to be more perfect than me; or it can be taken **objectively**...

On the contrary, I will never advise anyone to read it, except those who are willing to meditate seriously with me, and who can detach their minds from the commerce of the senses and deliver them entirely from all sorts of prejudices, which I know all too well to be very few in number. But for those who, without caring much for the order and connection of my reasons, amuse themselves by nitpicking at each of the parts, as many do—those, I say, will not profit much from the reading of this Treatise.
