# FIFTH OBJECTIONS

## Page 260

...having thus stripped the wax of all its forms, no more and no less than if they were its clothes, you believe you conceive more clearly and perfectly what it is. For I am willing to grant that you conceive that the wax, or rather the **substance** <note>In 17th-century philosophy, "substance" refers to the underlying reality of a thing that stays the same even when its outer qualities change.</note> of the wax, must be something different from all these forms; however, you cannot say that you truly conceive what it is, unless you intend to deceive us or unless you wish to be deceived yourself. For this substance is not made manifest to you in the way a man becomes manifest—a man of whom we had only glimpsed the cloak and the hat—when we come to take them off him to find out what he is or who he is. 

And afterwards, since you think you understand in some way what this thing is, tell us, I pray you, how do you conceive of it? Is it not as something **fusible** <note>Capable of being melted.</note> and **extended**? <term>Extended (étendue)</term> <note>For Descartes, the defining characteristic of physical matter is that it takes up space (extension).</note> For I do not think you conceive of it as a single point, even though it is such that it extends sometimes more and sometimes less. Now, this sort of extension cannot be infinite, but has its boundaries and limits; do you not also conceive of it as having some kind of shape? Then, conceiving it in such a way that it seems to you that you see it, do you not attribute to it some sort of color, however dark and confused? Certainly, as it appears to you to have more body and matter than a pure vacuum, it also seems more visible to you; and therefore, your **intellect** is merely a species of **imagination**. <note>Gassendi is arguing that Descartes isn't using "pure reason," but is still just forming mental pictures (imagining).</note> If you say that you conceive of it without extension, without shape, and without color, then tell us plainly: what is it?

What you say regarding the men whom we have seen and conceived of through the mind—of whom, nevertheless, we only perceived the hats or the clothes—does not show us that it is the **understanding** <note>The "intellect" or higher reasoning faculty.</note> rather than the **imaginative faculty** that judges. And in fact, does not a dog—in whom you do not admit a mind similar to your own—judge in the same way when, seeing nothing other than the cloak or the hat of his master, he nonetheless fails not to recognize him? Furthermore, even if his master is standing, lying down, leaning over, hunching, or stretching out, he always knows his master, who can exist under all these forms, but not more under one than the other, just like the wax? And when he runs after a hare, and after having seen it alive and whole, he sees it dead, skinned, and butchered into several pieces, do you think he does not believe it to be the same hare? # SYNOPSIS

## SYNOPSIS OF THE FIRST MEDITATION

In the first meditation, I set forth the reasons why we can generally doubt all things, and particularly material things; at least so long as we have no other foundations in the sciences than those we have had up to now. Now, although the utility of such a general doubt may not be apparent at first, it is nonetheless very great, in that it delivers us from all sorts of **prejudices**, <term>prejudices (préjugés)</term> <note>In this context, "prejudices" refers to preconceived notions or beliefs we have accepted since childhood without questioning them.</note> and prepares for us a very easy path to accustom our mind to detach itself from the senses: and finally, in that it makes it impossible for us to ever again doubt those things that we later discover to be true.

## SYNOPSIS OF THE SECOND MEDITATION

In the second meditation, the mind which—using its own freedom—supposes that all things of whose existence it has the slightest doubt do not exist, recognizes that it is absolutely impossible that it does not itself exist during this process. This is of very great utility, especially since by this means the mind easily distinguishes those things that belong to itself—that is to say, to the **intellectual nature**—from those that belong to the body.

But because it may happen that some will expect from me in this section reasons to prove the immortality of the soul, I consider it my duty to warn them here that, having tried to write nothing in this entire Treatise for which I did not have very exact demonstrations, I found myself obliged to follow an order similar to that used by **geometricians**, <term>geometricians (géomètres)</term> <note>Descartes refers to the "geometric method," a way of reasoning that starts with simple, undeniable truths (axioms) and builds up to complex conclusions through logical steps.</note> which is to set forth first all the things upon which the proposition one seeks depends, before concluding anything from it.

Now, the first and principal thing required for well... <note>The sentence ends abruptly at the bottom of the page.</note>

-># SYNOPSIS<-

knowing the immortality of the soul is to form a clear and distinct conception of it, and one entirely distinct from all the conceptions that one can have of the body: which was done in that place <note>Referring to the Second Meditation.</note>. It is required, besides this, to know that all the things we conceive clearly and distinctly are true, in the manner that we conceive them: which could not be proved before the Fourth Meditation. Furthermore, one must have a distinct conception of **bodily nature**, which is formed partly in this second, and partly in the Fifth and Sixth Meditations. And finally, one must conclude from all this that the things one conceives clearly and distinctly to be diverse substances—just as one conceives the **Mind** and the **Body**—are in effect substances really distinct from one another; and this is what is concluded in the Sixth Meditation. This is further confirmed in that same Meditation by the fact that we cannot conceive of any body except as **divisible**: whereas the mind, or the soul of man, can only be conceived as **indivisible**. For indeed, we cannot conceive of the half of any soul, as we can do with the smallest of all bodies; so that one recognizes that their natures are not only diverse, but even in some way contrary.

Now, I have not treated this matter further in this writing, both because this suffices to show clearly enough that the death of the soul does not follow from the <term>corruption of the body</term> <note>Decay or physical breaking down.</note>, and thus to give men the hope of a second life after death; and also because the premises from which one can conclude the immortality of the soul depend on the explanation of the whole of **physics**. First, to know that generally all <term>substances</term> <note>In philosophical terms, a 'substance' is something that exists independently, needing only God to exist.</note>—that is to say, all things that cannot exist without being created by God—are by their nature incorruptible, and that they can never cease to be, if God himself, by denying them his <term>concurrence</term> <note>Descartes refers here to the theological concept of "divine concurrence," the idea that God must actively "concur" or support the existence of every thing at every moment for it to continue existing.</note>, does not reduce them to nothingness. And subsequently, to remark that the body, taken in general, is a substance, which is why it also does not perish; but that the human body, insofar as it differs from other bodies, is composed only of a certain configuration of members and other similar <term>accidents</term> <note>Properties or characteristics (like shape or movement) that can change without the underlying substance disappearing.</note>: whereas the human soul is not thus composed of any accidents, but is a **pure substance**. For even though all its accidents change—for example, even though it conceives of certain things, wills others, and senses others, etc.—the soul nevertheless does not become something else: whereas the human body becomes another thing simply because the shape of some of its parts is changed. From this it follows that the human body may easily perish, but that the mind, or the soul of man (which I do not distinguish between), is immortal by its nature.

As, among others, this one: how the idea of a **supremely perfect being**, which is found within us, contains so much <term>objective reality</term> <note>The reality of a thing as it exists as an object of thought in the mind, representing a certain degree of perfection.</note>; that is to say, how it participates by representation in so many degrees of being and perfection that it must come from a **supremely perfect cause**. This I have clarified in those responses by the comparison of a highly ingenious and artificial machine, the idea of which is found in the mind of some craftsman; for just as the **objective craftsmanship** of this idea must have some cause—namely, either the knowledge of this craftsman, or that of someone else from whom he received this idea—likewise, it is impossible for the idea of God which is in us not to have God Himself as its cause.

### SYNOPSIS OF THE FOURTH MEDITATION

In the fourth, it is proved that all the things we conceive very clearly and very distinctly are all true; and at the same time, the nature of error or falsehood is explained. This must necessarily be known both to confirm the preceding truths and to better understand those that follow. However, it should be remarked that I do not treat **sin** there at all—that is, the error committed in the pursuit of good and evil—but only that which occurs in judgment and the discernment of the true and the false. And I do not intend to speak there of things belonging to faith, or the conduct of life, but only of those regarding **speculative truths**, which can be known with the help of <term>natural light</term> <note>The innate human capacity for reason, independent of divine revelation.</note> alone.

### SYNOPSIS OF THE FIFTH MEDITATION

In the fifth Meditation, besides the fact that **corporeal nature** <note>The nature of physical bodies or matter.</note> taken in general is explained, the existence of God is again demonstrated by a new reason. In this, nevertheless, perhaps some difficulties will also be encountered, but the solution will be seen in the responses to the objections made to me. And furthermore, I show in what way it is true that the very certainty of **geometrical demonstrations** depends on the knowledge of God.

It is not from today that I have noticed that, from my earliest years, I have accepted many false opinions as true, and that what I have since founded on such insecure principles could only be highly doubtful and uncertain. <note>This is the starting point of Descartes’ famous "Methodical Doubt." He realized that if his basic assumptions were wrong, everything he learned afterward was suspect.</note> And from then on, I rightly judged that I needed to seriously undertake, once in my life, to rid myself of all the opinions I had previously accepted into my belief <note>original: *créance*. But this undertaking seeming to me to be very great, I waited until I had reached an age so mature that I could not hope for another after it in which I would be more fit to execute it; which has made me delay so long that henceforth I would believe I was committing a fault if I still spent in deliberation the time that remains for me to act.

Today, then, quite opportunely for this purpose, I have freed my mind from all sorts of cares, and as I fortunately do not feel myself agitated by any passions, and have procured for myself a secure rest in a peaceful solitude, I will apply myself seriously and freely to the general destruction of all my former opinions. Now, for this purpose, it will not be necessary for me to show that they are all false, which I might perhaps never accomplish; but since reason already persuades me that I should no less carefully withhold belief from things that are not entirely certain and indubitable than from those that appear to me to be manifestly false, it will be enough for me to reject them all if I can find in each some reason for doubt; and for that, it will also not be necessary for me to examine each one in particular, which would be an infinite labor; but because the ruin of the foundations necessarily carries with it the rest of the building, I will first attack the principles <note>Descartes uses an architectural metaphor here: rather than knocking down every individual brick (every single thought), he intends to undermine the foundation (the basic principles of how we know things) so the whole structure falls at once.</note> upon which all my former opinions were supported.

But perhaps, even though the senses deceive us sometimes concerning things that are barely perceptible and very far away, there are nonetheless many others about which one cannot reasonably doubt, although we know them through their means. For example, that I am here, sitting by the fire, wearing a dressing gown, having this paper between my hands, and other things of this nature. And how could I deny that these hands and this body are mine, unless perhaps I compare myself to certain madmen <note>Descartes uses the term *insensés*, meaning those without sense or reason.</note>, whose brains are so troubled and clouded by the black vapors of bile <note>original: *noires vapeurs de la bile*. However, I must here consider that I am a man, and consequently that I am in the habit of sleeping, and of representing to myself in my dreams the same things, or sometimes less plausible things, than those madmen do while awake. How many times has it happened that I dreamt at night that I was in this place, that I was dressed, that I was by the fire, although I was quite naked in my bed? It certainly seems to me now that it is not with sleeping eyes that I look at this paper; that this head which I move is not drowsy; that it is with design and deliberate purpose that I stretch out this hand, and that I feel it; what happens in sleep does not seem so clear or so distinct as all this. But in thinking about it carefully, I remember having often been deceived while sleeping by similar illusions. And pausing on this thought, I see so clearly that there are no certain marks by which one can clearly distinguish waking from sleep, that I am quite astonished, and my astonishment is such that it is almost capable of persuading me that I am dreaming.

Let us suppose then, for now, that we are dreaming, and that all these particulars—namely, that we open our eyes, that we move our heads, that we stretch out our hands, and similar things—are only false illusions; and let us think that perhaps our hands, nor our whole body, are not such as we see them. For in truth, painters, even when they strive with the greatest artifice to represent sirens and satyrs through bizarre and extraordinary figures, cannot nonetheless give them entirely new forms and natures, but only create a certain mixture and composition of the limbs of various animals; or else if perhaps their imagination is extravagant enough to invent something so new that nothing like it has ever been seen, and that thus their work represents something purely feigned and absolutely false, certainly at the very least the colors from which they compose them must be real.

And for the same reason, even if these general things—namely, a body, eyes, a head, hands, and the like—could be imaginary, it must nonetheless be admitted that there are at least some other even simpler and more universal things that are true and existing, from the mixture of which, neither more nor less than from that of certain true colors, all these images of things that reside in our thought, whether true and real or feigned and fantastic, are formed.

Of this kind of things is *corporeal nature* <term>nature corporelle: the fundamental essence of physical matter as something that occupies space</term> in general and its *extension* <term>étendue: the principal attribute of matter, meaning it has length, breadth, and depth</term>; together with the *shape* <note>original: *figure*</note> of extended things, their quantity or *size*, and their *number*, as also the *place* where they are, the *time* that measures their *duration*, and other similar things. That is why perhaps we will not conclude poorly if we say that *physics*, *astronomy*, *medicine*, and all other sciences that depend on the consideration of composite things, are very doubtful and uncertain; but that *arithmetic*, *geometry*, and other sciences of this nature, which deal only with very simple and very general things, without caring much whether they exist in nature or not, contain something certain and indubitable; for, whether I am awake or asleep, two and three joined together will always form the number five, and the square will never have more than four sides; and it does not seem possible that truths so clear and so apparent could be suspected of any falsehood or uncertainty.

### FIRST MEDITATION 69

by whom I was made and created such as I am. Now, how do I know if he has not brought it about that there is no Earth, no Heaven, no extended body <term>corps étendu: in Cartesian philosophy, matter is defined by "extension," meaning it takes up physical space in three dimensions</term>, no figure, no magnitude, no place? And that nonetheless I have the sensation of all these things, and that all this seems to me to exist no differently than how I see it? And even as I judge sometimes that others are mistaken in the things they think they know best, how do I know if he has not brought it about that I am also mistaken every time I add two and three, or count the sides of a square, or judge something even easier, if one can imagine anything easier than that? But perhaps God has not willed that I be deceived in such a way, for he is said to be supremely good. However, if it were repugnant to his goodness to have made me such that I was always mistaken, it would also seem somewhat contrary to it to allow me to be mistaken sometimes; and yet I cannot doubt that he does allow it.

There will perhaps be people here who would rather deny the existence of a God so powerful than believe that all other things are uncertain: but let us not resist them for the moment, and let us suppose in their favor that everything said here about a God is a fable; nevertheless, in whatever way they suppose I have arrived at the state and the being I possess—whether they attribute it to some destiny or fate, or refer it to chance, or wish it to be through a continual sequence and connection of things, or finally by some other manner; since failing and being mistaken is an imperfection, the less powerful the author they assign to my origin, the more probable it will be that I am so imperfect that I am always mistaken. To which reasons I certainly have nothing to answer; but finally I am constrained to admit that there is nothing of all I once believed to be true of which I cannot in some way doubt. And this not through thoughtlessness or levity, but for very strong and maturely considered reasons. So that henceforth I must no less carefully withhold my belief from them than from what would be patently false, if I wish to find anything certain and assured in the sciences <note>original: "sciences"; here meaning all organized fields of knowledge, including philosophy and physics</note>.

But it is not enough to have made these remarks; I must also take care to remember them; for these old and ordinary opinions still return often to my thought; the long and familiar acquaintance they have had with me gives them the right to occupy my mind against my will, and to make themselves almost masters of my belief;

and I will never break the habit of deferring to them and placing my trust in them, so long as I consider them as they truly are—namely, as being in some way doubtful, as I have just shown, and yet highly probable, such that one has much more reason to believe them than to deny them.

This is why I think I will not do wrong if, by taking a deliberately contrary stance, I deceive myself and pretend for a time that all these opinions are entirely false and imaginary; until finally, having so balanced my old and new prejudices that they cannot tip my opinion more to one side than the other, my judgment may no longer be mastered by bad habits and turned away from the right path that can lead it to the knowledge of truth.

I will consider myself as having no hands, no eyes, no flesh, no blood, as having no senses, but falsely believing I have all these things; I will remain stubbornly attached to this thought; and if by this means it is not in my power to arrive at the knowledge of any truth, at the very least it is in my power to suspend my judgment <term>suspension of judgment: the act of withholding assent to any proposition that is not completely certain</term>: this is why I will take careful heed not to receive any falsehood into my belief, and will prepare my mind so well against all the ruses of this great deceiver that, however powerful and cunning he may be, he will never be able to impose anything upon me.

But this undertaking is painful and laborious, and a certain laziness draws me imperceptibly back into the course of my ordinary life. And just like a slave who enjoyed an imaginary freedom in his sleep, when he begins to suspect that his freedom is only a dream, fears waking up and conspires with his pleasant illusions to be deceived by them longer, so I fall back imperceptibly...

## SECOND MEDITATION

->*Of the nature of the human Mind,*<-
->*And that it is easier to know than the Body.*<-

That we must reject things where there is the slightest doubt, until we have encountered something certain. — That it will be a significant achievement if we can find just one certain thing. — That we must therefore reject as false everything we have ever known through the senses. — That while one doubts everything in this way, one cannot doubt that one is, and that this proposition *I am*, is necessarily true. <note>This is the foundation of the famous principle "I think, therefore I am" (cogito, ergo sum).</note> — That being thus certain that one exists, it is necessary to examine *what* one is. — That for this purpose it is appropriate to examine what we believed ourselves to be previously. — That we are nothing of what we previously believed ourselves to be, except precisely a thinking thing. <term>thinking thing: "res cogitans" in Latin; for Descartes, this is a being that doubts, understands, affirms, denies, wills, refuses, and also imagines and feels.</term> — That nothing that can be understood by the imagination belongs to this knowledge of ourselves. — What a thinking thing is. — Why we believe we know bodily things more distinctly than this thinking thing. — Consideration of the knowledge of sensible things through the examination of a piece of wax. <note>The "Wax Argument" is used to show that we perceive the essence of objects through the mind, not just the senses, because the wax's physical properties change when melted, yet we know it is the same wax.</note> — That everything we believe we know distinctly in this piece of wax does not fall under the senses. — That it is therefore by the understanding alone that we know what this piece of wax is. — Why it is difficult to agree with this truth. — That it serves to prove that we have a mind. — And that this mind is more distinctly known to us than any other thing. — That there is, therefore, nothing easier to know than our mind.

The meditation I made yesterday has filled my mind with so many doubts that it is no longer within my power to forget them; and yet I do not see in what way I might resolve them. It is as if I had suddenly fallen into very deep water, and I am so surprised that I can neither plant my feet on the bottom nor swim to keep myself above. I will nevertheless make an effort, and once again follow the same path I entered yesterday, by distancing myself from everything in which I can imagine the slightest doubt, just as if I knew that it were absolutely false; and I will always continue on this path until I have <note>The text cuts off here, but Descartes is about to reach his "Archimedean point" of certainty.</note>

<summary>Descartes begins his Second Meditation by outlining his plan to find a single point of absolute certainty, eventually concluding that while he can doubt the physical world, he cannot doubt his own existence as a "thinking thing."</summary>

...encountered something certain, or at least, if I can do nothing else, until I have learned for certain that there is nothing in the world that is certain.

Archimedes, to pull the terrestrial globe from its place and transport it to another location, asked for nothing but a point that was firm and immovable <note>original: "un point qui fût ferme et immobile." This refers to the famous quote attributed to the Greek mathematician Archimedes: "Give me a place to stand, and I will move the Earth."</note>; thus I will have the right to conceive high hopes if I am lucky enough to find just one thing that is certain and indubitable.

I suppose, then, that all the things I see are false; I persuade myself that nothing has ever existed of all that my memory, filled with lies, represents to me: I think I have no senses; I believe that the body, shape, extension, movement, and place are but fictions of my mind. <term>extension: "étendue" in French; for Descartes, this refers to the fundamental property of physical matter—occupying space in length, width, and depth.</term> What, then, can be esteemed true? Perhaps nothing else, except that there is nothing in the world that is certain.

But how do I know if there is not something else, different from those I have just judged uncertain, about which one cannot have the least doubt? Is there not some God or some other power who puts these thoughts into my mind? That is not necessary; for perhaps I am capable of producing them myself. Am I, then, at the very least, not something? But I have already denied that I had any senses or any body; I hesitate, nonetheless: for what follows from that? Am I so dependent on the body and the senses that I cannot exist without them? But I persuaded myself that there was nothing at all in the world, that there was no sky, no earth, no minds, nor any bodies: did I not then also persuade myself that I was not? Far from it; I certainly existed if I persuaded myself, or even if I thought anything at all: but there is a some-kind-of very powerful and very cunning deceiver <note>Often referred to as the "Evil Demon" or "Malicious Genius," this is a thought experiment Descartes uses to test the strength of his doubt.</note> who employs all his industriousness to always deceive me: there is then no doubt that I am, if he deceives me; and let him deceive me as much as he will, he could never make it so that I am nothing as long as I think I am something. So that after having thought about it well and having carefully examined everything, finally one must conclude and hold as constant that this proposition, *I am, I exist*, is necessarily true every time that I utter it, or that I conceive it in my mind. <note>This is the definitive moment of the "Cogito." While the phrase "I think, therefore I am" is more famous, Descartes here emphasizes that the very act of thinking or being deceived confirms his existence.</note>

But I do not yet know clearly enough what I am, I who am certain that I am: so that from now on I must take careful care not to imprudently take some other thing for myself, and thus not to mistake myself in this knowledge that I...

Therefore, I will now consider entirely anew what I believed myself to be before I entered into these recent thoughts; and from my old opinions, I will strip away everything that can be even slightly contested by the reasons I have just alleged, so that there remains precisely only that which is entirely certain and indubitable. What, then, did I previously believe myself to be? Without difficulty, I thought that I was a man. But what is a man? Shall I say that he is a **rational animal**? <term>rational animal: In French "animal raisonnable." This was the traditional Scholastic definition of humanity based on Aristotle. Descartes rejects it here because it requires defining "animal" and "rational," leading to further complexity.</term> No, certainly not; for I would then have to research what an animal is, and what "rational" is, and thus from a single question I would slide insensibly into an infinity of others more difficult and more tangled, and I would not wish to abuse the little time and leisure remaining to me by employing it to unravel such difficulties. 

Instead, I will stop here to consider the thoughts that were previously born of themselves in my mind, and which were inspired in me only by my own nature when I applied myself to the consideration of my being. I considered myself, first, as having a face, hands, arms, and this whole **machine** <note>Descartes famously viewed the physical body as a biological machine governed by mechanical laws, much like a clock.</note> composed of bones and flesh, such as it appears in a corpse, which I designated by the name of **body**. I considered, furthermore, that I nourished myself, that I walked, that I felt, and that I thought, and I referred all these actions to the **soul**; but I did not stop to think what this soul was; or if I did, I imagined that it was something extremely rare and subtle, like a wind, a flame, or a very thin air that was insinuated and spread throughout my grosser parts. 

As for the body, I had no doubt at all about its nature; rather, I thought I knew it very distinctly; and if I had wished to explain it according to the notions I then held, I would have described it in this way: by **body**, I mean everything that can be bounded by some shape; which can be contained in some place and fill a space in such a way that every other body is excluded from it; which can be perceived either by touch, sight, hearing, taste, or smell; which can be moved in several ways, not indeed by itself, but by something foreign by which it is touched and from which it receives an impression. For as for having the power to move itself, as well as to feel or to think, I did not believe at all that these belonged to the nature of the body; on the contrary, I was rather astonished to see that...

...struck, it will emit a sound. In short, all the things that can distinctly make a body known are found in this one.

But look, even as I speak, it is brought near the fire; what remained of its flavor exhales, the smell evaporates, its color changes, its shape is lost, its size increases, it becomes liquid, it grows hot, one can hardly handle it, and although one strikes it, it will no longer emit any sound. Does the same wax remain after this change? It must be admitted that it does; no one doubts it, no one judges otherwise. What was it, then, that I knew in this piece of wax with such distinction? Certainly, it could be nothing of all those things I noticed by means of the senses, since everything that fell under taste, smell, sight, touch, and hearing has changed, and yet the same wax remains. 

Perhaps it was what I am thinking now: namely, that this wax was neither that sweetness of honey, nor that pleasant scent of flowers, nor that whiteness, nor that shape, nor that sound, but only a body that a moment ago appeared to me under those forms, and which now makes itself felt under others. But what, precisely speaking, do I imagine when I conceive of it in this way? Let us consider it attentively and, removing everything that does not belong to the wax, let us see what remains. Certainly, nothing remains but something <term>extended: For Descartes, "extension" (occupying space in three dimensions) is the essential property of all physical matter.</term>, flexible, and changeable. Now, what is this "flexible and changeable"? Does it mean that I imagine this wax, being round, is capable of becoming square, and of passing from a square to a triangular shape? No, certainly not, since I conceive of it as being capable of receiving an infinite number of similar changes, and I could not, nevertheless, run through this infinity with my imagination; consequently, this conception I have of the wax is not achieved by the faculty of imagination. 

What now of this extension? Is it not also unknown? For it becomes greater when the wax melts, greater still when it boils, and even greater as the heat increases; and I would not clearly and truly conceive what the wax is if I did not think that even this piece we are considering is capable of receiving more varieties in extension than I have ever imagined. 

We must then agree that I could not even understand by the imagination what this piece of wax is, and that it is my <term>understanding: Also called the intellect; the mind's capacity for logic and pure reason, separate from sensory images.</term> alone which perceives it. I say "this piece of wax" in particular...

## SECOND MEDITATION

...for regarding wax in general it is even more evident. But what is this piece of wax which can only be understood by the <term>understanding: The intellectual faculty of the mind that grasps concepts, as opposed to the senses or imagination.</term> or by the mind? Certainly, it is the same one that I see, that I touch, that I imagine, and finally it is the same that I have always believed it was from the beginning. Now, what is highly noteworthy here is that its perception is neither an act of vision, nor of touch, nor of imagination, and never was, though it seemed so before; rather, it is solely an **inspection of the mind**, which can be imperfect and confused, as it was before, or clear and distinct, as it is now, depending on whether my attention is directed more or less to the things within it and of which it is composed.

However, I cannot be surprised enough when I consider how much weakness and tendency my mind has to lead me insensibly into error. For even though I consider all this within myself without speaking, words nevertheless stop me, and I am almost deceived by the terms of ordinary language. For we say that we "see" the same wax, if it is present, and not that we **judge** it to be the same from its having the same color and shape. From this, I would almost want to conclude that one knows the wax through the vision of the eyes, and not by the sole inspection of the mind. If by chance I did not look from a window at men passing in the street, at the sight of whom I do not fail to say that I "see" men, just as I say that I see wax; and yet, what do I see from this window, other than hats and coats which could cover <term>artificial machines: Descartes is referring to automatons—mechanical figures popular in the 17th century—to argue that the senses alone cannot distinguish a human from a robot.</term> that might move only by springs? But I **judge** that they are men, and thus I comprehend by the sole power of judging which resides in my mind what I believed I saw with my eyes.

A man who strives to raise his knowledge above the common level should be ashamed to find reasons for doubt in the forms of speech invented by the <term>vulgar: In this context, "vulgar" refers to the general public or common folk, rather than something offensive.</term>. ->## SECOND MEDITATION<-

...external qualities, and that, just as if I had stripped away its clothing, I consider it entirely naked, it is certain that although some error might still be found in my judgment, I nonetheless cannot conceive of it in this way without a human mind.

But finally, what shall I say of this mind—that is, of myself? For until now I admit nothing within myself except for the mind. <note>Descartes is currently operating under his "method of doubt," having temporarily set aside the belief that he has a physical body.</note> What then? I, who seem to conceive this piece of wax with such clarity and distinctness, do I not know myself not only with much more truth and certainty, but also with far more distinctness and clarity? For if I judge that the wax is or exists because I see it, certainly it follows much more evidently that I am, or that I myself exist, because I see it. For it may be that what I see is not actually wax; it may also be that I do not even have eyes to see anything; but it cannot be that when I see, or (a distinction I do not make here) when I **think** I see, that I who think am not something.

Likewise, if I judge that the wax exists because I touch it, the same thing will follow—namely, that I am. And if I judge this because my imagination or any other cause convinces me of it, I will always reach the same conclusion. And what I have noted here regarding the wax can be applied to all other things that are external to me and are found outside of me. Furthermore, if the notion or <term>perception: In this context, not just physical seeing, but the mental grasping of an idea.</term> of the wax seemed clearer and more distinct to me after not only sight or touch, but many other causes made it more manifest, how much more evidence, distinctness, and clarity must I admit I now possess in knowing myself? For all the reasons that serve to know and conceive the nature of the wax, or of any other body whatsoever, prove much better the nature of my mind. And there are so many other things found within the mind itself which can contribute to the clarification of its nature that those depending on the body, like these, hardly deserve to be taken into account.

But at last, I have insensibly returned to where I intended. For since it is now manifest to me that even bodies are not properly known by the senses or by the faculty of imagination, but by the <term>understanding: The intellectual power of the mind used to grasp truths through reason rather than physical sensation.</term> alone, and that they are not known because they are seen or touched, but only because they are understood or rightly grasped by thought, I see clearly that there is nothing easier for me to know than my mind.

<summary>Descartes concludes that the act of perceiving external objects like wax proves the existence and nature of the mind more effectively than it proves the existence of the objects themselves. He establishes that the mind (the intellect) is the primary and most certain source of knowledge, surpassing both the senses and the imagination.</summary>

# THIRD MEDITATION

### *That God Exists.*

That by detaching ourselves from the senses, we come to know ourselves very clearly as a <term>thinking thing</term> <note>original: "chose qui pense" or "res cogitans"; Descartes' definition of the mind as a substance whose essence is thought.</note>. — That all the things we conceive very clearly and very distinctly are true. — That we previously lacked clear and distinct ideas of several things that we now recognize as very uncertain, despite having once believed them to be very certain. — That what can cause us to doubt the things we conceive very distinctly is the possibility that perhaps God takes pleasure in deceiving us. — That it is therefore necessary to examine if there is a God, and if so, whether he is a <term>deceiver</term> <note>Descartes refers to the "malicious demon" or "deceiving God" hypothesis: the fear that our logic itself might be manipulated by a higher power.</note>, if we wish to be certain of anything. — That to examine the truth or error of our thoughts, it is appropriate to divide them into certain genres. — That our thoughts are either ideas, or <term>affections</term> <note>In 17th-century philosophy, "affections" refer to volitions, emotions, or desires—movements of the will rather than just mental images.</note>, or judgments. — That ideas, taken in themselves, are not false. — Nor are affections. — How it happens that there is error in our judgments. — Three kinds of ideas that are within us. — Two reasons that persuaded us that the ideas which seem to come to us from objects are similar to those objects. — That the first of these reasons is not convincing. — Nor the second, either. — That we have believed, without any certain judgment, that there were things outside of us which caused ideas in us that were similar to them. — How our ideas, considered as such, are more perfect than one another. — That every <term>efficient cause</term> <note>The primary source or agent that brings an effect into being.</note> has at least as much perfection as its effect. — How it follows from this that the <term>objective perfection</term> <note>The degree of reality or "perfection" represented by the content of an idea, rather than the idea as a mental event.</note> of an idea must be present <term>formally</term> or <term>eminently</term> <note>Scholastic terms: "formally" means the cause has the property itself (e.g., a hot stove causes heat); "eminently" means the cause has the property in a higher, more superior form (e.g., God creating light).</note> in its cause. — That if we have any idea whose objective perfection is in us neither formally nor eminently, there is then something outside of us which is the cause of it. — An enumeration of our ideas. — How the ideas we have of men, Angels, and animals can come from ourselves. — Those we have of corporeal things. — Those we have of sensible things. — Those we have of <term>substance</term>, duration, number, etc. — Even those we have of <term>extension</term> <note>The physical quality of taking up space.</note>, figure, situation, etc. — But that the idea we have of God cannot come from us, and that consequently there is a God. — That we conceive of the infinite, that is to say, God, through a true idea; and that it is in some way more primary in us than the idea of ourselves. — That this idea of God is in no way false. —

That on the contrary it is very true. — And very clear and very distinct. — That even though we do not understand the infinite, it does not cease to be true. — That regardless of what supposition one makes, it is impossible that the idea of a God comes from us. — That the use of the senses makes us easily forget the reasons for this truth. — That we are not the cause of ourselves. — First reason. — Second reason. — That even though we suppose we have always existed, the nature of our life's duration proves there is a cause that makes us exist — That this cause is different from ourselves. — That it is impossible it could be anything other than God. — Why one cannot pretend that several causes concurred in our production. — Nor that our parents produced us, or preserve us, from which we must conclude that there is a God. — That this idea of God is natural to us. — That it comes from God who actually and infinitely possesses all the perfections it contains. — From which it is evident that he cannot be a deceiver. — That one cannot linger too long in contemplating and adoring this all-perfect God. — And that in this consists the <term>Sovereign Good</term> <note>The "Sovereign Good" (Summum Bonum) refers to the highest possible good or the ultimate goal of human life, which Descartes identifies here with the contemplation of God.</note> of this life.

<margin>1<insert>st</insert></margin>
I will now close my eyes, I will stop my ears, I will turn away all my senses, I will even erase from my thought all images of corporeal things, or at least, because this can hardly be done, I will consider them as vain and false; and thus conversing only with myself, and considering my interior, I will try to make myself gradually better known and more familiar to myself. I am a <term>thinking thing</term> <note>original: "chose qui pense"; the fundamental definition of the self established in the Second Meditation, often known by the Latin term "res cogitans."</note>, that is to say, a thing that doubts, affirms, denies, knows few things, is ignorant of many, loves, hates, wills, does not will, imagines also, and feels. For, as I have remarked before, although the things I feel and imagine are perhaps nothing at all outside of me and in themselves, I am nonetheless certain that these ways of thinking that I call sensations and imaginations, insofar as they are only ways of thinking, certainly reside and are found within me. But another path now presents itself to investigate whether, among the things whose ideas I possess within me, there are some that exist outside of me. From this it follows, not only that nothingness cannot produce anything, but also that what is more perfect—that is, what contains more reality in itself—cannot be a consequence of and dependent upon the less perfect. This truth is not only clear and evident regarding those effects which possess that reality which philosophers call <term>actual or formal</term> <note>original: "actuelle ou formelle." <margin>Continuous creation</margin>
Even if I were to suppose that perhaps I have always been as I am now, I still could not escape the force of this reasoning, and I would still recognize that it is necessary for God to be the author of my existence. For the entire duration of my life can be divided into an infinite number of parts, each of which does not depend in any way on the others; thus, from the fact that I existed a short time ago, it does not follow that I must exist now, unless at this very moment some cause produces and creates me, so to speak, anew—that is to say, "conserves" or sustains me. In fact, it is a very clear and evident thing (to all those who consider the nature of time with attention) that a <term>substance</term> <note>In 17th-century philosophy, a "substance" is an independent entity that can exist on its own—here referring to the soul or mind.</note>, in order to be conserved at every moment that it lasts, needs the same power and the same action that would be necessary to produce and create it anew if it did not yet exist. In this way, the <term>natural light</term> <note>Descartes' term for the innate power of human reason to perceive truth clearly and distinctly.</note> makes us see clearly that conservation and creation differ only in our way of thinking, and not in reality.

I must therefore only ask and consult myself here to see if I have in me any power or any virtue by means of which I can ensure that I, who exist now, will still exist a moment later. For since I am nothing but a <term>thinking thing</term> <note>Original: "chose qui pense." This relates to his famous "Cogito," defining the self as a mind or consciousness.</note> (or at least since we are only dealing precisely with that part of myself so far), if such a power resided in me, I certainly should at the very least be conscious of it and have knowledge of it; but I feel no such power within me, and by that I clearly know that I depend on some being different from myself.

<margin>B. Causes inferior to God</margin>
But perhaps that being on whom I depend is not God, and I am produced either by my parents or by some other causes less perfect than Him? Far from it; that cannot be. For as I said previously, it is very evident that there must be at least as much reality in the cause as in its effect. Therefore, since I am a thinking thing, and have in me some idea of God, whatever the cause of my being may eventually be, it must necessarily be admitted that it is also a thinking thing, and that it possesses in itself the idea of all the perfections that I attribute to God. Then one can again inquire whether this cause holds its origin and its existence from itself, or from something else; for if it holds it from itself, it follows from the reasons I have previously...

...acquired this idea: for I have not received it through the senses, and it has never presented itself to me unexpectedly, as the ideas of sensible things usually do when these things present themselves or appear to present themselves to the external organs of the senses; it is also not a pure production or fiction of my mind, for it is not in my power to take anything away from it nor to add anything to it; and consequently there remains nothing else to say except that this idea was born and produced with me from the moment I was created, just as the idea of myself is.

# FOURTH MEDITATION

->*Of Truth and Error.*<-

That after having detached the mind from the senses, it is easy to direct it toward intelligible things. — That the knowledge of God is a means to arrive at the knowledge of other things. And that it is impossible for God to deceive us. — That thus, by making good use of the reason he has given us, we can never err. — That it does not follow from this that we should never err <note>Descartes is distinguishing between our *capacity* to avoid error and the fact that we often do err in practice.</note>. — That since error is nothing but a defect <term>défaut</term> <note>In this context, a "defect" refers to a lack of some power or knowledge, rather than a positive "thing" created by God.</note>, it is enough to be a finite being to be capable of erring. — That it seems, nonetheless, that error is not purely a defect, but the privation of some perfection. — And that it seems impossible that God would have deprived us of any perfection that was due to us. — That this should not cause doubt regarding his existence, as his ends are impenetrable, and there is even a certain rashness in seeking them out. — That, moreover, one must not examine God's works separately to understand their perfection <note>Descartes suggests that something might appear imperfect when viewed in isolation, but perfect when seen as part of the entire universe.</note>. — That our errors depend on the combination of two causes: the understanding <term>entendement</term> and the will <term>volonté</term>. — That there is never, strictly speaking, any error in our understanding. — That our will or free will <term>franc arbitre</term> is the most ample and the most perfect of all our faculties. — In what free will consists; # FOURTH MEDITATION

...possible causes of our errors have been reported above. — And that the means to arrive at the knowledge of truth have been provided there.

I have become so accustomed these past few days to detaching my mind from the senses, and I have so accurately noticed that there are very few things known with certainty regarding bodily things, while there are many more known to us regarding the human mind, and even more still regarding God himself, that it will now be easy for me to turn my thoughts away from the consideration of sensible or imaginable things, to direct them toward those which, being stripped of all matter, are purely intelligible <note>Intelligible things are those understood by the intellect alone, without the need for mental "pictures" or sensory input.</note>.

And certainly, the idea I have of the human mind—insofar as it is a thinking thing, and not extended in length, width, and depth, and participating in nothing that belongs to the body—is incomparably more distinct than the idea of any bodily thing. And when I consider that I doubt—that is, that I am an incomplete and dependent thing—the idea of a complete and independent being—that is, of God—presents itself to my mind with such distinction and clarity. From the mere fact that this idea is found within me, or that I who possess this idea exist, I conclude so evidently that God exists, and that my own existence depends entirely on him at every moment of my life, that I do not think the human mind can know anything with more evidence and certainty. And already I seem to discover a path that will lead us from this contemplation of the true God (in whom all the treasures of science and wisdom are contained) to the knowledge of the other things in the universe.

For, firstly, I recognize that it is impossible that he should ever deceive me, since in all fraud and deception there is found some kind of imperfection; and although it seems that the power to deceive is a mark of subtlety or power, nevertheless the will to deceive undoubtedly testifies to weakness or malice. And, therefore, this cannot be found in God.

Next, I know by my own experience that there is in me a certain faculty of judgment, or of discerning the true from the false, which I have undoubtedly received from God, as well as everything else that is within me and that I possess; and since it is impossible that he would wish to deceive me, it is also certain that he did not give it to me in such a way that I could ever fail when I use it properly.

And there would remain no doubt regarding this, if it did not seem that one could draw this consequence: that I therefore...

# FOURTH MEDITATION

...I can never be deceived; for, if everything in me comes from God, and if he has placed in me no faculty for failing, it seems that I should never be mistaken. It is also true that when I consider myself only as coming from God, and when I turn myself entirely toward him, I discover in myself no cause of error or falsehood. But immediately afterward, returning to myself, experience makes me realize that I am nevertheless subject to an infinity of errors. In seeking their cause, I notice that there is presented to my thought not only a real and positive idea of God—that is, of a sovereignly perfect being—but also, so to speak, a certain negative idea of nothingness <note>original: "néant". This refers to the concept of non-being or the total absence of perfection.</note>, that is, of what is infinitely removed from every kind of perfection. I see that I am like a middle point between God and nothingness, placed between the sovereign being and non-being. Insofar as a sovereign being produced me, there is nothing truly found in me that could lead me into error; but if I consider myself as participating in some way in nothingness or non-being—that is, insofar as I am not myself the sovereign being and that I lack many things—I find myself exposed to an infinity of failings, so that I should not be surprised if I am mistaken.

And thus I recognize that error, as such, is not something real that depends on God, but that it is only a defect; and therefore, to fail, I do not need a faculty that was given to me by God specifically for that purpose. Instead, it happens that I am mistaken because the power God gave me to discern the true from the false is not infinite within me.

However, this does not yet entirely satisfy me, for error is not a pure negation—that is, it is not the simple defect or lack of some perfection that is not owed to me—but it is a privation <note>Descartes uses "privation" to mean the lack of a knowledge or faculty that a human being feels they ought to possess, rather than just something they happen to lack.</note>, or the lack of some knowledge that it seems I ought to have.

Now, considering the nature of God, it does not seem possible that he has placed in me any faculty which is not perfect in its kind, that is, which lacks some perfection due to it. For if it is true that the more expert the craftsman, the more perfect and accomplished are the works that come from his hands, what thing could have been produced by this sovereign creator of the universe that is not perfect and entirely finished in all its parts? And certainly, there is no doubt that God could have created me such that I would never be mistaken; it is also certain that he always wills what is best. Is it, then, a better thing that I should be able to be mistaken than not to be able to be so?

<summary>Descartes explores why humans err despite being created by a perfect God, concluding that we exist as a "middle point" between God's perfect being and the "nothingness" of non-being. He distinguishes between simple ignorance and "privation," questioning why a perfect Creator would allow His handiwork to be capable of error.</summary>

# FOURTH MEDITATION

<margin>II a)</margin> Considering this attentively, the first thought that comes to me is that I should not be astonished if I am unable to understand why God does what he does; and that I must not, for that reason, doubt his existence, just because I perhaps see by experience many other things that exist, even though I cannot understand for what reason or how God made them. For, knowing already that my nature is extremely weak and limited, and that God’s nature, on the contrary, is immense, incomprehensible, and infinite, I no longer have any difficulty in recognizing that there are an infinity of things within his power whose causes surpass the reach of my mind. This reason alone is sufficient to persuade me that the entire class of causes that we are accustomed to derive from a "purpose" <note>original: "de la fin." This refers to "final causes," the Aristotelian idea that we can explain things in nature by their intended goal or purpose. Descartes famously rejected this, arguing we cannot know God's purposes.</note> is of no use in physical or natural things; for it does not seem to me that I could, without rashness, search for and undertake to discover the impenetrable purposes of God.

<margin>b)</margin> Furthermore, it also occurs to me that one should not consider a single creature in isolation when seeking to determine if God’s works are perfect, but rather all creatures together as a whole. For the same thing that might perhaps, with some degree of reason, seem very imperfect if it were alone in the world, remains very perfect when considered as a part of this entire universe. And although, since I formed the design of doubting all things, I have so far only certainly known my own existence and that of God, nevertheless, since I have recognized the infinite power of God, I cannot deny that he has produced many other things—or at least that he could produce them—such that I exist and am placed in the world as a part of the universality of all beings.

<margin>II a)</margin> Following this, when I come to look at myself more closely and consider what my errors are (which alone testify to the imperfection within me), I find that they depend on the cooperation of two causes: namely, the faculty of knowing which is in me, and the faculty of choosing, or my free will; that is to say, from my understanding <note>original: "entendement." The capacity to perceive ideas or concepts.</note> and my will together.

<margin>b)</margin> For through the understanding alone, I neither assert nor deny anything, but I only conceive the ideas of things that I may assert or deny. Now, considering it precisely in this way, one can say that no error is ever found in it, provided that one takes the word "error" in its proper sense. And even though there may be an infinity of things in the world of which I have no idea in my understanding, one cannot say for that reason that it is deprived of these...

<summary>Descartes argues that human error does not imply God is a deceiver, but rather reflects the limits of the human mind compared to God's infinite nature. He introduces the idea that error arises from the interaction between our limited understanding and our unlimited free will.</summary>

...ideas, as something that is owed to its nature, but only that it does not possess them; for indeed, there is no reason that could prove that God ought to have given me a larger and more ample faculty of knowledge than that which he has given me. Regardless of how skillful and learned a craftsman I imagine him to be, I must not think that he was required to put into each of his works all the perfections he is capable of bestowing upon some.

<margin>c)</margin>
I also cannot complain that God has not given me a free will <term>libre arbitre: the capacity to choose between different courses of action without being forced</term> or a will that is sufficiently ample and perfect; for, in fact, I experience it to be so ample and so extended that it is not enclosed within any boundaries. What seems particularly remarkable to me here is that, of all the other things within me, there is none so perfect or so great that I do not clearly recognize it could be even greater and more perfect. For example, if I consider the faculty of conceiving <note>the intellect’s ability to grasp ideas</note> that is in me, I find that it has a very small range and is greatly limited; at the same time, I can form the idea of another faculty that is much more ample, and even infinite. From the mere fact that I can represent this idea to myself, I recognize without difficulty that such an infinite faculty belongs to the nature of God. In the same way, if I examine memory, or imagination, or any other faculty within me, I find none that is not very small and limited, and which in God is not immense and infinite. It is only the will alone, or the sole liberty of free choice, that I experience in me to be so great that I cannot conceive the idea of any other more ample and extended. Thus, it is primarily the will that makes me know that I bear the image and likeness of God <note>Descartes is referencing the Biblical idea from Genesis that humans are created in God's image, identifying this "likeness" specifically as our capacity for free choice</note>. For although the will is incomparably greater in God than in me—whether because of the knowledge and power joined with it (making it firmer and more effective), or because of its object (since it extends to infinitely more things)—it does not, however, seem any greater to me if I consider it formally and precisely in itself.

For the will consists solely in the fact that we can do a thing, or not do it (that is, affirm or deny, pursue or shun a thing); or rather, it consists solely in the fact that, to affirm or deny, pursue or shun the things that the understanding <note>the faculty of the mind that perceives or thinks about objects</note> proposes to us, we act in such a way that we do not feel any external force constraining us. To be free, it is not necessary that I be indifferent toward choosing one of two opposites; rather, the more I lean toward one, whether I know...

He defines freedom not as mere indifference, but as the ability to act without external constraint when the intellect presents a choice.</summary>

# FOURTH MEDITATION

...evidently because the good and the true meet there; and whether God so disposes the interior of my thought, I choose and embrace it all the more freely. Certainly, divine grace and natural knowledge, far from diminishing my liberty, rather increase and strengthen it. Thus, that **indifference** <note>In this context, indifference refers to a state of indecision where the mind lacks enough evidence to lean toward one choice over another.</note> I feel when I am not pulled toward one side rather than another by the weight of any reason is the lowest degree of liberty; it reveals a lack in knowledge rather than a perfection in the **will** <term>volonté: the faculty of the mind that makes choices or decisions</term>. If I always clearly knew what was true and good, I would never be at pains to deliberate what judgment or choice I should make; thus I would be entirely free without ever being indifferent.

From all this, I recognize that neither the power of willing, which I have received from God, is in itself the cause of my errors (for it is very ample and perfect in its kind), nor is the power of understanding or conceiving. Since I conceive nothing except by means of this power that God has given me for conceiving, it is certain that everything I conceive, I conceive correctly, and it is not possible for me to be deceived in that.

Where then do my errors arise? They come from this alone: that since the **will** is much more ample and extended than the **understanding** <term>entendement: the intellect or the capacity to perceive and process information</term>, I do not contain it within the same limits, but instead extend it to things that I do not understand. Because the will is indifferent to these things, it easily goes astray and chooses the false instead of the true, and evil instead of good. This is what causes me to be deceived and to sin.

<margin>x</margin>
For example, when I was examining these past few days whether anything truly existed in the world, and I recognized that from the mere fact that I was examining this question it followed very evidently that I myself existed, I could not prevent myself from judging that a thing I conceived so clearly was true. This was not because I felt forced by any external cause, but only because a great clarity in my understanding was followed by a great inclination in my will; and I was moved to believe this with all the more liberty as I found myself with less indifference.

On the contrary, at present I do not only know that I exist insofar as I am something that thinks, but there also presents itself to my mind a certain idea of corporeal nature. This causes me to doubt whether this thinking nature which is in me—or rather, which I am myself—is different from this corporeal nature, or else...

# FOURTH MEDITATION

...if both are but one and the same thing; and I assume here that I do not yet know any reason that persuades me of one rather than the other. From this, it follows that I am entirely indifferent to denying it, asserting it, or even abstaining from giving any judgment on it.

<margin>x|</margin>
And this **indifference** <note>In Cartesian philosophy, "indifference" is not a lack of interest, but a state where the mind has no clear evidence to tip the scales toward one choice or another.</note> does not extend only to things of which the **understanding** <term>entendement: the intellect or the mind's capacity to perceive ideas</term> has no knowledge, but generally also to all those that it does not discover with perfect clarity at the moment the **will** <term>volonté: the faculty of making choices or decisions</term> deliberates upon them. For however probable the conjectures may be that make me inclined to judge something, the mere knowledge that they are only conjectures, and not certain and indubitable reasons, is enough to give me reason to judge the opposite. I have experienced this sufficiently in recent days, when I set aside as false everything I had previously held to be very true, for the sole reason that I noticed it could be doubted in some way.

Now, if I abstain from giving my judgment on a thing when I do not conceive it with enough clarity and distinction, it is evident that I am doing the right thing and am not deceived. But if I decide to deny or assert it, then I am not making proper use of my **free will**; and if I assert what is not true, it is obvious that I am mistaken. Even if I happen to judge according to the truth, this happens only by chance, and I still fail and make bad use of my free will; for the **natural light** <note>The "natural light" of reason is a central concept for Descartes; it represents the God-given ability to recognize truth through clear and logical intuition.</note> teaches us that the knowledge of the understanding must always precede the determination of the will.

<margin>x x</margin>
And it is in this misuse of free will that we find the **privation** <note>Descartes uses "privation" to describe error as a "lack" or "absence" of correct action, rather than a positive thing created by God.</note> which constitutes the form of error. This privation, I say, is found in the action insofar as it proceeds from me, but it is not found in the faculty I received from God, nor even in the action insofar as it depends on Him.

For I certainly have no reason to complain that God has not given me a more ample intelligence or a more perfect natural light than what He has given me, since it is the nature of a **finite understanding** to not understand many things, and the nature of a created understanding to be finite. On the contrary, I have every reason to give Him thanks that, although He owed me nothing, He nevertheless gave me all the small amount of perfection that is in me; I am far from conceiving such unjust thoughts as to imagine that He has unfairly taken away or withheld from me the other perfections He did not give me.

# FOURTH MEDITATION

I also have no reason to complain that He has given me a **will** <term>volonté: the faculty of choice or free will</term> more ample than my **understanding** <term>entendement: the intellect or capacity for knowledge</term>, since the will consists of only one thing, and is as if indivisible <note>Descartes argues that while knowledge can be gained in degrees, the will is "all or nothing"—you either have the power to choose or you do not.</note>; it seems that its nature is such that nothing could be taken from it without destroying it. Indeed, the more extensive it is, the more I have reason to thank the goodness of Him who gave it to me.

And finally, I must not complain that God cooperates with me in forming the acts of this will—that is, the judgments in which I am mistaken—because those acts are entirely true and absolutely good insofar as they depend on God; there is, in a sense, more perfection in my nature because I can form them than if I could not. As for the **privation** <term>privation: the absence of a quality that should normally be present</term>, in which alone the formal reason for error and sin consists, it does not require any cooperation from God, because it is not a thing or a being. If we relate it to God as its cause, it should not be called "privation," but only **negation** <term>négation: a simple absence or "not-having" of something that is not naturally required</term>, according to the meaning given to these words in **the school** <note>original: "l'école." This refers to **Scholasticism**, the traditional philosophy taught in universities of Descartes' time, which heavily used Aristotelian logic.</note>.

For indeed, it is not an imperfection in God that He has given me the liberty to give my judgment, or not to give it, on certain things of which He has not placed a clear and distinct knowledge in my understanding; but undoubtedly it is an imperfection in me that I do not make good use of this liberty, and that I rashly give my judgment on things that I conceive only with obscurity and confusion.

I see, nonetheless, that it was easy for God to ensure that I never deceived myself, even though I remained free and possessed limited knowledge: namely, if He had given my understanding a clear and distinct intelligence of all the things upon which I would ever deliberate, or even if He had simply engraved so deeply in my memory the resolution never to judge anything without conceiving it clearly and distinctly that I could never forget it. And I well notice that, insofar as I consider myself all alone, as if there were only me in the world, I would have been much more perfect than I am if God had created me such that I never failed. But I cannot for that reason deny that it is in some way a greater perfection in the universe that some of its parts are not exempt from defect while others are, rather than if they were all alike.

And I have no right to complain that God, having placed me in the world, did not wish to place me in the rank of the most noble and most perfect things; indeed, I have reason...

->QUATRIÈME MÉDITATION 107<-

to be content with the fact that, even if He [God] has not granted me the perfection of never erring by the first means I described above—which depends on a clear and evident knowledge of all things I might deliberate upon <note>The "first means" of avoiding error would be to have perfect knowledge of everything, a trait reserved for God.</note>—He has at least left within my power the other means. This means is to hold firmly to the resolution of never pronouncing my **judgment** <term>jugement: the act of the will deciding that something is true or false</term> on things whose truth is not clearly known to me. For although I experience in myself this weakness of being unable to keep my mind continuously fixed on the same thought, I can nonetheless, through attentive and frequently repeated **meditation** <term>méditation: here, a focused intellectual exercise designed to retrain the mind</term>, imprint it so strongly in my memory that I never fail to remember it whenever I have need of it, and in this way acquire the habit of not erring. And insofar as it is in this that the greatest and principal perfection of man consists, I consider myself to have gained no small thing today by this meditation, having discovered the cause of error and falsity.

And certainly there can be no other cause than the one I have just explained: for every time I keep my **will** <term>volonté: the faculty of choice</term> so strictly within the boundaries of my knowledge that it makes no judgment except on things clearly and distinctly represented to it by the **understanding** <term>entendement: the faculty of the mind that perceives ideas</term>, it is impossible for me to be mistaken. This is because every clear and distinct conception is undoubtedly "something," and therefore it cannot take its origin from **nothingness** <term>le néant: non-being or the void</term>, but must necessarily have God as its author—God, I say, who being supremely perfect, cannot be the cause of any error. Consequently, one must conclude that such a conception or judgment is true.

Moreover, I have not only learned today what I must avoid in order to no longer fail, but also what I must do to reach the knowledge of the truth. For certainly I shall reach it if I fix my attention sufficiently on all the things I conceive perfectly, and if I separate them from those others which I conceive only with confusion and obscurity. To this, from now on, I shall take careful heed.

<summary>Descartes concludes that error is avoidable if we resolve to only judge what we clearly and distinctly understand. He argues that since clear perceptions come from a perfect God, they must be true, providing a reliable method for seeking knowledge.</summary>
<keywords>will, understanding, error, judgment, God, truth, clear and distinct ideas, perfection, habit, meditation</keywords>

### FIFTH MEDITATION

-> *Of the essence of material things,* <-

That before examining the existence of material things, it is necessary to consider the ideas we have of them. — That we have a clear and distinct idea of **extension** <term>étendue: the property of taking up space in length, width, and depth, which Descartes considers the defining characteristic of physical matter</term> in length, width, and depth, and of several of its properties. — That we even know very clearly several particulars concerning numbers, figures, movement, etc. — That we have within us the ideas of several things whose nature is true and immutable. — That the ideas of these things have not come to us through the mediation of the senses and that they are necessarily true. — How it follows from this that there is a God. — A reason that seems to prove the contrary. — That this reason is a pure **sophism** <term>sophisme: a fallacious or deceptive argument that sounds plausible</term>. — That since it is impossible to think of God without attributing all sorts of perfections to him, his existence—which one concludes from this—is not a result of a mere supposition. — And that the idea we have of God is not something feigned or imaginary. — That only the things we conceive clearly and distinctly can entirely persuade us. — That there is nothing that is absolutely easier for us to know than God. — That on the certainty of his existence necessarily depends the certainty of other things. — And that otherwise one can have only vague and uncertain knowledge. — Even in the things one believes to be most certain. — But that it is not the same when one has the knowledge of a God. — And that it provides us with a certain means of arriving at the knowledge of an infinity of things.

There remain many other things for me to examine regarding the attributes of God and regarding my own nature, that is to say, that of my mind: but I will perhaps resume that inquiry another time. Now (after having noted what must be done or avoided to arrive at the knowledge of the truth), what I principally have to do is to try to emerge and rid myself of all the doubts into which I have fallen these past days, and to see if nothing certain can be known regarding material things. But before I examine whether such things exist outside of me,

### FIFTH MEDITATION

I must consider their ideas, insofar as they exist in my thought, and see which ones are distinct and which <gloss>are confused</gloss>.

First, I distinctly imagine that quantity which philosophers commonly call <term>continuous quantity</term> <note>original: "quantité continue"; this refers to the concept of space as something that can be infinitely divided and measured, forming the basis of geometry</note>, or rather the extension in length, width, and depth which is found in this quantity, or rather in the thing to which it is attributed. Furthermore, I can count within it several different parts, and attribute to each of these parts all sorts of sizes, shapes, positions, and movements; and finally, I can assign all sorts of durations to each of these movements.

And I do not only know these things with distinction when I consider them thus in general; but also, however little I apply my attention to them, I come to know an infinite number of particulars regarding numbers, figures, movements, and other similar things, whose truth is so evident and accords so well with my nature that, when I begin to discover them, it does not seem to me that I am learning anything new, but rather that I am remembering what I already knew before—that is, that I perceive things which were already in my mind, even though I had not yet turned my thought toward them.

And what I find most remarkable here is that I find within me an infinite number of ideas of certain things which cannot be considered a mere nothing, even though perhaps they have no existence outside of my thought, and which are not invented by me, although it is within my power to think of them or not; instead, they have their own true and immutable natures. As an example, when I imagine a <term>triangle</term> <note>Descartes argues that mathematical objects like triangles have an "essence"—a set of rules that define them—that remains true even if no physical triangle actually exists</note>, even if there were perhaps no such figure anywhere in the world outside of my thought, and never had been, there nonetheless exists a certain nature, or form, or determined essence of this figure, which is immutable and eternal, which I have not invented, and which does not depend in any way on my mind; this is evident because one can demonstrate various properties of this triangle—namely, that its three angles are equal to two right angles, that the greatest angle is supported by the greatest side, and other similar properties. These I now recognize very clearly and very evidently to be in it, whether I want to or not, even though I had not thought of them in any way before when I first imagined a triangle; and therefore it cannot be said that I have feigned or invented them.
