### FIFTH MEDITATION

And I have no need here to object to myself that perhaps this idea of the triangle came to my mind through the medium of my senses, because I have occasionally seen triangular-shaped bodies; for I can form in my mind an infinite number of other figures of which there cannot be the slightest suspicion that they ever fell under the notice of my senses, and yet I am still able to demonstrate various properties regarding their nature, just as I can for the triangle. These properties must certainly all be true, since I conceive them clearly; and therefore they are something, and not a mere nothing: for it is very evident that everything which is true is something, truth being one and the same thing with being; and I have already amply demonstrated above that all things which I know clearly and distinctly are true. And even if I had not demonstrated it, the nature of my mind is such that I could not prevent myself from esteeming them as true, so long as I conceive them clearly and distinctly: and I remember that even when I was still strongly attached to the objects of the senses, I had held among the most constant truths those which I conceived clearly and distinctly regarding figures, numbers, and other things belonging to arithmetic and geometry.

<margin>+</margin> Now, then, if from the mere fact that I can draw the idea of something from my thought, it follows that everything which I recognize clearly and distinctly as belonging to that thing does in fact belong to it, can I not draw from this an argument and a demonstrative proof of the existence of God? It is certain that I find the idea of him within me—that is, the idea of a **supremely perfect being**—no less than I find the idea of any figure or number whatsoever: and I know no less clearly and distinctly that an actual and eternal existence belongs to his nature, than I know that everything I can demonstrate regarding some figure or number belongs truly to the nature of that figure or number; and therefore, even if all that I have concluded in the preceding Meditations were found to be untrue, the existence of God should pass in my mind at least as being as certain as I have hitherto esteemed all mathematical truths which regard only numbers and figures: although, in truth, this may not at first appear entirely manifest, but seems to have some appearance of a **sophism** <note>original: "sophisme"; a clever but false argument, especially one used to deceive.</note>. <summary>Descartes argues that clear mathematical truths are objective "beings" and uses this as a foundation for his Ontological Argument: that existence is a necessary property of a supremely perfect being, just as three sides are necessary to a triangle.</summary>

### FIFTH MEDITATION

...preme being. But nonetheless, when I think about it more carefully, I find clearly that existence can no more be separated from the essence <note>In philosophy, "essence" refers to the fundamental nature or "what-ness" of a thing, defining what it is, while "existence" refers to the fact that it actually is.</note> of God than the magnitude of its three angles being equal to two right angles can be separated from the essence of a straight-lined triangle, or the idea of a valley from the idea of a mountain. Thus, there is no less contradiction in conceiving of a God (that is, a supremely perfect being) who lacks existence (that is, who lacks some perfection) than there is in conceiving of a mountain that has no valley.

But even though I cannot indeed conceive of a God without existence, any more than a mountain without a valley, it does not follow from the mere fact that I conceive a mountain with a valley that there is any mountain in the world. Similarly, even though I conceive of God as existing, it does not seem to follow from this that God exists; for my thought imposes no necessity upon things. Just as it is up to me to imagine a winged horse, even though none actually have wings, so too I might perhaps attribute existence to God, even if no God existed.

Far from it; it is here that a fallacy <note>original: "sophisme," a deceptive or flawed argument that sounds plausible.</note> lies hidden under the appearance of this objection. For from the fact that I cannot conceive of a mountain without a valley, it does not follow that there is any mountain or any valley in the world, but only that the mountain and the valley—whether they exist or not—are inseparable from one another. However, from the mere fact that I cannot conceive of God except as existing, it follows that existence is inseparable from him, and <unclear>therefore that he</unclear> <note>Text damaged; likely "partant qu'il"</note> truly exists. This is not because my thought makes it so, or because it imposes any necessity on things; on the contrary, the necessity of the thing itself—that is, the necessity of God’s existence—compels me to have this thought. For it is not within my power to conceive of a God without existence (that is, a supremely perfect being without a supreme perfection) in the same way that I am free to imagine a horse either with or without wings.

For is there anything in itself more clear and more manifest than to think that there is a God—that is to say, a sovereign and perfect being, in whose idea alone necessary or eternal existence is comprised, and who consequently exists?

And although, to properly conceive this truth, I have needed a great application of mind, nevertheless at present I do not hold myself merely as assured of it as of all that seems most certain to me: but besides that, I remark that the certainty of all other things depends on it so absolutely that without this knowledge it is impossible to ever be able to know anything perfectly.

For even though I am of such a nature that, as soon as I understand something very clearly and very distinctly, I cannot prevent myself from believing it to be true; nevertheless, because I am also of such a nature that I cannot keep my mind continually attached to the same thing, and because I often remember having judged a thing to be true when I cease to consider the reasons that obliged me to judge it so, it can happen during that time that other reasons present themselves to me, which would easily make me change my opinion if I were ignorant that there were a God; and thus I would never have a true and certain <term>science</term> <note>Descartes uses "science" (from the Latin *scientia*) to mean systematic, unshakable knowledge, rather than the modern experimental method.</note> of anything whatsoever, but only vague and inconstant opinions.

### FIFTH MEDITATION

<margin>|</margin>...I am unaware that there is a God: for I could persuade myself that I was so made by nature that I might easily be deceived, even in the things that I believe I understand with the most evidence and certainty; especially seeing as I remember having often regarded many things as true and certain, which afterwards other reasons led me to judge as absolutely false.

But after having recognized that there is a God, because at the same time I also recognized that all things depend on him, and that he is not a deceiver, and that consequently I have judged that everything I conceive clearly and distinctly cannot fail to be true—even if I no longer think of the reasons for which I judged this to be true, provided only that I remember having clearly and distinctly understood it—no contrary reason can be brought against me that would ever make me doubt it, and thus I have a true and certain <term>science</term> <note>original: "science." In the 17th century, this referred to a body of certain, demonstrated knowledge rather than just the "natural sciences" we think of today.</note> of it. 

And this same knowledge extends also to all the other things that I remember having formerly demonstrated, such as the truths of geometry and other similar matters: for what can be objected to me to force me to call them into doubt? Will it be that my nature is such that I am very prone to being mistaken? But I already know that I cannot be mistaken in judgments where I clearly know the reasons. Will it be that I formerly regarded many things as true and certain, which I later recognized to be false? But I had not known any of those things clearly or distinctly, and, not yet knowing this rule by which I assure myself of the truth, I had been led to believe them by reasons that I have since recognized to be less strong than I had then imagined. What further objection can then be made? Will it be that perhaps I am dreaming (as I had myself objected earlier) or indeed that all the thoughts I have now are no truer than the reveries we imagine while asleep? But even if I were dreaming, everything that presents itself to my mind with <term>evidence</term> <note>original: "évidence." For Descartes, "evidence" is a technical term for a truth so clear and distinct that it is impossible for the mind to doubt it while attending to it.</note> is absolutely true.

And to make this very manifest, I first note the difference that exists between **imagination** and **pure intellection**, or conception. For example, when I imagine a triangle, I not only conceive that it is a figure composed of three lines, but along with that, I envision these three lines as present by the power and internal application of my mind; and this is properly what I call "imagining." ### SIXTH MEDITATION

<note>This page begins mid-sentence, continuing a list of reasons why the author previously doubted his senses.</note> second, because not yet knowing—or rather pretending not to know—the author of my being, I saw nothing that could prevent me from having been made by nature in such a way that I was deceived even in those things which seemed most true to me.

And as for the reasons that had previously persuaded me of the truth of sensible things, I did not have much trouble answering them. For since nature seemed to lead me toward many things from which reason turned me away, I did not think I should trust the teachings of this nature very much. And although the ideas I receive through the senses do not depend on my will, I did not think I should conclude from that that they proceeded from things different from myself, since perhaps there may be within me some faculty (although it has been unknown to me until now) which is their cause and which produces them.

But now that I begin to know myself better and to discover more clearly the author of my origin <note>Descartes refers here to God, whom he has proved to be a non-deceiver in the previous Meditations.</note>, I do not think, in truth, that I should rashly admit all the things that the senses seem to teach us, but neither do I think that I should generally call them all into doubt.

And first, because I know that all the things I conceive clearly and distinctly can be produced by God exactly as I conceive them, it is sufficient that I can clearly and distinctly conceive one thing without another to be certain that the one is distinct or different from the other, because they can be set apart, at least by the omnipotence of God; and it does not matter by what power this separation is made for me to be obliged to judge them as different. Therefore, from the very fact that I know with certainty that I exist, and that yet I do not notice that any other thing necessarily belongs to my nature or my essence except that I am a **thinking thing**, I rightly conclude that my essence consists in this alone: that I am a **thinking thing** or a <term>substance</term> <note>In 17th-century philosophy, a "substance" is something that can exist by itself, without needing anything else to exist.</note> whose entire essence or nature is only to think. And although perhaps, or rather certainly (as I will soon say), I have a body to which I am very closely joined, nevertheless, because on the one hand I have a clear and distinct idea of myself insofar as I am only a <term>chose qui pense</term> <note>original: "chose qui pense" (thinking thing). This is the mind.</note> and not <term>étendue</term> <note>original: "étendue" (extended). "Extension" refers to the property of taking up physical space in three dimensions.</note>, and on the other I have a distinct idea of the body insofar as it is only an **extended thing** and which does not think at all, it is certain that I—that is, my soul, by which I am what I am—is entirely and truly distinct from my body and that it can be or exist without it.

Furthermore, I find in myself various <term>thinking faculties</term> <note>These are specific powers of the mind, like imagining or feeling, as opposed to pure reasoning.</note> which each have their own particular way of operating: for example, I find in myself the faculties of <term>imagining</term> and <term>sensing</term>. I can clearly and distinctly conceive of myself as a complete being without these faculties, but I cannot conceive of them without me—that is, without an <term>intelligent substance</term> <note>The mind or soul.</note> to which they are attached or to which they belong. This is because, in the notion we have of these faculties—or, to use the language of the Schools <note>Descartes refers to "Scholasticism," the traditional philosophy taught in universities at the time, which blended Church doctrine with Aristotle's logic.</note>, in their <term>formal concept</term>—they include some kind of <term>intellection</term> <note>The act of the mind understanding something.</note>. From this, I perceive that they are distinct from me in the same way that <term>modes</term> <note>A "mode" is a specific quality or state of a substance, like "roundness" is a mode of a ball.</note> are distinct from the things they belong to.

I also recognize some other faculties, such as the ability to change location, to take on various postures, and other similar movements. These cannot be conceived, any more than the preceding ones, without some substance to which they are attached, nor consequently can they exist without it. But it is very evident that these faculties, if it is true that they exist, must belong to some <term>corporeal substance</term> or <term>extended substance</term> <note>Physical matter, which Descartes defines primarily as something that takes up space (extension).</note>, and not to an intelligent substance; for in our clear and distinct concept of them, some kind of extension is included, but no intelligence or thought at all.

Furthermore, I cannot doubt that there is in me a certain passive faculty of sensing—that is, a power of receiving and recognizing the <term>ideas</term> of sensible things. However, this would be useless to me, and I could not use it in any way, if there were not also—either in me or in something else—another active faculty capable of forming and producing these ideas. Now, this active faculty cannot be in me insofar as I am only a "thinking thing," since it does not presuppose my thought, and also because these ideas are often presented to me without my contributing to them in any way, and even often against my will. Therefore, this faculty must necessarily exist in some substance different from myself. In this other substance, all the reality that exists "objectively" in the ideas produced by this faculty must be contained either <term>formally</term> or <term>eminently</term> <note>Descartes is using a logic of "cause and effect." If I have an idea of a tree, the cause of that idea must either be a physical tree (formal reality) or something even more powerful, like God, who contains the "idea" of a tree in a higher form (eminent reality).</note>, as I have noted previously. This substance is either a <term>body</term>—that is, a corporeal nature in which is contained "formally" everything that is "objectively" represented in these ideas—or it is <term>God</term> himself, or some other <term>creature</term> more noble than a body, in which this same reality is contained "eminently."

   But we also deceive ourselves often enough, even in the things toward which we are directly carried by nature, as happens to the sick when they desire to drink or eat things that can harm them. But certainly, although regarding a dropsical body it is only an external label when we say its nature is corrupted, when without needing to drink it still has a dry and parched throat; nevertheless, regarding the whole composite—that is to say, of the mind, or the soul united to the body—it is not a pure label, but indeed a true error of nature that it feels thirst when it is very harmful for it to drink; and therefore it still remains to be examined how the goodness of God does not prevent the nature of man, taken in this way, from being faulty and deceptive.

To begin this examination, then, I first remark here that there is a great difference between the mind and the body in that the body, by its nature, is always divisible, and the mind is entirely indivisible. For indeed, when I consider it—that is to say, when I consider myself insofar as I am only a **thinking thing** <note>original: "chose qui pense" — Often referred to by the Latin term *res cogitans*, this is the core of Descartes' identity: a being that doubts, understands, affirms, and denies.</note>, I cannot distinguish any parts in myself, but I know and conceive very clearly that I am a thing...

This would be enough to teach me that the mind or the soul of man is entirely different from the body, if I had not already learned it enough elsewhere.

I also notice that the mind does not receive the impression from all parts of the body immediately, but only from the brain, or perhaps even from one of its smallest parts, namely that where the faculty they call the <term>common sense</term> <note>original: "sens commun" — A traditional philosophical term for the place in the brain where all sensory information is gathered and unified. I notice, moreover, that the nature of the body is such that none of its parts can be moved by another part slightly distant from it, without it being able to be moved in the same way by each of the parts between them, even if that more distant part does not act at all. For example, in the cord A B C D, which is pulled tight, if one happens to pull and move the last part D, the first part A will not be moved in any other way than it could also be if one pulled one of the middle parts B or C, and the last part D remained meanwhile immobile. # SIXTH MEDITATION

brain, it can happen that even though the nerve endings in the foot are not moved, but only some of the parts passing through the lower back or the neck, this nevertheless excites the same movements in the brain that would be excited by a wound received in the foot. Consequently, it is necessary for the mind to feel the same pain in the foot as if it had actually been injured there; and we must judge all our other sensory perceptions in the same way.

Finally, I notice that since each of the movements occurring in the part of the brain from which the mind immediately receives an impression causes only a single sensation, one could neither wish for nor imagine anything better than this: that this movement should cause the mind to feel—among all the sensations it is capable of causing—the one most suitable and most usually useful for the preservation of the human body when it is in full health.

Now, experience shows us that all the sensations nature has given us are of this kind; and therefore, nothing is found in them that does not manifest the power and goodness of God.

Thus, for example, when the nerves in the foot are moved forcefully and more than usual, their movement—passing through the <term>spinal cord</term> <note>original: "moelle de l’épine du dos" — literally "the marrow of the spine of the back."</note> to the brain—makes an impression there on the mind, causing it to feel something, namely pain, as if it were in the foot. By this sensation, the mind is warned and spurred to do its best to remove the cause of the pain, as something very dangerous and harmful to the foot.

It is true that God could have established human nature in such a way that this same movement in the brain made the mind feel something else entirely; for example, that it felt the movement itself as it exists in the brain, or in the foot, or in some other place between the foot and the brain, or indeed anything else imaginable. But none of those alternatives would have contributed as effectively to the preservation of the body as the sensation it actually feels.

Similarly, when we need to drink, a certain dryness arises in the throat which moves its nerves, and by their means, the internal parts of the brain; and this movement makes the mind feel the sensation of thirst. This is because, in that situation, nothing is more useful to us than knowing we need to drink to maintain our health; and the same logic applies to our other senses.

From this, it is entirely manifest that, notwithstanding the sov-

->### SIXTH MEDITATION<-

...sovereign goodness of God, human nature—insofar as it is composed of mind and body—cannot help but sometimes be faulty and deceptive. For if there is some cause that excites a movement, not in the foot, but in some part of the nerve stretching from the foot to the brain, or even in the brain itself (the same movement that usually occurs when the foot is injured), then pain will be felt as if it were in the foot, and the sense will naturally be deceived. This is because a single specific movement in the brain can only produce a single specific sensation in the mind. Since this sensation is much more frequently triggered by a cause that hurts the foot than by one located elsewhere, it is far more reasonable that it should always convey to the mind a pain in the foot rather than a pain in any other part. 

And if it happens that sometimes a dry throat does not arise, as it usually does, from the fact that drinking is necessary for the body's health, but from some entirely opposite cause—as happens to those who are <term>hydropical</term> <note>original: "hydropiques" — referring to dropsy, now known as edema, a condition where the body retains excess fluid, yet the patient feels intense thirst.</note>—it is nevertheless much better that it should deceive in that particular instance than if, on the contrary, it always deceived when the body was in good health; and the same applies to the other senses.

And certainly, this consideration is very useful to me, not only for recognizing all the errors to which my nature is subject, but also for avoiding or correcting them more easily. For I know that all my senses usually indicate what is true rather than what is false regarding things that concern the convenience or inconvenience of the body; and I can almost always use several of them to examine the same thing. Beyond that, I can use my memory to connect and join present knowledge with the past, and my <term>understanding</term> <note>original: "entendement" — the faculty of the intellect or reason.</note>, which has already discovered all the causes of my errors. Therefore, I should no longer fear that falsehood will be found in the things most commonly represented to me by my senses.

Indeed, I ought to reject all the doubts of these past days as hyperbolic and ridiculous—particularly that very general uncertainty regarding <term>sleep</term> <note>Descartes refers to his famous "Dream Argument" from the First Meditation, where he questioned if he could distinguish waking life from a dream.</note>, which I could not distinguish from being awake. For I now encounter a very notable difference between the two: our memory can never link and join our dreams with one another, and with the entire course of our lives, in the way it is accustomed to joining the things that happen to us while we are awake. In fact, if someone appeared to me suddenly while I was awake and disappeared in the same way, as do the images I see while sleeping—so that I could not notice where he came from or where he went—it would not be without rea-

<meta>catchword: rea- (reason)</meta>

<summary>Descartes concludes that while the mind-body connection can occasionally lead to sensory deception (like phantom limb pain or the thirst of a sick person), the system is designed by God for the body's survival. He ultimately rejects his previous radical doubt about the reality of the waking world, noting that waking life possesses a memory-based continuity that dreams lack.</summary>

But, because the demands of daily life often oblige us to make decisions before we have had the leisure to examine things so carefully, it must be admitted that human life is frequently subject to error in specific matters; and ultimately, we must acknowledge the infirmity and weakness of our nature.

### FIRST OBJECTIONS

RAISED BY MR. CATERUS, A LEARNED THEOLOGIAN FROM THE NETHERLANDS

->Against the *3rd*, *5th*, and *6th* Meditations.<-

# FIRST OBJECTIONS

...perhaps there was no need for it; for why should I not follow the straightest and least straying path? **I think, therefore I am**, or even, I am the mind itself and the thought itself; now this thought and this mind, either it exists by itself or by another; if by another, then by whom does that other exist? If it exists by itself, then it is God, for that which exists by itself would easily have given itself all things.

I pray this great personage <note>A respectful reference to René Descartes.</note> and conjure him not to hide himself from a reader who is eager to learn and who perhaps is not very intelligent. For this phrase **by self** <note>original: "par soi" or the Latin "per se." This is a crucial distinction in Scholastic logic regarding how something comes to exist.</note> is taken in two ways; in the first, it is taken positively, namely by itself as if by a cause, and thus what would be by itself and would give being to itself, if by a prior and premeditated choice it gave itself what it wanted, it would no doubt give itself all things and therefore it would be God. In the second, this phrase **by self** is taken negatively and is the same thing as **from itself** or **not by another**: and it is in this way (if I remember correctly) that it is understood by everyone.

Now, if something exists by itself, that is to say, not by another, how will you prove for that reason that it comprises everything and that it is infinite? For at present I will not listen to you if you say: since it is by itself, it will have easily given itself all things; especially since it is not by itself as if by a cause and since it was not possible for it, before it existed, to foresee what it could be in order to choose what it would be afterward. I remember having formerly heard <term>Suarez</term> <note>Francisco Suárez (1548–1617) was a Spanish Jesuit philosopher and theologian whose works were standard textbooks in the 17th century.</note> reason in this way: every limitation comes from a cause, for a thing is finite and limited either because the cause could not give it anything greater or more perfect, or because it did not want to: if, therefore, something exists by itself and not by a cause, it is true to say that it is infinite and not limited.

As for me, I do not entirely agree with this reasoning; for let a thing be by itself as much as you please, that is to say, let it not be by another, what could you say if this limitation comes from its internal and constituent principles, that is to say, from its very form and its essence, which nonetheless you have not yet proven to be infinite? Certainly, if you suppose that heat is heat, it will be heat by its internal and constituent principles, and not cold, even if you imagine that it is not by another that it is what it is. I do not doubt that Mr. <term>Descartes</term> <note>René Descartes (1596–1650), the author of the *Meditations on First Philosophy*.</note> does not lack reasons to substitute for what others have perhaps not sufficiently explained nor deduced clearly enough.

Finally, I agree with this great man in what he establishes

as a general rule *that those things we conceive very clearly and very distinctly are all true.* I even believe that everything I think is true, and for a long time now I have renounced all chimeras and all Beings of reason <note>In scholastic philosophy, "Beings of reason" (entia rationis) are things that exist only in the mind, like a mountain made of gold, as opposed to real things.</note>, for no power can turn away from its own object; if the will moves, it tends toward the good; the senses themselves are not mistaken: for sight sees what it sees, the ear hears what it hears, and if one sees tinsel <note>The original French "oripeau" refers to a thin layer of brass or copper that looks like gold.</note>, one indeed sees well: but one is mistaken when one determines by one's judgment that what one sees is gold. To which I also answer in few words: even though it is agreed that the supremely perfect being, by its very name, carries existence with it, nevertheless it does not follow that this same existence is actually something in nature, but only that with the concept or notion of the supremely perfect being, that of existence is inseparably joined. Similarly, even though I clearly and distinctly know the supreme Being, and even though the supremely perfect Being in its essential concept includes existence, it nevertheless does not follow that this existence is actually anything unless you assume that this supreme Being exists; for then, with all its other perfections, it will also actually include that of existence: and thus it must be proven elsewhere that this supremely perfect Being exists.

I will say little regarding the essence of the soul and its real distinction from the body; for I confess that this great spirit <note>Caterus is referring to René Descartes.</note> has already exhausted me so much that I can hardly go on. Here, gentlemen, are the things I had to say regarding what you proposed to me; it is now for you to be the judges. If you rule in my favor, it will not be difficult to persuade Mr. Descartes not to hold any ill will toward me for having contradicted him a little; but if you side with him, I immediately yield and confess myself defeated—and all the more willingly, as I would fear being defeated yet again. # AUTHOR'S REPLIES
## TO THE FIRST OBJECTIONS MADE BY MR. CATERUS
## LEARNED THEOLOGIAN OF THE NETHERLANDS
## Against the *3*<sup>rd</sup>, *5*<sup>th</sup> and *6*<sup>th</sup> *Meditations*.

->**GENTLEMEN,**<-

I confess to you that you have raised against me a powerful adversary, whose spirit and doctrine might have caused me much trouble, had this helpful and devout theologian not preferred to favor the cause of God and that of His weak defender rather than to combat it with open force. But although it was very honorable of him to act in such a manner, I could not exempt myself from blame if I tried to take advantage of it: therefore, my intention here is rather to reveal the artifice he used to assist me than to answer him as an opponent.

He began with a brief deduction of the principal reason I use to prove the existence of God, so that the readers might remember it all the better. Then, having succinctly granted the things he judged to be sufficiently demonstrated, and thus having supported them with his authority, he came to the heart of the difficulty, which is to know what must be understood here by the name *idea* and what cause this idea requires.

Now, I have written somewhere that the *idea* is the thing itself conceived or thought, insofar as it is objectively in the understanding; words which he pretends to understand quite differently than I intended them, in order to give me the opportunity to explain them more clearly. *To be*, he says, *objectively in the understanding, is to terminate the act of the understanding in the manner of an object <note>In Scholastic philosophy, "terminating an act" means being the target or end-point of a mental process.</note>, which is only an external denomination <note>original: "dénomination extérieure" — This refers to a property that is attributed to something because of its relationship to something else, rather than an inherent quality of the thing itself.</note>, and which adds nothing real to the thing, etc.* Here it must be noted that he is considering the thing itself, insofar as it is outside the understanding, in respect to which it is indeed an external denomination that it be objectively in the understanding; but I am speaking of the idea, which is never outside the understanding, and in respect to which being objectively <note>For Descartes, "objective reality" refers to the content of a thought—the thing as it exists in the mind—as opposed to "formal reality," which is the thing as it exists in the physical world.</note> signifies nothing other than being in the understanding in the manner that objects are accustomed to being there. Thus, for example, if someone asks what happens to the sun by the fact that it is objectively in my understanding,

...first: for certainly, from the fact that I cannot understand that, it does not follow that there must be a first one: any more than from the fact that I cannot understand an infinity of divisions in a finite quantity, it follows that one can arrive at a last one, after which this quantity can no longer be divided: but rather it follows only that my understanding, which is finite, cannot comprehend the infinite. # RESPONSES

...ly true when one restricts the meaning of **efficient** to those causes which are distinct from their effects, or which precede them in time. However, it seems that in this question, the term should not be so restricted. This is partly because such a restriction would make the question frivolous—for who does not know that a thing cannot be different from itself, nor precede itself in time?—and also because the **natural light** <term>natural light: the innate human capacity for reason, which Descartes believes allows us to discern truth clearly and distinctly</term> does not dictate that it is the specific nature of an **efficient cause** <term>efficient cause: the primary agent that produces an effect or brings something into being</term> to precede its effect in time. On the contrary, strictly speaking, a cause does not possess the name or the nature of an efficient cause except when it is actually producing its effect, and therefore it does not exist before the effect.

Indeed, the **natural light** dictates that there is nothing for which it is not permissible to ask why it exists, or for which one cannot seek the efficient cause. Or, if it has no such cause, we may ask why it does not need one. Consequently, if I thought that nothing could, in some way, stand in relation to itself as an efficient cause stands to its effect, I would be far from concluding that there is a "first cause." Rather, I would once again seek the cause of that very thing one calls "first," and thus I would never arrive at a primary cause. 

But I frankly admit that there can be something possessing a power so great and inexhaustible that it has never needed any help to exist, and does not need any now to be **preserved**, and which is thus, in a certain way, the **cause of himself**. I conceive of God in this way. For just as—even if I had existed from all eternity and thus nothing had existed before me—I see that the parts of time can be separated from one another, and thus from the fact that I exist now, it does not follow that I must still exist afterward, unless (so to speak) I am created anew at every moment by some cause. I would not hesitate to call the cause that continually creates me in this way—that is, the one who **preserves** me—an *efficient* cause. Thus, even though God has always existed, because it is He himself who in effect preserves His own being, it seems that He may quite properly be spoken of and called the ***cause of himself***. (However, it must be noted that I do not mean here a "preservation" that occurs through any real and positive influence of an efficient cause <note>Descartes is clarifying that God doesn't "act" on Himself like an outside force, but rather His very nature demands existence.</note>, but simply that the **essence** of God is such that it is impossible for Him not to be, or not to exist always).

This being established, it will be easy for me to respond to the distinction regarding the phrase *by itself* <note>original: "par soi"; in philosophical Latin, *per se*</note> that this very learned **theologian**...

### TO THE FIRST OBJECTIONS

...warns me that it must be explained; for even though those who, attaching themselves only to the proper and narrow meaning of **efficient**, think it is impossible for a thing to be the **efficient cause** <term>efficient cause: the primary agent or force that brings something into being or produces an effect</term> of itself, and do not notice here any other kind of cause that has a relation and analogy with the **efficient cause**; even though, I say, those people are not accustomed to understand anything else when they say that something is *of itself* <note>original: "par soi," often rendered in Latin as *per se*</note>, except that it has no cause; nevertheless, if they are willing to focus on the thing itself rather than the words, they will easily recognize that the negative sense of the phrase *of itself* <term>of itself: (Latin: *per se*) in philosophy, this refers to a thing that exists by its own nature rather than being brought into existence by an external cause</term> arises only from the imperfection of the human mind, and that it has no foundation in the things themselves. Instead, there is another positive sense drawn from the truth of things, upon which alone my argument is supported.

For if, for example, someone thinks that a body is *of itself*, he may understand by this nothing other than that this body has no cause. Thus, he does not assert what he thinks through any positive reason, but only in a negative way, because he knows no cause for this body. But this bears witness to some imperfection in his judgment; as he will easily recognize later if he considers that the parts of time do not depend on one another, and that, starting from his assumption that this body has been *of itself* until now—that is, without a cause—it does not follow that it must continue to exist in the future, unless there is in it some real and positive power which, so to speak, produces it continually <note>Descartes famously argued that existence is not a state but a continuous creation; a thing requires a cause to exist at this moment just as much as it did at the first moment of its creation</note>. For then, seeing that in the idea of a body he does not encounter such a power, it will be easy for him to infer from this that this body is not *of itself*; and thus he will take this phrase *of itself* positively. 

Similarly, when we say that God is *of himself*, we can also, in truth, understand this negatively, as meaning that he has no cause. But if we have previously searched for the cause of why he is, or why he does not cease to be, and if, considering the immense and incomprehensible power contained in his idea, we have recognized it as so full and so abundant that, in effect, it is the true cause of why he is and why he continues thus always to be, and that there can be no other cause but that one, we say that God is *of himself*, no longer negatively, but on the contrary, very positively. For even though there is no need to say that he is the **efficient cause** of himself, for fear that perhaps one might enter into a dispute over the word, nevertheless, because we see that what makes him exist *of himself*, or why he has no cause different from himself, does not proceed from nothingness, but from the real and true immensity of his...

<summary>Descartes distinguishes between a "negative" sense of existing "of oneself" (merely lacking a cause) and a "positive" sense (possessing an internal power that sustains existence). He argues that God exists "of himself" in this positive sense, as his infinite power acts as the reason for his continuous being.</summary>

Now, what is signified by a word does not, for that reason, appear to be <margin>3º</margin> true.

But my argument has been this. What we conceive clearly and distinctly to belong to the nature or the essence, or to the immutable and true form of something, can be said or affirmed with truth of that thing; but after we have carefully enough searched for what God is, we conceive clearly and distinctly that it belongs to His true and immutable nature that He exists; therefore, we can then affirm with truth <margin>a</margin> that He exists, or at least the conclusion is legitimate.

But the <term>major premise</term> <note>In a logical argument or syllogism, the "major" is the broad, general rule or principle.</note> also cannot be denied, because we have already agreed previously that everything we understand or <margin>b</margin> conceive clearly and distinctly is true.

But to remove the first part of this difficulty, we must make a distinction between <term>possible existence</term><note>The capacity of a thing to exist; it doesn't have to exist, but there is no logical contradiction in its existing.</note> and <term>necessary existence</term><note>Existence that is part of a thing's very essence; it would be a logical contradiction for such a thing not to exist.</note>, and remark that possible existence is contained in the notion or in the idea of all the things that we conceive clearly and distinctly, but that necessary existence is contained only in the idea of God alone.

For I do not doubt that those who will consider with attention this difference between the idea of God and all other ideas, will perceive very well that, although we never conceive other things except as existing, it does not follow nevertheless from there that they exist, but only that they *can* exist; this is because we do not conceive that it is necessary that actual existence be joined with their other properties. But from the fact that we conceive clearly that actual existence is necessarily and always joined with the attributes of God, it follows necessarily from there that God exists.

Then, to remove the other part of the difficulty, we must take care that the ideas which do not contain true and immutable natures, but only those feigned and composed by the <term>understanding</term><note>The faculty of the mind that perceives or grasps ideas, as opposed to the imagination.</note>, can be divided by the understanding itself—not only by an abstraction or restriction of its thought, but by a clear and distinct operation. For example, when I represent to myself a winged horse, or a lion actually existing, or a triangle inscribed in a square, I easily conceive that I can also, quite on the contrary, represent to myself a horse that has no wings, a lion that is not existing, and a triangle without a square; therefore, these things do not have true and immutable natures. 

But if I represent to myself a triangle or a square (I do not speak here of the lion or the horse, because their natures are not entirely known to us) then certainly all the things that I recognize to be contained in the idea of the triangle—such as its three angles being equal to <note>original: "deux droits"</note> two right angles <note>A classic geometric proof: the interior angles of any triangle always sum to 180 degrees (the equivalent of two 90-degree right angles).</note>, etc.—I will affirm with truth of a triangle; and of a square, I will affirm all that I find to be contained in the idea of the square. For although I can conceive of a triangle while restricting my thought so much that I do not conceive in any way that its three angles are equal to two right angles, I cannot nevertheless deny that property of it by a clear and distinct operation—that is to say, while understanding clearly what I am saying.

<margin>α</margin> But if I consider that in the idea of a very perfect body existence is contained—and this because it is a greater perfection to exist in reality and in the <term>understanding</term><note>The cognitive faculty of the mind; Descartes is referencing a classic philosophical principle that existing in reality is "more perfect" than existing only as a thought.</note> than to exist only in the understanding—I cannot conclude from this that this very perfect body exists, but only that it *can* exist. |

<margin>α</margin> For I recognize well enough that this idea was made by my own understanding, which has joined together all the bodily perfections; and also that existence does not result at all from the other perfections comprised in the nature of the body, because one can equally affirm or deny that they exist—that is to say, conceive of them as existing or non-existing.

<margin>β</margin> And furthermore, because in examining the idea of the body, I see in it no force by which it produces itself or preserves itself, I rightly conclude that <term>necessary existence</term><note>Existence that cannot fail to be; a being that exists by its own nature.</note>, of which alone we are speaking here, belongs as little to the nature of a body (no matter how perfect it may be) as it belongs to the nature of a mountain to have no valley, or to the nature of a triangle to have its three angles greater than two right angles.

<margin>γ</margin> But now, if we ask not about a body, but about a thing (whatever it may be) which has within itself all the perfections that can exist together, and seek to know if existence should be counted among them, it is true that at first we might doubt it; this is because our mind, which is finite, being accustomed to considering these perfections only separately, perhaps will not perceive at first glance how necessarily they are joined together. But if we examine carefully whether existence belongs to the <term>sovereignly powerful being</term><note>A common Cartesian term for God, emphasizing omnipotence as the source of necessary existence.</note>, and what sort of existence, we will be able to clearly and distinctly know: first, that at least *possible* existence belongs to him, as it does to all other things of which we have some distinct idea, even those composed by the fictions of our mind; afterwards, because we cannot think that his existence is possible without at the same time noticing his infinite power, we recognize that he can exist by his own force. From this, we conclude that he really exists, and that he has been from all eternity; for it is very manifest by the <term>natural light</term><note>The innate power of human reason to recognize self-evident truths.</note> that what can exist by its own force, exists.

<summary>Descartes argues that while we can imagine a "perfect body," it does not necessarily exist because it lacks the power to sustain itself. However, the idea of a "sovereignly powerful being" (God) implies existence because infinite power includes the force to exist by its own nature.</summary>

...always; and thus we will know that <term>necessary existence</term><note>The concept that a being must exist by its very nature and cannot be thought of as non-existent.</note> is contained in the idea of a sovereignly powerful being, not by a <term>fiction of the understanding</term><note>Something the mind invents or makes up, like a chimera or a flying horse, as opposed to a truth discovered by reason.</note>, but because it belongs to the true and immutable nature of such a being to exist. And it will be just as easy for us to know that it is impossible for this sovereignly powerful being not to have within itself all the other perfections contained in the idea, so that by their own nature, and without any fiction of the understanding, they are all joined together and exist in God. All of these things are manifest to anyone who thinks about them seriously, and they do not differ at all from what I have already written previously, except only in the way they are explained here, which I have expressly changed to accommodate the diversity of minds. And I will freely confess here that this argument is such that those who do not remember all the things that serve its demonstration will easily mistake it for a <term>sophism</term><note>A clever but false argument intended to deceive.</note>; and this made me doubt at the beginning whether I should use it, for fear of giving those who did not understand it an occasion to also distrust the others. But because there are only two ways by which one can prove that there is a God—namely, one by his effects, and the other by his essence or his very nature—and because I explained the first as much as possible in the **Third Meditation**, I believed that after that I should not omit the other.

Regarding the <term>formal distinction</term><note>A term from medieval philosophy (associated with Duns Scotus) describing a distinction between two properties of the same thing that are different in concept but cannot exist apart from one another.</note> that this very learned theologian <note>Descartes is referring to the author of the First Objections, the Dutch priest Johannes Caterus.</note> says he has taken from <term>Scotus</term><note>John Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), an influential Scholastic philosopher and theologian.</note>, I reply briefly that it does not differ at all from the <term>modal distinction</term><note>A distinction between a thing (a substance) and its "mode" or temporary state (like a body and its movement).</note>, and that it extends only to <term>incomplete beings</term>, which I have carefully distinguished from those which are <term>complete</term>. And in truth, it suffices to make one thing be conceived separately and distinctly from another by an abstraction of the mind which conceives of the thing imperfectly, but not to make two things be conceived as so distinct and separate from one another that we understand that each is a complete being, different from every other; for that, a <term>real distinction</term><note>The strongest form of distinction, where two things (like mind and body) can be clearly understood to exist independently of one another.</note> is necessary. Thus, for example, between the motion and the shape of the same body there is a formal distinction, and I can very well conceive of the motion without the shape, and the shape without the motion, and both without thinking particularly of the body that moves or has shape. But I cannot, nonetheless, fully and perfectly conceive of the motion without some body to which this motion is attached; nor the shape without some body in which this

<summary>Descartes defends his ontological argument for God's existence as a fundamental truth of reason rather than a mental invention. He also distinguishes between "formal" and "real" distinctions, arguing that properties like motion and shape cannot exist independently of a physical body.</summary>

...shape; nor finally can I pretend that motion exists in something in which shape cannot exist, or shape in something incapable of motion. But I fully conceive of what a body is (that is, I conceive of the body as a <term>complete thing</term><note>In Cartesian philosophy, a "complete thing" or substance is something that requires nothing but itself (and God’s concurrence) to exist, possessing a full set of essential attributes.</note>) by thinking only that it is an extended, shaped, and movable thing, etc., even though I deny it all the things that belong to the nature of the mind. And I also conceive that the mind is a complete thing, which doubts, understands, wills, etc., even though I deny that there is in it any of the things contained in the idea of the body. This could not be done at all if there were not a <term>real distinction</term><note>The "real distinction" (distinctio realis) is the metaphysical core of Descartes’ dualism, asserting that mind and matter are two entirely different types of substance.</note> between the body and the mind.

There, gentlemen, is what I have had to say in response to the subtle and obliging objections of your mutual friend. But if I have not been fortunate enough to satisfy him entirely, I pray that I may be informed of those points which deserve a fuller explanation, or perhaps even his censure; for if I can obtain this from him through your mediation, I shall remain infinitely obliged to all of you.

<summary>Descartes argues that the mind and body are distinct substances because each can be clearly and completely conceived without the properties of the other. This marks a concluding point in his reply to the first set of objections regarding his Meditations.</summary>

# SECOND SET OF OBJECTIONS

## COLLECTED BY THE REVEREND FATHER MERSENNE

### FROM THE VOICES OF VARIOUS THEOLOGIANS AND PHILOSOPHERS

### *Against the 2nd, 3rd, 4th, 5th, and 6th Meditations.*

->SIR,<-

Since, in order to confound the new <term>giants of this age</term><note>A rhetorical reference to atheists or skeptics who, like the giants of Greek mythology, were seen as challenging the divine order.</note> who dare to attack the author of all things, you have undertaken to strengthen his throne by demonstrating his existence; and since your design seems so well-conducted that good people may hope that henceforth no one will be found who, after having carefully read your *Meditations*, will not confess that there is an eternal God on whom all things depend; we have judged it appropriate to notify you, and at the same time to request that you shed such light on certain passages which we will mark for you below, that nothing remains in your entire work which is not, if possible, most clearly and most manifestly demonstrated. For inasmuch as you have, through continuous meditation over many years, so exercised your mind that things which seem obscure and uncertain to others may appear clearer to you—and you perhaps conceive them through a simple <term>inspection of the mind</term><note>Descartes uses this term (*mentis inspectio*) to describe a pure intellectual perception, distinct from the use of the senses or imagination.</note> without noticing the obscurity others find in them—it would be good for you to be warned of those points that need more clear and ample explanation and demonstration; and once you have satisfied this, we do not believe there will be anyone who can deny that the reasons you have begun to deduce for the glory of God and the public benefit should be taken as demonstrations.

First, you should remember that it was not in earnest truth, but only by a <term>fiction of the mind</term><note>The objectors are referring to Descartes' "methodological doubt," where he temporarily pretends everything is false to see what remains certain.</note> that you rejected, as much as was possible for you, all phantoms of bodies, to conclude that you are only a thinking thing; for fear that you might perhaps believe afterward that one could conclude that in fact and without fiction you are nothing other than a spirit, or a thinking thing; and this is all we have found worthy of observation concerning your first two Me-

This serves me as a foundation for thinking of any number whatsoever, and thus for adding one degree of perfection to another even unto infinity; just as, even if there were only one degree of heat or light in the world, I could nevertheless add and always imagine new ones even unto infinity. Why likewise might I not add to whatever degree of being I perceive within myself any other degree whatsoever and, from all the degrees capable of being added, form the idea of a perfect being?

Add to this that an atheist knows clearly and distinctly that the three angles of a triangle are equal to two right angles, even though he is nonetheless very far from believing in the existence of God—indeed, he denies it altogether. He does so because, he says, if God existed, there would be a <term>sovereign Being</term><note>A term for the supreme, most perfect existence.</note> and a sovereign good, which is to say, an infinite being; now, that which is infinite in every kind of perfection excludes everything else, whatever it may be—not only every kind of being and good, but also every kind of non-being and evil. In the fourth place, you deny that God can lie or deceive, even though there are <term>Scholastics</term><note>The traditional school of philosophy and theology dominant in European universities since the Middle Ages, which Descartes was seeking to replace.</note> who hold the opposite view, such as <term>Gabriel Ariminensis</term><note>Also known as Gregory of Rimini (c. 1300–1358), a prominent medieval philosopher and theologian.</note>, and some others who think that God lies, absolutely speaking—that is to say, that He signifies something to men contrary to His intention and contrary to what He has decreed and resolved. For instance, when He says to the people of Nineveh through His prophet, without adding any condition:

> *In forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown;* <note>Original: "Encore quarante jours, et Ninive sera subvertie." This refers to the biblical Book of Jonah. Since the city was spared after the people repented, the objectors argue that God's literal statement did not match His ultimate intent.</note>

If He hardened and blinded <term>Pharaoh</term><note>A reference to the Book of Exodus, where God is described as "hardening Pharaoh's heart" so that he would not let the Israelites go.</note>, and if He put a lying spirit in the prophets, how can you say that we cannot be deceived by Him? Could God not behave toward men as a doctor toward his patients, or a father toward his children—both of whom deceive so often, but always with prudence and for a useful purpose? For if God showed us the naked truth, what eye, or rather what mind, would have enough strength to endure it?

Furthermore, to tell the truth, it is not necessary to imagine a deceptive God in order for you to be deceived in the things you think you know clearly and distinctly, since the cause of this deception could be in yourself, even if you do not even think of it. For how do you know if your nature is not such that it is always mistaken, or at least very often? And from where have you learned that, concerning the things you think you know clearly and distinctly, it is certain that you are never deceived, and that you cannot be? For how many times have we seen people who were mistaken...

And therefore, this principle of clear and distinct knowledge must be explained so clearly and so distinctly that henceforth no one of a reasonable mind can be deceived in the things they believe they know clearly and distinctly; otherwise, we do not yet see how we can answer with certainty for the truth of anything.

In the fifth place, if the will can never fail, or does not sin when it follows and allows itself to be led by the clear and distinct lights of the mind that governs it—and if, on the contrary, it puts itself in danger of failing when it pursues and embraces the obscure and confused knowledge of the understanding—take care that it seems one could infer from this that the <term>Turks</term><note>A term commonly used in the 17th century to refer to Muslims or the Ottoman people.</note> and other <term>infidels</term><note>In this historical context, this refers to those who do not believe in the Christian faith.</note> not only do not sin when they do not embrace the Christian and Catholic religion, but even that they sin when they *do* embrace it, since they do not know its truth either clearly or distinctly. Furthermore, if this rule you establish is true, the will will only be permitted to embrace very few things, given that we know almost nothing with that clarity and distinction you require to form a certainty that cannot be subject to any doubt. Take care then, if you please, that in wanting to strengthen the side of truth, you do not prove more than is necessary, and that instead of supporting it, you do not overthrow it.

In the sixth place, in your responses to the previous objections, it seems you have failed to properly draw the conclusion from this argument: *That which we clearly and distinctly understand to belong to the nature, or to the essence, or to the immutable and true form of something, can be said or affirmed with truth of that thing;* but (*after we have carefully observed what God is*) *we clearly and distinctly understand that it belongs to His true and immutable nature that He exists;* the conclusion should be: therefore (after we have sufficiently and carefully observed what God is) we can say or affirm this truth, that it belongs to the nature of God that He exists. From this, it does not follow that God exists in fact, but only that He must exist if His nature is possible, or does not involve a contradiction; that is to say, that the nature or essence of God cannot be conceived without existence, such that if this existence is, He really exists. This relates to that argument which others propose in this manner: if it does not involve a contradiction that God is, it is certain that He exists; now, it does not involve a contradiction that He exists: therefore, etc.

<summary>The objectors argue that Descartes's "clear and distinct" criterion is too vague and could lead to religious skepticism or the justification of non-Christian faiths. They also challenge his proof of God, suggesting he only proves God must exist *if* such a being is possible, rather than proving He *actually* exists.</summary>

But the question lies in the <term>minor premise</term><note>In a formal logical argument (a syllogism), the minor premise is the second statement that links a specific case to a general rule.</note>, namely *that it does not involve a contradiction for Him to exist*, the truth of which some of our adversaries call into doubt, and others deny. Moreover, this clause of your reasoning—*after we have clearly enough recognized or observed what God is*—is assumed to be true, though not everyone agrees on this yet, given that you yourself admit that you only understand the infinite imperfectly. The same must be said of all His other attributes; for since everything in God is entirely infinite, what mind could understand even the smallest thing in God except very imperfectly? How, then, can you have clearly and distinctly enough observed what God is?

In the seventh place, we do not find a single word in your *Meditations* concerning the immortality of the human soul, which you nevertheless ought primarily to have proven, and made a very exact demonstration of it to confound those individuals unworthy of immortality, since they deny it and perhaps even detest it. But besides this, we fear that you have not yet sufficiently proven the distinction between the human soul and the body, as we already noted in the first of our observations. To this, we add that it does not seem to follow from this distinction of the soul from the body that the soul is <term>incorruptible</term><note>That which cannot decay, perish, or be destroyed.</note> or immortal; for who knows if its nature is not limited to the duration of bodily life, and if God has not so measured its powers and existence that it ends along with the body?

These, sir, are the matters upon which we desire you to bring greater light, so that the reading of your very subtle and, as we believe, very true *Meditations* may be profitable to everyone. This is why it would be a very useful thing if, at the end of your solutions, after first putting forward some definitions, postulates, and axioms, you were to conclude the whole according to the <term>method of geometers</term><note>A formal style of writing used by mathematicians like Euclid, which builds a system of truth step-by-step from simple definitions to complex proofs.</note>, in which you are so well-versed, so that your readers might see everything at once, as if in a single glance, to their satisfaction, and that you might fill their minds with the knowledge of the divinity.

<summary>In this concluding section of the Second Objections, critics challenge Descartes' claim to have a clear understanding of an infinite God and point out his failure to prove the immortality of the soul. They conclude by asking him to rewrite his arguments in a formal, geometric style for better clarity.</summary>

# AUTHOR'S RESPONSES

## TO THE SECOND OBJECTIONS COLLECTED FROM SEVERAL THEOLOGIANS AND PHILOSOPHERS, BY THE REVEREND FATHER MERSENNE

->Against the 2nd, 3rd, 4th, 5th, and 6th Meditations.<-

->GENTLEMEN,<-

It is with much satisfaction that I have read the observations you have made on my little treatise on <term>first philosophy</term><note>Also known as metaphysics; the study of the fundamental nature of reality, including the relationship between mind and matter.</note>; for they have made known to me the goodwill you have for me, your piety toward God, and the care you take for the advancement of His glory; and I cannot but rejoice not only that you have judged my reasons worthy of your censure, but also that you put forward nothing against them to which it seems to me I will not be able to respond easily enough.

In the first place, you warn me to remember that *it is not in earnest and in truth, but only by a fiction of the mind, that I have rejected the ideas or the <term>phantoms</term><note>In this context, "phantoms" refers to mental images or sensory perceptions of physical objects.</note> of bodies, to conclude that I am a thinking thing, for fear that perhaps I might consider that it follows from this that I am nothing but a thinking thing.* But I have already shown in my second Meditation that I had remembered it well enough, seeing as I included these words: *But it may also happen that these very things which I suppose to be nothing, because they are unknown to me, are not in fact different from the "me" whom I know: I know nothing of it, I am not disputing that now, etc.;* by which I intended expressly to warn the reader that I was not yet seeking in that place whether the mind was different from the body, but that I was only examining those of its properties of which I can have a clear and certain knowledge. And, insofar as I noted several of them there, I cannot admit without qualification what you add next: *That I do not know, nevertheless, what a <term>thinking thing</term><note>In Latin, "res cogitans." This is Descartes's famous definition of the soul or self as an entity whose essence is the act of thinking.</note> is.* For although I admit that I did not yet know if this thinking thing was at all different from the body, or if it was the same, I do not admit for that reason that I did not know it at all; for who has ever known anything so thoroughly that he knew there was nothing in it except that very thing which he knew? But we think all the better

He argues that he can know the mind's properties clearly even before he determines if the mind is separate from the physical body.</summary>

# RESPONSES TO THE SECOND OBJECTIONS

To know a thing means that there are many specific details within it that we recognize; thus, we have more knowledge of those with whom we converse every day than of those whose name or face alone we know. And yet, we do not judge these strangers to be entirely unknown to us. In this sense, I believe I have sufficiently demonstrated that the <term>mind</term><note>French: *esprit*. In Descartes's philosophy, this refers to the thinking substance or the soul, distinct from the physical body.</note>, considered apart from the things usually attributed to the body, is better known than the body considered without the mind. This is all I intended to prove in that second Meditation.

But I see well what you mean to say: namely, that having written only six meditations regarding <term>first philosophy</term><note>Metaphysics; the study of the fundamental nature of existence and knowledge.</note>, readers will be astonished that in the first two I conclude nothing other than what I have just mentioned. Because of this, they may find them too sterile and unworthy of being published. To this, I respond only that I do not fear that those who have read with judgment the rest of what I have written will have occasion to suspect that I lacked material; rather, it seemed very reasonable to me that things which require particular attention, and which must be considered separately from others, should be placed in separate meditations.

For this reason, knowing nothing more useful for achieving a firm and assured knowledge of things than if, before establishing anything, one were to become accustomed to doubting everything—and principally corporeal things—I could not dispense with giving this subject an entire meditation. This is true even though I had long ago seen several books written by the <term>skeptics and academics</term><note>Descartes refers here to ancient Greek skeptical traditions, such as the followers of Pyrrho or the members of Plato's Academy during its skeptical period, who argued that certain knowledge is impossible.</note> regarding this matter, and though it was not without some distaste that I chewed over such "common food." I would wish that readers would employ not only the little time it takes to read that meditation, but several months, or at least several weeks, in considering the things it treats before moving further; for in doing so, I have no doubt they would benefit much more from reading the rest.

Furthermore, because until now we have had no ideas of things belonging to the mind that were not very confused and mixed with the ideas of sensible things—and because this has been the first and main reason why no one has been able to understand clearly enough anything said of God and the soul—I thought I would achieve no small feat if I showed how one must distinguish the properties or qualities of the mind from the properties or qualities of the body, and how one must recognize them. For although...

# RESPONSES

...it has already been said by many that, to properly conceive of immaterial or metaphysical things, one must distance the mind from the senses; nevertheless, no one, as far as I know, had yet shown the means by which this can be done. Now the true and, in my judgment, the only means for this is contained in my **Second Meditation**; but it is such that it is not enough to have viewed it once; one must examine it often and consider it at length, so that the habit of confusing intellectual things with bodily ones—which has become rooted in us throughout the course of our lives—can be erased by a contrary habit of distinguishing them, acquired through the practice of several days. This seemed to me a sufficiently just cause for not treating any other matter in the second meditation.

You ask here how I demonstrate that the body cannot think: but forgive me if I respond that I have not yet given cause for this question, having only begun to treat it in the **Sixth Meditation** with these words:

> *it is enough that I can clearly and distinctly conceive of one thing without another to be certain that the one is distinct or different from the other, etc.*

And a little later:

> *Although I have a body that is very closely joined to me; nevertheless, because on one hand I have a clear and distinct idea of myself, insofar as I am only a **thinking thing** <term>thinking thing</term><note>original: "chose qui pense" (Latin: *res cogitans*); for Descartes, the fundamental essence of the mind is the act of thinking.</note> and not extended, and on the other, I have a clear and distinct idea of the body, insofar as it is only an **extended thing** <term>extended thing</term><note>original: "chose étendue" (Latin: *res extensa*); for Descartes, the fundamental essence of matter is that it occupies space (extension), having length, width, and depth.</note> and it does not think, it is certain that I—that is to say, my mind or my **soul** <note>original: "âme"; Descartes often uses mind (*esprit*) and soul (*âme*) interchangeably when referring to the thinking substance.</note>, by which I am what I am—is entirely and truly distinct from my body and that it can be or exist without it.*

To which it is easy to add: everything that can think is a mind or is called a mind. But since the body and the mind are <term>really distinct</term><note>A technical term in Cartesian philosophy meaning they are two different "substances" that can exist independently of one another.</note>, no body is a mind. Therefore, no body can think.

And certainly, I see nothing in this that you can deny; for will you deny that it is enough for us to clearly conceive of one thing without another to know that they are really distinct? Give us then some more certain sign of a real distinction, if indeed any can be given. For what will you say? Will it be that those things are really distinct, each of which can exist without the other? But again, I will ask you: how do you know that one thing can exist without another? For, in order for this to be a sign of distinction, it must be known.

Perhaps you will say that the senses make it known to you because you see one thing in the absence of the other, or...

<summary>Descartes explains that his Second Meditation is a mental exercise designed to separate the intellect from the senses, and he argues that the mind and body are distinct substances because they can be clearly and distinctly understood apart from one another.</summary>

# TO THE SECOND OBJECTIONS

...that you touch it, etc. But the faith of the senses is more uncertain than that of the understanding; and it can happen in many ways that one and the same thing appears to our senses under different forms, or in several places or manners, and thus it is taken for two. And finally, if you remember what was said about the **wax** <note>Descartes uses the example of a piece of wax in his *Second Meditation* to show that its sensory qualities (smell, color, shape) change when melted, yet the mind understands it is still the same wax. This proves that we know things through the intellect, not just the senses.</note> at the end of the **Second Meditation**, you will know that even bodies are not properly known by the senses, but by the understanding alone, in such a way that sensing one thing without another is nothing else but having the idea of one thing, and knowing that this idea is not the same as the idea of another: now this cannot be known otherwise than by the fact that one thing is conceived without the other; and this cannot be certainly known if one does not have a **clear and distinct idea** <term>clear and distinct idea</term><note>For Descartes, an idea is "clear" if it is present and apparent to an attentive mind, and "distinct" if it is so precise that it is distinguished from all other objects.</note> of these two things: and thus this sign of **real distinction** <term>real distinction</term><note>original: "réelle distinction"; a technical term for a difference between two "substances" (like mind and matter) that can exist independently of one another.</note> must be reduced to my own criterion in order to be certain.

If there are some who deny that they have distinct ideas of the **mind** and the **body**, I can do nothing else but pray them to consider with enough attention the things contained in that **Second Meditation**, and to notice that the opinion they hold—that parts of the brain work together with the mind to form our thoughts—is based on no positive reason, but only on the fact that they have never experienced being without a body, and that they have often been hindered by it in their operations. This is the same as if someone who, having had irons on his feet since childhood, believed that these irons were a part of his body, and that they were necessary for him to walk.

In the second place, when you say that we find within ourselves a sufficient foundation to form the **idea of God**, you say nothing contrary to my opinion; for I said myself in express terms at the end of the **Third Meditation**: *that this idea was born with me and that it does not come to me from anywhere other than myself.* I also admit that we could form it even if we did not know that there is a **Supreme Being** <term>Supreme Being</term><note>original: "souverain Etre"; referring to God as the highest and most perfect reality.</note>, but not if, in fact, there were no such being; for on the contrary, I have pointed out that the whole force of my argument consists in the fact that it would be impossible for the faculty of forming this idea to be in me if I had not been created by God.

And what you say of flies, plants, etc., proves in no way that some degree of **perfection** can be in an effect that was not previously in its **cause**. For either it is certain that there is no perfection in animals that lack reason which is not also found in inanimate bodies, or if there is...

...some [creature], that it comes to them from elsewhere; and that the sun, rain, and earth are not the total causes of these animals. <note>Descartes is responding to an objection about spontaneous generation—the then-common belief that small animals like flies could be produced by non-living matter like dirt or heat. It does not seem to me either that you prove anything against me by saying that *the idea of God which is in us is only a **being of reason*** <term>being of reason</term><note>original: "être de raison." And I have already sufficiently warned in several places that I was speaking only of the perfection, or **objective reality** <term>objective reality</term><note>original: "réalité objective." This refers to the reality of the "object" as it exists in the mind as an idea. Descartes argues that the "content" of an idea (its objective reality) must come from a cause that has at least as much "actual" reality.</note> of this idea of God, which requires a cause that contains in fact everything that is contained in the idea only objectively (or by representation), no less than the "objective artifice" or represented design in an artisan’s idea of a very complex machine requires a cause.

And certainly, I do not see what could be added to make it more clearly known that this idea cannot be in us if a Supreme Being does not exist; unless the reader, paying closer attention to the things I have already written, frees himself from the prejudices that perhaps obscure his natural light, and accustoms himself to give credence to primary notions (whose knowledge is so true and evident that nothing can be more so) rather than to obscure and false opinions that long usage has deeply engraved in our minds.

For, that there be nothing in an effect that was not in a similar or more excellent way in the cause, is a primary notion, and so evident that there is none clearer; and this other common notion, *that from nothing, nothing is made* <note>original Latin: "ex nihilo nihil fit." This is a fundamental principle of ancient and early modern philosophy.</note>, includes it within itself, because if one grants that there is something in the effect that was not in its [cause...]
