# TO THE SECOND OBJECTIONS

...cause, we must also agree that this proceeds from nothingness; and if it is evident that nothingness cannot be the cause of anything, it is only because in such a cause there would not be the same thing as in the effect.

It is also a **fundamental notion** <term>fundamental notion</term><note>Descartes uses this to describe a "self-evident truth" (Latin: *primis notio*) that the human mind recognizes as true through reason alone, without needing further proof.</note> that all the reality or all the perfection which is only **objectively** <term>objective reality</term><note>In 17th-century philosophy, "objective reality" refers to the reality of an object as it exists as a concept or "object of thought" in the mind, rather than as a physical thing in the world.</note> in ideas must be **formally** or **eminently** <term>formal and eminent reality</term><note>Formal reality refers to a thing actually existing as it is represented (e.g., a real sun). Eminent reality refers to a cause that has a higher or more perfect level of existence than the effect it produces.</note> in their causes; and every opinion we have ever held regarding the existence of things outside our mind is supported by this alone. For from where could the suspicion that they existed come to us, if not from the fact that their ideas came through the senses to strike our mind?

Now, that there is in us some idea of a supremely powerful and perfect Being, and also that the objective reality of this idea is found neither formally nor eminently within ourselves, will become manifest to those who think about it seriously and who are willing to take the trouble to meditate with me: but I cannot force it into the minds of those who read my ***Meditations*** only as a novel, for amusement, and without paying much attention. Now, from all this, one concludes most clearly that God exists. And yet, for the sake of those whose **natural light** <term>natural light</term><note>The innate human capacity for reason and discernment, which Descartes believes is a gift from God.</note> is so weak that they do not see that it is a fundamental notion that all the perfection which is objectively in an idea must be really in one of its causes, I have further demonstrated it in a way that is easier to conceive—by showing that the mind which possesses this idea cannot exist by itself; and therefore, I do not see what more you could desire for your consent, as you have promised.

Nor do I see that you prove anything against me by saying that I perhaps received the idea representing God *from thoughts I had before, from the teachings of books, from the talk and conversations of my friends, etc.*, and not from my mind alone. For my argument will always have the same force if, addressing those from whom it is said I received it, I ask them whether they have it by themselves or from someone else, instead of asking it of myself; and I will always conclude that He from whom it is first derived is God.

As for what you add in that place—that it could be formed from the consideration of **corporeal things** <term>corporeal things</term><note>Material or physical objects that occupy space, as opposed to spiritual or mental entities.</note>—this seems no more likely than if you said that we have no faculty for hearing, but that by the sight of colors alone we arrive at the knowledge of sounds. For one could say there is more analogy or relationship between colors and sounds than between things...

...corporeal things and God; and when you ask that I add something that raises us to the knowledge of the **immaterial or spiritual being** <term>immaterial or spiritual being</term><note>In Descartes's dualism, this refers to substances that do not take up physical space, such as the human soul and God.</note>, I can do no better than to refer you to my **second Meditation** <note>The second of his *Meditations on First Philosophy*, where he famously concludes "I think, therefore I am" (*Cogito, ergo sum*).</note>, so that at the very least you may recognize that it is not entirely useless; for what could I achieve here in one or two sentences, if I could move nothing forward by a long discourse prepared solely for this subject, to which it seems to me I have brought no less industry than to any other writing I have published.

Thus, when you speak here of a **most perfect bodily being**, if you take the name "most perfect" absolutely—so that you understand the body to be a being in which all perfections meet—you are saying things that contradict each other. This is because the nature of the body includes several imperfections; for example, that the body is divisible into parts, that each of its parts is not the other, and other such things; for it is a self-evident thing that it is a greater perfection to be indivisible than to be divisible, etc. But if you mean only that which is most perfect *within the category of bodies*, that is not the true God.

What you add regarding the idea of an **angel** <note>In 17th-century philosophy, angels were frequently used as examples of "finite spirits"—beings that are more perfect than humans but less than God.</note>, which is more perfect than we are—namely, that it is not necessary for it to have been placed in us by an angel—I easily agree with. As for those who deny having the idea of God within them, and who instead of it forge some idol, etc.—those people, I say, deny the name and grant the thing. ### TO THE SECOND OBJECTIONS

...from the fact that he senses within himself that it is impossible for him to think if he does not exist. For it is characteristic of our mind to form general propositions from the knowledge of particular ones. <note>Descartes is clarifying that the "Cogito" (I think, therefore I am) is an immediate internal awareness of one's own existence, which then allows the mind to understand the general principle that "to think, one must exist."</note>

Now, that an **atheist** can clearly know that the three angles of a **triangle** are equal to two right angles, I do not deny; but I maintain only that the **knowledge** <note>original: "connaissance"</note> he has of it is not a true **science**, because any knowledge that can be rendered doubtful should not be called by the name of **science**; and since it is supposed that this person is an atheist, he cannot be certain of not being deceived in things that seem very evident to him, as has already been shown previously; and even though perhaps this doubt does not occur to his mind, it can nevertheless come to him if he examines it, or if it is proposed to him by another; and he will never be beyond the danger of having it, if he does not first acknowledge a **God**. <margin>—|</margin> <note>In the 17th century, "science" referred to "perfect knowledge" that is absolutely certain. Descartes argues that without God as a guarantor of truth, even mathematical proofs could be a trick or a delusion.</note>

And it does not matter if perhaps he believes there are demonstrations to prove that there is no God; for these alleged demonstrations being false, one can always make him recognize their falsity, and then he can be made to change his opinion, which in truth will not be difficult, if for all reasons he brings only those that you allege here—that is to say, that the infinite in every kind of *perfection excludes any other sort of being, etc.* <note>Descartes is addressing a specific objection: the idea that if God is "everything" or "infinite," there would be no room for finite humans or the physical world to exist separately from Him.</note>

For, first of all, if he is asked where he got the idea that this exclusion of all other beings belongs to the nature of the **infinite**, he will have nothing he can answer pertinently: especially since by the name "infinite," we are not accustomed to understand that which excludes the existence of finite things, and he can know nothing of the nature of a thing that he thinks is nothing at all, and consequently has no nature, except what is contained in the single and ordinary meaning of the name of that thing.

Furthermore, of what use would the infinite power of this imaginary infinite be if it could never create anything? And finally, from the fact that we experience having within ourselves some **power of thinking**, we easily conceive that such a power can be in someone else, and even greater than in us: but even though we think that this power increases to infinity, we will not fear for that reason that our own becomes less. It is the same with all the other **attributes of God**, even the power of producing some effects outside of himself, provided that we suppose there is none in us that is not subject to the will of God; and therefore, he can be conceived as entirely infinite without any exclusion of **created things**.

<meta>This page continues Descartes’s response to the Second Objections, where he addresses the theological concern that if God is all-powerful, He might be a deceiver. Descartes argues that God's nature is fundamentally truthful.</meta>

### RESPONSES

In the fourth place. When I say that God cannot lie or be a deceiver, I believe I agree with all the theologians who have ever lived and who will ever live in the future. Everything you argue to the contrary has no more weight than if, after I had denied that God becomes angry or is subject to other passions of the soul, you were to object by citing those passages of Scripture where it seems that some human passions are attributed to Him.

For everyone is well enough acquainted with the distinction between those ways of speaking about God which Scripture commonly uses—which are accommodated to the capacity of the **common people** and contain some truth, but only in how they relate to men—and those ways of speaking which express a simpler and purer truth, one that does not change its nature even when it is not related to men. Everyone must use these latter expressions when philosophizing, and I was primarily obliged to use them in my *Meditations*, seeing as in that context I did not yet suppose that any man was known to me, nor did I consider myself as a composite of body and mind, but as a mind only.

From this it is evident that I did not speak in that place of the lie expressed by words, but only of the internal and <term>formal malice<note>In 17th-century philosophy, "formal" refers to the essential nature of a thing. "Formal malice" here means the inherent intention to do evil or deceive.</note></term> found in deception; although, nevertheless, those words you bring from the prophet—*Yet forty days and Nineveh shall be overthrown*—are not even a verbal lie, but a simple threat whose outcome depended on a condition <note>The condition was whether the people of Nineveh would repent, which they did.</note>. And when it is said that *God hardened Pharaoh’s heart*, or something similar, one must not think that He did this positively, but only negatively—namely, by not giving Pharaoh the <term>efficacious grace<note>A theological term for the divine influence that successfully moves a person's will toward a good action.</note></term> to convert.

I would not, however, wish to condemn those who say that God can utter, through His prophets, some verbal lie—such as those used by physicians when they deceive their patients to cure them—that is to say, a lie exempt from all the malice usually found in deception. But much more often, we see that we are actually deceived by that natural instinct given to us by God, as when a person with <term>dropsy<note>A historical term for edema, a condition where the body retains fluid. It causes intense thirst, though drinking more water can be harmful or even fatal to the sufferer.</note></term> is thirsty; for then he is actually pushed to drink by the nature given to him by God for the preservation of his body, even though this nature deceives him, since drinking must be harmful to him. However, I explained in the *Sixth Meditation* how this can be reconciled with the goodness and truth of God.

# TO THE SECOND OBJECTIONS

But in things that cannot be explained in this way—namely, in our clearest and most exact judgments—if these were false, they could not be corrected by other clearer ones, nor by the help of any other natural faculty. I boldly maintain that we cannot be deceived in these matters. Because God is the Supreme Being, he is also necessarily the supreme good and the supreme truth; consequently, it is contradictory for anything to come from him that <term>positively tends toward falsehood<note>Descartes argues that while we can make mistakes (privation of truth), God cannot be the direct cause of a "positive" or active error in our design.</note></term>. 

But since there can be nothing real in us that has not been given to us by him (as was demonstrated in proving his existence), and since we have within us a real faculty for knowing the true and distinguishing it from the false (as can be proven from the fact alone that we have in us the ideas of truth and falsehood), if this faculty did not lead toward the truth—at least when we use it as we should (that is, when we only give our consent to things we conceive clearly and distinctly, for one cannot imagine another proper use of this faculty)—it would not be without reason that God, who gave it to us, would be considered a deceiver.

And so, you see that after knowing that God exists, it is necessary to imagine that he is a deceiver if we want to cast doubt on the things we conceive clearly and distinctly; and because this cannot even be imagined, we must necessarily admit these things as most true and most certain.

But since I notice here that you are still lingering on the doubts I proposed in my first *Meditation*, and which I thought I had removed quite thoroughly in the following ones, I will explain here once again the foundation upon which it seems to me all human certainty can be supported.

First, as soon as we think we clearly conceive some truth, we are naturally inclined to believe it. And if this belief is so firm that we can never have any reason to doubt what we believe in this way, there is nothing further to seek; we have, regarding that matter, all the certainty that can reasonably be desired.

For what does it matter to us if, perhaps, someone imagines that this very thing—of whose truth we are so strongly persuaded—appears false in the eyes of God or the angels, and that therefore, absolutely speaking, it is false? Why should we trouble ourselves with this <term>absolute falsehood<note>The hypothetical idea that something could be true for humans but false from a "God's-eye view." Descartes dismisses this as irrelevant to human reason.</note></term>, since we do not believe it at all and do not have even the slightest suspicion of it? For we suppose...

...a belief or a conviction so firm that it cannot be shaken; which is, consequently, the same thing as a perfect certainty. But one may well doubt whether we possess any certainty of this nature, or any conviction that is truly firm and immutable.

And indeed, it is manifest that we cannot have such certainty regarding obscure and confused things, no matter how little obscurity or confusion we notice in them; for that obscurity, whatever it may be, is a sufficient cause to make us doubt those things. Nor can we have it regarding things that are perceived only by the senses, regardless of how much clarity there seems to be in their perception. This is because we have often noticed that error can exist in the senses—as when a <term>hydropic<note>Someone suffering from dropsy (edema). Descartes uses this medical example to show that the body’s "clear" signals, like thirst, can be deceptive when the body is ill.</note></term> person feels thirst, or when snow appears yellow to someone with <term>jaundice<note>A medical condition that causes yellowing of the skin and eyes; here used as a classic example of how physical illness can distort sensory perception.</note></term>. For the person with jaundice does not see the snow any less clearly or distinctly than we do when it appears white to us; it follows, then, that if such certainty can be had, it must be only regarding things that the mind conceives clearly and distinctly.

Now, among these things, there are some so clear and so simple that it is impossible for us to think of them without believing them to be true. For example: that I exist when I think, that things which have once been done cannot be undone, and other similar truths of which it is manifest that we have a perfect certainty.

For we cannot doubt these things without thinking about them, but we can never think about them without believing that they are true, as I have just said; therefore, we can only doubt them if we also believe them to be true—which is to say, we can never truly doubt them at all.

And it is of no use to say *that we have often experienced people being mistaken in things they thought they saw more clearly than the sun:* for we have never seen, neither we nor anyone else, that this has happened to those who derived all the clarity of their perception from the <term>intellect<note>In French, "entendement." Descartes uses this to mean the pure faculty of the mind, independent of the physical senses or the imagination.</note></term> alone; rather, it happens to those who have taken it from the senses or from some false prejudice. It is also useless to try to imagine that perhaps these things seem false to God or to angels, because the evidence of our perception will never allow us to listen to anyone who would try to imagine such a thing or who would try to persuade us of it.

There are other things that our intellect also conceives very clearly when we pay close attention to the reasons upon which their knowledge depends, and for that reason, we cannot doubt them at the time; but because we can forget these reasons, and yet remember...

And I reply that those who know God—to the extent that they know it is impossible for the faculty of <term>understanding<note>The intellect or the mind’s ability to perceive ideas.</note></term> given to them by Him to have anything other than the truth as its object—can have such conviction. In the fifth place, I am surprised that you deny that the <term>will<note>The faculty of choice or judgment. Descartes famously argued that error arises when the will extends further than the intellect—that is, when we choose to believe something we do not fully understand.</note></term> puts itself in danger of failing when it pursues and embraces the obscure and confused knowledge of the understanding. For what can make the will certain if that which it follows is not clearly known? And who has there ever been—be it a philosopher, a theologian, or simply a person using their reason—who has not confessed that the danger of failing to which we expose ourselves is lesser the clearer the thing we conceive is before we give our consent to it? Furthermore, those people sin who, without knowledge of the cause, deliver some judgment. Now, no conception is called obscure or confused except because there is something contained within it that is not known.

Therefore, what you object regarding the <term>faith<note>Religious belief or dogma.</note></term> that one must embrace has no more force against me than against all those who have ever cultivated human reason; and, to tell the truth, it has no force against anyone. For even though it is said that faith has obscure things as its object, nevertheless, the reason *why* we believe them is not obscure; rather, it is clearer than any <term>natural light<note>The "lumière naturelle" is the innate human capacity for reason and logic, which Descartes believes is a gift from God.</note></term>. This is because we must distinguish between the "matter"—or the thing to which we give our belief—and the "formal reason" that moves our will to give it. It is in this formal reason alone that we require there to be clarity and evidence. As for the matter, no one has ever denied that it can be obscure, or even obscurity itself; for when I judge that obscurity must be removed from our thoughts so that we may give them our consent without any danger of failing, it is that very obscurity that serves as my matter for forming a clear and distinct judgment.

Besides this, it must be noted that the clarity or evidence by which our will can be moved to believe is of two kinds: one that proceeds from the natural light, and the other that comes from divine grace.

...are not yet distinctly enough known. But the major premise of my argument was as follows:

That which we clearly and distinctly conceive to belong to the nature of something, that can be ***said*** or ***affirmed with truth of that thing***. That is to say, if being an animal belongs to the <term>essence<note>The "what-ness" or defining characteristics of a thing.</note></term> or to the nature of man, one can assert that man is an animal; if having three angles equal to two right angles belongs to the nature of a rectilinear triangle, one can assert that the rectilinear triangle has its three angles equal to two right angles; if existing belongs to the nature of God, one can assert that God exists, ***etc.*** And the <term>minor premise<note>The second, specific statement of a logical argument that links a particular case to the general rule.</note></term> was this: ***now it is the case that it belongs to the nature of God to exist***; from which it is evident that one must conclude as I have done—namely, ***therefore one can with truth assert of God that he exists***—and not as you wish: ***Therefore we can assert with truth that it belongs to the nature of God to exist***.

And therefore, to use the exception that you subsequently bring forward, you would have had to deny the major premise and say that what we clearly and distinctly conceive to belong to the nature of something cannot, for that reason, be ***said*** or ***affirmed*** of that thing, unless its nature is possible or does not involve a contradiction. But see, I pray you, the weakness of this exception: for either by this word "possible" you mean, as is usually done, everything that does not conflict with human thought—in which sense it is manifest that the nature of God, in the way I have described it, is possible, because I have supposed nothing in it except what we clearly and distinctly conceive must belong to it; and thus I have supposed nothing that conflicts with human thought or the human <term>concept<note>The mental representation or idea we have of a thing.</note></term>—or else you feign some other possibility on the part of the object itself,

# REPLIES

...which, if it does not agree with the preceding one, can never be known by the human understanding, and therefore, it has no more force to compel us to deny the nature of God or his existence than to destroy all the other things that fall under human knowledge. For, by the same reason that one denies that the nature of God is possible—even though no impossibility is encountered on the part of the concept or the thought, but on the contrary, all the things contained in this concept of the divine nature are so connected among themselves that it seems to us contradictory to say that there is any which does not belong to the nature of God—one could also deny that it is possible that the three angles of a triangle are equal to two right angles, or that he who is currently thinking exists; and for a much stronger reason could one deny that there is anything true of all the things we perceive through the senses, and thus all human knowledge will be overturned without any reason or foundation.

And as for this argument that you compare with mine, namely: *if it does not imply a contradiction that God exists, it is certain that he exists; but it does not imply one: therefore, etc.*, <note>Descartes is analyzing a specific syllogism provided by his objectors to see if it holds the same weight as his own argument.</note> materially speaking it is true, but formally it is a <term>sophism<note>An argument that seems correct but is actually logically flawed or deceptive.</note></term>. For, in the <term>major premise<note>The first part of a syllogism, containing a general statement.</note></term>, this word *it implies* <note>original: *il implique*, which in this context means "implies a contradiction."</note> concerns the concept of the cause by which God can be, and in the <term>minor premise<note>The second part of a syllogism, which offers a specific instance or condition.</note></term>, it concerns the sole concept of the existence and nature of God, as it appears from the fact that if one denies the major premise, it will have to be proved thus:

If God does not yet exist, it implies a contradiction that he exists because one could not assign a <term>sufficient cause<note>A principle in philosophy stating that nothing can exist or happen without a reason or cause enough to explain it.</note></term> to produce him; but it does not imply that he exists, as was granted in the minor premise; therefore, etc.

And if one denies the minor premise, it must be proved thus: that thing does not imply a contradiction in whose formal concept there is nothing containing a contradiction; but in the formal concept of the existence or the divine nature, there is nothing that contains a contradiction; therefore, etc. And thus this word *it implies* is taken in two different senses.

For it may be that one conceives nothing in the thing itself that prevents it from being able to exist, and yet one conceives something on the part of its cause which prevents it from being produced. <note>Descartes distinguishes between "internal possibility" (is the idea logically consistent?) and "external possibility" (is there a cause that can bring it into being?). For God, who is uncaused, these two must coincide.</note>

Now, even though we conceive God only very imperfectly, that does not prevent it from being certain that his nature is possible, or that it does not imply a contradiction.

Nor also that we cannot affirm with truth that we have examined it carefully enough, and clearly enough—

# REPLIES TO THE SECOND OBJECTIONS

...is sufficiently known (namely, as much as is enough to know that it is possible, and also that **necessary existence** belongs to it); for all impossibility, or if I may be permitted here to use the word of the school, all <term>implication<note>original: *implicance*. In Scholastic philosophy, this refers to a logical contradiction—where one part of a concept "implies" the negation of another part.</note></term> consists only in our concept, or thought, which cannot join ideas that contradict each other. It cannot consist in anything that is outside the **understanding**, because the very fact that a thing exists outside the understanding makes it manifest that it implies no contradiction, but is possible.

Now, the impossibility that we find in our thoughts comes only from the fact that they are obscure and confused, and there can be none in those that are clear and distinct. Therefore, so that we may be certain that we know the **nature of God** enough to know that there is no <note>In this context, "repugnance" means a logical incompatibility or contradiction.</note> repugnance in His existence, it is enough that we clearly and distinctly understand all the things we perceive to be in Him—even though these things are few in number compared to those we do not perceive (which are also in Him)—and that we notice that **necessary existence** is one of the things we thus perceive to be in God.

**In the seventh place.** I have already given the reason in the synopsis of my *Meditations* why I said nothing here concerning the **immortality of the soul**; I have also shown previously how I have sufficiently proven the distinction that exists between the **mind** and every kind of **body**.

As for what you add—that from the distinction of the soul from the body it does not follow that it is immortal, because, notwithstanding this, one could say that God made it of such a nature that its duration ends with that of the life of the body—I confess that I have nothing to answer; for I do not have so much presumption as to undertake to determine by the force of human reasoning a thing that depends only on the pure **will of God**.

Natural knowledge teaches us that the **mind** is different from the body, and that it is a **substance**, and also that the human body, insofar as it differs from other bodies, is only composed of a certain configuration of members and other similar <term>accidents<note>Non-essential properties or characteristics (like shape or size) that can change without the thing itself being destroyed.</note></term>. Finally, it teaches us that the death of the body depends only on some division or change of shape. Now, we have no argument nor any example that persuades us that the death or the annihilation of a substance such as the mind must follow from so slight a cause as a change of shape—which is nothing other than a <term>mode<note>A "mode" is a specific way in which a substance exists or is modified (for example, "squareness" is a mode of a physical body).</note></term>, and furthermore a mode not of the mind, but of the body, which is really distinct from the mind.

# REPLIES

And indeed, we have no argument or example that can persuade us that there are <term>substances<note>In Cartesian philosophy, a "substance" is a thing that requires nothing but itself (or God) in order to exist. Here, Descartes refers to the mind/soul as a thinking substance distinct from the body.</note></term> which are subject to being annihilated. And since He has now revealed to us that this will not happen, no doubt should remain for us regarding this.

Furthermore, I have much to thank you for because you deigned so obligingly, and with such frankness, to warn me not only of things that seemed worthy of explanation to you, but also of the difficulties that could be raised against me by atheists, or by some envious and slanderous people.

For even though I see nothing among the things you proposed that I had not previously rejected or explained in my *Meditations*—such as, for example, what you alleged regarding **flies produced by the sun**<note>Descartes is referring to the then-common belief in "spontaneous generation," the idea that life (like flies) could arise from non-living matter through the heat of the sun.</note>, the **Canadians, the Ninevites, the Turks**<note>These were common 17th-century examples used to discuss people living outside of Christian revelation or in different cultural contexts, often raised to challenge the idea of an innate, universal idea of God.</note>, and other similar things (which cannot enter the minds of those who, following the order of these *Meditations*, set aside for some time all things learned from the senses to take part in what pure and healthy reason dictates; which is why I thought I had already rejected all these things)—nevertheless, even though this is so, I judge that these objections will be very useful to my design. This is especially so because I do not expect to have many readers willing to bring so much attention to the things I have written that, having reached the end, they remember everything they read before; and those who do not do so will easily fall into difficulties for which they will later see I have provided satisfaction in this response, or at least they will take the opportunity from there to examine the truth more carefully.

Regarding the advice you give me to arrange my reasons according to the method of the **geometers**, so that readers can understand them all at once, I will tell you here in what way I have already tried to follow it before, and how I will try again hereafter.

In the way of writing of geometers I distinguish two things: namely, the **order** and the **manner of demonstrating**.

The **order** consists only in this: that the things proposed first must be known without the help of those that follow, and those that follow must then be dis-

<meta>This page continues Descartes’s explanation of his writing method. He justifies why certain topics, like the distinction between mind and body, were deferred to later sections of his Meditations to ensure a logical progression where each point builds upon the last.</meta>

<page-num>181</page-num>
<header>TO THE SECOND OBJECTIONS</header>

...[dispo]sed in such a way that they are demonstrated by the things that precede them alone; and certainly, I have tried as much as I could to follow this order in my *Meditations*. And this is what led me not to treat the distinction between the mind and the body in the second [Meditation], but only in the sixth, and why I deliberately omitted many things throughout this entire treatise, because they presupposed the explanation of several others.

The manner of demonstrating is twofold: one proceeds by <term>analysis<note>In the 17th century, "analysis" (or "resolution") referred to the method of discovery, where one starts from the result or a specific problem and works backward to find the underlying principles or causes.</note></term> or resolution, and the other by <term>synthesis<note>"Synthesis" (or "composition") is the method of formal proof, starting from established definitions and axioms to reach a conclusion, much like a textbook in geometry.</note></term> or composition.

Analysis shows the true path by which a thing was methodically discovered, and makes it clear how effects depend on causes; so that if the reader is willing to follow it and cast their eyes carefully over everything it contains, they will understand the thing thus demonstrated no less perfectly, and make it no less their own, than if they had discovered it themselves.

But this kind of demonstration is not suited to convince stubborn or inattentive readers: for if one allows even the smallest detail it proposes to escape without notice, the necessity of its conclusions will not appear; and it is not the custom to express very amply the things that are clear enough in themselves, even though these are usually the ones that require the most careful attention.

Synthesis, on the contrary, by a completely different path and as if by examining causes by their effects (even though the proof it contains is often also of effects by their causes), truly demonstrates clearly what is contained in its conclusions. It uses a long series of definitions, requests, axioms, theorems, and problems, so that if any consequence is denied, it shows how they are contained in the antecedents, and it wrenches consent from the reader, however obstinate and stubborn they may be. But it does not give, as the other does, complete satisfaction to the minds of those who desire to learn, because it does not teach the method by which the thing was discovered.

The ancient <term>geometers<note>Descartes is referring to classical Greek mathematicians like Euclid or Archimedes. He suggests they kept their "analytical" methods of discovery secret to make their final "synthetic" proofs seem more impressive.</note></term> were accustomed to using only this synthesis in their writings, not because they were entirely ignorant of analysis, but, in my opinion, because they set such a high value on it that they reserved it for themselves alone, as an important secret.

For my part, I have followed only the analytical path in my *Meditations*, because it seems to me to be the truest and the most appropriate for teaching; but as for synthesis,

<summary>Descartes distinguishes between "analysis" (the method of discovery) and "synthesis" (the method of formal proof). He explains that he chose the analytical method for his Meditations because it allows the reader to truly understand and "own" the knowledge, rather than just being forced to agree with a technical argument.</summary>

attention. For by the very fact that someone prepares themselves to
impugn the truth, they make themselves less fit to understand it,
insofar as they turn their mind away from considering the
reasons that persuade them of it, in order to apply it to the search
for those that destroy it.

### FIRST OBJECTION.

It appears clearly enough from what has been said in this Meditation that there is no certain and evident mark by which we can recognize and distinguish our dreams from our waking state and from a true perception of the senses; and consequently that these images or these phantasms <note>original: "fantômes" — in 17th-century philosophy, this term referred to mental images or sensory appearances rather than supernatural spirits.</note> that we feel while awake (no more and no less than those we perceive while asleep) are not qualities attached to external objects, and are not sufficient proof to show that these external objects truly exist. Therefore, if we follow only the testimony of our senses without the help of any other reasoning, we will have just cause to doubt whether anything exists or not. 

We therefore recognize the truth of this Meditation. But since Plato spoke of this uncertainty regarding sensible things <note>Things perceived through the five senses.</note>, as did several other ancient philosophers before and after him, and since it is easy to notice the difficulty of discerning being awake from sleep, I would have wished that this excellent author of new speculations <note>Hobbes is being somewhat dismissive here, suggesting Descartes is trying to present old ideas as "new theories."</note> had abstained from publishing such old things.

### SECOND OBJECTION TO THE SECOND MEDITATION.

#### *On the nature of the human mind.*

I am a thinking thing; that is very well said. For from the fact that *I think*, or that I have an idea, whether waking or sleeping, one infers that *I am thinking*: for these two things, *I think* and *I am thinking*, mean the same thing. From the fact that *I am thinking*, it follows that *I am*, because that which thinks is not a nothing. But where our author adds, "that is to say, a mind, a soul, an understanding, a reason": from there a doubt arises. For this reasoning does not seem to me well-deduced to say *I am thinking, therefore, I am a thought*, or indeed, *I am intelligent, therefore, I am an understanding*. For in the same way I could say, *I am walking, therefore I am a walk*. <note>Hobbes is using a "reductio ad absurdum" here to argue that just because you are performing an action (thinking), it doesn't mean you *are* the faculty itself (the mind).</note>

Mr. Descartes therefore takes the intelligent thing and the intellection <term>intellection<gloss>the act or process of the mind understanding something</gloss></term>, which is its act, for the same thing; or at least he says that the thing which understands is the same as the understanding, which is a power or faculty of an intelligent thing. Nevertheless, all philosophers distinguish the subject from its faculties and its acts, that is to say, from its properties and its essences <note>original: "essences" — the fundamental nature of what a thing is.</note>; for the thing itself that exists is one thing, and its essence is another; it could therefore be that a thing that thinks is the subject of the mind, reason, or understanding, and consequently that it is something <term>corporeal<gloss>physical or material; having a body</gloss></term>, the contrary of which is assumed or put forward, but is not proved. And yet it is in this that the foundation of the conclusion lies, which it seems Mr. Descartes wishes to establish.

In the same place he says: *I know that I exist, and I seek what I am, I whom I know to be.* Now, it is very certain...

<header>AND RESPONSES</header>

...that this notion and knowledge of myself, taken so precisely, does not depend at all on things whose existence is not yet known to me.

It is very certain that the knowledge of this proposition, *I exist*, depends on this one: *I think*, as he has very well taught us; but from where does our knowledge of this one—*I think*—come? Certainly, it comes from nothing other than the fact that we cannot conceive of any act without its subject, such as thought without a thing that thinks, knowledge without a thing that knows, and walking without a thing that walks.

And from this, it seems to follow that a thing that thinks is something corporeal; for the subjects of all acts seem to be understood only under a corporeal nature, or under the nature of matter, as he himself showed a little later by the example of the wax. This wax, although its color, its hardness, its shape, and all its other "acts" <note>In 17th-century philosophy, "acts" or "accidents" refer to the changing qualities or behaviors of a substance, rather than the substance itself.</note> are changed, is always conceived to be the same thing—that is to say, the same matter subject to all these changes. Now, it is not through another thought that I infer that I think: for although someone can think that they have thought (which is nothing more than a memory), nevertheless it is quite impossible to think that one thinks, or to know that one knows: for this would be an interrogation that would never end: "how do you know that you know that you know that you know," etc.

And therefore, since the knowledge of this proposition, *I exist*, depends on the knowledge of this one, *I think*, and the knowledge of this latter depends on the fact that we cannot separate thought from a matter that thinks, it seems that one should rather infer that a thinking thing is material rather than immaterial.

---

RESPONSE.

Where I said, "that is to say, a *mind*, a *soul*, an *understanding*, a *reason*, etc.," I did not mean by these names the faculties alone, but the things endowed with the faculty of thinking, as one is accustomed to understand by the first two, and often enough by the last two as well. This is something I have explained so often, and in such express terms, that I do not see that there was any reason to doubt it.

And there is no relationship or correspondence here between walking and thinking, because walking is never understood as anything other than the action itself; but thought is sometimes taken for the action, sometimes for <note>Descartes is beginning to explain that "thought" can refer to the mental activity itself or the underlying substance that performs it, a distinction he claims does not apply to physical actions like walking.</note>

And I do not fear that his method—which is to join several things together in this way—will be found more suitable for reaching the knowledge of the truth than mine, by which I distinguish each thing as much as I can. But let us dwell no longer on words; let us come to the matter in question.

*It may be,* he says, *that a thing that thinks is something corporeal; the contrary of this is assumed or asserted, but is not proved.* On the contrary, I have not asserted the opposite at all, nor did I use it in any way as a foundation; rather, I left it entirely undetermined until the Sixth Meditation, in which it is finally proved.

Afterwards, he says quite correctly that we cannot conceive of any act without its subject, such as a thought without a thing that thinks, because the thing that thinks is not "nothing." But it is without any reason, and against all good logic—and even against the ordinary way of speaking—that he adds that from this it seems to follow that a thing that thinks is something corporeal. For while the subjects of all acts are indeed understood as being substances (or if you prefer, as <term>matters<note>In the philosophical language of the time, "matter" could mean "the subject of a discussion" or "the underlying substance," not just physical material.</note></term>, namely metaphysical matters), it does not follow from this that they are bodies. On the contrary, all logicians, and almost everyone with them, are accustomed to saying that among substances, some are spiritual and others are corporeal. I also did not speak in that passage about the formal nature of the mind, nor even that of the body.

# AND REPLIES

...that a thought cannot be the subject of another thought. For who has ever suggested such a thing but him? But I will attempt here to explain in a few words the entire matter in question.

It is certain that thought cannot exist without a thing that thinks, and in general, no <term>accident<note>In 17th-century philosophy, an "accident" is a quality or property (like color or shape) that cannot exist on its own but must belong to a "substance."</note></term> or any act can exist without a <term>substance<note>The underlying "thing" or "stuff" that possesses properties. For example, a chair is the substance, and "being red" is the accident.</note></term> of which it is the act. But since we do not know the substance immediately by itself, but only because it is the subject of certain acts, it is quite fitting to reason—and even common usage requires it—that we call by different names those substances which we know to be the subjects of several entirely different acts or accidents. After doing so, we should examine whether these different names signify different things, or one and the same thing.

Now, there are certain acts that we call *corporeal*, such as size, shape, motion, and all other things that cannot be conceived without <term>local extension<note>The property of taking up physical space in a specific location.</note></term>; and we call the substance in which they reside by the name *body*. One cannot imagine that there is one substance that is the subject of shape, and another that is the subject of local motion, etc., because all these acts agree with one another in that they presuppose extension. Following this, there are other acts that we call *intellectual*, such as understanding, willing, imagining, sensing, etc., all of which agree with one another in that they cannot exist without thought, or perception, or consciousness and knowledge. The substance in which they reside we name *a thinking thing*, or a *mind*, or any other name we please, provided that we do not confuse it with corporeal substance; this is because intellectual acts have no affinity with corporeal acts, and thought—which is the common reason in which they agree—differs totally from extension, which is the common reason of the others.

But after we have formed two clear and distinct concepts of these two substances, it is easy to know, by what was said in the <term>Sixth Meditation<note>The final part of Descartes's "Meditations on First Philosophy," where he argues that the mind and body are distinct and can exist without each other.</note></term>, whether they are but one same thing, or whether they are two different things.

...is nonetheless distinct from me: in the same way that walking (as was said above) is distinct from the person who walks. ### REPLY.

I do not deny that I, who think, am distinct from my thought, in the same way that a thing is distinct from its <term>mode<note>In 17th-century philosophy, a "mode" is a specific state or "way" of being. For example, "roundness" is a mode of a ball.</note></term>. But when I ask "what is there, then, that is distinct from my thought?" I am referring to the various ways of thinking listed there, and not to my <term>substance<note>The underlying "thing" that possesses qualities or performs actions. Descartes argues the "self" is a thinking substance.</note></term>. And when I add, "what is there that one can say is separate from myself?" I mean only that all these ways of thinking within me cannot exist outside of me. I do not see that there is any room for doubt here, nor why I am blamed for obscurity.

### FOURTH OBJECTION.

*I must therefore agree that I cannot even understand through my imagination what this piece of wax is, and that only my understanding alone understands it.*

There is a great difference between *imagining*—that is, having some mental image—and *conceiving* through the understanding—that is, concluding by reasoning that something is or exists. However, Mr. Descartes has not explained the difference to us. The ancient <term>Peripatetics<note>Followers of Aristotle. Their philosophy was the standard "old guard" that Descartes was trying to replace.</note></term> also taught quite clearly that substance is not perceived by the senses, but is gathered through reason.

What shall we say now if, perhaps, reasoning is nothing more than the assembling and linking of names by the word *is*? From this, it would follow that through reason we conclude nothing at all regarding the nature of things, but only regarding their titles. That is to say, we simply see whether we join the names of things correctly or incorrectly, according to the conventions we have made by our own whims regarding their meanings. If this is indeed the case, as it may well be, reasoning will depend on names, and names on the imagina-

### REPLY.

I explained in the second Meditation the difference between the **imagination** and the **pure concept of the understanding** or the mind. I did this using the <term>example of the wax<note>Descartes famously described how a piece of wax changes all its sensory qualities (smell, color, shape) when melted, yet we still know it is the same wax. He argued this knowledge comes from the mind, not the senses.</note></term>, where I showed which things we imagine about it and which things we conceive through the understanding alone. Elsewhere, I have also explained how we understand a thing differently than we imagine it. For instance, to imagine a **pentagon**, a specific mental effort is required to make that figure (the five sides and the space they enclose) present to us as if it were before our eyes; however, we do not need this effort simply to conceive of it. Now, the connection made during reasoning is not a connection of names, but rather a connection of the things signified by those names; I am surprised that the contrary could even occur to anyone.

For who doubts that a Frenchman and a German can have the same thoughts or reasoning regarding the same things, even though they conceive of entirely different words? And does this philosopher not condemn himself when he speaks of the "conventions" we have made according to our own <term>fancy<note>Or "imagination." Descartes is pointing out that if words were just arbitrary sounds with no underlying meaning, communication would be impossible.</note></term> regarding the meaning of words? If he admits that something is signified by words, why does he not want our discourse and reasoning to be about the *thing* signified rather than the words alone? Certainly, with the same logic and reason that he concludes the mind is a "movement," he could also conclude that the earth is the heavens, or anything else he pleases. This is because there are no two things in the world between which there is as little similarity as there is between movement and the mind, which belong to two entirely different categories.

<meta>This page continues the "Third Objections" to René Descartes’s *Meditations on First Philosophy*. While the previous page featured Descartes defending his view that the mind is distinct from the body, we now return to the objections raised by the English philosopher Thomas Hobbes. Hobbes is arguing against Descartes's definition of an "idea." For Hobbes, an idea is strictly a mental image derived from the senses, which leads him to claim that we cannot truly have an "idea" of God or angels.</meta>

### THIRD OBJECTIONS

...thinks of a man, a <term>chimera<note>A mythological creature composed of parts from different animals; in philosophy, it often refers to a mere figment of the imagination or an impossible concept.</note></term>, the sky, an angel, or *God*.

When I think of a man, I represent to myself an **idea** or an **image** composed of color and shape, concerning which I may doubt whether it carries the likeness of a man or not. The same is true when I think of the sky. When I think of a **chimera**, I represent to myself an **idea** or an **image**, concerning which I may doubt whether it is the portrait of some animal that does not exist, but which could be or could have been in the past, or else which has never existed at all.

And when someone thinks of an **angel**, sometimes the image of a flame presents itself to his mind, and sometimes that of a young child with wings; regarding this, I think I can say with certainty that it bears no resemblance to an angel, and therefore that it is not the **idea** of an angel. However, believing that there are invisible and <term>immaterial<note>Not made of physical matter.</note></term> creatures who are the ministers of God, we give the name "angel" to a thing we believe or suppose to exist, even though the **idea** under which I imagine an angel is nevertheless composed of the ideas of visible things.

It is the same with the venerable name of **God**, of whom we have no image or idea; this is why we are forbidden from worshipping him under an image, for fear that it might seem to us that we are conceiving him who is inconceivable.

We therefore do not have within us, it <unclear>seems</unclear>, any **idea** of God; but, just like a <term>person born blind<note>original: "aveugle-né"</note></term> who has often approached a fire and felt its heat, recognizes that there is something by which he has been warmed, and hearing that this thing is called "fire," concludes that fire exists, yet nevertheless does not know its shape or color, and has, truth be told, no **idea** or image of fire that presents itself to his mind.

In the same way, man, seeing that there must be some cause for his images or his ideas, and for that cause another first cause, and so on, is finally led to an end or to a supposition of some **eternal cause** which, because it never began to be, can have no cause preceding it; this leads him to conclude necessarily that there is an **Eternal Being** who exists. And yet, he has no **idea** that he could say is that of this **Eternal Being**; rather, he names or calls by the name of **God** this thing which faith or his reason persuades him of.

Now, since *Mr. Descartes* proceeds from this supposition—namely, that we have within us the idea of *God*—to the proof of this proposition that *God* (*that is to say, an All-Powerful, most wise Being, Creator of the Universe, etc.*) exists, he ought to have better explained this idea of *God*, and from there...

By the name "idea," he [Hobbes] wishes only for us to understand here the images of material things depicted in the physical <term>phantasy<note>Originally from the Greek *phantasia*, this refers to the capacity of the mind to form or store mental images. And I have used this word because it was already commonly accepted by philosophers to signify the forms of the conceptions of the divine <term>intellect<note>The faculty of understanding or reasoning. ### EIGHTH OBJECTION.

*But the other idea of the sun is derived from the reasons of astronomy—that is, from certain notions that are naturally within me.*

It seems that there cannot be more than one idea of the sun at the same time, whether it is seen by the eyes or conceived by reasoning to be many times larger than it appears to the sight. For this latter "idea" is not truly the idea of the sun, but rather a consequence of our reasoning, which teaches us that the idea of the sun would be many times larger if it were viewed from much closer. It is true that at different times there can be different ideas of the sun—for instance, if at one time it is viewed only with the naked eye, and at another through a telescope <note>original: "lunette d'approche"</note>. However, the principles of astronomy do not make the idea of the sun larger or smaller; they only teach us that the sensible <term>sensible: that which is perceived through the senses</term> idea of the sun is deceptive.

### REPLY.

I reply once again that what is claimed here *not* to be an idea of the sun—yet which is nevertheless described—is exactly what I call by the name "idea." As long as this philosopher refuses to agree with me on the meaning of words, he can raise no objection against me that is not trivial <note>original: "frivole"</note>.

->NINTH OBJECTION.<-

*For in fact, those ideas that represent substances to me are undoubtedly something more, and possess, so to speak, more objective reality <note>In Cartesian philosophy, "objective reality" refers to the degree of perfection or "being" represented by an idea in the mind, rather than the modern sense of "unbiased truth."</note> than those that represent only modes or accidents. Just as that idea by which I conceive of a supreme, eternal, infinite, all-knowing, all-powerful God, and the universal creator of all things outside of himself, also undoubtedly has more objective reality within itself than those ideas by which finite substances are represented to me.*

I have already remarked several times before that we have no idea of God nor of the soul; I now add: nor of substance <note>A "substance" is a technical term for something that exists in itself, like a piece of wood or a human mind, rather than existing as a property of something else.</note>. For I certainly admit that substance—insofar as it is a material thing capable of receiving various accidents <note>An "accident" or "mode" is a quality that can change, such as color, shape, or position, without the thing itself ceasing to exist.</note> and subject to their changes—is perceived and proven through reasoning; however, it is not conceived, and we have no idea of it. If this is true, how can one say that the ideas representing substances are "something more" and have "more objective reality" than those representing accidents? Furthermore, it seems that Mr. Descartes has not sufficiently considered what he means by these words: *have more reality*. Does reality admit of "more" and "less"? Or, if he thinks one thing is "more" of a thing than another, let him consider how it is possible for this to be made clear to the mind and explained with all the clarity and evidence required in a demonstration, and with which he has often treated other matters.

---

->REPLY.<-

I have said several times that I use the name "idea" for that which reason makes known to us, as well as for all the other things we conceive, in whatever way we conceive them. And I have sufficiently explained how reality admits of "more" and "less" by saying that a substance is something more than a mode; and if there are "real qualities" or "incomplete substances," they are also something more than modes, but something less than complete substances; and finally, if there is an infinite, independent substance, this substance has more being, or more reality, than a finite and dependent substance. This is so manifest in itself that there is no need to provide a more ample explanation.

### TENTH OBJECTION.

There remains then only the idea of God, in which it must be considered if there is something that could not have come from myself. By the name of God, I understand a substance that is infinite, independent, supremely intelligent, supremely powerful, and by which not only myself, but all other things that exist (if there are others) have been created. All of these things, to tell the truth, are such that the more I think about them, the less they seem to me to be able to come from myself alone. And consequently, it must be concluded from all that has been said before, that God necessarily exists.

Considering the attributes of God—in order that we might have an idea of them and see if there is something in that idea which could not have come from ourselves—I find, if I am not mistaken, that neither the things we conceive by the name of God come from us, nor is it necessary that they come from anywhere other than external objects. For by the name of God I understand a substance, that is to say, I understand that God exists (not by an idea, but through reasoning); I understand that this substance is infinite (meaning that I can neither conceive nor imagine its limits <note>The original French uses "termes," referring to the boundaries or end-points of a thing.</note>, or its final parts, without being able to imagine others beyond them), from which it follows that the name *infinite* does not provide us with the idea of divine infinity, but rather with the idea of our own boundaries and limits. I also understand that this substance is independent, meaning I conceive of no cause from which God could come. From this, it appears that I have no other idea that corresponds to this name of "independent," except for the memory of my own ideas, which all have their beginning at various times, and which, consequently, are dependent.

Therefore, to say that God is independent is to say nothing other than that God is among the number of things whose origin I cannot imagine; just as saying that God is *infinite* is the same as if we said He is among those things whose limits we do not conceive. And thus, this entire idea of God is refuted; for, what kind of idea is it that has no end and no origin?

*Supremely intelligent.* I also ask by what idea Mr. Descartes conceives of God’s intellection <note>In this context, the act of understanding or the operation of the intellect.</note>.

*Supremely powerful.* I also ask by what idea His power—which regards future things, that is to say, non-existent things—is understood.

Certainly, for my part, I conceive of power through the image or memory of past things, reasoning in this way: he has done thus, therefore he was able to do thus; therefore, as long as he exists, he

*Creator of all things that are in the world.* I can form some image of creation by means of things I have seen; for example, from having seen a man being born, and who has grown from an almost inconceivable smallness to the form and size he has now; and no one, in my opinion, has any other idea attached to this name of "creator." ->RESPONSE.<-

None of those things we attribute to God can come from external objects as if from an exemplary cause <term>exemplary cause: a model or pattern that an artist or creator follows to produce an effect</term>; for there is nothing in God similar to external things, which is to say, to corporeal things. For who is he who conceives of something without perceiving it, and who consequently does not have this form, or this idea of intellection? When he extends this to infinity, he forms the idea of the divine intellect; and what I say of this perfection should be understood in the same way for all the others.

Finally, when I say that some idea is born with us <note>This refers to Descartes’s famous concept of "innate ideas."</note>, or that it is naturally imprinted on our souls, I do not mean that it is always present to our thought, for in that case there would be no such ideas; rather, I mean only that we have within ourselves the faculty <term>faculty: a natural power or inherent mental capacity</term> to produce it.

### ELEVENTH OBJECTION.

And the entire force of the reasoning I used to prove the existence of God consists in this: that I see it would not be possible for my nature to be such as it is—that is to say, that I should have the idea of God within me—if God did not truly exist, namely that same God of whom I have the idea within me. 

Since, therefore, it is not a demonstrated fact that we have the idea of God within us, and since the Christian religion obliges us to believe that God is inconceivable—that is to say, in my opinion, that one cannot have an idea of Him—it follows that the existence of God has not been demonstrated, and much less the creation of the world.

### RESPONSE.

When it is said that God is inconceivable, this is understood to mean a conception that encompasses Him totally and perfectly <note>Descartes draws a distinction here between "conceiving" (having a mental representation) and "comprehending" (fully grasping the infinite, which a finite mind cannot do).</note>. For the rest, I have already explained so many times how we have the idea of God within us that I cannot repeat it here again without wearying the readers.

<meta>This page continues the exchange between the objector (Thomas Hobbes) and René Descartes. that there is no need for any positive faculty <term>positive faculty: a real, existing power of the mind, rather than just a lack of one</term> to be ignorant; but as for error, it is not so manifest a thing: for it seems that if stones and other inanimate things are incapable of error, it is only because they do not have the faculty of reasoning or imagining; from which we must conclude that to be capable of error one needs an understanding, or at least an imagination, both of which are positive faculties granted to all those who are mistaken, but also to them alone.

Besides this, Mr. Descartes adds: *I perceive that my errors depend on the concurrence of two causes, namely, the faculty of knowing which is in me, and the faculty of choosing, or rather my free will.* This seems to me to contain a contradiction with the things that were said before. It should also be noted here that the liberty of free will <note>original: "franc-arbitre"</note> is assumed without being proved, even though this assumption is contrary to the opinion of the Calvinists <note>The Calvinists of the 17th century held a strict view of predestination, which many saw as incompatible with the kind of free will Descartes describes.</note>.

### RESPONSE.

Even though to err one needs the faculty of reasoning (or, to put it better, of judging—that is, of affirming and denying) insofar as error is a defect of that faculty, it does not follow from this that this defect is real; no more than blindness is called real, even though stones are not said to be blind simply because they are not capable of seeing. I am quite astonished that I have not yet been able to find in all these objections any conclusion that seems to me to be properly drawn from its principles.

I have assumed or advanced nothing regarding freedom except what we feel every day within ourselves, and which is very well known by the natural light <term>natural light: the innate human capacity for reason and clear intuition, which Descartes believed allows us to recognize fundamental truths</term>: and I cannot understand why it is said here that this is repugnant to, or contradicts, what was said before.

But even though there may be many who, considering the preordination of God, cannot understand how our freedom can subsist and harmonize with it, there is nevertheless no one who, looking at themselves, does not feel and experience that the will and freedom are but one and the same thing, or rather that there is no difference between what is voluntary and what is free. And this is not the place to examine what the opinion of the Calvinists is on this matter.

## THIRTEENTH OBJECTION.

*For example, while examining these past few days whether anything truly existed in the world, and taking notice that from the very fact that I examined this question, it followed very evidently that I myself existed, I could not prevent myself from judging that a thing I conceived so clearly was true; not that I found myself forced by an external cause, but only because a great clarity in my understanding was followed by a great inclination in my will, and thus I was moved toward believing with all the more liberty as I found myself with less indifference.* <note>Descartes defines "indifference" not as a lack of caring, but as a state where the mind sees no reason to choose one side over the other. For him, the highest form of freedom is not having a "choice," but being so convinced by the truth that you cannot help but follow it.</note>

This way of speaking—*a great clarity in the understanding*—is metaphorical, and therefore is not suitable for use in a logical argument. Now, someone who has no doubt about an error still claims to have a similar clarity, and their will has no less an inclination to affirm what they do not doubt than the person who possesses perfect knowledge. This "clarity" can therefore easily be the reason why someone holds and stubbornly defends a certain opinion, but it cannot make them know with certainty that the opinion is true.

Furthermore, not only knowing that a thing is true, but also believing it, or giving it one’s admission and consent, are things that do not depend on the will at all. For things that are proven to us by good arguments, or told to us as believable—whether we wish it or not—we are constrained to believe them. It is quite true that affirming or denying, supporting or refuting propositions, are acts of the will; but it does not follow that our internal consent and admission depend on the will.

*And consequently, the conclusion that follows is not sufficiently demonstrated: "And it is in this misuse of our liberty that the deprivation which constitutes the form of error consists."*

---

## RESPONSE.

It matters little whether this way of speaking—*a great clarity*—is suitable or not for use in a formal argument, provided that it is suitable for explaining our thought clearly, as it indeed is. For there is no one who does not know that by this phrase, *a clarity in the understanding*, one means a clarity or <term>perspicuity: the quality of being clear and easily understood</term> of knowledge that perhaps not everyone has who thinks they have it; but that does not prevent it from differing greatly from a stubborn opinion which has been conceived without an evident perception.

<note>original: "clarté, entendement, volonté, indifférence, perspicuité, perception, liberté, erreur, objection, réponse"</note>

<summary>This page contains Thomas Hobbes's critique of Descartes's "clarity" as a mere metaphor and his argument that belief is involuntary. Descartes responds by defending "clarity" as a precise description of the intellectual perception that distinguishes true knowledge from mere stubborn opinion.</summary>

<keywords>clarity, intellect, will, indifference, free will, nature of error, Thomas Hobbes, René Descartes, epistemology</keywords>

Now, when it is said here that whether we wish to or not, we give our assent to the things we clearly conceive, it is the same as saying that whether we wish to or not, we will and desire good things when they are clearly known to us. For this way of speaking—*whether we do not wish to*—has no place on such occasions, because it is a contradiction to will and not to will the same thing at the same time. <note>Hobbes is pointing out a logical flaw: if our "will" is automatically drawn to what the "intellect" sees clearly, then "not wishing" to believe it is impossible. He views this as a linguistic confusion rather than a psychological insight.</note>

### FOURTEENTH OBJECTION CONCERNING THE FIFTH MEDITATION.

### *On the essence of material things.*

*As, for example, when I imagine a triangle, even if there is perhaps no such figure anywhere in the world outside of my thought, and there never has been, there is nonetheless a certain nature, or form, or determined essence of this figure, which is immutable and eternal, which I have not invented, and which does not depend in any way on my mind; as is evident from the fact that one can demonstrate various properties of this triangle.* <note>This is a famous passage where Descartes argues that mathematical truths (like the properties of a triangle) are "discovered" by the mind rather than "created" by it. He believes these essences exist as eternal truths even if no physical triangle exists.</note>

If there is no triangle anywhere in the world, I cannot understand how it has a "nature," for that which is nowhere is nothing at all, and therefore has no being or nature. The idea that our mind conceives of a triangle comes from another triangle we have seen, or one we have invented based on things we have seen. But once we have applied the name "triangle" to the thing from which we think the idea of the triangle takes its origin, the name remains even if that thing perishes. Similarly, if we have once conceived in our thought that all the angles of a triangle taken together are equal to two right angles, and we have given this other name to the triangle—*that it is a thing which has three angles equal to two right angles*—even if there were no triangle in the world, the name would nonetheless remain. And thus the truth of this proposition will be eternal: that a triangle is a thing that has three angles equal to two right angles. However, the nature of the triangle will not be eternal because of this; for if it happened by chance that every triangle generally perished, its nature would also cease to be. <note>Hobbes is arguing from the perspective of "Nominalism"—the idea that "essences" or "natures" are just names and mental labels we use to group similar things together, rather than being real, eternal things in themselves.</note>

In the same way, the proposition *man is an animal* <note>original: "l'homme est un animal"</note> will be eternally true because of the names; but supposing the human race were annihilated, there would no longer be a human nature.

From which it is evident that essence, insofar as it is distin-

<header>AND RESPONSES</header>

It seems that just as the image of a man in the mind is related to that man, so essence is related to existence; or rather, as the proposition *Socrates is a man* is related to the proposition *Socrates is* or *exists*, so the essence of Socrates is related to the existence of that same Socrates. Now, the statement *Socrates is a man*, when Socrates does not exist, signifies nothing other than a collection of names; and the word *is* or *to be* carries with it the idea of the unity of a thing designated by two names. <note>Hobbes is arguing for "nominalism"—the idea that "man" or "triangle" are just labels we use to group ideas, and they have no real "essence" or "nature" outside of our language and the actual existence of individual things.</note>

## RESPONSE.

The distinction between essence and existence is known to everyone; and what is said here regarding "eternal names," instead of concepts or ideas of an eternal truth, has already been sufficiently refuted and rejected. <note>Descartes dismisses Hobbes's linguistic argument, standing by his belief that mathematical and logical truths (essences) are real and discoverable by the mind, not just names we made up.</note>

# FIFTEENTH OBJECTION ON THE SIXTH MEDITATION.

## On the existence of material things.

> *For God having given me no faculty to know that this is the case (namely, that God by Himself or through some creature more noble than the body sends me ideas of the body) but, on the contrary, having given me a great inclination to believe they are sent to me, or that they arise from corporeal things, I do not see how one could excuse Him from deceit if indeed these ideas came from elsewhere or were sent to me by other causes than corporeal things; and therefore it must be admitted that corporeal things exist.* <note>Descartes argues that since we have a powerful, natural instinct to believe that our sensations (like seeing a tree) come from actual physical objects, and since God gave us this instinct and is not a deceiver, physical objects must actually exist.</note>

It is a common opinion that doctors do not sin when they deceive the sick for their own health, nor fathers who deceive their children for their own good, and that the evil of deceit consists not in the falsehood of words, but in the malice of the one who deceives. <note>Hobbes is using the concept of a "pious fraud"—the idea that lying can be a good thing if it serves a noble purpose.</note> Let <term>Monsieur Descartes</term> <note>original: "Monsieur Descartes"</note> therefore consider whether this proposition—*God can never deceive us*—is true when taken universally. For if it is not true in every possible case, then this conclusion—"therefore corporeal things exist"—is not valid.

# THIRD OBJECTIONS AND RESPONSES

I have frankly admitted that we are often [deceived], but only that we are not so when our error would make God appear to have a will to deceive, which cannot be in Him; and there is also here a consequence that does not seem to me well-deduced from his principles. <note>Descartes is arguing that while humans make mistakes, God—being perfect—would not create a universe where we are systematically deceived about the most basic truths of reality, as that would imply God is malicious.</note>

->FINAL OBJECTION<-

For I now recognize that there is a very notable difference between the one and the other (that is, between being awake and dreaming) in that our memory can never link and join our dreams to one another, and with the whole course of our life, in the same way it is accustomed to join the things that happen to us while awake.
I ask, then, whether it is a certain thing that a person, dreaming that they doubt whether they are dreaming or not, cannot also dream that their dream is joined and linked with the ideas of a long series of past events. If they can, then those things which seem to the sleeper to be the actions of their past life can be taken for true, just as if they were awake. Furthermore, since—as he says himself—all the certainty of science and all its truth depends solely on the knowledge of the true God, either an atheist cannot recognize that they are awake through the memory of their past life’s actions, or else a person can know they are awake without the knowledge of the true God. <note>Hobbes is challenging Descartes’s "dreaming test." Descartes argued that life has a continuity that dreams lack. Hobbes points out that a dreamer could simply "dream" that their life is continuous, making the distinction useless without God.</note>

->RESPONSE<-

Someone who sleeps and dreams cannot perfectly and truly join and assemble their daydreams with the ideas of past things, even though they might dream that they are assembling them. For who denies that a sleeper can be mistaken? But later, once awake, they will easily recognize their error.
And an atheist can recognize that they are awake by the memory of the actions of their past life, but they cannot know that this sign is sufficient to make them certain that they are not mistaken, if they do not know that they were created by God, and that God cannot be a deceiver. <note>This is a famous and controversial point in Descartes's philosophy: he argues that while an atheist can know facts (like 2+2=4 or that they are currently awake), they can never have "perfect science" or absolute certainty because they have no guarantee that their mind isn't fundamentally broken or being manipulated by a higher power.</note>
