### FOURTH OBJECTIONS

->WRITTEN BY MR. ARNAULD, DOCTOR OF THEOLOGY.<-

->A letter from the same to the Reverend Father Mersenne.<-

### MY REVEREND FATHER,

I count among the most remarkable benefits the communication that has been shared with me through your efforts of the *Meditations* of Mr. Descartes; but as you knew their value, so too have you sold them to me very dearly, since you would not make me a participant in this excellent work until I had first obligated myself to tell you my feelings on it. This is a condition to which I would never have committed myself if the desire to know beautiful things were not so violent within me, and against which I would willingly protest if I thought I could as easily obtain from you an exception for having let myself be carried away by this laudable curiosity, just as in the past the <term>praetor</term><note>A high-ranking Roman magistrate who had the power to grant legal remedies or "exceptions" if a contract was signed under duress or fear.</note> granted them to those from whom fear or violence had wrung consent.

For what do you want from me? My judgment regarding the author? Not at all; you have long known the high esteem in which I hold his person and the value I place on his mind and his doctrine; nor are you unaware of the troublesome business which currently keeps me occupied. And if you have a better opinion of me than I deserve, it does not follow that I have no knowledge of my own lack of capacity; however, what you wish to submit to my examination requires a very high degree of <term>competence</term><note>The original French "suffisance" here refers to intellectual ability or adequacy for the task.</note> along with much tranquility and leisure, so that the mind, being freed from the clutter of worldly affairs, may think only of itself. This, as you rightly judge, cannot be done without very profound meditation and a great <term>recollection of spirit</term><note>A state of deep inward focus and spiritual gathering of one's thoughts, common in meditative practices.</note>. I will nevertheless obey since you wish it, but on the condition that you will be my guarantor, and that you will answer for all my faults. Now, although philosophy alone can boast of having given birth to this work, nevertheless because our author—in this, being very modest—comes to present himself before the tribunal of theology, I shall play here...

## On the Nature of the Human Mind.

The first thing I find here worthy of note is to see that Mr. Descartes establishes as the foundation and first principle of his entire philosophy what Saint Augustine—a man of very great intellect and singular <term>doctrine</term><note>In this context, "doctrine" refers to Augustine's comprehensive system of learning and teaching in both sacred and secular matters.</note>, not only in matters of theology but also concerning philosophy—had taken as the base and support of his own. This is a famous precursor to Descartes' "I think, therefore I am."</note> These words are echoed by those of our author: *But there is a certain very powerful and very cunning deceiver who employs all his industry to always deceive me*. It is therefore certain that I exist, if he deceives me. But let us continue, and so as not to wander from our subject, let us see how from this principle one can conclude that our mind is distinct and separate from the body.

I can doubt whether I have a body; indeed, I can even doubt whether there are any bodies in the world, and nonetheless I cannot doubt that I am or that I exist while I doubt or while I think.

Therefore I, who doubt and who think, am not a body; otherwise, by doubting the body, I would be doubting myself.

Even if I were to stubbornly maintain that there are no bodies in the world, this truth nevertheless remains: I am something, and consequently I am not a body. Certainly, this is subtle; but someone might say (as our author even objects to himself): from the fact that I doubt, or even that I deny that there is any body, it does not follow from this that there are none.

Thus, by an abstraction of the mind, it can be conceived with this single faculty as a "thinking thing," even though, in reality, the properties and qualities of a body belong to all things that have the power to think; just as quantity can be conceived as length alone, even though in reality there is no quantity where width and depth do not accompany length.

What increases this difficulty is that this power of thinking seems to be attached to physical organs, since in children it appears dormant, and in the insane it seems altogether extinguished and lost—an objection primarily raised against us by those impious persons and "soul-murderers" <note>Arnauld uses this strong language to describe materialists who argue that the soul dies with the body.</note>.

That is what I had to say regarding the real distinction between the mind and the body; but since Monsieur Descartes has undertaken to demonstrate the immortality of the soul, one may rightly ask if it follows clearly from this distinction. For according to the principles of <term>ordinary philosophy</term><note>'Ordinary philosophy' refers to Scholasticism, the traditional Aristotelian system taught in 17th-century universities.</note>, this does not follow at all, seeing as they usually say that the souls of beasts are distinct from their bodies, and yet they perish with them.

I had extended this writing this far, and my intention was to show how—according to the principles of our author (which I thought I had gathered from his way of philosophizing)—the immortality of the soul is easily concluded from the real distinction between the mind and the body. However, a summary of the six *Meditations* written by the same author was then placed in my hands. In addition to the great light it sheds on his whole work, it contained the same reasons on this subject that I had been meditating upon to solve this question.

As for the "souls of beasts," he has already made his opinion well enough known in other places: that they have no soul at all, but rather only a body shaped in a certain way and composed of several different organs arranged so that all the operations we observe in them can be performed in and by that body.

But there is reason to fear that this opinion will not find credit in the minds of men unless it is supported and proven by very strong reasons. For this...

According to the ancient theory of the four humors, an excess of phlegm was thought to cause dullness or physical interference with the senses.</note></term>. This is what the same Saint Augustine says in the first book of his *Soliloquies*, chapter 4, where he states that he has experienced many times that, in matters of geometry, the senses are like ships.

> *For, he says, when I allowed myself to be led by my senses to the place I intended to go for the establishment and proof of some geometric proposition, I had no sooner left them than, coming to go over in my thought all the things they seemed to have taught me, I found my mind as unsteady as the steps of those who have just been put ashore after a long voyage. This is why I think that one could sooner find the art of navigating on land than be able to understand geometry through the sole mediation of the senses, although it seems, however, that they are of no small help to those who are beginning to learn it.*

The first reason our author brings forward to demonstrate the existence of God—which he undertook to prove in his third Meditation—contains two parts: the first is that God exists because His idea is in me; and the second is that I, who have such an idea, can only come from God.

<meta>This page continues Antoine Arnauld’s critique of René Descartes. Having previously discussed the distinction between the soul and body and the nature of "animal spirits," Arnauld now pivots to a technical critique of Descartes' theory of ideas. Specifically, he challenges Descartes’ claim that certain ideas can be "materially false," using the example of cold being a "privation" (an absence) rather than a positive force.</meta>

->FOURTH OBJECTIONS<-

...materially, to be false; which seems to me to be **in conflict** with his principles.

But for fear that in such an obscure matter I cannot explain my thought clearly enough, I will use an example to make it more evident. If, he says, cold is merely a **privation** <note>In the philosophy of the time, a "privation" is the absence of a quality that should be present—like blindness is the absence of sight, or cold is the absence of heat.</note> of heat, the idea that represents it to me as a positive thing will be **materially false**.

On the contrary, if cold is only a privation, there can be no idea of cold that represents it to me as a positive thing, and here our author confuses **judgment** with the **idea**.

For what is the idea of cold? It is cold itself insofar as it exists <term>objectively in the understanding<note>original: "objectivement dans l’entendement." In Cartesian philosophy, "objective being" refers to the content or object as it exists in the mind, rather than as a physical thing in the world.</note></term>: but if cold is a privation, it could not exist objectively in the understanding through an idea whose objective being is a positive being: therefore, if cold is only a privation, the idea of it can never be positive, and consequently there can be no idea that is <term>materially false<note>Descartes used this term to describe an idea that provides "material" for an error, such as representing "nothing" as if it were "something." Arnauld argues this is a contradiction.</note></term>.

This is confirmed by the same argument that Monsieur Descartes employs to prove that the idea of an infinite being is necessarily true: for, he says, although one might feign that such a being does not exist, one cannot nevertheless feign that its idea represents nothing real to me.

The same thing can be said of every positive idea; for although one might feign that cold—which I think is represented by a positive idea—is not a positive thing, one cannot nonetheless feign that a positive idea represents nothing real and positive to me, given that ideas are not called "positive" according to the "being" they have as modes or manners of thinking—for in that sense they would all be positive—but they are so called from the **objective being** they contain and represent to our mind. Hence, this idea may well not be the idea of cold, but it cannot be false.

But, you will say, it is false for the very reason that it is not the idea of cold; on the contrary, it is your **judgment** that is false if you judge it to be the idea of cold: but as for the idea itself, it is certain that it is very true. Just as the idea of God must not be called materially false, even if someone might transfer and apply it to a thing that is not God, as idolaters have done.

Finally, this idea of cold, which you say is materially false, what does it represent to your mind? A privation: then it is true; a positive being: then it is not...

<summary>Arnauld critiques Descartes' concept of "materially false" ideas, arguing that an idea itself cannot be false; error only occurs when the human judgment misinterprets what the idea represents.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Antoine Arnauld’s critique of René Descartes. ->FOURTH OBJECTIONS<-

...not the idea of cold; and furthermore, what is the cause of this **positive objective being**, which according to your opinion makes this idea materially false? It is, you say, myself insofar as I participate in <term>nothingness<note>In this context, "nothingness" or "non-being" refers to human limitation or imperfection. Arnauld is pointing out a logical flaw: if something exists (even just as an idea), it must have a cause; Descartes claims this "false idea" comes from our lack of perfection, which Arnauld sees as deriving something from nothing.</note></term>. Therefore, the positive objective being of some idea can come from nothingness, which nevertheless is entirely repugnant to your primary foundations.

But let us come to the second part of this demonstration, in which it is asked whether I, who have the idea of an infinite being, can exist through anyone other than an infinite being, and principally whether I can exist through myself. Mr. Descartes maintains that I cannot exist through myself, insofar as if I gave myself being, I would also give myself all the perfections of which I find some idea within me. But the author of the <term>first objections<note>The "first objections" were written by Johan de Kater (Caterus), a Dutch theologian and contemporary of Descartes.</note></term> replies very subtly: <term>being by oneself<note>original: "être par soi." This relates to the concept of *aseity*, or existing by one's own nature rather than being caused by another.</note></term> must not be taken positively, but negatively, so that it is the same thing as "not being through another." Now, he adds, if something exists by itself—that is, not through another—how will you prove from that that it encompasses everything and that it is infinite; for right now I am not listening to you if you say: since it exists by itself, it will have easily given itself all things; especially since it does not exist by itself as if by a cause, and since it was not possible for it, before it existed, to foresee what it could be in order to choose what it would be afterward.

To respond to this argument, Mr. Descartes maintains that this way of speaking—"being by oneself"—should not be taken negatively but positively, even with regard to the existence of God: in such a way that God does, in some sense, the same thing with regard to Himself as the <term>efficient cause<note>An "efficient cause" is the primary source of change or rest; in simple terms, the "maker" or "producer" of a thing. Arnauld is uncomfortable with the idea of God "making" Himself, as a cause usually precedes its effect in time or logic.</note></term> does with regard to its effect. This seems to me a bit bold, and not to be true.

This is why I agree with him in part, and in part I do not. For I certainly admit that I cannot exist by myself except positively, but I deny that the same must be true of God; on the contrary, I find a manifest contradiction in the idea that something exists by itself positively, and as if by a cause. This is why I conclude the same thing as our author, but by a completely different path, in this manner.

To exist by myself, I would have to exist by myself positively, and as if by a cause; therefore, it is impossible for me to exist by myself; the <term>major premise<note>In a formal logical argument (a syllogism), the major premise is the general statement that forms the basis of the conclusion.</note></term> of this argument is proven by what he himself says: that since the parts of time can be separated and do not depend on one another, it does not follow from the fact that I exist now that I must exist in the future, unless there is within me some **real and positive power** that creates me anew, as it were, at every moment.

### FOURTH OBJECTIONS

As for the minor premise—namely, that I cannot exist by myself positively and as if by a cause—it seems so manifest by the <term>natural light<note>In 17th-century philosophy, "natural light" (*lumière naturelle*) refers to the innate power of human reason to recognize self-evident truths without the need for external proof.</note></term> that it would be in vain to stop to prove it, since it would be wasting time to prove something well-known by using something less known. Our author even seems to have recognized its truth when he did not dare to deny it openly. For I pray you, let us carefully examine these words from the response to the first objections:

*I did not say,* he says, *that it is impossible for a thing to be the <term>efficient cause<note>The agent or force that actually produces an effect or brings something into being. For example, a carpenter is the efficient cause of a table.</note></term> of itself; for although that is manifestly true when one restricts the meaning of "efficient" to those kinds of causes which are different from their effects, or which precede them in time, it does not seem, nevertheless, that in this question it should be so restricted, because the natural light does not dictate to us that it is the property of the efficient cause to precede its effect in time.*

That is all very well regarding the first part of this distinction; but why has he omitted the second? And why did he not add that the same natural light does not dictate that it is the property of the efficient cause to be different from its effect, if not because the natural light would not allow him to say it?

And in truth, since every effect is dependent on its cause and receives its being from it, is it not very evident that the same thing cannot depend upon nor receive being from itself?

Furthermore, every cause is the cause of an effect, and every effect is the effect of a cause, and therefore there is a **mutual relationship** between the cause and the effect; now, there can be no mutual relationship except between two things.

Moreover, one cannot conceive without absurdity that a thing receives being, and that nevertheless this same thing has being before we have even conceived that it has received it. Yet this would happen if we attributed the notions of cause and effect to the same thing in regard to itself. For what is the notion of a cause? To give being. What is the notion of an effect? To receive it. Now, the notion of the cause naturally precedes the notion of the effect.

Now, we cannot conceive of a thing under the notion of a cause, as giving being, if we do not conceive that it has it; for no one can give what he does not have. Therefore, we first conceive that a thing has being before we conceive that it has received it; and nevertheless, in the one who receives, receiving precedes having.

### FOURTH OBJECTIONS

...existence except for the one who already possesses it; now, if he already possesses it, why would he give it to himself?

Finally, he says that *it is manifest by the natural light that creation is distinguished from conservation only by a distinction of reason*; <note>Descartes argued that "continuous creation" is necessary because existence doesn't carry over from one moment to the next; God must constantly "re-create" or "conserve" everything.</note> but it is also manifest by the same natural light that nothing can create itself, nor consequently can it conserve itself.

If we descend from the general thesis to the specific case of God, the matter will be, in my opinion, even more manifest—namely, that God cannot exist by Himself *positively*, but only *negatively*, which is to say, not by another.

Firstly, this is evident from the very reason Monsieur Descartes brings forward to prove that if a body exists *by itself*, it must exist by itself *positively*. *For*, he says, *the parts of time do not depend upon one another; and therefore, from the fact that one supposes a body has existed by itself until now, which is to say without a cause, it does not follow from this that it must still exist in the future, unless there is some real and positive power in it which, so to speak, continually reproduces it.*

But this reasoning is so far from being applicable when it concerns a supremely perfect and infinite being that, on the contrary, for entirely opposite reasons, one must conclude quite differently. For in the idea of an infinite being, the infinity of his duration is also contained; that is to say, it is not enclosed by any limits, and therefore it is indivisible, permanent, and subsisting all at once. In this infinity, one cannot—without error, or at least only improperly due to the imperfection of our minds—conceive of a past or a future.

From this it is manifest that one cannot conceive of an infinite being existing, even for a single moment, without simultaneously conceiving that he has always been and will eternally be (as our author himself says in another place); and therefore, it is a superfluous thing to ask why he perseveres in existence.

Indeed, as Saint Augustine teaches (who, after the sacred authors, has spoken of God more highly and more worthily than any other), in God there is no past nor future, but a continual present. <note>Augustine’s view of "eternal present" means God exists outside of time altogether, seeing all moments at once.</note> This clearly shows that one cannot, without absurdity, ask why God perseveres in existence, seeing as this question manifestly involves a "before" and an "after," a past and a future, which must be banished from the idea of an infinite being.

Furthermore, one cannot conceive that God exists by himself *positively*, as if he were himself first produced;

<meta>This page continues Antoine Arnauld’s critique of René Descartes. Arnauld is arguing against Descartes' idea that God is the "efficient cause" of Himself. ### FOURTH OBJECTIONS

...for he would have had to exist before existing; rather, it is only (as our author declares in several places) because, in effect, he conserves himself.

But <term>conservation</term> <note>The theological and philosophical idea that God must continuously sustain the existence of all created things, otherwise they would vanish.</note> is no more suited to an infinite being than is a first <term>production</term> <note>The initial act of being created or brought into existence.</note>. For what is conservation, I ask you, if not a continual reproduction of a thing? From this, it follows that every conservation presupposes a first production. It is for this very reason that the name "continuation," as well as "conservation," being names of <term>potentiality</term> <note>original: "puissance." In Scholastic philosophy, "potentiality" is the capacity to become or receive something, as opposed to being "actuality."</note> rather than <term>act</term> <note>original: "acte." The state of being fully realized or complete.</note>, carry with them some capacity or disposition to receive existence. But the infinite being is a **pure act**, incapable of such dispositions.

Let us conclude, then, that we cannot conceive of God existing "by himself" in a positive sense, except because of the imperfection of our own minds, which conceive of God in the same way we conceive of created things. This will be even more evident through this other reason:

One does not ask for the <term>efficient cause</term> <note>The primary agent or force that produces an effect or brings a thing into existence.</note> of a thing except regarding its existence, and not regarding its essence. For example, when one asks for the efficient cause of a triangle, one asks who made it so that this triangle exists in the world; but it would be absurd for me to ask for the efficient cause of why a triangle has its three angles equal to two right angles. To the person making such a request, one would not respond with an efficient cause; rather, one must simply answer that such is the nature of the triangle. This is why mathematicians, who do not concern themselves much with the existence of their objects, do not provide any demonstrations using efficient or final causes.

Now, it is no less a part of the essence of an infinite being to exist—or even, if you prefer, to persevere in being—than it is part of the essence of a triangle to have its three angles equal to two right angles. Therefore, just as one should not answer a person asking why a triangle has its three angles equal to two right angles by citing an efficient cause, but only by saying that such is the immutable and eternal nature of the triangle; so too, if someone asks why God is, or why he does not cease to be, one must not seek an efficient cause (or a "quasi-efficient" cause) either inside or outside of God. (For I am not arguing here about the name, but about the thing itself.) Instead, one must say it is for this reason: because such is the nature of the **supremely perfect being**.

This is why, regarding what Monsieur Descartes says—that the **natural light** <note>The innate human capacity for reason, granted by God, which allows us to discern fundamental truths.</note> dictates to us that there is nothing for which we are not permitted to ask why it exists, or for which we cannot seek the efficient cause, or else...

<summary>Arnauld argues that God does not need a "cause" to exist because existence is part of His very essence, just as geometric properties are part of a triangle's essence. ### FOURTH OBJECTIONS

...it has none, to ask why it does not need one.

I reply that if one asks why God exists, one must not respond by citing an <term>efficient cause</term> <note>The primary agent or force that produces an effect or brings a thing into existence.</note>, but only because He is God—that is to say, an <term>infinite being</term>. If one asks what the <term>efficient cause</term> is, one must reply that He has no need of one; and finally, if one asks why He has no need of one, one must reply it is because He is an <term>infinite being</term>, for whom <term>existence</term> is His <term>essence</term> <note>In theology, this means that God’s very nature is "to be"; He does not receive existence from elsewhere.</note>. For it is only in those things where it is possible to distinguish actual <term>existence</term> from <term>essence</term> that there is a need for an <term>efficient cause</term>.

Consequently, what he adds immediately after the words I have just cited destroys itself; namely: "if I thought," he says, "that nothing could in any way be toward itself what the <term>efficient cause</term> is toward its <term>effect</term>, far from concluding from this that there is a <term>first cause</term>, I would, on the contrary, search again for the <term>cause</term> of that very thing one calls the <term>first</term>, and thus I would never arrive at a first."

For on the contrary, if I thought that for anything whatsoever one must seek an <term>efficient cause</term> (or a "quasi-efficient" cause), I would have it in mind to seek a <term>cause different</term> from that thing. This is because it is manifest that nothing can, in any way, be toward itself what the <term>efficient cause</term> is toward its <term>effect</term>.

Now, it seems to me that our author must be warned to consider all these things diligently and with attention, because I am certain there are few theologians who would not be offended by this proposition: namely, that God is of Himself "positively," and as if by a <term>cause</term>.

I am left with only one doubt, which is to know how he can defend himself from committing a **circle** <note>The "Cartesian Circle" is a famous logical critique: Descartes proves God exists by relying on clear and distinct perceptions, but then says we can only trust clear and distinct perceptions because God exists.</note> when he says that we are only assured that the things we conceive clearly and distinctly are true because God is, or exists.

For we cannot be assured that God is, except because we conceive this very clearly and very distinctly; therefore, before being assured of the <term>existence</term> of God, we must be assured that all things we conceive clearly and distinctly are true.

I will add one thing that had escaped me: namely, that this proposition seems false to me, which <term>Monsieur Descartes</term> gives as a very constant truth: that nothing can be in him, insofar as he is a thinking thing, of which he has no knowledge. For by this phrase, "in him, insofar as he is a thinking thing," he means nothing other than his spirit...

### *Things that might give pause to the Theologians.*

Finally, to conclude a discourse that is already all too tedious, I wish to treat these matters here as briefly as possible; my intention in this regard is merely to point out the difficulties, without dwelling on a more exact dispute.

First, I fear that some may take offense at this free way of philosophizing by which all things are called into doubt. And indeed, our author himself confesses in his *Method* <note>René Descartes, *Discourse on the Method* (1637).</note> that this path is dangerous for weak minds; I admit, however, that he tempers the grounds for this fear somewhat in the summary of his first *Meditation*.

Nonetheless, I do not know if it would not be appropriate to provide it with a preface in which the reader is warned that one does not doubt these things seriously and in earnest, but only so that—having set aside for a time everything that could leave the slightest doubt, or, as our author puts it elsewhere, *which could give our mind the most hyperbolic <note>Exaggerated or extreme; in this context, doubting even the most obvious truths for the sake of philosophical rigor.</note> occasion for doubt*—we might see if, after this, there is no way to find some truth so firm and so certain that even the most stubborn could in no way doubt it. And also, instead of these words: *not knowing the author of my origin*, I would think it better to put *pretending not to know.*

In the fourth *Meditation*, which deals with truth and falsehood, I would wish, for several reasons that would be long to recount here, that M. Descartes, in his summary or in the very fabric of this *Meditation*, would warn the reader of two things.

The first is that when he explains the cause of error, he intends to speak primarily of that which is committed in the discernment of truth and falsehood, and not of that which occurs in the pursuit of good and evil.

This page picks up with a warning that some readers might interpret this method wrongly or find it offensive if not properly contextualized.</meta>

### FOURTH OBJECTIONS

[take it] badly, it seems to me that it is a matter of prudence, and that order itself, of which our author seems so protective, requires that all things which do not serve the subject and which can give rise to various disputes should be cut out, for fear that, while the reader wastes time uselessly disputing superfluous things, he might be distracted from the knowledge of necessary ones.

The second thing for which I would like our author to provide some warning is that, when he says we should only give our belief to things we conceive clearly and distinctly, this should be understood only for things concerning the sciences and which fall under our understanding <note>Arnauld is distinguishing between "Speculative Truth" (science/logic) and "Revealed Truth" (religion/morality).</note>, and not for those regarding faith and the actions of our life: this is why he has always condemned the arrogance and presumption of those who *opine*—that is, those who presume to know what they do not know—but he has never blamed the just persuasion of those who believe with prudence.

*For*, as Saint Augustine very judiciously remarks in chapter xv of *The Profit of Believing* <note>original: *De Utilitate Credendi*, a foundational work by Augustine on the relationship between faith and reason.</note>: There are three things in the human mind which have a close relationship with each other and seem almost to be one and the same thing, but which must nonetheless be very carefully distinguished: namely, *understanding, believing, and opining*.

*He understands* <note>original: *entend*</note> who grasps something through certain reasons. *He believes* who, carried by the weight and credit of some grave and powerful authority, holds as true the very thing he does not grasp through certain reasons. *He opines* <note>In this context, "to opine" (opiner) means to hold an ungrounded opinion or to guess without certainty.</note> who persuades himself, or rather presumes to know, what he does not know.

Now, it is a shameful thing and quite unworthy of a man to opine, for two reasons: the first, because a person is no longer in a state to learn if he has already persuaded himself that he knows what he is ignorant of; and the second, because presumption is in itself the mark of an ill-formed mind and a man of little sense.

Therefore, what we understand, we owe to reason; what we believe, to authority; what we opine, to error. I say this so that we may know that by adding faith, even to things we do not yet grasp, we are exempt from the presumption of those who opine.

For those who say that one must believe nothing but what we know, only try to avoid falling into the fault of those who opine, which, in effect, is shameful and blameworthy in itself. But if someone considers with care the great difference there is between he who presumes to know what he does not know and he who believes what he knows, although he does not understand [it]...

But what I foresee theologians will be most offended by is that, according to his principles, it does not seem that the things the Church teaches us regarding the sacred mystery of the Eucharist <note>The Christian sacrament of Holy Communion. The theological problem Arnauld raises is how the "accidents" (appearance) of bread can remain if the "substance" (the essence) changes into the body of Christ.</note> can persist and remain in their entirety.

*For we hold as an article of faith that, the substance of the bread being removed from the Eucharistic bread, the accidents alone remain: now these accidents are extension, shape, color, smell, taste, and the other sensible qualities.*

Of sensible qualities <note>Properties of an object perceived by the senses, like color or bitterness.</note> our author recognizes none, but only certain different movements of the small bodies surrounding us, by means of which we feel these different impressions, which we then call by the names of color, taste, smell, etc. Thus, only shape, extension, and mobility remain. But our author denies that these faculties <note>Here used in the sense of "properties" or "modes."</note> can be understood without some substance in which they reside, and consequently also that they can exist without it; which he even repeats in his replies to the first Objections.

He also recognizes no other distinction between these modes <term>modes (the specific ways a substance exists, like a specific shape)</term> or affections and the substance than a "formal" distinction. This does not seem sufficient for things so distinguished to be separated from one another, even by the omnipotence of God.

I do not doubt that Mr. Descartes, whose piety is well known to us, will diligently examine and weigh these matters. I trust he will judge that one must carefully ensure that, in trying to support God's cause against the impiety of the freethinkers <note>original: *libertins* — in the 17th century, this referred to those who rejected religious authority or lived without moral restraint.</note>, he does not seem to have placed weapons in their hands to combat a faith founded by the authority of God—the very authority he defends, and through which he hopes to reach that immortal life he has undertaken to persuade men of.

# AUTHOR’S REPLIES
## TO THE FOURTH OBJECTIONS MADE
### BY MONSIEUR ARNAULD, DOCTOR OF THEOLOGY.

->*Letter from the Author to the Reverend Father Mersenne.*<-

### MY REVEREND FATHER,

It would have been difficult for me to wish for a more clear-sighted or more helpful <note>The original French "officieux" here means "obliging" or "serviceable," rather than the modern English sense of being meddlesome.</note> examiner of my writings than the one whose remarks you have sent me. He treats me with such gentleness and courtesy that I can see clearly his intention was not to say anything against me, nor against the subject I have treated. Nevertheless, he has examined what he challenged with such care that I have reason to believe nothing escaped him. Furthermore, he presses so vigorously against the things that could not obtain his approval that I have no reason to fear anyone will think that mere politeness caused him to conceal anything. For this reason, I am not so much troubled by the Objections he has made as I am glad that there are no more things in my writing which he contradicts.

### Reply to the first part.

#### ON THE NATURE OF THE HUMAN MIND.

I will not pause here to thank him for the assistance he has given me by strengthening my position with the authority of Saint Augustine <note>A foundational Christian philosopher (354–430 AD). Arnauld had pointed out that Descartes' "I think, therefore I am" was anticipated by Augustine’s "If I am mistaken, I am" (*Si fallor, sum*).</note>, nor for the fact that he proposed my reasons in such a way that he seemed to fear others might not find them strong and convincing enough.

But I will state first at what point I began to prove how—from the fact that I know nothing else belonging to my essence (that is, to the essence of my mind) except that I am a thinking thing—it follows that there is indeed nothing else that belongs to it. This occurs in the same place where I proved that God is, or exists.

# REPLIES TO THE FOURTH OBJECTIONS

God, I say, who can do all the things that I conceive clearly and distinctly as possible.

For although perhaps there are many things in me that I do not yet know (just as I indeed supposed in that place that I did not yet know that the mind had the power to move the body, or that it was substantially united to it), nevertheless, since what I know to be in me is sufficient for me to subsist with that alone, I am certain that God could create me without those other things I do not yet know; and therefore, those other things do not belong to the <term>essence</term><note>In philosophy, an "essence" is the fundamental nature of a thing—the qualities that make it what it is and without which it could not exist.</note> of my mind.

For it seems to me that none of the things without which another can exist is included in its essence; and even though the mind is of the essence of man, it is nevertheless not, strictly speaking, part of the essence of the mind that it be united to a human body.

I must also explain here what my thought is when I say that one cannot infer a <term>real distinction</term><note>A "real distinction" is a technical term meaning that two things are truly separate entities (substances) that can exist independently of one another, rather than just being different ways of thinking about the same thing.</note> between two things from the fact that one is conceived without the other by an <term>abstraction</term><note>Abstraction is a mental process where we focus on one aspect of a thing while ignoring others (like thinking of a leaf's color without thinking of its shape).</note> of the mind which conceives the thing imperfectly, but only from the fact that each of them is conceived without the other fully, or as a <term>complete thing</term><note>Descartes defines a "complete thing" (*res completa*) as a substance that possesses everything necessary to exist on its own.</note>.

For I do not think that to establish a real distinction between two things, an entire and perfect knowledge is necessary, as <term>Monsieur Arnauld</term><note>Antoine Arnauld (1612–1694), the theologian who provided these critiques, was a leading figure in the Jansenist movement and a brilliant logic scholar.</note> claims; but there is this difference: a knowledge, to be entire and perfect, must contain within itself each and every property that is in the thing known; and it is for this reason that only God alone knows that He has entire and perfect knowledge of all things.

But although a <term>created understanding</term><note>This refers to the human intellect, which—unlike God's infinite mind—is "created" and therefore limited in its scope.</note> may perhaps indeed have entire and perfect knowledge of several things, it can never know that it has them unless God himself reveals it specifically; for to ensure that one has a full and entire knowledge of something, it is only required that the <term>power of knowing</term><note>The capacity of the human mind to grasp truths.</note> within him equals that thing, which can be done easily; but to ensure that he knows he has such a knowledge—or rather, that God has put nothing more into that thing than what he knows of it—his power of knowing would have to equal the infinite power of God, which is entirely impossible.

Now, to know the real distinction that exists between two things, it is not necessary that the knowledge we have of these things be entire and perfect, even if we do not know at the same time that it is such; but we can never know this, as I have just proven;

<summary>Descartes argues that because he can clearly conceive of himself as a thinking thing without needing a body, God is capable of creating the mind and body as separate entities. He clarifies that a "real distinction" between things only requires perceiving them as "complete," even if our human knowledge of them isn't as perfect as God's.</summary>

...therefore it is not necessary that it be entire and perfect. This is why, where I said that it is not enough for a thing to be conceived without another by an <term>abstraction</term> <note>Abstraction is a mental operation where we focus on one quality of an object while ignoring others—like thinking of the "redness" of an apple without thinking of its "roundness." Descartes is arguing that the separation of mind and body is not just a mental trick, but a recognition of their different natures.</note> of the mind that conceives the thing imperfectly, I did not intend for it to be inferred from this that, to establish a **real distinction**, one needed an entire and perfect knowledge, but only a knowledge such that we do not make it imperfect and defective by the abstraction and restriction of our mind.

For there is a great difference between having an entirely perfect knowledge—of which no one can ever be certain unless God himself reveals it—and having a knowledge that is perfect to the point that we know it has not been rendered imperfect by any abstraction of our mind.

Thus, when I said that one must "fully conceive" a thing, it was not my intention to say that our conception had to be entire and perfect, but only that we should know it well enough to know that it was *complete*.

This I thought was manifest, as much by the things I had said before as by those that follow immediately after; for a little earlier I had distinguished "incomplete beings" from those that are "complete," and I had said that it was necessary that each of the things that are really distinguished be conceived as a **being by itself** <note>original: "Être par soi." This is a central concept in metaphysics referring to something that can exist on its own, without needing to be a property or part of something else.</note> and distinct from every other.

And a little later, in the same sense that I said I fully conceived what the body is, I added in the same place that I also conceived the mind to be a complete thing—taking these two ways of speaking, *fully conceiving* and *conceiving that it is a complete thing*, to have one and the same meaning.

But one may here rightly ask what I mean by a *complete thing*, and how I prove that, for the *real distinction*, it is enough that two things be conceived one without the other as two *complete things*.

To the first demand I answer that by a complete thing, I mean nothing other than a **substance** <note>A substance is a fundamental entity that carries properties but is not itself a property of something else. For example, a chair is a substance; its color is a property.</note> clothed in forms or attributes that are sufficient to let me know that it is a substance.

For as I have already remarked elsewhere, we do not know substances immediately by themselves; but because we perceive certain forms or attributes which must be attached to something in order to exist, we call that thing to which they are attached by the name of substance.

If, after this, we wished to strip this same <term>substance</term> <note>In 17th-century philosophy, a "substance" is a thing that can exist on its own, unlike a "mode" or "quality" (like the color red) which must belong to something else.</note> of all those attributes that make it known to us, we would destroy all the knowledge we have of it. Thus, we might indeed be able to say something about the substance, but everything we said would consist only of words whose meaning we would not clearly and distinctly conceive.

I am well aware that there are substances commonly called "incomplete." But if they are called so because, by their nature, they cannot subsist all alone and without being supported by other things, I confess it seems to me that there is a contradiction in their being "substances"—that is, things that subsist by themselves—and also being "incomplete"—that is, things that cannot subsist by themselves. It is true that in another sense they can be called incomplete, not because they have anything incomplete insofar as they are substances, but only insofar as they relate to some other substance with which they compose a <term>whole by itself</term> <note>Original: "un tout par soi". This refers to a unified entity, like a human being, rather than a mere collection of parts like a pile of stones.</note> that is distinct from any other.

Thus, the hand is an incomplete substance if you relate it to the whole body of which it is a part; but if you consider it on its own, it is a complete substance. Similarly, the mind and the body are incomplete substances when they are related to the human being they compose; but when considered separately, they are complete substances.

For just as being extended, divisible, shaped, and so on, are forms or attributes through which I know that substance called **body**, so too being intelligent, willing, doubting, and so on, are forms through which I know that substance called **mind**. And I understand no less that the thinking substance is a complete thing than I understand the extended substance to be one.

And what <term>Mr. Arnauld</term> <note>Antoine Arnauld (1612–1694) was a prominent Jansenist theologian and philosopher who provided the Fourth Set of Objections to Descartes' Meditations.</note> added cannot be said in any way: namely, that perhaps the body relates to the mind as the <term>genus</term> to the <term>species</term>. <note>In logic, a "genus" is a general category (like "Animal") and a "species" is a specific type within it (like "Human"). Thus, for example, we easily conceive of "shape" without thinking of a "circle" (though this conception is not distinct unless it is related to some particular shape, nor is it of a complete thing unless it includes the nature of the body), but we cannot conceive of any...

### TO THE FOURTH OBJECTIONS

...we conceive clearly and distinctly the mind without the body, and reciprocally the body without the mind.

In the third place, even though the concept, or the idea of the triangle inscribed in a semi-circle, might be such that it does not contain the equality that exists between the square of the base and the squares of the sides <note>This refers to the Pythagorean theorem ($a^2 + b^2 = c^2$). In a triangle inscribed in a semi-circle where the base is the diameter, the triangle is always a right-angled triangle.</note>, it cannot nevertheless be such that one conceives that no proportion which might exist between the square of the base and the squares of the sides belongs to this triangle; and therefore, as long as one is ignorant of what this proportion is, one cannot deny any except that which one clearly knows does not belong to it—which can never be understood as the proportion of equality that exists between them.

But there is nothing contained in the concept of the body of what belongs to the mind, and reciprocally in the concept of the mind nothing is included of what belongs to the body.

This is why, although I have said that it is enough that I can conceive clearly and distinctly one *thing* without another, etc., one cannot for that reason form this <term>minor premise</term> <note>original: "mineure." In formal logic, a syllogism consists of a major premise, a minor premise, and a conclusion. Descartes is arguing that Arnauld's logic fails at the second step.</note>: "Now, it is the case that I conceive clearly and distinctly that this triangle is right-angled, even though I doubt, or I deny, that the square of its base is equal to the squares of its sides," etc.

Firstly, because the proportion which exists between the square of the base and the squares of the sides is not a complete thing.

Secondly, because this proportion of equality can only be clearly understood in a right-angled triangle.

And in the third place, because a triangle itself could not be distinctly conceived if one denies the proportion which exists between the squares of its sides and of its base.

But now it is necessary to pass to the second demand, and show how it is true that from the fact alone that I conceive clearly and distinctly one *substance* without another, I am assured that they mutually exclude one another, and are really distinct; which I show in this manner.

The *notion of the substance* is such that it is conceived as a thing which can exist by itself, that is to say, without the help of any other substance; and there has never been anyone who has conceived two substances by two different concepts who has not judged that they were really distinct.

That is why, if I had not sought a greater certainty than the common one, I would have been content to have *shown in the second Meditation that the mind is conceived as a subsisting thing, although one attributes to it nothing of what belongs to the body, and that in the same way the*

<header>REPLIES</header>

the body is conceived as a subsisting thing <note>A "subsisting thing" refers to a substance that can exist independently of other things.</note>, even though we attribute nothing to it that belongs to the mind; and I would have added nothing further to prove that the mind is really distinguished from the body, especially since we are accustomed to judge that all things are, in fact and according to the truth, exactly as they appear to our thought.

But, insofar as among those <term>hyperbolic doubts</term> <note>These are extreme, "exaggerated" doubts Descartes used as a tool to see if anything was absolutely certain—such as the possibility that an "evil demon" was deceiving him about the existence of the world.</note> that I proposed in my first Meditation, there was this one: namely, that I could not be certain *that things were in fact and according to the truth as we conceive them*, so long as I supposed that I did not know the author of my origin. Everything I said about God and truth in the 3rd, 4th, and 5th Meditations serves this conclusion of the <term>real distinction</term> <note>Descartes’ famous "dualism": the idea that the mind and the body are two completely different types of things (substances) that can exist without each other.</note> of the mind from the body, which I finally completed in the sixth.

I conceive very well, says Mr. Arnauld, *the nature of the triangle inscribed in the semi-circle without knowing that the square of its base is equal to the squares of its sides.* <note>This refers to the Pythagorean theorem. In geometry, any triangle drawn inside a semi-circle where one side is the diameter will always be a right-angled triangle.</note> To which I reply that this triangle can indeed be conceived without one thinking of the proportion between the square of its base and the squares of its sides, but one cannot conceive that this proportion should be *denied* of this triangle—that is to say, one cannot think that it does not belong to its nature. Now, it is not the same with the mind; for not only do we conceive that it exists without the body, but we can also deny that any of the things belonging to the body belong to the mind; for it is the very nature of <term>substances</term> <note>A substance is a fundamental building block of reality that does not need anything else to exist (except God).</note> to mutually exclude one another.

And what Mr. Arnauld added is in no way contrary to my view, namely, that it is no wonder if, when *from the fact that I think I come to conclude that I am, the idea that I then form of myself represents me only as a thinking thing*: for in the same way, when I examine the nature of the body, I find nothing in it that experiences thought; and one could not have a stronger argument for the distinction between two things than when, by considering them both separately, we find nothing in one that is not entirely different from what is found in the other.

I also do not see why this argument seems to prove too much; for I do not think that to show one thing is truly distinct from another one can say anything less than that by the omnipotence of God it can be separated from it: and it seemed to me that I had taken care quite carefully so that no one could think that man is nothing but a spirit using or making use of a body.

# TO THE FOURTH OBJECTIONS

For even in that sixth Meditation, where I spoke of the distinction of the mind from the body, I also showed that it is <term>substantially united</term> <note>This is a key Cartesian concept: even though the mind and body are different "substances," they are joined together to form a single unit—the human being.</note> to it: and to prove it, I used reasons which are such that I have no memory of ever having read any elsewhere that were stronger or more convincing.

And just as someone who said that a man's arm is a substance <term>really distinct</term> <note>In philosophy, a "real distinction" means the two things can exist independently of one another, usually by the power of God.</note> from the rest of his body would not, for that reason, deny that it belongs to the essence of the whole man; and just as he who says that this same arm belongs to the essence of the whole man does not, for that reason, give cause to believe that it cannot <term>subsist by itself</term> <note>To "subsist by itself" means to exist as a complete thing without needing to be attached to something else.</note>; so I do not think I have proven too much in showing that the mind can be without the body, nor have I said too little in saying that it is substantially united to it. This is because this substantial union does not prevent us from having a clear and distinct idea, or concept, of the mind alone as a complete thing. Therefore, the concept of the mind differs greatly from that of a surface or a line, which cannot be understood as complete things if, besides length and width, one cannot also attribute depth to them.

And finally, from the fact that *the faculty of thinking is dormant in children, and that in the mad it is not, in truth, extinguished, but* DISTURBED, it must not be thought that it is so attached to the bodily organs that it cannot exist without them. For, from the fact that we often see it hindered by these organs, it in no way follows that it is produced by them; and it is not possible to provide any reason for such a claim, however slight it might be.

I do not deny, nevertheless, that this close bond between the mind and the body, which we experience every day, is the reason why we do not easily discover, without deep meditation, the real distinction that exists between the two.

But, in my judgment, those who frequently turn over in their minds the things I wrote in my second Meditation will easily persuade themselves that the mind is not distinguished from the body by a mere fiction or abstraction of the intellect, but that it is known as a distinct thing because it is indeed so in fact.

I shall say nothing in response to what Mr. Arnauld has added here regarding the immortality of the soul, since that is not contrary to my views; but as for what concerns the <term>souls of beasts</term> <note>Descartes famously argued that animals were "automata" or complex machines without conscious minds or immortal souls, a point Arnauld questioned.</note>, although the consideration of them does not belong here, and although I cannot say more without an explanation of my entire system of physics than what I have already said in the fifth part—

He also refutes the idea that the mind is produced by the body simply because physical conditions, like childhood or madness, can interfere with thought.</summary>

# RESPONSES

As a result, even in us, it is not the mind (or the soul) that directly moves the external limbs; rather, it can only determine the course of that very subtle fluid called the <term>animal spirits</term> <note>Despite the name, "animal spirits" were not "souls." Descartes imagined them as a very fine, fast-moving wind or fluid—similar to hydraulic fluid—that flowed from the heart through the brain and into the muscles to trigger movement.</note>. This fluid, flowing continually from the heart through the brain and into the muscles, is the cause of all the movements of our limbs, and it can often cause several different movements as easily as any other. Moreover, the mind does not always determine these movements; for among the movements that occur within us, there are several that do not depend on the mind at all. These include the beating of the heart, the digestion of food, nutrition, the breathing of those who sleep, and even in those who are awake, walking, singing, and other similar actions when they are performed without the mind thinking about them. And when those who fall from a height put their hands forward to save their head, it is not by the counsel of their reason that they perform this action; it does not depend on their mind, but only on the fact that their senses, being affected by the present danger, cause a change in their brain which determines the animal spirits to pass from there into the nerves in the manner required to produce this movement—exactly as in a machine, and without the mind being able to prevent it.

Now, since we experience this in ourselves, why should we be so astonished if the light reflected from the body of a wolf into the eyes of a sheep has the same power to excite in it the movement of flight?

After noting this, if we wish to reason a little to discover whether some movements of beasts are similar to those performed in us through the ministry of the mind, or rather to those which depend only on the animal spirits and the disposition of the organs, we must consider the differences between the two, which I explained in the fifth part of the *Discourse on the Method*, for I do not think any others can be found; and then it will be easily seen that all the actions of beasts are only similar to those we perform without our mind contributing to them.

Because of this, we will be obliged to conclude that we do not, in effect, recognize in them any other principle of move-

### RESPONSE TO THE OTHER PART.

#### Of God.

Up to this point, I have tried to resolve the arguments proposed to me by Mr. Arnauld, and have made it my duty to withstand all his efforts; but henceforth, imitating those who have to deal with too strong an opponent, I will try instead to avoid the blows rather than directly opposing their violence.

He treats only three things in this part, which can easily be agreed upon according to how he understands them; but I took them in another sense when I wrote them, a sense which also seems to me capable of being received as true.

The first is that some <term>ideas</term> <note>In Cartesian philosophy, an "idea" is any object of thought, whether a sensation, a memory, or a concept.</note> are materially false—that is to say, in my sense, they are such that they give the judgment matter or occasion for error; but he, considering <term>ideas taken formally</term> <note>To consider an idea "formally" is to look at it simply as a mental act, rather than looking at what that idea represents (the "objective" reality).</note>, maintains that there is no falsehood in them.

For since ideas themselves are nothing but forms, and they are not composed of matter, whenever they are considered insofar as they represent something, they are not taken *materially*, but *formally*; whereas if they were considered not insofar as they represent one thing or another, but only as being operations of the understanding, one could indeed say that they would be taken materially, but then they would not relate at all to the truth or falsity of objects.

That is why I do not think they can be said to be materially false in any other sense than the one I have already explained; that is to say, whether cold is a positive thing or a privation, I do not have a different idea of it for that reason, but it remains the same in me as I have always had, which I say gives me matter or occasion for error if it is true that cold is a privation and that it does not have as much reality as heat; especially since, coming to consider both these ideas according to how I received them from the senses, I cannot recognize that there is more reality represented to me by the one than by the other.

And certainly, I have not confused judgment with the idea: for I have said that in the latter a material falsity was encountered, but in judgment there can be no other than a formal one. Moreover, in all the rest of my writings, I have always maintained this same distinction. These words sufficiently testify that I believed something existed which does not need an efficient cause.

Now, what thing can be such, except God? And even a little later, I said that there was in God such a great and inexhaustible power that He never had need of any help to exist, and that He still does not need any to be preserved, so that He is, in some way, the cause of Himself.

In that context, those words—"the cause of Himself"—cannot in any way be understood as the efficient cause; they mean only that this inexhaustible power in God is the cause or the reason why He does not need a cause.

immensity of essence is very <term>positive</term> <note>In 17th-century philosophy, "positive" refers to something that has actual, real being or power, rather than just the absence of something.</note>, for this reason I said that the cause, or the reason why God has no need of a cause, is *positive*. This could not be said in the same way of any finite thing, even if it were very perfect in its own kind. 

For if one were to say that a finite thing existed by itself, that could only be understood in a *negative* way, insofar as it would be impossible to provide any reason drawn from the *positive* nature of that thing by which we should conceive that it would not need an <term>efficient cause</term> <note>The "efficient cause" is the external agent or force that brings something into existence, like a builder for a house.</note>.

And so, in all other places, I have compared the <term>formal cause</term> <note>The "formal cause" refers to the essence or definition of a thing—what makes it what it is.</note>, or the reason taken from the essence of God—which ensures he has no need of a cause to exist nor to be preserved—with the <term>efficient cause</term>, without which finite things cannot exist. In this way, it is easy to see from my own terms that it is entirely different from the <term>efficient cause</term>.

And no place will be found where I have said that God preserves himself by a <term>positive influence</term> <note>An "influence" here refers to a continuous flow of power or action that maintains something's existence over time.</note> in the same way that created things are preserved by him; rather, I have only said that the immensity of his power, or of his essence, which is the cause of why he has no need of a preserver, is a *positive* thing.

And therefore, I can easily admit everything that Monsieur <term>Arnauld</term> <note>Antoine Arnauld (1612–1694) was a prominent French theologian and mathematician who provided one of the most rigorous sets of objections to Descartes' Meditations.</note> puts forward to prove that God is not the <term>efficient cause</term> of himself and that he does not preserve himself by any <term>positive influence</term>, or else by a <term>continual reproduction of himself</term>, which is all that can be inferred from his reasons.

But he will also not deny, as I hope, that this immensity of power which ensures that God has no need of a cause to exist is in him a *positive* thing, and that in all other things one can conceive of nothing similar that is *positive*, by reason of which they would not need an <term>efficient cause</term> to exist; this is all I wished to signify when I said that no thing could be conceived to exist by itself except *negatively*, save for God alone; and I had no need to put forward anything further to answer the difficulty that was proposed to me.

But since Monsieur <term>Arnauld</term> warns me here so seriously that there will be few theologians who are not offended by this proposition—namely, that God is by himself *positively*, and as if by a cause—I will state here the reason why this way of speaking is, in my opinion, not only very useful in this matter, but even necessary and very far removed from anything that could give rise or occasion to take offense at it.

I know that our theologians, in dealing with divine matters, do not use the name *cause* at all when discussing the <term>procession</term> <note>In theology, "procession" describes how the Son and the Holy Spirit originate from the Father within the Trinity.</note> of the persons of the most Holy Trinity, and that where the Greeks used the terms <note>original: "αἰτίον"</note> *cause* and <note>original: "ἀρχήν"</note> *principle* interchangeably, our theologians prefer to use only the name *principle* as a very general term, for fear that they might otherwise give occasion to judge that the Son is less than the Father.

But where there can be no similar occasion for error, and when it is not a question of the persons of the Trinity but only of the unique essence of God, I do not see why we must so strictly avoid the name *cause*, especially when we have reached a point where it seems very useful to employ it, and in some way necessary.

Now, this name cannot be more usefully employed than for demonstrating the existence of God; and the necessity of using it cannot be greater than if, without using it, this existence cannot be clearly demonstrated.

And I think it is manifest to everyone that the consideration of the <term>efficient cause</term> <note>The "efficient cause" is the primary agent that produces an effect or brings something into being.</note> is the first and primary means—not to say the one and only means—that we have to prove the existence of God.

Now, we cannot make use of this means if we do not grant our mind the license to search for the efficient causes of all things that are in the world, without excepting even God himself; for for what reason should we except him from this search before it has been proven that he exists?

One can therefore ask of each thing whether it exists *by itself* or *by another*; and certainly, by this means, one can conclude the existence of God, even if one does not explain in formal and precise terms how these words *to be by itself* <note>original: "être par soi"</note> ought to be understood.

For all those who follow only the guidance of the <term>natural light</term> <note>The "natural light" refers to human reason or the innate capacity to recognize truth without the aid of divine revelation.</note> immediately form within themselves, in this encounter, a certain concept that participates in both the efficient cause and the <term>formal cause</term> <note>The "formal cause" is the essence or definition that makes a thing what it is.</note>, and which is common to both. This is to say: that which is *by another* exists by that other as by an efficient cause; and that which is *by itself* exists as if by a formal cause—that is, because it has such a nature that it has no need of an efficient cause. This is why I did not explain this in my *Meditations*, and I omitted it as being a thing manifest in itself that did not need any explanation.

But when those whom long habit has confirmed in the opinion that nothing can be the efficient cause of itself, and who are careful to distinguish this cause from the formal one, see that one asks whether something is *by itself*, it easily happens that they do not car- <note>The original French "ne por-" is the beginning of "ne portent" (do not carry/bring), cut off by the page break.</note>

But to respond to this pertinently, I judge that it is necessary to show that between the efficient cause properly so called and "no cause," there is a middle ground: namely, the *positive essence of a thing*. To this essence, the idea or concept of the efficient cause can be extended in the same way that we are accustomed to extending the concept of the largest circular line imaginable in geometry to the concept of a straight line, or the concept of a rectilinear polygon with an indefinite number of sides to the concept of a circle.

And I do not think I could have ever explained this better than when I said that *the meaning of the efficient cause must not be restricted in this question to those causes which are different from their effects, or which precede them in time; both because it would be a trivial and useless thing—since everyone knows that a thing cannot be different from itself, nor precede itself in time—and because one of these two conditions can be removed from its concept while the notion of the efficient cause remains entirely intact.*

For it is evident that it is not necessary for a cause to precede its effect in time, since it only possesses the name and nature of an efficient cause at the moment it produces its effect, as has already been stated.

But because the other condition <note>That is, the condition that the cause must be a different entity from the effect.</note> cannot be likewise removed, one must only infer that this is not an efficient cause properly so called—which I admit—but not that it is not a positive cause at all, which by analogy can be related to the efficient cause; and this alone is required for the question at hand. And when one adds, *if something is such, it will give itself all the perfections of which it has the ideas, if it were true that it did not have them yet*: this means that it is impossible for it not to actually possess all the perfections of which it has the ideas. This is because the <term>natural light</term> <note>The "natural light" refers to the human capacity for reason or innate intellectual intuition.</note> makes us realize that a thing whose essence is so immense that it does not need an efficient cause to exist, also does not need one to possess all the perfections of which it has the ideas; its own essence gives it <term>eminently</term> <note>To possess a quality "eminently" means to possess it in a higher, more perfect form than the way it appears in other things.</note> everything that we can imagine could be given to other things by an efficient cause.

And these words, *if it does not have them yet it will give them to itself*, serve only as an explanation; for by the same natural light we understand that this thing cannot have, at the moment I am speaking, the power and the will to give itself something new, but rather that its essence is such that it has possessed from all eternity everything that we can now think it would give itself if it did not have it yet.

And nevertheless, all these ways of speaking, which have a relationship and analogy with the efficient cause, are very necessary to guide the natural light in such a way that we conceive these things clearly: just as there are several things demonstrated by **Archimedes** concerning the sphere and other figures composed of curved lines, by comparing these same figures with those composed of straight lines; which he would have had difficulty making understood if he had used any other method.

And just as these types of demonstrations are not at all disapproved of—even though the sphere is considered there as a figure that has many sides—likewise I do not think I can be criticized here for having used the analogy of the efficient cause to explain things that belong to the <term>formal cause</term> <note>The "formal cause" refers to the internal structure or essence of a thing that explains why it is what it is. And it must be noted that I have attributed to God the dignity of being the cause in such a way that one cannot infer from this that I have also attributed to Him the imperfection of being the effect. But when I take the entire essence of a thing as the <term>formal cause</term> <note>A "formal cause" explains what a thing is by its very definition or nature, rather than what physical agent made it.</note>, I am merely following in the footsteps of Aristotle. He extends this to all the essences of all things because he is not dealing in that passage with the causes of a physical composite—any more than I am doing here—but generally with the causes from which one can derive some knowledge.

Now, to show that it was difficult in the question proposed not to attribute the name of "cause" to God, there is no better proof than this: that even though Mr. Arnauld tried to conclude the same thing as I did by another path, he nevertheless did not succeed, at least in my judgment.

For after having amply shown that God is not the efficient cause of Himself, because it is in the nature of an efficient cause to be different from its effect; and having also shown that He is not "of Himself" *positively*—understanding by this word "positively" a positive influence from a cause—and also that, truth be told, He does not "preserve" Himself—taking the word preservation to mean a continual reproduction of the thing (on all of which points I agree with him)—after all that, he wants once again to prove that God should not be called the efficient cause of Himself. This is because, he says, the efficient cause of a thing is only sought by reason of its existence, and never by reason of its essence. Now, it is no less a part of the essence of an infinite being to exist than it is of the essence of a triangle to have its three angles equal to two right angles. This <term>syllogism <note>A form of logical reasoning where a conclusion is drawn from two premises (e.g., All men are mortal; Socrates is a man; therefore, Socrates is mortal).</note></term> can easily be turned back against its author in this way: Although one cannot ask for the <term>efficient cause <note>The primary source of change or rest; in simple terms, the "maker" or "producer" of a thing.</note></term> in regards to the essence of a thing, one can nevertheless ask for it in regards to its existence; but in God, essence is not distinguished from existence, therefore one can ask for the efficient cause of God.

But to reconcile these two things, one must say that to someone asking why God exists, one should not, in truth, answer by citing an efficient cause properly speaking, but only by the essence of the thing itself, or perhaps by the <term>formal cause <note>The nature or "definition" of a thing that makes it what it is.</note></term>. Because in God existence is not distinguished from essence, this formal cause has a very close relationship with the efficient cause, and therefore can be called a "quasi-efficient cause."

Finally, he adds *that to someone who asks for the efficient cause of God, one must answer that He has no need of one: and again, to someone who asks why He has no need of one, one must answer: because He is an infinite being whose existence is His essence; for only those things in which it is permitted to distinguish actual existence from essence have need of an efficient cause.*

From this he infers that what I had said before is entirely overturned; namely, *if I thought that nothing could in any way be toward itself what the efficient cause is toward its effect, I would never reach a first cause in seeking the causes of things;* which, however, does not seem to me overturned at all, not even slightly weakened or shaken. It is certain that the main force, not only of my demonstration, but also of all those that can be brought to prove the existence of God through effects, depends entirely on this. Indeed, almost all theologians maintain that no proof can be offered unless it is drawn from effects.

And consequently, far from bringing any clarification to the proof and demonstration of God's existence when he does not allow us to attribute to Him the analogy of the efficient cause in relation to Himself, he instead obscures it and prevents readers from being able to understand it—particularly toward the end, where he concludes *that if he thought it necessary to seek the efficient or quasi-efficient cause of every thing, he would seek a cause different from that thing.*

And how, finally, would they stop at God as the **first cause**, and place in Him the end of their search, if they thought that the efficient cause of each thing must necessarily be sought as something different from that thing?

Certainly, it seems to me that Monsieur Arnauld has done the same thing here as if—after Archimedes <note>Archimedes (c. 287–212 BC) was a Greek mathematician who used the "method of exhaustion" to calculate the area and volume of curved shapes by treating them as if they were made of many straight-edged shapes.</note>, speaking of the things he demonstrated regarding the sphere by analogy to **rectilinear figures** <note>A geometric shape made entirely of straight lines.</note> inscribed within that same sphere, had said: "If I thought that the sphere could not be taken for a rectilinear or quasi-rectilinear figure whose sides are infinite, I would attribute no force to this demonstration, because it is not true if you consider the sphere as a curvilinear figure, as it indeed is, but rather if you consider it as a rectilinear figure where the number of sides is infinite";

If, I say, Monsieur Arnauld, not finding it good that the sphere should be called such, and nevertheless desiring to retain the demonstration of Archimedes, said: "If I thought that what is concluded here should be understood of a rectilinear figure whose sides are infinite, I would not believe this at all regarding the sphere, because I have a certain knowledge that the sphere is not a rectilinear figure."

By these words, it is certain that he would not be doing the same thing as Archimedes, but on the contrary, he would be creating an obstacle for himself, and would prevent others from properly understanding the demonstration.

I have deduced this here at greater length than the matter perhaps seemed to deserve, in order to show that I take careful care not to put even the slightest thing in my writings that **theologians** might justly censure.

<margin>Finally, I have already shown clearly enough, in the responses to the second objections, that I have not fallen into the error called the **circle** <term>Cartesian Circle <note>A famous critique of Descartes' logic: he argues that we know God exists because we perceive Him clearly and distinctly, but we only know our clear perceptions are true because God exists.
