I do this by making a distinction between the things that we do, in fact, conceive very clearly, and those things which we remember having formerly conceived very clearly.

Thus, when we prepare to use some faculty, if that faculty is in our mind, we immediately acquire an actual knowledge of it; therefore, we can certainly deny it is there if we cannot acquire this actual knowledge of it.

And certainly it was not my intention here to define anything regarding the nature of <term>accidents</term> <note>In the philosophy of the time, "accidents" were properties like color, smell, or texture that were thought to "inhere" in a substance but were not the substance itself.</note>, but I only proposed what seemed to me at first glance; and finally, from what I said—that <term>modes</term> <note>Descartes used "modes" to describe the way a substance is organized, such as its shape or motion.</note> cannot be conceived without some **substance** in which they reside—one should not infer that I have denied that by the **omnipotence of God** they can be separated from it, because I hold it as very certain, and firmly believe, that God can do an infinity of things that we are not capable of understanding or conceiving.

But, to proceed here with more frankness, I will not hide that I am persuaded that there is nothing else by which our senses are touched than this single **surface** <note>original: "superficie"</note> which is the boundary of the dimensions of the body that is felt or perceived by the senses; for it is on the surface alone that contact is made, which is so necessary for sensation that I estimate that without it, not one of our senses could be moved. And I am not alone in this opinion; **Aristotle** himself, and many other philosophers before me, held it. Thus, for example, **bread and wine** are not perceived by the senses except insofar as their surface is touched by the sensory organ, either immediately or mediately by means of the air or other bodies, as I believe—or else, as several philosophers say, by means of <term>intentional species</term> <note>original: "espèces intentionnelles". This refers to a Scholastic theory where objects sent out "likenesses" of themselves through the air to reach the eyes or ears.</note>.

And it must be noted that it is not only the external figure of bodies, which is felt by the fingers and the hand, that should be taken for this surface; but one must also consider all those small intervals that are, for example, between the tiny parts of the flour of which the bread is composed, as also between the particles of the **brandy** <note>original: "eau-de-vie"</note>, the fresh water, the vinegar, the dregs, or the tartar, from the mixture of which the wine is composed, and likewise between the small parts of other bodies, and to think that all the small surfaces that terminate these intervals form part of the surface of each body.

For in truth, these small parts of all bodies having various shapes and sizes and different movements, they can never be so well arranged nor so precisely joined together that there do not remain several intervals around them, which are nonetheless not empty, but are filled with air or some other matter; as is seen in bread, where they are quite wide and can be filled not only with air, but also with water, wine, or some other liquid. It must also be noted that this surface is not only moved as a whole when the entire mass of the bread is carried from one place to another, but that it is also moved in part when some of its small parts are agitated by the air or by other bodies entering its pores: so much so that if there are bodies of such a nature that some of their parts, or all those that compose them, move continually (which I believe to be true of several parts of the bread and of all those of the wine), it must also be conceived that their surface is in continual motion.

Finally, it must be noted that by the surface of the bread or wine, or of any other body whatsoever, we do not here mean any part of the substance, nor even of the quantity of that same body, nor any parts of the other bodies surrounding it, but only *this boundary which is conceived as the intermediary between each of the particles of this body and the bodies surrounding them, and which has no other entity than a <term>modal</term> one.* <note>For Descartes, a "mode" is a state or quality of a substance—like its shape or position—rather than a "thing" in itself. Now, there is no one who thinks that by "species" anything else is meant here than what is precisely required to touch the senses. And there is also no one who believes in the conversion of the bread into the body of Christ, who does not think that this body of Christ is precisely contained under the same surface under which the bread would be contained if it were present; although nonetheless it is not there as if properly in a place, but sacramentally, and in that manner of existing which—although we can hardly express it in words—nonetheless after our spirit is enlightened by the lights of faith, we can conceive as possible for God, and which we are obliged to believe very firmly. For in truth, the church has never taught (at least that I know), that the <term>species</term> <note>In this context, "species" refers to the outward appearances (taste, smell, color) of the bread and wine that remain after the substance has changed.</note> of bread and wine that remain in the sacrament of the Eucharist are <term>real accidents</term> <note>A "real accident" was a philosophical concept suggesting that a property, like the color red, could exist as a "thing" even if the object it belonged to was gone. Descartes argues this is unnecessary and confusing.</note> which subsist miraculously all on their own after the substance to which they were attached has been removed.

But because perhaps the first theologians who undertook to explain this question by the reasons of <term>natural philosophy</term> <note>The historical term for what we now call science, particularly the study of the physical world.</note> were so strongly persuaded that these accidents which touch our senses were something real, different from the substance, that they did not even think one could ever doubt it, they had supposed—without any valid reason, and without having thought much about it—that the species of bread were real accidents of this nature; following which they put all their study into explaining how these accidents can subsist without a subject. In which they found so many difficulties that this alone should have made them judge that they had turned away from the right path, just as travelers do when some path has led them to places full of thorns and inaccessible. For, first, they seem to contradict themselves (at least those who hold that objects only move our senses by means of contact), when they suppose that something else is still required in objects to move...

<summary>Descartes argues that his physical theory—defining the "species" of the Eucharist as the surface boundary of the object—aligns better with Church doctrine than the traditional scholastic reliance on "real accidents." He asserts that all sensation is fundamentally a form of touch and that the "species" are simply what is required for the senses to be affected.</summary>

Furthermore, the human mind cannot conceive that the <term>accidents</term> <note>In traditional philosophy, "accidents" are properties like color, smell, or taste that "happen" to a thing but are not its essential nature (substance).</note> of the bread are real, and that they nevertheless exist without its substance, unless it conceives of them in the manner of substances: so that there seems to be a contradiction if the entire substance of the bread is changed—as the church believes—and yet something real remains that was previously in the bread; because one cannot conceive of anything real remaining except that which subsists, and even though we call it an accident, we nevertheless conceive of it as a substance.

And it is in effect the same thing as if one were to say that, in truth, all the substance of the bread is changed, but that nevertheless that part of its substance which we call a "real accident" remains: in which words, if there is no contradiction, certainly in the concept there appears to be much. But who could deny that when it is permitted—and when no reason, neither theological nor even philosophical, obliges us to embrace one opinion rather than another—we should primarily choose those that cannot give occasion nor pretext to anyone to distance themselves from the truths of the faith? 

Now, that the opinion which admits "real accidents" does not accommodate itself to the reasons of theology, I think that is seen here clearly enough; and that it is entirely contrary to those of philosophy, I hope soon to demonstrate evidently in a treatise on principles <note>This refers to his *Principles of Philosophy*, published in 1644.</note> which I intend to publish, and to explain there how color, flavor, weight, and all the other qualities that touch our senses, depend only in that regard on the external surface of bodies. Moreover, one cannot suppose that accidents are real without adding—to the miracle of <term>transsubstantiation</term> <note>The doctrine that the substance of bread and wine changes into the body and blood of Christ.</note>, which alone can be inferred from the words of <term>consécration</term>—a new and incomprehensible miracle without necessity, by which these real accidents exist in such a way in the substance of bread that they are not themselves made of substances: this repugns not only human reason, but even the axiom of the <term>théologiens</term> <note>Specifically, Catholic Scholastic theologians.</note> who say that the words of consecration operate nothing [other than] what they signify, and who do not want...

one should not attribute to a miracle those things that can be ex-

entirely removed by the explanation I give to these
things. For so far from it being the case, according to the explanation I
give, that there is a need for some miracle to preserve the
<term>accidents</term> <note>Sensible qualities like color, taste, and smell.</note> after the substance of the bread is removed; on
the contrary, without a new miracle (namely, one by which the
dimensions were changed) they could not be removed.
And history teaches us that this has sometimes
happened, when instead of the consecrated bread there appeared flesh
or a small child in the hands of the priest: for never
has it been believed that this happened by a cessation of the miracle,
but it has always been attributed to a new miracle.
Furthermore, there is nothing in this that is incomprehensible or
difficult: that God, the creator of all things, can change
one substance into another, and that this latter substance
remains precisely beneath the same <term>surface</term> <note>Descartes argues that we don't perceive the "inside" of a thing, only the boundary where it touches our senses.</note> in which the
first was contained. Nor can anything be said that is more
conformable to reason, or more commonly received
by philosophers, than that not only every sensation,
but generally every action of one body upon another,
occurs through contact, and that this contact can only be at the
surface: from which it follows evidently that the same surface
must always act or be acted upon in the same way, whatever
change occurs in the substance that it covers.

This is why, if I am permitted here to tell the truth without
envy, I dare to hope that the time will come when this opi-
nion, which admits "real accidents," will be rejected by
theologians as unsafe for the faith, repugnant to rea-
son, and entirely incomprehensible, and that mine will be
received in its place as certain and indubitable. This
I believed I should not hide here, in order to prevent as much
as possible for me the calumnies of those who, wishing to
appear more learned than others, and being unable to suffer
that anyone propose any opinion different from theirs that is
esteemed true and important, are accustomed to say that it
is repugnant to the truths of faith, and try to abolish by autho-
rity what they cannot refute by reason. But I appeal
from their sentence to that of good and orthodox theologians,
to the judgment and censure of whom I shall sub-
mit myself always very willingly.

# FIFTH OBJECTIONS
## MADE BY MR. GASSENDI AGAINST THE SIX MEDITATIONS.

->*Mr. Gassendi to Mr. Descartes.*<-

**SIR,**

The Reverend Father Mersenne <note>Marin Mersenne (1588–1648) was a monk and mathematician who acted as a central hub for scientific and philosophical correspondence in 17th-century Europe.</note> has done me a great favor by sharing these sublime Meditations you have written regarding <term>first philosophy</term> <note>Metaphysics: the branch of philosophy that deals with the first principles of things, including abstract concepts such as being, knowing, substance, and cause.</note>; for truly, the grandeur of the subject, the strength of the thoughts, and the purity of your style have pleased me extraordinarily. Indeed, to tell the truth, it is with great pleasure that I see you working so successfully, with such wit and courage, toward the advancement of the sciences, and that you are beginning to reveal to us things that have remained unknown to all past centuries. 

Only one thing has troubled me: that he desired of me that, if after reading your Meditations any doubts or hesitations remained in my mind, I should write to you about them. For I judged well that I would reveal nothing other than the deficiency of my own mind if I did not agree with your reasons—or rather my <term>temerity</term> <note>Rashness or excessive boldness.</note>, if I dared to propose the slightest thing against them. Nevertheless, I could not refuse the requests of my friend, thinking that you will take in good part a project that comes more from him than from me, and knowing, moreover, that you are so kind that you will easily believe I had no other thought than to simply propose my doubts and difficulties to you. 

And certainly, it will be quite enough if you have the patience to read them from one end to the other. For as for thinking that they ought to move you, or give you the slightest distrust of your reasonings, or oblige you to waste time responding to them that you should better employ elsewhere—I am far from such a thought and would not advise it. I would not even dare to propose them to you without blushing, being certain that there is not one among them which has not passed through your mind many times, and which you have not either expressly dismissed or judged should be left aside. I propose them, then, but with no other design than that of a simple proposition, which I make

## AGAINST THE FIRST MEDITATION.

### *Of things that can be called into doubt.*

Regarding the First Meditation, there is no need for me to dwell on it much; for I approve of the plan you have taken to rid yourself of all kinds of prejudices. There is only one thing I do not well understand, which is to know why you did not prefer simply, and in few words, to hold all the things you had known until then as uncertain, in order afterwards to set aside those you would recognize as true, rather than holding them all as false—not so much stripping yourself of an old prejudice as clothing yourself in a completely new one. And notice how it was necessary, to obtain this from yourself, to imagine a deceiving God, or some sort of <term>evil genius</term> <note>original: "mauvais génie." In Descartes’ philosophy, this is a hypothetical powerful being who exerts all its power to deceive the mind, used as a tool for radical doubt.</note> who employed all his industry to deceive you, although it seems that it would have been enough to cite as the reason for your mistrust the limited light of the human mind and the mere weakness of nature. Besides this, you pretend that you are sleeping, so that you may have the occasion to call all things into doubt, and so that you might take for illusions everything that happens here below. 

But can you, for all that, exert enough power over yourself as to believe that you are not awake, and that all the things that are and that pass before your eyes are false and deceitful? Whatever you say about it, no one will be convinced that you are fully persuaded that there is nothing true in all that you have ever known: and that the senses, or sleep, or God, or an evil genius have continually imposed upon you. Would it not have been something more worthy of the candor of a philosopher and the zeal for truth to state things simply, in good faith, and as they are, rather than, as one might object to you, resorting to this <term>artifice</term> <note>original: "machine." Gassendi uses this word to imply an elaborate or artificial rhetorical device, similar to a "deus ex machina" in theater.</note>, forging these illusions, seeking these detours and these novelties? Nevertheless, since you have found it good thus, I will not contest it further.

<summary>Pierre Gassendi begins his critique by questioning Descartes' method of "radical doubt," arguing that it is unnecessarily theatrical and artificial to pretend everything is false or to invent an "evil genius" when simply acknowledging human fallibility would suffice.</summary>

# FIFTH OBJECTIONS

## AGAINST THE SECOND MEDITATION.

### *On the nature of the human mind; and that it is easier to know than the body.*

1. Regarding the second [Meditation], I see that you are not yet out of your enchantment and illusion, and nonetheless that through these phantoms you still perceive that at the very least it is true that you, who are thus charmed and enchanted, are something; this is why you conclude that this proposition, *I am, I exist* <note>original: "je suis, j'existe"</note>, every time you utter it, or conceive it in your mind, is necessarily true. But I do not see that you had any need for such a grand apparatus <note>The "apparatus" refers to the elaborate mental exercise of doubting everything, including the senses and mathematics.</note>, since you were already otherwise certain of your existence, and you could have inferred the same thing from any other of your actions, it being manifest by the <term>natural light</term> <note>original: "lumière naturelle." In 17th-century philosophy, this refers to the innate human capacity for reason, which allows one to recognize fundamental truths without external help.</note> that everything that acts, is, or exists.

You add to this that nevertheless you do not yet know well enough what you are: I know that you say this in earnest, and I grant it to you very willingly, for it is in this that the entire knot of the difficulty consists; and, in effect, this was all you needed to investigate without so many detours and without employing all this supposition.

Following this, you propose to examine what you have thought yourself to be until now, so that after having stripped away everything that can admit the slightest doubt, nothing remains but what is certain and unshakable. Certainly, you can do this with everyone's approval. Having attempted this fine design and then finding that you have always believed yourself to be a man, you ask yourself this question: *What then is a man?* Or rather, after having deliberately rejected the ordinary definition, you stop at the things that formerly presented themselves to you at first glance; for example, that you have a face, hands, and all these other members that you called by the name of body; as also that you are nourished, that you walk, that you feel, and that you think, all of which you attributed to the soul. I grant you all of this, provided that we guard ourselves against the distinction you place between the mind and the body. You say that you did not stop then to think about what the soul was, or else if you did stop, that you imagined it was something very subtle, similar to wind, fire, or air, infused and spread throughout the grosser parts of your body: this certainly is worthy of remark; but as for the body, you in no way doubted that it was a...

...It seemed to me, you say, that I felt several things while sleeping that I have since recognized I did not feel at all. ...do not depend at all on the <term>rational soul</term><note>In Aristotelian philosophy, the "rational soul" is the highest part of the soul unique to humans, responsible for reason, as opposed to the "vegetative" or "sensitive" souls shared with plants and animals.</note>, and that they can be exercised before it is introduced into the body, just as they are exercised every day in beasts, which you maintain have no reason at all. Be that as it may, I am quite willing for you to be called *a mind* from now on, and for you to be precisely nothing but *a thing that thinks*.

You add that thought alone cannot be separated from you. One cannot deny you this, especially if you are nothing but a mind—and if you do not wish to admit any other distinction between the substance of the soul and your own than that which is called in the schools a <term>distinction of reason</term><note>A scholastic term referring to a distinction that exists only in our minds/concepts, rather than a "real" distinction between two different objects in the world.</note>. However, I hesitate, and do not know well if, when you say *that thought is inseparable from you*, you mean that, as long as you exist, you never cease to think. Certainly this has much in common with that thought of some ancient philosophers who, to prove that the human soul is <term>immortal</term><note>original: "immortelle"</note>, said that it was in a continual motion—that is to say, in my view, that it always thought. And therefore, it is no wonder if the things that present themselves and strike the senses themselves make a stronger impression on the mind than those that the mind figures and represents to itself based on the model and occasion of things that have touched its senses. For not only do they manifest themselves by several different operations, but besides that, they make themselves known by several <term>accidents</term><note>In this context, "accidents" are the observable properties or qualities of a thing (like its color or smell) that are not part of its essential nature.</note> that are very sensible and very evident, such as by size, shape, solidity, color, flavor, etc. So, although they are outside of you, one should not be surprised if you know and understand them more distinctly than yourself. But, you say, I have my seat in the brain; and there, without changing my dwelling, I receive all that is reported to me by the <term>spirits</term><note>Descartes and his contemporaries believed in "animal spirits," a very subtle fluid that flowed through the nerves to carry sensory information to the brain and motor commands to the muscles.</note> that flow along the nerves: and thus, properly speaking, the sensation that is said to occur throughout the whole body is made and accomplished in me. I grant this; but there are likewise nerves in animals, there are spirits, there is a brain, and in that brain there is a knowing principle which receives in the same way that which is reported to it by the spirits, and which finishes and completes the sensation. You will say that this principle is nothing other in the brains of animals than what we call <term>fantasy</term><note>From the Greek "phantasia," referring to the faculty of the mind that produces or stores mental images.</note>, or else the imaginative faculty. I asked you just now for an argument or a certain mark by which you might make us know that you are something other than a human fantasy, but I do not think that you can bring any. I know well that you could show us operations much more elevated than those performed by animals: but just as man, though he be the noblest and most perfect of animals, is nevertheless not removed from the number of **animals**; so although this proves very well that you are the most excellent of all fantasies or imaginations, you will nonetheless always be deemed to be of their number. And if you wish, beyond that, to infer something from this perception of the **substance** of the wax, you can conclude nothing else but that, just as we conceive of this substance only very confusedly, and as a "certain I-know-not-what," similarly the mind can only be conceived in this way; so that one can in all truth repeat here what you said elsewhere: *this I-know-not-what of yourself.*

You conclude: *but finally here I have imperceptibly returned to where I intended, for since it is now a thing known to me that the mind and even bodies are not properly conceived by the senses or by the imaginative faculty, but by the understanding alone, and that they are not known from being seen or touched, but only from being understood, or well-grasped by thought, I know very clearly that there is nothing easier for me to know than my mind.* This is well said by you; but as for me, I do not see how you can infer that one can clearly know anything else about your mind except that it exists. This is why I also do not see that what was promised by the very title of this meditation—namely, that through it the human mind would be made easier to know than the body—has been accomplished. For your design was not to prove the existence of the human mind, or that its existence is clearer than that of the body, since it is certain that no one doubts its existence; you undoubtedly wanted to make its nature more manifest than that of the body, and nevertheless I do not see that you have done so in any way. In speaking of the nature of the body, you

# FIFTH OBJECTIONS

you said yourself, O mind <note>original: "ô esprit"; Gassendi addresses Descartes as "O mind" or "O spirit" throughout this section to mock Descartes' insistence that he is nothing but a thinking thing.</note>, that we know many things about it <note>Referring to the body or the physical wax discussed on the previous page.</note>, such as extension, shape, motion, the occupation of space, etc. But what have you said about yourself? Except that you are not a collection of bodily parts, nor air, nor a wind, nor a thing that walks or senses, etc. But even if we granted you all these things (though you have nonetheless refused some of them), it is still not what we were expecting. For in truth, all these things are only negations, and we are not asking you to tell us what you are *not*, but rather to teach us what you *are*.

That is why you finally say that *you are a thing that thinks, that is to say, which doubts, affirms, denies, etc.*

But first, saying that you are *a thing* is not saying anything known, for this word is a general term—vague, broad, indeterminate—and it applies to you no more than to everything else in the world, and to everything that is not pure nothingness.

You are a thing, which is to say you are not nothing; or to put it in other words that mean the same thing, you are something. But a stone is also not nothing, or if you prefer, it is something; and a fly likewise, and everything else in the world.

Furthermore, saying that you are *a thing that thinks* is indeed saying something known, but it was not previously unknown, nor was it what was being asked of you: for who doubts that you are a thing that thinks?

But what we do not know, and what we therefore desire to learn, is to know and penetrate the interior of this **substance** <term>Substance: In 17th-century philosophy, the underlying reality or "stuff" that supports properties like thinking or shape.</term> whose property is thinking. Therefore, since this is what we seek, you should conclude not just that you are a thing that thinks, but rather what is this thing that has the property of thinking?

What then! If one asked you to give us a knowledge of wine more exact and more elevated than the common sort, would you think you had satisfied the request by saying that wine is a liquid thing, pressed from grapes, which is sometimes white and sometimes red, which is sweet, which intoxicates, etc.?

But would you not rather try to discover and reveal as much as possible the interior of its substance, showing how this substance is composed of spirits <note>original: "esprits ou eaux-de-vie"; here referring to the volatile chemical essence of a substance.</note>, of **phlegm** <note>In early modern chemistry, the watery, tasteless part of a substance.</note>, of **tartar** <note>The acidic sediment found in wine, then considered one of its primary chemical building blocks.</note>, and of several other parts mixed together in a precise proportion and balance?

Thus, since we expect from you—and you promise us—a knowledge of yourself more exact than the ordinary, you can see that it is not enough to tell us, as you do, that you are a thing that thinks, doubts, understands, etc.,

## AGAINST THE THIRD MEDITATION.

### *Of God; that he exists.*

1. *First, from the fact that you have recognized that the clear and distinct knowledge of this proposition,* I am a thinking thing, *is the cause of the certainty you have of it, you infer that you can establish as a general rule, that the things we conceive very clearly and very distinctly are all true.* But, although until now no more assured rule of our certainty could have been found amidst the obscurity of human affairs, nevertheless, seeing that so many great minds—who seem to have been destined to know several things very clearly and very distinctly—have judged that the truth was hidden in the heart of God himself or in the depths of the abyss <note>This is a reference to the ancient philosopher Democritus, who famously claimed that "truth lies at the bottom of a well."</note>, is there not reason to suspect that this rule might be false? And certainly, after what the skeptics <note>The Skeptics were a school of philosophy that argued human beings can never reach absolute certainty about the nature of reality, only about how things appear to them.</note> say, whose arguments you are not unaware of, what truth can we answer for as a thing clearly known, except that it is true that things appear as they appear to each person? 

For example, I feel manifestly and distinctly that the flavor of the melon is very pleasant to my taste; therefore it is true that the flavor of the melon appears to me in this way. But for that to make it true that the flavor is such *within* the melon itself, how could I believe it—I, who in my youth, and in a state of perfect health, judged it quite differently, because I then manifestly felt another flavor in the melon? I even see even now that several people judge it differently: I see that several animals who have a very exquisite sense of taste and very vigorous health have different sensations than mine. Is it then that the truth is repugnant <note>In this context, "repugnant" means "incompatible" or "self-contradictory."</note> and is opposed to itself, or rather is it not that a thing is not true in itself, even though it is conceived clearly and distinctly? But rather, that it is true only that it is thus clearly and distinctly conceived. It is almost the same...

And thus the idea of God does indeed represent all these things, but it does not for that reason have more objective reality than finite things taken all together have—from the ideas of which this idea of God was composed, and afterward enlarged in the manner I have just described. # FIFTH OBJECTIONS

...only from something outside of yourself. Furthermore, what is there in these ideas that you could not have formed and composed yourself from the things you have previously seen and learned? Certainly, if you conceived God as he is, you would be right to believe that you had been instructed and taught by God himself; but all these attributes that you give to God are nothing other than a collection of certain perfections that you have noticed in some men or in other creatures, which the human mind is capable of extending, joining together, and amplifying as it pleases, as has already been observed several times.

You say that, *although you can have the idea of substance from yourself because you are a substance, you cannot nevertheless have from yourself the idea of infinite substance because you are not infinite.* <note>In 17th-century philosophy, a "substance" refers to a thing that can exist by itself, such as a physical body or a mind.</note> But you are greatly mistaken if you think you have the idea of an infinite substance; this idea can only exist in you by name alone, and in the way that men are able to understand the infinite—which is, in effect, to not understand it at all. Thus, it is not necessary that such an idea emanated from an infinite substance, since it can be formed by joining together and amplifying the perfections that the human mind is capable of conceiving, as has already been said. Unless, perhaps, you mean to say that when the ancient philosophers—by multiplying the ideas they had of this visible space, of this world, and of the few principles of which it is composed—formed the ideas of an infinitely extended world, an infinity of principles, and an infinity of worlds, they did not form these ideas by the power of their own thought, but that these ideas were sent into their minds by a world truly infinite in its extension, by a true infinity of principles, and by an infinity of actually existing worlds.

As for what you say—that *you conceive the infinite by a true idea*—certainly, if it were true, it would represent the infinite to you as it is in itself, and consequently you would understand what is most essential to it and what is currently at issue, namely infinity itself. But your thought always ends at something finite, and you say nothing but the mere name of "infinite," because you cannot understand what is beyond your comprehension; so much so that one can rightly say that you only conceive the infinite through the mere negation of the finite. <note>Gassendi argues here for "Empiricism": the belief that all our ideas come from sensory experience. He suggests "infinite" is just a word we use to say "not-finite," rather than a positive concept we truly understand.</note> And it is not enough to say that *you conceive more reality in an infinite substance than in a finite one*; for it would...

<summary>Gassendi argues that the human idea of God is not "divinely implanted," but rather a mental construction made by amplifying human perfections and negating the concept of limits. He challenges Descartes' claim that we have a clear and "true" understanding of infinity.</summary>

# FIFTH OBJECTIONS

In fact, to speak truly, you do not conceive of any more reality, insofar as you only extend finite substance; then you imagine that there is more reality in what is thus enlarged and extended by your thought than in that same thing when it is shortened and not extended—unless you also want those philosophers <note>Gassendi likely refers here to the Epicureans or other ancient atomists who theorized an infinite number of worlds.</note> to have indeed conceived of more reality when they imagined several worlds than when they conceived of only one. And on this point, I will remark, in passing, that the reason why our mind becomes more confused the more it increases and amplifies some kind of species or idea <term>species: in 17th-century philosophy, this refers to the mental representation or "image" of an object used by the mind to understand it</term> is because it then displaces this species from its natural state, removes the distinction of its parts, and stretches it in such a way—making it so thin and delicate—that it finally vanishes and dissipates. I will not stop to say that the mind is similarly confused for an entirely opposite reason: namely, when it diminishes and shrinks too much an idea it had previously conceived under some sort of greatness.

You say that it does not matter that you cannot comprehend the infinite, nor even many things within it, but that it is enough for you to conceive of a few things clearly so that it may be true to say that you have a very true, very clear, and very distinct idea of it. Quite the contrary: it is not true that you have a true idea of the infinite, but rather only of the finite—if it is true that you do not understand the infinite, but only the finite. One could say at most that you know a part of the infinite, but not, for that reason, the infinite itself; just as one could certainly say that someone who had never seen anything but the opening of a cave <note>This is a subtle nod to Plato’s Allegory of the Cave, suggesting Descartes is mistaking a small shadow for the whole of reality.</note> would have knowledge of a part of the world, but one could not say that he would have the idea of the whole world. Thus, he would appear completely ridiculous if he persuaded himself that the idea of such a small portion was the true and natural idea of the whole world. 

But, you say, it is the nature of the infinite not to be understood by you, who are finite. Certainly, I believe so; but it is not the nature of a true idea of the infinite to represent only a very small part of it—or rather, nothing at all—since there is no proportion between this part and the whole. It is enough, you say, that you conceive of these few things very distinctly: yes, just as it is enough to see the tip of the hair of someone of whom one wishes to have a true idea. Would a painter not have failed if, to represent me faithfully on a canvas, he had only drawn one of my hairs, or even the tip of one of them? Now, it...

<meta>This page continues Pierre Gassendi’s systematic critique of René Descartes’ "Third Meditation." In the previous section, Gassendi argued that our human mind cannot truly grasp the infinite; he suggested that when we try to imagine "the infinite," we are merely stretching out finite concepts until they become blurry and vanish. He now concludes that point and moves to Descartes' claim that our awareness of our own "imperfection" implies a prior knowledge of a "perfect" being (God).</meta>

# FIFTH OBJECTIONS

...it is true, however, that there is a proportion not only much smaller, but even infinitely smaller, between everything we know of the infinite and the infinite itself than there is between one of my hairs—or even the very tip of one of them—and my whole body. In short, your entire reasoning proves nothing regarding God that it does not also prove regarding an infinity of worlds <note>Gassendi is likely referencing the "atomist" philosophers like Epicurus and Lucretius, who believed in an infinite number of universes. He is arguing that if Descartes' logic holds for God, it should also "prove" the existence of these infinite worlds.</note>. Indeed, it was much easier for those ancient philosophers to form and conceive ideas of such worlds through the clear and distinct knowledge they had of this current world, than it is for us to conceive of a God or an infinite Being through the knowledge of your "substance," <term>substance: in 17th-century philosophy, this refers to the fundamental "stuff" or essence that makes up a thing (like the "thinking stuff" of the mind)</term> the nature of which is not yet known to you.

8. After this, you make the following argument: *For how would it be possible for me to know that I doubt and that I desire—that is to say, that I lack something and that I am not entirely perfect—if I did not have in myself any idea of a being more perfect than my own, by comparison with which I might recognize my defects?* <note>Descartes argues that you can't know you are "less than" something unless you have a benchmark of "perfection" to compare yourself against.</note> But if you doubt something, if you desire something, or if you recognize that you lack some perfection, what is so marvelous about that? After all, you do not know everything, you are not present in all things, and you do not possess everything. You acknowledge, you say, that you are not perfectly complete; certainly, I believe you, and you can say so without envy and without doing yourself any wrong. Therefore, you conclude: *there exists something more perfect than I*. And why not?

However, that which you desire is not always more perfect in every respect than you are. For example, when you desire bread, that bread you desire is not more perfect in every way than you or your body; rather, it is only more "perfect" <note>In this context, "perfect" retains its Latin root *perfectus*, meaning "complete" or "finished." Gassendi is playing with the idea that bread "completes" the lack caused by hunger.</note> than the hunger or emptiness that is in your stomach. How then will you conclude that something more perfect than you exists? You do so by observing the universality of things, in which you, the bread, and all other things are contained. Since every part of the universe has some perfection in itself, and some parts serve to "perfect" or complete others, it is easy to conceive that there is more perfection in the "whole" than in any single part. Consequently, since you are only a part of this whole, you must necessarily recognize something more perfect than yourself.

In this way, you can possess within you the idea of a being more perfect than your own, and by comparing yourself to it, you recognize your defects. This is to say nothing of the fact that there may be other parts in this universe more perfect than you; if that is the case, you can desire what they have, and through comparison with them, your own defects can be recognized.

<summary>Gassendi challenges Descartes' "benchmark" argument, suggesting that our awareness of our own limits comes from comparing ourselves to the physical universe and our needs, rather than from an innate idea of an infinite God. He famously uses the "bread" analogy to show that we desire things to fill a lack, not because those things are inherently "more perfect" than our entire being.</summary>

# FIFTH OBJECTIONS

For you could have known a man who was stronger, healthier, more vigorous, better built, more learned, more moderate, and therefore more perfect than yourself; and it was not difficult for you to conceive the idea of him. By comparing yourself to this idea, you could recognize that you do not possess as much health, strength, or, in a word, as many perfections as he possesses.

A little later, you pose this objection to yourself: *but perhaps I am something more than I think, and all these perfections that I attribute to God are in some way in me potentially, even if they do not yet produce themselves or manifest through their actions—as might happen if my knowledge increases more and more to infinity. But to this you reply: even if it were true that my knowledge acquired new degrees of perfection every day, and that there were many things in me potentially <term>potentially: from the Latin 'potentia,' meaning a capacity or power to become something that is not yet fully realized</term> which are not yet there actually, nevertheless none of this belongs to the idea of God, in which nothing is found merely potentially, but everything is there actually <term>actually: from the Latin 'actus,' meaning something fully realized or in its final, completed state</term> and in effect; and indeed, is it not an infallible argument of imperfection in my knowledge that it increases little by little and grows by degrees?* 

But one can reply to this that while it is quite true that the things you conceive in an idea are "actually" present within that same idea, they are not, because of that, "actually" present in the thing itself of which it is the idea. Thus, an architect imagines the idea of a house, which is truly composed "actually" of walls, floors, roofs, windows, and other parts according to the design he has made; yet neither the house nor any of its parts exist "actually" yet, but only "potentially." In the same way, the idea that the ancient philosophers <note>Gassendi is likely referring to the Atomists like Epicurus, who proposed that space is infinite and contains an infinite number of worlds.</note> had of an infinity of worlds contains, in effect, infinite worlds; but you would not say because of that that these infinite worlds actually exist. Therefore, whether there is something in you "potentially" or whether there is nothing at all, it is enough that your idea or knowledge can increase and grow by degrees, and one must not infer from this that what is represented or known by that idea exists "actually." 

Regarding what you remark after this—namely, that your knowledge will never be actually infinite—this must be granted to you without contest. But you must also know that you will never have a true and natural idea of God; there will always remain much more (and even infinitely more) for you to know of Him than of someone of whom you have seen only the very tip of their hair. For I am willing to grant that you have not seen this man in his entirety; nonetheless, you have...

And it is also not necessary that this mark be something different from this same work: but from this alone that God created me, it is very credible that he produced me in some way in his image and likeness, and that I conceive this resemblance in which the idea of God is contained by the same faculty by which I conceive myself—that is, when I reflect upon myself, not only do I know that I am an imperfect, incomplete, and dependent thing on another, which incessantly tends and aspires toward something better and greater than I am, but I also know at the same time that he on whom I depend possesses in himself all these great things toward which I aspire, and of which I find the ideas in me—not indefinitely and only potentially, but that he enjoys them in fact, actually and infinitely, and thus that he is God.*

Certainly all these things are very specious <note>In this context, "specious" means something that looks attractive or plausible on the surface but may lack a solid logical foundation.</note> and very beautiful, and I do not say that they are not true: but I would still like to ask you from what antecedents you deduce them? For, to stop no longer on what I objected previously, if it is true that the idea of God is in us like the mark of the craftsman impressed upon his work, tell me, I pray you, what is the manner of this impression? What is the form of this mark? And how do you make the discernment of it? For if it is not different from the work or from the <term>thing itself</term> <note>original: "chose même"; referring to the human being or soul as the creation of God.</note>, then you yourself are nothing but an idea; you are nothing else but a mode or way of thinking? Are you both the mark impressed and the subject of the impression? You say *that this is very believable, because he created you.* On the contrary, for that very reason it is unbelievable. For the work is never similar to the workman, except when it is engendered by him through a communication of nature <note>Gassendi is using a scholastic distinction: a child is "engendered" and shares its father’s human nature, but a table is "created" and does not share the nature of the carpenter.</note>. And even that is understood assuming that you were created by God, which you have not yet proven. You conceive, you say, *this resemblance, in the same way that you conceive that you are an incomplete, dependent thing, and one that aspires constantly to greater and better things.* But why is this not rather a mark of dissimilarity, since God, on the contrary, is most perfect, most independent, and most self-sufficient, being most great and most good? 

Not to mention that when you conceive of yourself as dependent, you do not for that reason immediately conceive that the one on whom you depend is anyone other than your parents; or if you do conceive that he is someone else, there is no reason why you should believe yourself to be like him. Not to mention also that it is strange why the rest of men—or, if you prefer, of minds—do not conceive the same thing as you, especially since there is no reason to believe that God has not imprinted the idea of himself upon them as he has done in you. And certainly this alone is more than enough to show that it is not an idea imprinted by the hand of God, seeing as if that were the case, all men would have it imprinted in the same way in their minds and would conceive of God in the same way and under the same form; everyone would attribute the same things to him, everyone would have the same feelings about him; and yet we clearly see the opposite. But that is already more than enough regarding this matter.

-># FIFTH OBJECTIONS<-

this distinction is subtle enough, it nonetheless does not entirely satisfy. For, although God does not concur <note>In 17th-century philosophy, "concurrence" refers to the idea that God must continuously support and cooperate with every action of a created being for it to happen.</note> in the privation found in the act—which is precisely what we call error and falsehood—He nonetheless concurs in the act itself; without His concurrence, there would be no privation at all. Furthermore, He is Himself the author of the power that is mistaken or that errs, and consequently, He is the author of an impotent power. Thus, it seems that the defect encountered in the act should not be referred so much to the power itself, which is inherently weak and powerless, but to the one who is its author. Having been able to make it powerful, or even more powerful than was necessary, He willed to make it as it is. 

Certainly, just as one does not blame a locksmith for not having made a large key to open a small cabinet, but rather for having made a small one with an improper or difficult shape for opening it; so, in truth, it is not a fault in God that, in wanting to give a <term>faculty of judgment</term> <note>The mental ability to decide if something is true or false.</note> to a puny creature such as man, He did not give him one so great that it could suffice to understand everything, or most things, or the highest and most elevated things. But without doubt, there is reason to wonder why, among the few things He willed to submit to man’s judgment, there is almost none where the power He gave him does not prove to be short, uncertain, and powerless.

3. After this, you investigate *where your errors come from and what their cause might be*. And first, I do not dispute here why you call the *understanding* the *only faculty of knowing ideas*—that is, the power to apprehend things simply and without any affirmation or negation—and why you call the *will*, or *free choice*, the *faculty of judging*—that is, that to which it belongs to affirm or deny, to give consent or to refuse it. I only ask why you restrict the understanding within certain limits, while you give none to the will or to the freedom of choice? For, to tell the truth, these two faculties seem to be of equal extent, or at the very least the understanding seems to have as much extent as the will, since the will cannot move toward any thing that the understanding has not previously foreseen.

I said that the understanding had at least as much extent: for it even seems that it extends further than the will, seeing that not only does our will or free choice not move toward anything, and we give no judgment, and consequently make no choice, and have no love or aversion for whatever

Regarding this, it is not only true but also such that the whole preceding Meditation—without which this could have been understood—seems to have been useless and superfluous. For you will notice that we objected to you from the beginning that very often we are mistaken, even when it seems to us that we know a thing so clearly and distinctly that we do not think we could know anything more clearly or distinctly. You even raised this objection to yourself, and yet we are still waiting for this rule or this method, which it seems to me you should primarily work on.

It is a resemblance, I say, of singular natures, regarding which the understanding has taken the occasion to form a concept, or idea, or form of a "common nature," from which nothing must deviate if it is to be a man.

This being thus explained, I say the same of your triangle or of its nature; for it is quite true that the triangle you have in your mind is like a rule that serves you to examine whether something should be called by the name of "triangle"; but one must not, for that reason, think that this triangle is something real, or a true nature existing outside of the understanding, since it is the mind alone that has formed it upon the model of material triangles that the senses have made it perceive, and from which it has gathered all the...

Therefore, it seems, it should have been said either that omnipotence, for example, can no more be separated from the essence of God than that equality of the magnitude of its angles can be separated from the essence of the triangle; or else that existence can no more be separated from the essence of God than existence can be separated from the essence of the triangle. For in this way, both comparisons would have been well made, and not only would the first have been granted to you, but also the last; and nevertheless, this would not have been a convincing proof of the necessary existence of a God, any more than it follows necessarily that there is any triangle in the world, even though its essence and its existence are indeed inseparable, whatever division our mind might make of them—that is, even though the mind conceives of them separately; in the same way that it can also separately conceive of the essence and the existence of God.

It must then be noted that you place <term>existence</term> <note>The state of being or reality.</note> among the divine perfections, and yet you do not place it among those of a triangle or a mountain, even though it is just as much—and according to the manner of being of each—the perfection of the one as of the other. a singular perfection and merely one among others, but only as a form or an act by which the thing itself and its perfections exist, and without which neither the thing nor its perfections would be at all.

From this it follows that we do not say that existence is "in" a thing as a perfection; nor, if a thing lacks existence, do we say it is "imperfect" or deprived of a perfection, so much as we say it is nothing, or that it does not exist at all.

This is why, just as in counting the perfections of a triangle you do not include existence, nor do you conclude from them that the triangle exists, so too in your enumeration of God's perfections you ought not to have included existence to conclude from there that God exists—unless you wished to take as a proven fact the very thing that is being disputed, and turn the question itself into a starting principle. <note>Gassendi is accusing Descartes of "begging the question" (*petitio principii*): assuming that God exists in the definition of God, and then using that definition to "prove" he exists.</note>

Gassendi argues that once a specific person dies, their "essence" doesn't linger in reality; it only remains as a concept in our minds.</note>

But it was not very difficult for you to solve a sophism that you invented yourself, especially since you used such a manifest contradiction—namely, that "an existing God does not exist"—and did not treat the horse or the mountain in the same way (that is, as "existing").

But if, just as you included the valley with the mountain and the wings with the horse in your comparison, you had likewise considered God alongside knowledge, power, or other attributes, then the difficulty would have been complete and quite well-established. It would then have been up to you to explain to us how it can be that we can conceive of a creeping mountain or a winged horse without thinking that they exist, and yet it is supposedly impossible to conceive of an all-knowing and all-powerful God without at the same time conceiving of Him as existing.

conceived, no contrary reason can be brought against me that would ever make me call it into doubt, and thus I have a true and certain <term>science</term> <note>In the 17th century, "science" referred to a systematic, demonstrated body of knowledge, rather than the modern experimental sciences.</note> of it; and this same science also extends to all the other things that I remember having formerly demonstrated, such as the truths of geometry and other similar matters.

To this, Sir, seeing that you speak so seriously, and believing also that you say it in all earnestness, I do not see that I have anything else to say except that it will be difficult for you to find anyone who is persuaded that you were formerly less assured of the truth of geometric demonstrations than you are now that you have acquired the knowledge of a God. For, in effect, these demonstrations are of such evidence and certainty that, without waiting for our deliberation, they pull consent from us by themselves, and once they are understood, they do not allow our mind to remain any longer in suspense regarding the belief it ought to have in them; so much so that I estimate you have as much reason not to fear in this the ruses of that <term>evil genius</term> <note>original: "mauvais génie." This refers to Descartes's famous skeptical hypothesis of a powerful being who might deceive him about even the simplest mathematical truths.</note> who tries incessantly to surprise you, as when you maintained so affirmatively that it was impossible for you to be mistaken regarding that antecedent and its consequence, *I think, therefore I am* <note>original: "je pense donc je suis," the French translation of the famous Latin "cogito ergo sum."</note>, even though at that time you were not yet assured of the existence of a God. And even though it be very true (as indeed there is nothing more true) that there is a God, who is the author of all things and who is not a deceiver: nevertheless, because that does not seem to be as evident as are the demonstrations of geometry (of which no other proof is needed except that there are several who call into question the existence of God, the creation of the world, and many other things which are said of God, and that not one calls into doubt the demonstrations of geometry), who will be he who can allow himself to be persuaded that these [geometric truths] borrow their evidence and their certainty from the others? And who can believe that Diagoras, Theodorus <note>Diagoras of Melos and Theodorus of Cyrene were famous atheists of antiquity, often cited in philosophical debates about the necessity of religious belief for moral or intellectual certainty.</note>, and all other similar atheists, cannot be made certain of the truth of these sorts of demonstrations? And finally, where will you find anyone who, being questioned on the certainty he has that in every right-angled triangle the square of the base is equal to the squares of the sides, would answer that he is assured of it because he knows that there is a God who cannot be a deceiver, and who is himself the author of this truth, and of all the things that are in the world? but rather, where is he who will not answer that he is assured of it because he knows that certainly, and that he is strongly persuaded of it by a most infallible demonstration?

### AGAINST THE SIXTH MEDITATION.

->*On the existence of material things,*<-

1. I dwell only on the fact that you distinguish here, once again, imagination from intellection <term>intellection</term> <note>Also called "pure understanding," this is the mind's ability to grasp abstract concepts (like the idea of a thousand-sided shape) without needing a mental picture.</note>, or pure conception. For, as I have already remarked before, these two operations seem to be the actions of the same faculty; and if there is some difference between them, it can only be a matter of degree. Indeed, take care, as I shall prove this by the very points you put forward.

You said previously that *to imagine is nothing other than to contemplate the figure or the image of a corporeal thing*, and here you agree that to conceive or to understand is to contemplate a triangle, a pentagon, a chiliogon <term>chiliogon</term> <note>A polygon with 1,000 sides.</note>, a myriagon <term>myriagon</term> <note>A polygon with 10,000 sides.</note>, and other similar things, which are figures of corporeal things. But we must observe here how, little by little and as if by degrees, the distinction is lost and the confusion increases. For it is certain that you will represent or imagine, or even conceive, a square more confusedly than a triangle, but more distinctly than a pentagon; and the latter more confusedly than a square, and more distinctly than a hexagon, and so on, until you can no longer propose anything clearly to yourself; and because then, whatever conception you have, it cannot be clear or distinct, you likewise neglect to make any effort of mind.

This is why, if, when you conceive a figure distinctly and with some noticeable effort, you wish to call this way of conceiving both an imagination and an intellection at once, and if, when your conception is confused and you conceive a figure with little or no mental effort, you wish to call that by the name of intellection alone, you will certainly be permitted to do so. But you will not find, for all that, that you have grounds to establish more than one kind of internal knowledge, for which it will always be merely an accidental thing whether you conceive some figure with more or less strength, or more or less distinctly. ### FIFTH OBJECTIONS

*You then say that the power of imagining within you, insofar as it differs from the power of conceiving, is not required for your essence—that is, the essence of your mind;* but how could this be, if both are but one and the same power or faculty, whose functions differ only by degree? You add that the mind, when imagining, turns toward the body, and when conceiving, it considers itself or the ideas it has within. Now, it is not my intention to argue here about the truth of our senses. For, although deception or <term>falsehood</term> <note>Gassendi is making a classic philosophical distinction: the senses themselves are passive and do not "lie"; rather, the mind makes an error when it interprets the data they provide.</note> is not strictly within the sense—which does not act, but simply receives images and reports them as they appear and as they must necessarily appear because of the disposition of the sense, the object, and the <term>medium</term> <note>The substance through which light or sound travels, such as air or water.</note>—but rather is in the judgment or in the mind, which does not apply all the required circumspection and does not take care that distant things, for the very reason that they are distant, or even for other causes, must appear to us smaller and more confused than when they are closer to us, and so on; nevertheless, from whatever side the error comes, one must admit that it exists. The only difficulty is knowing whether it is therefore true that we can never be certain of the truth of anything that the sense has made us perceive.

But certainly, I do not see that there is much need to trouble oneself with settling a question that so many daily examples decide so clearly. I answer only to what you say, or rather to what you object against yourself: it is quite certain that when we look closely at a tower and almost touch it with our hand, we no longer doubt that it is square, even though when we were a bit further away we had reason to judge that it was round, or at least to doubt whether it was square or round, or some other shape.

Similarly, that feeling of pain which seems to still be in the foot or the hand, even after those limbs have been severed from the body, may indeed sometimes deceive those whose limbs have been cut off—and this because of the <term>animal spirits</term> <note>In 17th-century physiology, these were thought to be very fine, active fluids that traveled through the nerves to transmit movement and sensation.</note> which used to be carried into those limbs and cause the sensation there; however, those who have all their limbs healthy and intact are so certain of feeling pain in the foot or the hand when a wound is still fresh and recent that it is impossible for them to doubt it.

Thus, although we might think that our nature is such that we could be mistaken even in things that seem most true to us, we also know that our nature allows us to know the truth. Just as we are sometimes mistaken—for example, when a <term>sophism</term> <note>A clever but false argument intended to deceive; a logical fallacy.</note> tricks us, or when a stick is halfway in the water <note>A reference to the "bent stick" illusion, where refraction makes a straight stick appear bent when submerged.</note>—so too do we sometimes know the truth, such as in geometric demonstrations or when seeing a stick that is out of the water. For these truths are so apparent that it is impossible for us to doubt them. And even if we had reason to distrust the truth of all our other knowledge, could we at least not doubt this: that all things appear to us exactly as they appear? It is impossible for it not to be absolutely true that they appear to us in this way. And although reason often turns us away from many things toward which nature seems to lead us, this does not take away the truth of the <term>phenomena</term> <note>From the Greek word for "appearances"; things as they appear to our senses rather than as they might be in themselves.</note>, nor does it prevent it being true that we see things as we see them. But this is not the place to consider how reason opposes the impulse of the senses, nor whether it is perhaps in the same way that the right hand might support the left when it lacks the strength to support itself, or if it is in some other manner.

3. This was undoubtedly the goal you were aiming for. Therefore, since it is in this that the main difficulty lies, it is necessary to stop here for a moment to see how you untangle yourself from it. First, we are dealing here with a distinction between the mind or soul of man and the body; but which body do you mean to speak of? Certainly, if I have understood correctly, it is that gross body which is composed of limbs; for these are your words: *I have a body to which I am joined;* and a little later: *it is certain that I, that is, my mind, is distinct from my body, etc.*

But I must caution you, O *spirit*, that the difficulty does not concern this massive and coarse body. That would be well and good if I were objecting to you according to the thought of certain philosophers who held that you were that perfection called by the Greeks <term>entelechy</term> <note>original: *ἐντελέχεια* (entelecheia). In Aristotelian philosophy, this refers to the "actuality" or "perfection" of a body that has life potentially.</note>, **the act**, **the form**, **the species**, or to speak in ordinary terms, **the mode** of the body. Truly, those who hold this view do not believe that you are any more distinct or separable from the body than its shape or any other of its modes. This remains true whether they consider you the entire soul of the human being, or a virtue or added power which the Greeks call a **potential understanding** <note>original: *νοῦς δυνάμει* (nous dynamei)</note> or a **passive understanding** <note>original: *νοῦς παθητικὸς* (nous pathetikos)</note>. But I wish to deal with you more generously, considering you as an **active understanding** <note>original: *νοῦς ποιητικὸν* (nous poietikon)</note> and even as something **separable** <note>original: *χωριστὸν* (chōriston)</note>, though in a different way than those philosophers imagined.

For those philosophers believed that this *active understanding* was common to all men (or even to all things in the world) and that it acted upon the *potential understanding*—to make it understand—in the same way that light acts upon the eye to make it see. This is why they were accustomed to compare it to the light of the sun, and consequently to regard it as something foreign and coming from without. For my part, I consider you instead (since I see that this pleases you) as a certain spirit or a **particular understanding** that rules within the body.

I repeat once more that the difficulty is not to know whether you are separable or not from this massive and coarse body (which is why I said a little earlier that it was not necessary to resort to the power of God to make those things separable which you conceive of separately), but rather to know whether you yourself are not some other body—perhaps a more subtle and refined body, diffused within this thick and massive body, or residing only in one of its parts. Furthermore, do not think you have shown us thus far that you are a purely spiritual thing that holds nothing of the body. When in the *second Meditation* you said *that you were not a wind, a fire, a vapor, or an air*, you must remember that I pointed out to you that you said this without any proof.

*You also said that you were not disputing those things in that place; but I do not see that you have treated them since, or that you have brought forward any reason to prove that you are not a body of this nature. I was still waiting for you to do so here; and nevertheless, if you say or prove anything, it is only that*

4. But, you say, *on the one hand I have a clear and distinct idea of myself, insofar as I am only a thinking thing, and not extended; and on the other, I have a distinct idea of the body, insofar as it is only an extended thing, and that it does not think at all.* But first, as for the idea of the body, it seems to me there is not much need to trouble ourselves: for if you said that of the idea of the body in general, I would be obliged to repeat here what I have already objected to you, namely, that you must first prove that thought cannot belong to the essence or the nature of the body. Thus we would fall back into our first difficulty, since the question is to know whether you, who think, are not perhaps a **subtle and refined body** <note>Gassendi is referring to the "animal spirits" or very fine matter that some contemporary materialist thinkers believed constituted the soul.</note>, as if it were a thing repugnant to the nature of the body to think.

But because in saying this you only mean to speak of this massive and coarse body, from which you maintain you are distinct and separable, I also somewhat agree that you can have an idea of the body; but supposing, as you say, that you are a thing which is not **extended** <term>extension</term> <note>In 17th-century philosophy, "extension" refers to the quality of taking up space—having length, width, and depth. Descartes defined matter as "extension."</note>, I absolutely deny that you could have an idea of it.

For, I pray you, tell us how you think that the **species** <note>original: *l'espèce*. In Scholastic philosophy, a "species" is the mental representation or image of an object that allows us to perceive it.</note>, or the idea of the body which is extended, can be received in you—that is to say, in a substance which is not extended? For either this species proceeds from the body, and in that case it is certain that it is corporeal and that its parts are outside of one another, and therefore that it is extended; or else it comes from elsewhere and makes itself felt by another way; however, because it is always necessary that it represent the body which is extended, it must also have parts, and thus be extended. Otherwise, if it has no parts, how will it be able to represent? If it has no extension, how will it be able to represent a thing which has it? If it is without shape, how will it make a shaped thing felt? If it has no position, how will it make us conceive of a thing that has parts, some high, others low, some to the right, others to the left, some in front, others behind, some curved, others straight; if it is without variety, how will it represent the variety of colors, etc. Therefore, the idea of the body is not entirely without extension, but if it has extension and you have none, how is it that you will be able to receive it? How will you be able to adjust and apply it to yourself? How will you make use of it? And how, finally, will you feel it little by little fade and vanish?

### FIFTH OBJECTIONS ###

Furthermore, regarding the idea of yourself, I have nothing to add to what I have already said, primarily regarding the Second Meditation. For by this it is clearly seen that it is far from the case that you have a **clear and distinct** idea of yourself; on the contrary, it seems you have none at all. For even though you certainly know that you think, you nevertheless do not know what kind of thing you are, you who think. Thus, although this single operation <note>The "operation" here refers to the act of thinking.</note> is clearly known to you, the principal matter is hidden: knowing what this **substance** <term>substance</term> <note>In 17th-century philosophy, a 'substance' is the underlying reality or "stuff" that possesses qualities or performs actions.</note> is which has thinking as one of its operations. 

Hence, it seems to me that I can very well compare myself to a blind man who, feeling heat and being warned that it comes from the sun, would think he had a clear and distinct idea of the sun; for if someone asked him what the sun is, he could answer that it is something that warms. But, you will say, I do not only say here that I am a thing that thinks; I also add that I am a thing that is not **extended** <term>extension</term> <note>Descartes defined physical matter as "extension," meaning it takes up space (length, width, and depth). To be "unextended" is to exist without taking up any space at all.</note>. 

However, without pointing out that this is something you assert without proof (though it is the very matter in question between us), tell me, I pray, do you think you have a clear and distinct idea of yourself for that reason? You say you are not an extended thing; certainly, I learn from this what you are *not*, but not what you *are*. What then! To have a clear and distinct idea of something—that is, a true and natural idea—is it not necessary to know the thing positively in itself, and so to speak, affirmatively? Is it enough to know that it is not such-and-such a thing? Would a person have a clear and distinct idea of **Bucephalus** <note>The famous warhorse of Alexander the Great, often used in logic examples of the time.</note> if they only knew at least that he was not a fly? 

But not to dwell on this further: you are then, you say, a thing that is not extended. But I ask you: are you not diffused throughout the whole body? Certainly, I do not know what you will have to answer, for although I considered you at the beginning as being only in the brain, that was nevertheless only by conjecture rather than a true belief that it was your opinion. I based my conjecture on those words which follow a little later, when you say that the soul does not receive the impression of all parts of the body immediately, but only from the brain, or perhaps even from one of its smallest parts <note>Descartes famously argued that the soul resides in the pineal gland, a tiny structure in the center of the brain, which he called the "seat of the soul."</note>. But I was not for that reason entirely certain if you were only in the brain, or even in one of its parts, seeing as you could be spread throughout the whole body and only feel in a single part, as we ordinarily say—

<summary>Gassendi argues that Descartes fails to define what the mind actually is, noting that defining something by what it is "not" (unextended) provides no real knowledge of its nature. He questions whether the mind is localized in the brain or diffused throughout the entire body.</summary>

If you say this, how, I pray you, do you understand it? Can one and the same thing be entirely in several places at once? I am willing to grant that faith teaches us this regarding the sacred mystery of the **Eucharist**; but here I am speaking of you; and besides the fact that you are a natural thing, we are examining things here only insofar as they can be known by **natural light** <term>natural light</term> <note>The 'natural light' refers to human reason and intellect, distinct from divine revelation.</note>. And, this being so, can one conceive that there are several places and yet not several things housed there? Are not a hundred places more than one? And if a thing is entirely in one place, can it be in others, unless it is outside of itself, just as that first place is outside the others? Answer this however you like, but at the very least it will be an obscure and uncertain thing to know if you are entirely in each part, or if you are not rather in each of the parts of your body according to each of the parts of yourself; and as it is much more manifest that nothing can be in several places at once, so it will always be more evident that you are not entirely in each part, but only a whole in the whole, and therefore that you are diffused through the whole body according to each of your parts, and thus that you are not without extension.

Let us now think that you are only in the **brain** <note>Descartes famously argued that the soul's primary seat was the pineal gland within the brain.</note> or even in one of its smallest parts: you see that the same problem always remains, because however small this part may be, it is nonetheless extended, and you as much as it: and therefore you are extended, and you have small parts that correspond to all of its parts. I cannot believe it, but suppose it were a point; nevertheless, if it is a **physical point** <term>physical point</term> <note>A 'physical point' refers to the smallest possible unit of matter that still possesses physical dimensions, unlike a mathematical point which is purely theoretical and dimensionless.</note>, the same...

But let us grant that it could be there and pass through; nevertheless, you—who exist thus in a point where there are neither countries nor regions, where there is nothing to the right or left, up or down—cannot discern from which direction things come or what report they give you.
