However, why should I linger here so long, since it is up to you to show us that you are a thing that has no extension, and consequently is not corporeal? And I do not think you wish to draw proof from what is commonly said—that man is composed of body and soul—as if one should conclude that because the name "body" is given to one part, the other should no longer be called so; for if that were the case, you would give me occasion to distinguish it in this way: Man is composed of two kinds of body, namely, a coarse one and a **subtle** <gloss>fine or gas-like</gloss> one, such that while the common name "body" is attributed to the first, one gives the other the name "soul" or "spirit." Besides, the same could be said of other animals, to whom I am sure you will not grant a spirit similar to yours: it will be quite enough for them if you leave them in possession of their soul <note>Descartes famously argued that animals were mere "automata" or machines without conscious minds. When you therefore conclude *that it is certain that you are distinct from your body*, you see well that this can easily be granted to you; but not that, for this reason, you are not corporeal at all, rather than being a kind of very subtle and very fine body, distinct from that other which is massive and coarse.

You add, and therefore that you can exist without it; but when one has granted you that you can exist without this coarse and heavy body—just as a fragrant vapor, leaving an apple, spreads through the air—what gain or advantage will you get from that? Certainly it will be a bit more than those philosophers I mentioned before intended, who believed that through death you were entirely annihilated, no more and no less than a shape that is so lost by the change of its surface that it exists no longer. For not being merely a **mode** <term>mode</term> <note>A "mode" is a quality or state of a substance. All of which things, however, I still object to you, not as doubting the conclusion you intended <note>Gassendi is careful to note that he agrees with Descartes' religious conclusion—that the soul is immortal—but he disagrees with the logical "proofs" Descartes uses to get there.</note>,

5. After this, you infer several other things which are consequences of this matter, upon each of which I do not wish to dwell. I only remark that you say that nature teaches you, through these feelings of pain, hunger, thirst, *etc.*, that you are not merely lodged in your body, ***just as a pilot in his ship*** <note>Descartes uses this famous analogy to argue that our relationship with our bodies is more intimate than a sailor's relationship with a boat; we don't just "observe" our body's damage, we "feel" it.</note>; but beyond that, you are most closely conjoined to it, and so **confused** <note>In this 17th-century context, "confused" refers to being "fused together" or "blended" (*confusio* in Latin), rather than being mentally muddled.</note> and mixed with it that you compose a single whole with it. For if this were not so, you say, when my body is wounded, I, who am only a thinking thing, would not feel pain because of it; but I would perceive this wound by the understanding alone, just as a pilot perceives by sight if something breaks in his vessel. And when my body needs to drink or eat, I would simply know that, even without being warned by confused feelings of hunger and thirst; for indeed these feelings of hunger, thirst, pain, *etc.*, are nothing other than certain confused ways of thinking, which depend upon and arise from the union and, so to speak, the mixture of the mind with the body.

To be sure, all of this is very well said, but it still remains to be explained how this conjunction and quasi-intermingling or confusion can apply to you, if it is true, as you say, that you are immaterial, indivisible, and without any **extension** <term>extension</term> <note>For Descartes, "extension" is the essential property of matter: the fact that it occupies space and has dimensions. Since the soul is "unextended," it has no size or location.</note>; for if you are no larger than a point, how are you joined and united to the whole body, which is of such notable size? How, at least, are you conjoined to the brain, or to one of its smallest parts, which—as I have said before—could not be so small that it lacks some size or extension? If you have no parts, how are you mixed or almost mixed with the most subtle parts of this matter with which you confess to be united, since there can be no mixture unless there are parts capable of being mixed with one another? And if you are entirely distinct, how are you confused with this matter, and do you compose a whole with it? And since every composition, conjunction, or union occurs only between parts, must there not be a certain proportion between these parts? But what proportion can be conceived between a corporeal thing and an incorporeal one? Can we understand how, for example, in a **pumice stone** <note>A porous volcanic rock. Gassendi uses it as an example of two physical substances (the stone and the air in its pores) being mixed, to show that even that requires both to be physical.</note>, the air and the stone are so mixed and united together that a true and natural composition results from it? And yet there is a greater proportion between the stone and the air, which are both bodies, than between the body and the mind, which is entirely immaterial.

<summary>Gassendi challenges Descartes' claim that the mind and body are "intermingled" into a single whole, arguing that an immaterial, spaceless soul could not possibly mix with a physical, extended body. He questions how something without parts or size could have any "proportion" or physical relationship with matter.</summary>

<header>FIFTH OBJECTIONS</header>

Furthermore, shouldn't every union occur through the very close and intimate contact of the two things joined? But, as I was saying just now, how can contact happen without a body? How can a physical thing embrace one that is <term>incorporeal</term> <note>Non-physical; something that does not take up space.</note>, so as to keep it united and joined to itself; or else, how can that which is incorporeal attach itself to what is physical, to be reciprocally united and joined to it, if there is nothing at all in the soul by which it can join itself to the body, or by which it can be joined to it? On this point, I pray you to tell me—since you admit yourself that you are subject to the feeling of pain—how do you think you are capable of this feeling, being of the nature and condition that you are (that is, incorporeal and <term>unextended</term>)? <note>In Cartesian philosophy, "extension" is the defining characteristic of matter—it takes up space. To be "unextended" means to have no length, width, or depth.</note> For the impression or feeling of pain, if I have understood it correctly, comes only from a certain "distraction" or separation of parts, which happens when something slides and wedges itself between those parts in such a way that it breaks the continuity that existed there before. And indeed, the state of pain is a certain state "against nature"; but how can a thing be put into a state against nature if, by its very nature, it is always uniform, simple, unchanging, indivisible, and incapable of receiving change? And since pain is an alteration—or at least never happens without alteration—how can a thing be altered if it is less divisible than a geometric point, and cannot be made into something else or cease to be what it is without being altogether annihilated? Moreover, when pain comes from the foot, the arm, and several other parts together, must there not be diverse parts within you in which you receive these feelings differently, for fear that this feeling of pain might be confused and seem to you to come from only a single part? But, to put it in a word, this general difficulty always remains: to know how that which is physical can make itself felt by, and have communication with, that which is not physical, and what proportion can be established between the one and the other.

6. I pass over in silence the other things you pursue quite amply and equally, to show that there is something else besides God and yourself that exists in the world. For firstly, you infer that you have a body and physical faculties, and furthermore that there are several other bodies around yours which send their <term>species</term> <note>original: "espèces"; a Scholastic term referring to the "images" or "sensory data" that objects were thought to transmit to our sense organs.</note> into the organs of your senses, and thus pass from there to you, which cause in you feelings of pleasure and pain that teach you what you must pursue and avoid regarding these bodies.

From all of these things, you finally draw this fruit,

<header>FIFTH OBJECTIONS</header>

What remains to be known is that since all the feelings you have usually report to you the truth rather than the false, regarding the conveniences or inconveniences of the body, you no longer have reason to fear that the things the senses show you every day are false. You say the same of the dreams that occur while you sleep; because they cannot be joined with all the other actions of your life, like the things that happen when you are awake, whatever truth is in your thoughts must inevitably be found in those you have while awake rather than in your dreams. *And since God is not a deceiver, it follows, you say, necessarily that you are not deceived in this, and that what appears so clearly to you while awake cannot but be entirely true.* Now, as your piety seems laudable to me in this, so must it be admitted that it is with great reason that you have finished your work with these words: *that the life of man is subject to many errors and that we must of necessity recognize the weakness and infirmity of our nature.* <note>Descartes concludes his Sixth Meditation by acknowledging that despite God's goodness, human nature is limited and prone to occasional sensory error.</note>

These, Monsieur, are the remarks that came to my mind regarding your Meditations; but I repeat here what I said at the beginning: that they are not of such importance that you should trouble yourself over them, for I do not consider my judgment to be such that you should take much account of it. For, just as when a food is pleasant to my taste which I see is unpleasant to that of others, I do not claim for that reason to have a better taste than another; so when an opinion pleases me which cannot find belief in the mind of another, I am very far from thinking that mine is the truest. I believe rather that it was very well said that everyone abounds in his own sense <note>original: "chacun abonde en son sens"; a common 17th-century rendering of the Latin biblical phrase from Romans 14:5, *unusquisque in suo sensu abundet*, meaning everyone is entitled to their own judgment.</note>, and I would hold that there would be almost as much injustice in wanting everyone to be of the same opinion as in wanting everyone's taste to be similar. I say this to assure you that I do not prevent you from making whatever judgment you please of these observations, or even from holding them in no esteem; it will be enough for me if you recognize the affection I have for your service and if you take some account of the respect I have for your virtue. Perhaps it will have happened that I have said something a bit too thoughtlessly, as there is nothing where those who dispute let themselves be more easily carried away: if that were so, I disavow it entirely and willingly consent to it being struck from my writing: for I can protest to you that my first and only design in this has been to maintain the honor of your friendship, and to keep it whole and inviolable. Farewell.

# AUTHOR’S REPLIES

## TO THE FIFTH OBJECTIONS MADE BY MISTER GASSENDI.

->*Mister Descartes to Mister Gassendi.*<-

Sir,

You have contested my *Meditations* with a discourse so elegant and so carefully researched, and which seemed to me so useful for further clarifying the truth, that I believe I owe you much for having taken the trouble to set your hand to it, and I am not a little obliged to the Reverend Father Mersenne <note>Marin Mersenne (1588–1648) was a French priest and mathematician who served as a central "clearinghouse" for scientific ideas, coordinating the series of Objections and Replies that accompany Descartes' Meditations.</note> for having urged you to undertake it. For he, who has always been most eager to seek the truth—especially when it may serve to increase the glory of God—rightly recognized that there were no better means for judging the truth of my demonstrations than to submit them to the examination and censure of several persons recognized as more learned than others, in order to see if I could respond pertinently to all the difficulties that might be proposed by them. To this end, he challenged several people; he obtained it from some, and I rejoice that you also acceded to his request.

For even though you have not so much employed the reasons of a philosopher to refute my opinions as the artifices of an orator to elude them, that does not fail to be very agreeable to me—and all the more so because I conjecture from this that it is difficult to bring against me reasons different from those contained in the previous objections that you have read. For certainly, if there had been any, they would not have escaped you; and I imagine that your entire design in this was only to warn me of the means which those persons—whose minds are so plunged in and attached to the senses that they can conceive of nothing without <term>imagining</term> <note>In the 17th century, "imagination" specifically referred to the ability to form mental images of physical objects, which Descartes argued was inferior to pure, abstract intellectual understanding.</note> it, and who, therefore, are not suited for metaphysical speculations—might use to elude my reasons, and to give me the opportunity at the same time to forestall them. Therefore, do not think that, in responding to you here, I intend to respond to a perfect and subtle philosopher, such as I know you to be, but as if you were one of those men of

<summary>Descartes begins his formal response to Pierre Gassendi’s critique, politely suggesting that Gassendi’s objections rely more on rhetorical flair than philosophical substance. He frames the exchange as a helpful exercise in addressing common misconceptions held by those who rely too heavily on their physical senses.</summary>

# REPLIES TO THE FIFTH OBJECTIONS

...flesh <note>Gassendi had addressed Descartes as "O Soul" (*O Anima*) to mock his dualism; Descartes retaliates here by addressing Gassendi as "O Flesh" (*O Caro*), implying Gassendi is too focused on the material world.</note> whose face you borrow, I shall address to you only the response that I would wish to make to them.

### *Regarding the things that were objected against the First Meditation.*

You say that you approve of the design I had to deliver the mind from its ancient prejudices <note>In 17th-century philosophy, "prejudices" (*préjugés*) refers to "pre-judgments"—ideas we accept as true in childhood before we have the capacity to reason for ourselves.</note>, which is indeed such that no one can find fault with it. But you would wish that I had discharged it simply and in few words—that is to say, in a word, negligently and without so many precautions—as if it were such an easy thing to deliver oneself from all the errors with which we are imbued from our infancy, and as if one could do too exactly what no one doubts must be done. But certainly, I see well that you have wished to indicate to me that there are many who say with their mouths that one must carefully avoid bias, but who nevertheless never avoid it, because they do not study at all how to rid themselves of it, and persuade themselves that one should not hold as prejudices what they have once received as true. Certainly, you play their character perfectly well here, and omit nothing of what they might object to me; but nevertheless, you say nothing that tastes even slightly of philosophy.

For, either you say that there was no need to feign a deceiving God <note>Descartes’ famous thought experiment where he imagines a powerful being might be tricking his senses and logic to ensure his doubt is absolute.</note>, nor that I was sleeping; a philosopher would have believed himself obliged to add the reason why such things cannot be called into doubt, or if he had no reason, as in truth there is none, he would have abstained from saying it. Nor would he have added that it was sufficient in that place to allege as the reason for our mistrust the dim light of the human mind or the weakness of our nature; for it is of no use, for correcting our errors, to say that we are mistaken because our mind is not very clairvoyant, or that our nature is infirm: for that is the same as if we said that we err because we are subject to error. 

And certainly, one cannot deny that it is more useful to take heed, as I have done, of all the things where it can happen that we err, lest we give them our belief too lightly. A philosopher would not have said, either, that by holding all things to be *false* I do not so much strip myself of my old *prejudices* as I clothe myself in a completely *new* one; or rather, he would have first tried to show that such a supposition could lead us into error. But, quite to the contrary, you assert a little later that it is not possible that I could obtain this from myself—to doubt the truth and certainty of those things that I have supposed to be false; that is—

<summary>Descartes defends his method of radical doubt, arguing against Gassendi’s claim that such deep skepticism is unnecessary or creates new prejudices. He insists that simply acknowledging human fallibility is not enough to actually correct deep-seated errors.</summary>

...that is to say, so that I might clothe myself in this new prejudice <note>In the 17th century, a "prejudice" (*préjugé*) was not necessarily a social bias, but a "pre-judgment"—an idea accepted as true before it has been examined by reason.</note> which you feared I would let myself be biased by. 1. Regarding what I said—that I did not yet sufficiently know what a thinking thing is—it is not true, as you claim, that I said this in earnest, for I explained it in its proper place; nor is it true that I said I had no doubt about what the nature of the body consisted of, or that I did not attribute to it the faculty of self-movement; nor that I imagined the soul as a wind or a fire, and other such things which I only reported in that place according to the common opinion <note>original: *vulgaire*; in 17th-century philosophy, the "vulgar" or "common" opinion refers to the unexamined beliefs of the general public before they are subjected to rigorous logic.</note>, to show later that they were false. But with what faithfulness can you say that I attribute to the soul the faculties of walking, feeling, being nourished, etc., so that you might add immediately after these words: *I grant you all that, provided we guard against your distinction between the mind and the body*: for in that very place I said in express terms that nutrition should be attributed only to the body; and as for feeling and walking, I also attribute them for the most part to the body, and I attribute nothing to the soul regarding them except that alone which is a thought.

Furthermore, what reason do you have to say *that there was no need for such a great apparatus to prove my existence*; certainly, I believe I have very good reason to conjecture from your own words that the apparatus I used was not yet great enough, since I have not yet been able to make you understand my thought well. For when you say that I could have concluded the same thing from any other of my actions indifferently, you are quite mistaken, because there is not a single one of which I am entirely certain (I mean that <term>metaphysical certainty</term> <note>Metaphysical certainty refers to a level of truth so absolute that it is impossible to even imagine it being false, unlike "moral certainty," which is just "good enough" for daily life.</note> which alone is at issue here) except for thought. For example, this consequence would not be valid: *I walk, therefore I am*, except insofar as the internal knowledge I have of it is a thought, from which alone this conclusion is certain, and not from the movement of the body, which can sometimes be false, as in our dreams, although it then seems to us that we are walking. Thus, from the fact that I think I am walking, I can very well infer the existence of my mind, which has this thought, but not the existence of my body, which is walking. It is the same with all the others.

9. And I do not see what more you could desire regarding this, unless you wish to be told what color, what smell, and what flavor the human mind has, or of what <term>salt, sulfur, and mercury</term> <note>These three elements—salt, sulfur, and mercury—were known as the "Tria Prima" in early modern chemistry and alchemy. Descartes is mocking the idea that the mind can be understood through material chemistry.</note> it is composed; for do you wish us to pass it through an <term>alembic</term> <note>An alembic is a glass or metal device used for distillation in alchemy and early chemistry.</note>, as if by a kind of chemical operation, to know what enters into the composition of its essence, as one might do with wine? Such a request is certainly worthy of you, <note>Descartes frequently addressed Gassendi as "O Flesh" (Latin: *O Caro*) to mock Gassendi's materialist philosophy, which Descartes felt focused too much on the body and not enough on the soul.</note> **O flesh**, and of all those who, conceiving of nothing except confusedly, do not know what one ought to seek in each thing.

But as for me, I have never thought that to make a substance manifest, anything more was needed than to discover its various attributes; so that the more attributes of a substance we know, the more perfectly we also know its nature. And just as we can distinguish several different attributes in the wax—one being that it is white, another that it is hard, another that from being hard it becomes liquid, etc.—there are just as many in the mind: one being that it has the power to know the whiteness of the wax, another that it has the power to know its hardness, another that it can know the change of this hardness or the liquefaction, and so on. For one may know the hardness who, for that reason, will not know the whiteness (such as a person born blind), and so it goes for the rest. From this, one clearly sees that there is no thing of which we know as many attributes as our own mind; because for every attribute we know in other things, we can count just as many in the mind for the very fact that the mind knows them: and therefore its nature is better known than that of any other thing.

Finally, you reproach me here in passing because, having admitted nothing in myself but the mind, I nevertheless speak of the wax that I see and touch, which surely cannot be done without eyes or hands; but you should have noticed that I expressly warned that I was not dealing here with sight or touch, which are performed through the mediation of bodily organs, but with the mere *thought* of seeing and touching, which does not require these organs, as we experience every night in our dreams. And certainly you noticed this very well, but you merely wanted to show how many absurdities and unjust <term>cavillations</term> <note>From the Latin *cavillatio*, meaning a petty, frivolous, or sophistical objection designed to confuse an argument rather than find the truth.</note> those are capable of inventing who work not so much to conceive a thing well as to attack and contradict it.

### *Concerning the objections raised against the Third Meditation.*

1. Cheer up! Finally you bring some reason against me here, something I had not noticed you doing until now; for, to prove that it is not a certain rule that *the things we conceive very clearly and very distinctly are all true*, you say that a number of great minds, who seem as though they ought to have known many things very clearly and very distinctly, have judged that truth was hidden in the bosom of God himself, or in the deep abyss. In this, I admit that it is very well argued from the authority of others; but you should remember, **O flesh**, <note>original: "ô chair" (Latin: *O Caro*). Descartes addresses Gassendi this way to mock his opponent's materialist philosophy, which suggests that the soul is just a physical substance.</note> that you are speaking here to a mind that is so detached from bodily things that it does not even know if there have ever been any men before it, and which therefore is not much moved by their authority. What you then allege regarding the <term>skeptics</term> <note>A school of philosophy that argues that certain knowledge is impossible.</note> is a common refrain which is not bad, but which proves nothing, any more than what you say about people who would die for the defense of their false opinions; this is because one cannot prove that they clearly and distinctly conceive what they assert with such stubbornness. Finally, what you add—that one should not work so hard to confirm the truth of this rule as to provide a good method for knowing whether or not we are mistaken when we think we clearly conceive something—is very true. But I also maintain that I have done exactly this in its proper place, first by removing <term>prejudices</term> <note>In Cartesian philosophy, "prejudices" refer to the unexamined beliefs we adopt in childhood before our reason is fully developed.</note>, then by explaining all the principal ideas, and finally by distinguishing clear and distinct ideas from those that are obscure and confused.

2. Certainly I admire your reasoning by which you want to prove that all our ideas are foreign or come from the outside, and that there are none that we ourselves have formed, *because*, you say, *the mind has not only the faculty of conceiving foreign ideas, but it also has that of assembling, dividing, extending, shortening, composing, etc., them in many ways*: from which you conclude that the idea of a <term>chimera</term> <note>A mythological creature made of parts from different animals. In philosophy, it represents a mental construct that has no external reality.</note> which the mind makes by composing, dividing, etc., is not made by it, but that it comes from the outside or is foreign. But you could also in the same way prove that <term>Praxiteles</term> <note>A famous sculptor of ancient Greece.</note> made no statues, since he did not derive from himself the marble upon which he could carve them; and one could also say that you did not make these objections because you composed them of words that you did not invent, but that you borrowed from others. But certainly neither the form of a chimera consists...

I also marvel that you maintain that the idea of what is named in general *a thing* cannot be in the mind if the ideas of an animal, a plant, a stone, and all the <term>universals</term> <note>General concepts or categories, such as "beauty" or "humanity," that represent a class of things rather than a specific individual.</note> are not there together: as if, to know that I am a thing that thinks, I had to know animals and plants, because I must know what is named *a thing*, or else what *a thing* is in general. You are also no more truthful in all that you say regarding the truth.

And finally, since you <term>impugn</term> <note>To challenge, call into question, or attack as false.</note> only things about which I have affirmed nothing, you arm yourself in vain against ghosts.

3. To refute the reasons for which I estimated that one could doubt the existence of material things, you ask here why then I walk upon the earth, etc., in which it is evident that you fall back into the first difficulty; for you take as a foundation that which is in controversy and which needs proof—namely, that it is so certain that I walk upon the earth, that it cannot in any way be doubted.

And when, to the objections that I made to myself, and for which I have given the solution, you wish to add this other one—namely, why then in a person born blind is there no idea of color, or, in a deaf person, of sounds and the voice?—you show clearly that you have no objection of any consequence; for how do you know that in a person born blind there is no idea of colors? Seeing as we sometimes experience that even though we have our eyes closed, there are nevertheless excited within us feelings of color and light; and, even if one granted you what you say, would not he who denied the existence of material things have just as good a reason to say that a person born blind has no ideas of colors because his mind is deprived of the faculty of forming them, as you have to say that he has no ideas of them because he is deprived of sight.

What you add regarding the two ideas of the sun proves nothing; but when you take them both for one and the same, because they relate to the same sun, it is the same as if you said that the true and the false do not differ when they are said of the same thing; and when you deny that one should call by the name of "idea" that which we infer from the reasons of astronomy, you restrict the name of "idea" to only those images depicted in the <term>fantasy</term> <note>In 17th-century philosophy, the "fantasy" (or *phantasia*) referred to the imagination, the faculty of the mind that holds and manipulates sensory images.</note>, against what I have expressly established.

4. You do the same when you deny that one can have a true idea of <term>substance</term> <note>The underlying reality or "thing" that supports qualities; for example, a piece of wax is the substance that supports the qualities of yellowness or softness.</note>, because, you say, substance is not perceived by the imagination, but by the <term>understanding</term> <note>In 17th-century philosophy, the "understanding" (intellect) is the mind’s ability to grasp abstract truths, whereas "imagination" is the ability to form mental images of physical objects.</note> alone. But I have already protested several times, O flesh, that I wish to have nothing to do with those who are willing to use only their imagination and not their understanding.

But where you say that *the idea of substance has no reality that it has not borrowed from the ideas of <term>accidents</term> <note>The non-essential properties of a thing, such as its color, weight, or smell, which cannot exist without a substance to inhabit.</note>, in which or in the manner of which it is conceived*, you clearly show that you have no distinct idea of it. This is because substance can never be conceived in the manner of accidents, nor can it borrow its reality from them; quite the contrary, accidents are commonly conceived by philosophers as substances—namely, when they conceive them as real things. For no reality (that is, no <term>entity</term> <note>A being or thing with its own existence.</note> more than a <term>modal</term> <note>Related to "modes," which are specific ways a substance exists; for instance, a specific shape is a "mode" of a physical object.</note> one) can be attributed to accidents that is not borrowed from the idea of substance.

Finally, where you say that *we only form the idea of God based on what we have learned and heard from others, attributing to Him, following their example, the same perfections that we have seen others attribute to Him*, I would have liked you to also add: where then did those first men, from whom we learned and heard these things, get this same idea of God? For if they had it from themselves, why can we not have it from ourselves? And if God revealed it to them, it follows that God exists.

And when you add that *he who speaks of an infinite thing gives a name he does not understand to a thing he does not comprehend*, you make no distinction between <term>intellection</term> <note>The act of the mind understanding a concept.</note>—which is consistent with the capacity of our mind, and which everyone recognizes within themselves regarding the infinite—and the complete and perfect conception of things (that is, one which includes everything intelligible within them). This latter kind of conception is such that no one has ever had it, not only of the infinite, but perhaps not even of any other thing in the world, however small it may be. And it is not true that we conceive of the infinite by the negation of the finite, since, on the contrary, all limitation contains within itself the negation of the infinite.

5. You say many things here to make it seem as if you contradict me, and yet you say nothing against me, since you conclude the same thing as I do. 6. If you had any reasons to prove the existence of material things, you would undoubtedly have reported them here. As for what you say regarding ideas, that needs no response, because you restrict the name "idea" only to images depicted in the <term>fantasy</term> <note>In early modern philosophy, "fantasy" or *fantaisie* refers to the faculty that generates mental images based on the senses.</note>, while I extend it to everything that we conceive through thought.

But I ask you, in passing, by what argument do you prove that *nothing acts upon itself*? For it is not your custom to use arguments and to prove what you say; you prove this by the example of the finger which cannot strike itself, and of the eye which cannot see itself except in a mirror. ...that it is not the eye that sees itself, nor the mirror, but rather the mind, which alone knows the mirror, the eye, and itself. "Formally" means the cause has the same property as the effect (e.g., a hot fire makes a hot coal). 7. You say nothing here that you have not already said before, and that I have not entirely refuted. I will only caution you here regarding the idea of the infinite, which you say cannot be true unless I comprehend the infinite, and that what I know of it is at most only a part of the infinite—and even a very small part which represents the infinite no better than the portrait of a single hair represents an entire man. I will caution you, I say, that it is a contradiction for me to comprehend something, and for what I comprehend to be infinite; for to have a true idea of the infinite, it must in no way be comprehended, especially since incomprehensibility itself is contained within the <term>formal reason</term> <note>The "formal reason" (*raison formelle*) refers to the essential definition or the core nature of a concept that makes it what it is.</note> of the infinite. And nevertheless, it is a manifest thing that the idea we have of the infinite represents not only one of its parts, but the infinite as a whole, according to how it must be represented by a human idea; although it is certain that God or some other intelligent nature could have another much more perfect one—that is to say, much more exact and distinct than that which men have—in the same way that we say that someone who is not versed in geometry nevertheless has the idea of the whole triangle when he conceives it as a figure composed of three lines, although geometers may know several other properties of the triangle and notice many things in its idea that the other does not observe there. For just as it is enough to conceive of a figure composed of three lines to have the idea of the whole triangle, so it is enough to conceive of a thing that is not enclosed within any limits to have a true and entire idea of the whole infinite.

8. You fall into the same error here when you deny that we can have a true idea of God: for even though we do not know every single thing that is in God, nevertheless everything we do know to be in him is entirely true. As for what you say—that bread is no more perfect than the one who desires it, and that just because I conceive of something as being actually contained in an idea, it does not follow that it is actually in the thing the idea represents, and also that I pass judgment on what I do not know, and other such things—all of this, I say, shows only that you rashly wish to attack many things whose meaning you do not comprehend. For, from the fact that someone desires bread, one does not infer that the bread is more perfect than him, but only that he who has need of bread is less perfect than when he has no such need. And from the fact that something is contained in an idea, I do not conclude that this thing actually exists, except when no other cause can be assigned for that idea than the very thing it represents as actually existing. What I have demonstrated could not be said of many worlds, nor of any other thing whatsoever, except for God alone. Nor do I judge what I do not know, for I have provided the reasons for the judgment I was making, which are such that you have not yet been able to refute even the slightest of them.

9. When you deny that we need the concurrence and continual influence of the "First Cause" <note>A philosophical term for God, viewed as the original source of all motion and existence.</note> to be preserved, you deny something that all metaphysicians affirm as most manifest, but which the less scholarly often do not think about. This is because they focus their thoughts only on those causes known in the schools as <term>causes of becoming <note>original: *secundum fieri*</note></term>—that is, causes upon which effects depend for their production—and not on those they call <term>causes of being <note>original: *secundum esse*</note></term>—that is, causes upon which effects depend for their subsistence and continuation in existence. Thus, the architect is the cause of the house, and the father the cause of his son, only in terms of their production; this is why, once the work is finished, it can subsist and remain without that cause. But the sun is the cause of the light that proceeds from it, and God is the cause of all created things, not only regarding what depends on their production, but even regarding their conservation or their duration in being. This is why He must always act upon His effect in the same way to preserve it in the initial existence He gave it. And this is demonstrated very clearly by what I have explained regarding the independence of the parts of time—which you attempt in vain to evade.

if one adds or subtracts anything at all, it immediately becomes the idea of another thing; thus was the idea of Pandora <note>In Greek mythology, Pandora was the first woman, created by various gods who each gave her a different gift—or "perfection"—making her a composite creation.</note> fashioned in the past; and thus have all the ideas of false gods been made by those who did not properly conceive the idea of the true God. For do not think that the idea we have of God is formed gradually from the accumulation of the perfections of creatures; it is formed entirely, and all at once, from our mind's conception of the **infinite being**, who is incapable of any kind of increase.

Certainly, it seems that you would then be more worthy of laughter than of an answer. He uses the analogy of a famous painter, Apelles, to explain how a creator’s style or "likeness" can be identified in their work.</meta>

...of Apelles were made in the likeness of Alexander, <note>Apelles of Kos was the renowned court painter to Alexander the Great; Descartes uses this famous historical pairing to illustrate the relationship between a creator and their subject.</note> would you say that Alexander therefore resembles a painting, and yet that paintings are composed of wood and colors, and not of flesh like Alexander? For it is not in the essence of an image to be in all things similar to the thing of which it is an image, but it is enough that it resembles it in some respect. And it is very evident that this admirable and most perfect power of thinking that we conceive to be in God is represented by the power that is in us, although ours is much less perfect. And when you prefer to compare the creation of God with the operation of an architect rather than with the generation of a father, <note>Descartes is distinguishing between "artifice" (making something external like a building) and "nature" (bringing forth something that shares one's essence, like a child).</note> you do so without any reason. For, even though these three ways of acting are totally different, the distance is nevertheless not so great from natural production to divine production as it is from artificial production to that same divine production. But you will not find that I have said there is as much of a relationship between God and us as there is between a father and his children; nor is it true either that there is never any relationship between the craftsman and his work, as appears when a painter makes a portrait that resembles himself.

But with how little fidelity do you report my words when you pretend that I said I conceive this *likeness* that I have with God in that I know that *I am an incomplete and dependent thing*, given that, on the contrary, I only said that to show the difference between God and us, for fear that anyone should think I wished to make men equal to God, and the creature equal to the Creator. For in that very place I said that I did not only conceive that I was in this regard much inferior to God, and that I nonetheless aspired to greater things than I possessed, but also that these greater things to which I aspired were found in God actually and in an infinite manner—in which things I nevertheless found something similar in myself, since I dared in some way to aspire to them.

Finally, when you say there is reason to wonder *why the rest of men do not have the same thoughts of God as those I have, since he has imprinted his idea in them as well as in me*, it is the same as if you wondered why, everyone having the notion of a triangle, everyone nevertheless does not notice as many properties in it, and that there are even perhaps some who falsely attribute several things to it.

### *Concerning the things that were objected against the Fourth Meditation.* <note>The Fourth Meditation, titled "Of Truth and Error," explores why humans are capable of making mistakes if they were created by a perfect God.</note>

1. I have already sufficiently explained what kind of idea we have of nothingness, and how we participate in non-being, by calling this idea "negative." I meant nothing more than that we are not the <term>Supreme Being</term> <note>original: "le souverain Être"</note> and that we lack many things. But you search everywhere for difficulties where none exist.

And when you say that among the works of God, I see some that are not entirely finished, you are inventing something that I never wrote and never even thought. I said only that if certain things were considered, not as parts of the entire universe, but as detached wholes and individual things, then they might appear imperfect.

Everything you then bring up regarding <term>final causes</term> <note>In philosophy, a "final cause" is the purpose or "end" for which something exists—for example, the "purpose" of an eye is to see. Descartes famously rejected looking for these in science.</note> must be redirected toward the <term>efficient cause</term>. <note>The "efficient cause" is the agent or mechanism that brings something into being—for example, the biological processes that form an eye.</note> Thus, regarding the admirable use of every part in plants and animals, etc., it is right to admire the hand of God who made them, and to know and glorify the craftsman by inspecting his works, but not to guess for what purpose he created each thing. And although in matters of <term>ethics</term>, where it is often permitted to use conjectures, it is sometimes a pious thing to consider what purpose we might guess God proposed for the government of the universe; certainly in <term>physics</term>, <note>In the 17th century, "physics" referred to the general study of nature and the physical world.</note> where all things must be supported by solid reasons, this would be foolish. We cannot pretend that some purposes are easier to discover than others, for they are all equally hidden in the unfathomable abyss of his wisdom. Nor should you pretend that there is no man who can understand other causes; for there is not one that is not much easier to know than the purpose God set for himself. Even those examples you bring to show the difficulty are not so difficult that I do not know someone who is convinced they understand them. Finally, since you ask me so ingenuously what ideas I think my mind would have had of God and of itself if, from the moment it was infused into the body, it had remained there until now with eyes closed, ears plugged, and without any use of the other senses, I reply to you just as ingenuously and sincerely that (provided we suppose it was neither hindered nor helped by the body in its thinking and meditating) I do not doubt that it would have had the same ideas that it has now, except that they...

What you then allege against the <term>universals</term> <note>General concepts like "humanity" or "circularity" that apply to many individual things.</note> of the <term>dialecticians</term> <note>Scholastic philosophers who relied heavily on formal logic and traditional Aristotelian categories.</note> does not concern me at all, since I conceive of them in an entirely different way than they do.

It is just as when we cast our eyes on a map where there are some lines arranged and set in such a way that they represent a man’s face; then this sight does not excite in us the idea of those same lines so much as the idea of a man. This would not happen if the face of a man were not known to us elsewhere, and if we were not more accustomed to thinking of the face than of its individual lines, which often we could not even distinguish from one another when we are a little distance away. Thus, certainly, we could never know the geometric triangle by the one we see traced on paper, if our mind had not had the idea of it from elsewhere.

it must be understood here. Furthermore, necessary existence is truly a property of God in the strictest sense, because it belongs to Him alone, and it is only in Him that it forms part of His essence. And yet, I do not deny that "possible existence" is a perfection in the idea of a triangle, just as "necessary existence" is a perfection in the idea of God; for this makes it more perfect than the ideas of all those <note>Descartes refers to "chimeras," which in philosophy are impossible or imaginary concepts that cannot exist in reality.</note> chimeras which we suppose cannot be produced. Therefore, you have in no way diminished the force of my argument, and you remain deceived by that very <term>sophism</term> <note>A clever but false argument intended to deceive.</note> which you claimed was so easy to resolve. 

As for what you add next, I have already replied sufficiently, and you are greatly mistaken when you say that the existence of God is not demonstrated in the same way as one demonstrates that every rectilinear triangle has its three angles equal to two right angles; for the reasoning is identical in both, except that the demonstration proving the existence of God is much simpler and more evident than the other. Finally, I shall pass over the rest in silence, because when you say that I do not explain things enough and that my proofs are not convincing, I think that, with better reason, one could say the same of you and your own arguments.

For in the true idea of the spirit, there is nothing contained but thought alone with all its attributes, among which there are none that are corporeal.

I will say nevertheless in passing *that I would very much like to know upon what you base yourself to say that I spoke of the massive and coarse body rather than of the <term>subtle and thin body</term>;* <note>Early modern thinkers often distinguished between "coarse" matter (rocks, flesh) and "subtle" matter (like air, fire, or "animal spirits") which was thought to be nearly invisible and highly mobile.</note> *it is, you say, because I said that I have a body to which I am joined, and also that it is certain that I—that is to say, my soul—is distinct from my body; where I confess that I do not see why these words could not just as well be applied to the subtle and imperceptible body as to that which is more coarse and palpable; and I do not believe that this thought could occur to the mind of anyone other than you.* Furthermore, I showed clearly in the second Meditation that *the <term>mind</term>* <note>Descartes uses "mind" (esprit) and "soul" (âme) almost interchangeably here to refer to the thinking, non-material part of a human.</note> *could be conceived as an existing <term>substance</term>,* <note>In philosophy, a "substance" is something that can exist by itself without needing something else to hold it up (like a color needs an object, but an object is a substance).</note> *even before we know if there is any wind, any fire, any vapor, any air, or any other body in the world at all, however subtle and thin it might be;* but as for knowing if in fact it was different from the body, I said in that place that *this was not the place to treat it: having reserved that for this sixth Meditation, it is also there where I have treated it amply, and where I have decided this question by a very strong and true demonstration.* But you, on the contrary, confusing the question concerning how the mind can be conceived with the one regarding what it is in fact, show nothing else except that you have understood nothing distinctly of all these things.

4. You ask here how I estimate that the <term>species</term> <note>In this context, a philosophical term for the "image" or "representation" of an object that the mind perceives.</note> or the idea of the body, which is <term>extended</term>, <note>Having "extension" (étendu) means taking up physical space—the primary characteristic of matter for Descartes.</note> can be received in me who am a...

a non-extended thing. I respond to this that no <term>corporeal species</term> <note>original: "espèce corporelle." In the philosophy of the time, a "species" was a mental image or representation of a physical object that was thought to travel from the object to the senses.</note> is received into the mind, but that the conception or pure <term>intellection</term> <note>The act of understanding through pure reason, without needing to "see" an image in the mind's eye.</note> of things, whether corporeal or spiritual, occurs without any image or corporeal species; and as for the **imagination**, which can only be of corporeal things, it is true that to form one there is a need for a species which is a true body and to which the mind applies itself, but not one which is received into the mind.

What you say about the idea of the sun—that a man born blind forms it based on the simple knowledge he has of its heat—can be easily refuted; for this blind man may well have a clear and distinct idea of the sun as a thing that heats, even though he does not have the idea of it as a thing that shines and illuminates. And it is without reason that you compare me to this blind man: firstly, because the knowledge of a **thinking thing** extends much further than that of a heating thing—indeed, it is more ample than any knowledge we have of any other thing whatsoever, as I have shown in its proper place—and also because there is no one who can show that this idea of the sun formed by this blind man does not contain everything that can be known about it, except for the person who, being endowed with the sense of sight, knows in addition its shape and its light. But as for you, not only do you know no more than I do regarding the mind, but you do not perceive in it all that I see there; so that in this, it is rather you who resemble a blind man, and I can at most, in your regard, be called only "squint-eyed" or "dim-sighted," along with all the rest of men.

Furthermore, I did not add that the mind was not <term>extended</term> <note>Taking up physical space; having length, width, and depth.</note> to explain what it is and make its nature known, but only to warn that those people are mistaken who think it is extended. Just as if there were some who wanted to say that **Bucephalus** <note>The famous horse of Alexander the Great; Descartes uses him here as a symbol for a purely physical creature.</note> is a piece of music, it would not be in vain or without reason for others to deny it. And truly, in everything you add here to prove that the mind has extension—insofar as, you say, it uses the body, which is extended—it seems to me that you reason no better than if, from the fact that Bucephalus neighs and thus produces sounds which can be related to music, you drew the conclusion that Bucephalus is therefore a piece of music. For even though the mind is united to the whole body, it does not follow from this that it is extended throughout the whole body, because it is not the nature of the mind to be extended, but only to think. And it does not conceive of extension by means of an extended species which is within it, although it imagines it by turning and applying itself to a corporeal species...

<summary>Descartes argues that the mind's ability to think about physical objects does not make the mind physical itself. 5. What you say here concerning the union of the mind with the body is similar to the preceding difficulties. You offer no objection at all against my reasoning, but instead merely propose the doubts that seem to you to follow from my conclusions, although in truth they only come to your mind because you wish to subject to the examination of the **imagination** things which, by their nature, are not subject to its **jurisdiction**. <note>Descartes distinguishes between the "intellect" (which understands abstract truths) and the "imagination" (which can only "see" physical shapes). He argues that we cannot use the imagination to understand the soul because the soul has no shape.</note> Thus, when you wish to compare the mixture of body and mind with that of two bodies mixed together, it is enough for me to reply that no comparison should be made between these things, because they are of two totally different **genres**, and one must not imagine that the mind has parts, even though it conceives of parts within the body. For, who taught you that everything the mind conceives must actually be within it? Certainly, if that were the case, when it conceives of the **grandeur of the universe**, it would also have that grandeur within itself, and thus it would not only be extended, but would even be larger than the entire world.

6. You say nothing here that contradicts me, yet you do not fail to say a great deal; from which the reader may learn that the strength of your arguments should not be judged by the prolixity of your words.

Until now, the mind has conversed with the flesh and, as was reasonable in many matters, it has not followed its sentiments. <note>In the preceding exchange, Gassendi had addressed Descartes as "O Mind" (*O Mens*), and Descartes had addressed Gassendi as "O Flesh" (*O Caro*). This was a rhetorical way of highlighting their disagreement over whether the soul is physical or spiritual.</note> But now I drop the mask and recognize that I am truly speaking to Monsieur Gassendi, a person as commendable for the integrity of his character and the candor of his spirit as for the depth and subtlety of his **doctrine**, and whose friendship will always be very dear to me; I also protest, as he himself may know, that I will always seek, as much as possible, opportunities to earn it. For this reason, I beg him not to take it ill if, in refuting his **objections**, I have used the liberty common to **philosophers**, just as for my part I assure him that I found nothing in them that was not very agreeable to me. But above all, I was delighted that a man of his merit, in a discourse so long and so carefully researched, brought forward no reason that could destroy or overturn mine, and that he opposed nothing against my conclusions to which it was not very easy for me to respond.

<meta>This page marks the beginning of the Sixth Objections to Descartes’ Meditations. While the previous page (351) concluded Descartes’ rebuttal to the Fifth Objections (Gassendi), this section shifts to a collective critique from a group of unnamed theologians and philosophers who challenge the foundational certainty of the "Cogito."</meta>

### SIXTH OBJECTIONS
### MADE BY VARIOUS THEOLOGIANS AND PHILOSOPHERS.

After having read your **Meditations** with care, along with the answers you gave to the difficulties previously raised against you, several doubts remain in our minds that we would like you to resolve.

The *first* is that it does not seem to be a very certain argument for our existence that we think; for, to be certain that you think, you must first know what thinking—or thought—is, and what your existence is. Given your ignorance of these two things, how can you know that you think or that you exist? Since, therefore, when you say **I think**, you do not know what you are saying, and when you add **therefore I am**, you do not understand yourself either. Indeed, you do not even know if you are saying or thinking anything at all, since it is necessary for you to know that you know what you are saying, and again to know that you know that you know what you are saying—and so on to infinity. <note>This is a classic "infinite regress" argument, suggesting that if every thought requires a prior thought to validate it, we can never reach a foundation of certain knowledge.</note> It is evident that you cannot know if you exist, or even if you think.

But, to come to the *second doubt*, when you say *I think, therefore I am*, <note>original: "je pense, donc je suis"</note> could one not say that you are mistaken—that you do not think at all, but are merely moved, and that you are nothing other than a **corporeal movement**? <note>Physical motion of the body or its parts.</note> No one has yet been able to understand your reasoning by which you claim to have demonstrated that there is no corporeal movement that can legitimately be called by the name of "thought." For do you believe you have so thoroughly cut and divided all the movements of your **subtle matter** <term>subtle matter: In Cartesian physics, these are extremely fine, fast-moving particles that fill all space and were thought to explain phenomena like light, heat, and magnetism without needing a vacuum.</term> that you can be certain and persuade us—who are very attentive and consider ourselves clear-sighted enough—that it is impossible for our thoughts to be spread throughout these corporeal movements?

The *third doubt* is not at all different from the second. Although some **Fathers of the Church** <note>Authoritative early Christian theologians whose writings helped establish Church doctrine.</note> believed, along with all the **Platonists**, that angels were corporeal—which is why the **Council of the Lateran** <note>The critics likely refer to the Fourth Lateran Council (1215) or more likely the Second Council of Nicaea (787), which discussed the depiction of angels in art, implying they had some form of "body" to be painted.</note> decreed that they could be depicted—and that they held the same view regarding the **rational soul** <note>The part of the human soul responsible for reason and intellect, distinguished from the "sensitive" soul found in animals.</note> that...

### SIXTH OBJECTIONS 353

...some among them have believed [the soul] to be passed down from father to son; <note>The authors refer to "traducianism," an old theological view that the soul is generated by the parents along with the body, rather than being a separate substance created by God.</note> they have nevertheless all stated that angels and the soul possessed thought. This leads us to believe their opinion was that thought could be produced by **corporeal movements**, or that angels themselves were nothing but corporeal movements from which they did not distinguish thought.

This can also be confirmed by the thoughts that monkeys, dogs, and other animals have; and indeed, dogs bark while sleeping, as if they were pursuing hares or thieves. They also know very well when awake that they are running, and when dreaming that they are barking—even though we acknowledge, along with you, that there is nothing in them that is distinct from the body. Now, if you say that dogs do not know they are running or thinking, besides the fact that you say this without proof, it is perhaps true that they make a similar judgment about us: namely, that we do not know if we are running or thinking when we perform one or the other of these actions. For, after all, you do not see the internal way of acting they have within them, any more than they see yours. 

In the past, there have been great figures—and there are still some today—who do not deny **reason** to the beasts. We are so far from being persuaded that all their operations can be sufficiently explained by means of **mechanics**, <term>mechanics</term> <note>Descartes famously argued that animals are "automata" or machines without souls; his critics here find this idea "ridiculous."</note> without attributing to them any sense, soul, or life, that on the contrary, we are ready to maintain, against all opposition, that such a thing is entirely impossible and even ridiculous.

And finally, if it is true that monkeys, dogs, and elephants act in such a way in all their operations, many will be found who will say that all human actions are also similar to those of machines, and who will no longer wish to admit any sense or understanding in man; seeing as, if the weak reason of beasts differs from that of man, it is only by a matter of degree ("the more and the less"), which does not change the nature of things.

The *fourth* **scruple** <note>A "scruple" here refers to a nagging doubt or a point of contention.</note> concerns the science of an **atheist**. He maintains that his knowledge is very certain—and even, according to your own rule, very evident—when he asserts that if equals are taken from equals, the remainders will be equal; or that the three angles of a rectilinear triangle are equal to two right angles, and other similar things. He cannot think of these things without believing they are very certain. He maintains this to be so true that even if there were no God, or even if it were impossible for there to be one (as he imagines), he would feel no less assured of these truths than if one truly existed: and of...

For how could that be, if the intellect itself has no other uncertainty than that which it borrows from senses that are well-disposed? And in fact, do we not see that it cannot correct the error of any of our senses unless another sense has first pulled it from the error in which it found itself? For example, a stick appears broken in the water because of refraction: who will correct this error? Will it be the intellect? Not at all, but the sense of touch. It is the same for all the others. And therefore, if you can once have all your senses well-disposed, and they always report the same thing to you, hold it for certain that you will acquire through their means the greatest certainty of which a man is naturally capable; but if you trust too much in the reasonings of your mind, be assured of being often deceived, for it happens quite commonly that our intellect deceives us in things it had held to be indubitable.

These are the points in which our main difficulties consist: to which you will also add some certain rule and infallible marks by which we can know with certainty, when we conceive one thing so perfectly without the other, that it is true that the one is so distinctly...

Thus, just as one would conclude poorly by saying that the Son and the Holy Spirit are essentially distinguished from the Father, or that they can be separated from Him, in the same way, it will never be granted to you that thought—or rather the human mind—is really distinguished from the body, even though you clearly conceive of one without the other and can deny one of the other, and even though you recognize that this is not achieved through any abstraction <note>In philosophy, "abstraction" is the mental act of focusing on one quality of an object while ignoring others; the objectors argue Descartes is merely ignoring the body rather than proving the soul is a separate thing.</note> of your mind. But certainly, if you fully satisfy all these difficulties, you must be assured that there will be nothing left to overshadow the concerns of our theologians.

### ADDITION.

I shall add here what several others have proposed to me, so that I will not need to respond to them separately, as their subject matter is nearly the same.

Persons of very great intellect and rare learning have posed the following three questions to me:

The first is how we can be certain that we have a clear and distinct idea of our soul <note>French: *âme*. In this context, it refers to the "thinking thing" or the mind.</note>?

The second is how we can be certain that this idea is entirely different from all other things?

The third is how we can be certain that it has nothing within itself belonging to the body?

It concludes with three specific questions regarding the clarity and exclusivity of the idea of the soul.</summary>

# SIXTH OBJECTIONS

The following was also sent to me with this title:

## FROM PHILOSOPHERS AND GEOMETRICIANS

### To Monsieur Descartes.

->SIR,<-

Regardless of the care we take in examining whether the idea we have of our mind—that is to say, whether the notion or concept of the human mind <term>mind</term> <note>French: *esprit*. In 17th-century philosophy, this term refers specifically to the thinking part of a human being, often used interchangeably with "intellect."</note>—contains nothing corporeal <term>corporeal</term> <note>Relating to the physical body or matter.</note> in itself, we nonetheless do not dare to assert that thought cannot in any way belong to a body agitated by secret movements. For, seeing that there are certain bodies that do not think at all and others that do, would we not pass for **sophists** <note>In this context, a "sophist" is someone who uses clever but fallacious or misleading arguments.</note> in your eyes, and would you not accuse us of too much audacity, if despite this we wanted to conclude that there is no body that thinks? We even find it difficult not to believe that you would have been right to mock us if we had been the first to forge this argument concerning ideas—the one you use for proof of a God and the **real distinction** <note>French: *distinction réelle*. A technical term in Cartesian philosophy meaning that two things are separate substances and can exist independently of one another by the power of God.</note> between the mind and the body—and if you had then subjected it to the scrutiny of your *analysis*. It is true that you seem to be so strongly convinced and preoccupied by it that it appears you have placed a veil before your own mind, which prevents you from seeing that all the operations and properties of the **soul** <note>French: *âme*. While *esprit* focuses on the intellect, *âme* often refers to the vital principle that animates the body.</note> you notice in yourself depend purely on the movements of the body; or else, untie the knot which, in your judgment, keeps our spirits chained and prevents them from rising above body and matter.

The knot we find in this is that we understand perfectly well that two and three joined together make the number five, and that if equal things are taken from equal things, the remainders will be equal; we are convinced of these truths, and a thousand others, as well as you. Why then are we not similarly convinced by means of your ideas, or even our own, that the human soul is really distinct from the body, and that God exists? You will perhaps say that you cannot instill this truth in our minds if we do not meditate with you; but we have to answer you that we have read your *Meditations* more than seven times with an attention of spirit almost like that of angels, and that nevertheless we are not yet persuaded. This term covers both the "spirit" and the "intellect" or "thinking thing."</note> are not of such great weight and such authority that learned men, who strive as much as they can to raise their minds above matter, could and should entirely submit to them.

On the contrary, we believe that you will confess the same along with us, if you would take the trouble to reread your *Meditations* with the same spirit, and put them through the same examination as you would if they had been proposed to you by an enemy. Finally, since we do not know at all to what extent the power <note>French: *vertu*. In 17th-century physics and philosophy, this refers to the inherent capability or "faculty" of a substance to produce an effect.</note> of bodies and their movements can extend—given that you yourself confess there is no one who can know all that God has put or can put into a subject without a particular revelation from Him—how could you have learned that God has not placed this power and property of thinking, doubting, etc., into some bodies?

These, Sir, are our arguments, or if you prefer, our **prejudices**, for which, if you provide the necessary remedy, we could not express to you how many thanks we would owe you, nor how great our obligation to you would be for having so well cleared the ground of our minds as to have made them capable of receiving the seed of your doctrine with profit. May God grant that you may happily succeed in this, and we pray that He may be pleased to reward your piety, which does not allow you to undertake anything that you do not sacrifice entirely to His glory.

<meta>This page contains the opening of René Descartes’ "Replies to the Sixth Objections." On the previous page, a group of anonymous theologians and mathematicians challenged Descartes’ claim that he could prove the separation of the mind and body. They argued that human reason might not be capable of knowing if God had given physical matter the power to think. Here, Descartes begins his rebuttal by addressing the nature of self-awareness and how we distinguish between different concepts like "thought" and "motion."</meta>

<header>THE AUTHOR’S REPLIES</header>

## TO THE SIXTH OBJECTIONS MADE BY VARIOUS THEOLOGIANS, PHILOSOPHERS, AND GEOMETERS.

1. It is a most certain fact that no one can be sure whether they are thinking or existing if they do not first know what "thought" and "existence" are. This does not mean one needs a **reflective knowledge** or one acquired through a logical demonstration—and even less does it require a science *about* that science (where one knows that they know, and then knows that they know they know, and so on to infinity, as it would be impossible to ever have such knowledge of anything at all). Rather, it is enough that one knows this through that power of **inner awareness** <note>French: *reconnaissance intérieure*. Descartes refers to a direct, intuitive grasp of one's own mental states that precedes formal reasoning.</note> which always precedes acquired knowledge. This awareness is so natural to all people regarding thought and existence that, although we might pretend we do not have it—perhaps being blinded by certain **prejudices** <note>In Cartesian philosophy, "prejudices" are the false or unexamined beliefs we absorb in childhood before we begin to reason for ourselves.</note> and paying more attention to the sound of words than their true meaning—it is nonetheless impossible for us not to actually possess it. Thus, when someone perceives that they are thinking, and it follows very clearly that they exist, even if they have perhaps never before bothered to ask what "thought" and "existence" are, they cannot help but know both well enough to be fully satisfied on the matter.

2. It is also completely impossible that someone who, on one hand, knows they are thinking, and who also understands what it is to be moved, could ever believe they are mistaken and that they aren't actually thinking, but only being moved. Because they have an idea or notion of **thought** that is entirely different from that of **bodily motion**, they must necessarily conceive of one as being different from the other. However, because we are too accustomed to assigning many different properties to the same subject that have no affinity with one another, it is possible that a person might doubt—or even claim—that it is the same "thing" within them that thinks and is moved. Now, it must be noted that things for which we have different ideas can be taken as one and the same thing in two ways: namely, either in **unity and identity of nature**, or only in **unity of composition**. <note>Descartes distinguishes between things that are essentially the same "by nature" (like a shape and the surface it belongs to) and things that are only joined together "by composition" (like a pilot in a ship, or the mind and the body).</note> Thus, for example, it is quite true that the idea of shape is not the [same as...]

<summary>Descartes argues that self-awareness of one's own thought and existence is an innate "inner awareness" rather than a learned science. He begins to distinguish between the mental concept of thinking and the physical concept of movement, introducing the difference between things that are essentially identical versus those merely joined together.</summary>

Finally, regarding the question proposed to me in this place—namely, whether I have so thoroughly cut and divided, by means of my analysis, all the movements of my <term>subtle matter</term> <note>Descartes’ "subtle matter" was a theoretical fluid substance made of tiny particles that he believed filled the universe and transmitted physical forces.</note> that I am not only certain, but can even demonstrate to very attentive people who consider themselves quite perceptive, that it is contradictory for our thoughts to be spread out in bodily movements (that is, as I see it, that our thoughts are nothing other than bodily movements)—I reply that, for my part, I am very certain of it. However, I do not promise to be able to persuade others, regardless of the attention they bring or the capacity they think they have, at least so long as they apply their minds only to things that are merely imaginable, and not to those that are purely intelligible. It is easy to see that those who imagine that the distinction or difference between thought and movement must be known through the dissection of some subtle matter are doing exactly that; for this difference can only be known by those who realize that the <term>idea</term> of a thinking thing and that of an extended or mobile thing are entirely diverse and mutually independent of one another. It is contradictory for things that we conceive clearly and distinctly as being diverse and independent to be unable to be separated, at least by the <term>omnipotence of God</term> <note>Descartes often appeals to God's power as a logical guarantee: if we can clearly conceive of two things existing apart, God is capable of separating them, proving they are truly distinct substances.</note>. Thus, every time we encounter them together in the same subject—such as thought and bodily movement in the same man—we should not for that reason estimate that they are one and the same thing in **unity of nature**, but only in **unity of composition**.

The passages you cite from *Ecclesiastes* are also not at all against me: for it must be noted that Solomon, in this book, does not speak in the voice of the impious, but in his own. Having previously been a sinner and an enemy of God, he then repents for his faults and confesses that as long as he had only wanted to use the light of human wisdom to guide his actions, without referring it to God—nor looking upon it as a benefit from His hand—he had never been able to find anything that satisfied him entirely, or that he did not see as filled with vanity. This is why in various places he exhorts and urges men to turn to God and do penance, notably in chapter 11, verse 9, with these words: *and know*, he says, *that God will bring you into judgment for all your actions*, which he continues in the following verses until the end of the book. But above all, one must take care with these words, *which are done under the sun*, for they are frequently repeated throughout this book and always denote natural things to the exclusion of the subordination and dependence they have on God; because God, being raised above all things, cannot be said to be contained among those which are only "under the sun"; so that...

But to entirely refute the opinion of those who admit real accidents <term>real accidents: a Scholastic theory that qualities like color, taste, or heat are "things" that could theoretically be separated from the objects they belong to.</term>, it seems to me there is no need for me to produce other reasons than those I have already advanced; for, firstly, since no sensation occurs without contact, nothing can be sensed except the surface of bodies. Now, if there are real accidents, they must be something different from this surface, which is nothing other than a mode; therefore, if they exist, they cannot be sensed. But who has ever thought they existed except because they believed they were sensed? 

Furthermore, it is an entirely impossible thing, and one that cannot be conceived without repugnance and contradiction, that there should be real accidents, because everything that is "real" can exist separately from any other subject. Now, that which can thus exist separately is a substance and not an accident. And it is of no use to say that real accidents cannot naturally be separated from their subjects, but only by the omnipotence of God. For to be "done naturally" is nothing other than to be done by the ordinary power of God, which differs in no way from his extraordinary power: and which, putting nothing new into things, does not change their nature either. So, if everything that can exist naturally without a subject is a substance, everything that can also exist without a subject through the power of God—however extraordinary it may be—must also be called by the name of substance. 

I confess, indeed, that one substance can be applied to another substance; but when that happens, it is not the substance that takes the form of an accident, but only the mode or the way in which this happens: for example, when a garment is put on a man, it is not the garment, but *being dressed* which is an accident. # RESPONSES
