8. When one attentively considers the immensity of God, it is clearly evident that it is impossible for there to be anything that does not depend on Him—not only everything that exists, but even that there is no order, no law, nor any reason for goodness and truth that does not depend on Him. Otherwise (as I said a little earlier), He would not have been entirely indifferent <note>In this context, "indifference" refers to God’s absolute freedom. Descartes argues that God is not forced by logic or morality to act; rather, logic and morality exist because God chose them.</note> to creating the things He created. For if some reason or appearance of goodness had preceded His preordination, it would undoubtedly have determined Him to do what was best; but on the contrary, because He determined Himself to make the things that are in the world, for that reason—as it is said in *Genesis*—they are "very good." This is to say that the reason for their goodness depends on the fact that He willed to make them so. 

And there is no need to ask in what category of cause this goodness, or all other truths (both mathematical and metaphysical), depend on God. For the categories of causes having been established by those who perhaps did not think of this specific reason for causality, it would not be surprising if they had given it no name; nevertheless, they have indeed given it one, for it can be called the efficient cause <term>efficient cause: the primary source of change or the "agent" that brings something into being, like a builder is the efficient cause of a house.</term>. In the same way, the will of a king can be called the efficient cause of a law, even though the law itself is not a natural being, but only (as they say in the Schools <note>Referring to the Scholastic philosophers of the medieval universities.</note>) a "moral being." 

It is also useless to ask how God could have made it so, from all eternity, that two times four were not eight, etc.; for I readily admit that we cannot understand this. But since, on the other hand, I understand very well that nothing can exist in any kind of being whatsoever that does not depend on God, and that it was very easy for Him to ordain certain things such that men could not understand how they could have been otherwise than they are, it would be entirely contrary to reason to doubt the things we understand very well simply because of some other things we do not understand, and which we see no reason why we should understand. Thus, one must not think that eternal truths depend on the *human understanding or on the existence of things, but only on the will of God, who, like a sovereign legislator, has ordained and established them from all eternity.*

<summary>Descartes argues that all truths—including mathematical laws like 2+2=4 and moral goodness—are not independent of God, but are products of His sovereign will. 9. To properly understand the certainty of the senses, one must distinguish between three different degrees of sensation. In the first degree, one should precisely consider nothing other than what external objects cause immediately in the bodily organ, which can be nothing else but the movement of the particles of that organ, and the change of shape and position resulting from that movement. The second degree contains everything that results immediately in the mind from the fact that it is united to the bodily organ thus moved and disposed by its objects; such are the feelings of pain, tickling, hunger, thirst, colors, sounds, tastes, smells, heat, cold, and other similar sensations which we said in the sixth *Meditation* arise from the union, or as it were, the mingling of the mind with the body. And finally, the third degree comprises all the judgments we have been accustomed to making since our youth concerning the things around us, on the occasion of the impressions or movements made in our sense organs. 

For example, when I see a stick, one must not imagine that little fluttering images—commonly called <term>intentional species<note>original: "espèces intentionnelles"; a Scholastic concept where objects were thought to emit "likenesses" of themselves that traveled through the air to the senses. Descartes argues instead for a mechanical explanation of light.</note></term>—fly out from it through the air and pass into my eye. Rather, it is only that rays of light reflected from this stick excite certain movements in the optic nerve, and by its means in the brain itself, just as I have explained at length in the *Dioptrics*. And it is in this movement of the brain, which we have in common with animals, that the first degree of sensation consists. 

From this first degree follows the second, which extends only to the perception of the color and light reflected from this stick; this arises because the mind is so intimately conjoined with the brain that it feels and is, so to speak, touched by the movements occurring within it. This is all that should be attributed to "sense" if we wish to distinguish it exactly from the understanding. For if, from this sensation of color which I feel as an impression, I come to judge that this stick which is outside of me is colored—and if from the extent of that color, its boundaries, and its position relative to the parts of my brain, I determine something regarding the size, shape, and distance of that same stick—it is nevertheless manifest that this depends on the understanding alone, even though we are accustomed to attributing it to the senses (which is why I have assigned it to a third degree of sensation). I even demonstrated in the *Dioptrics* that size, distance, and shape are only perceived by reasoning, by deducing them from one another. But there is only this...

<meta>This page continues Descartes’ explanation of the three degrees of sensation. -># RESPONSES<-

the difference is that we attribute to the **understanding** <note>French: *entendement*; the faculty of the mind that deals with logic and clear reasoning.</note> those new and unusual judgments we make concerning things that present themselves to our senses; whereas we attribute to the **senses** those judgments we have been accustomed to making since our childhood regarding sensible things, triggered by the impressions they make on our sense organs. The reason for this is that custom makes us reason and judge so quickly about these things (or rather, makes us remember the judgments we made about them in the past) that we no longer distinguish this way of judging from the simple apprehension or perception of our senses.

From this, it is clear that when we say the certainty of the understanding is greater than that of the senses, our words mean nothing more than that the judgments we make at a more advanced age—based on new observations we have made—are more certain than those we formed in our infancy without any reflection. This cannot be doubted. It is certain that we are not talking here about the first or second degree of sensation, since there can be no falsehood in them.

Therefore, when someone says that a stick appears broken in the water because of <term>refraction<note>The bending of light as it passes from one medium (air) into another (water), which creates the visual illusion of a straight object being bent.</note></term>, it is the same as saying it appears to us in such a way that a child would judge it to be broken, and which also causes us—according to the <term>prejudices<note>In this historical context, "prejudices" refers to "pre-judgments" or ideas we accept as true before we have the capacity to reason for ourselves.</note></term> we have been accustomed to since childhood—to judge the same thing. 

But I cannot agree with what is added next: namely, that this error is not corrected by the understanding, but by the sense of **touch** <note>French: *l'attouchement*; the tactile sense.</note>. For although this sense makes us judge that a stick is straight—and does so through that way of judging we have been accustomed to since childhood, which can consequently be called "sensation"—this is nevertheless not enough to correct the error of sight. Beyond this, it is necessary that we have some **reason** which teaches us that, in this instance, we should trust the judgment we make following our touch rather than the one to which the sense of sight seems to lead us. Since this reason has not been in us since our childhood, it cannot be attributed to the senses, but to the understanding alone. Therefore, in this very example, it is the understanding alone that corrects the error of the sense. It is impossible to ever provide an example in which the error comes from having trusted the operation of the mind more than the perception of the senses.

I had had others before, and I found that the main reason was that from my youth I had made several judgments regarding natural things (as those which were to contribute much to the preservation of my life, in which I was only just entering), and that I had always since retained the same opinions I had had of them previously. And although it had knowledge of its own nature, and had no less the idea of **thought** than that of **extension** <note>term: *extension* (French: *étendue*); the defining characteristic of physical matter for Descartes—the fact that it takes up space.</note> within itself, nevertheless because it conceived nothing purely intellectual without imagining at the same time something corporeal, it took one for the other and applied to the body all the notions it had of intellectual things. And since I had never since freed myself from these prejudices, there was nothing I knew distinctly enough that I did not suppose to be corporeal, although I often formed such ideas of these very things that I supposed to be corporeal, and had such notions of them that they represented spirits rather than bodies. 

For example, when I conceived of **gravity** <note>original: *pesanteur*; in this era, gravity was often understood as an internal "heaviness" or "tendency to fall" rather than a modern gravitational force.</note> as a **real quality** <note>term: *qualité réelle*; a Scholastic term for a property that was thought to have its own existence independent of the object it belongs to.</note>, inherent and attached to massive and coarse bodies, even though I called it a quality in as much as I related it to the body in which it resided, nevertheless, because I added the word "real," I thought in effect it was a **substance** <note>Descartes defines "substance" as a thing that can exist on its own; here he argues he was mistakenly treating weight as if it were a separate thing from the object.</note>, just as a garment considered in itself is a substance, though when related to a dressed man it can be called a quality; and thus, although the mind is a substance, it can nonetheless be called a quality in regard to the body to which it is united. 

And although I conceived that gravity is spread throughout the entire body that is heavy, I did not attribute to it the same kind of extension that constitutes the nature of the body, for that extension is such that it excludes all penetrability of parts; and I thought there was as much gravity in a mass of gold, or some other metal the length of one foot, as there was in a piece of wood ten feet long; indeed, I even estimated that all this gravity could be contained under a **mathematical point**. And even when this gravity was thus equally extended throughout the body, I saw that it could exert all its force in each of its parts, because, in whatever way this body was suspended by a rope, it pulled with all its weight, as if all that weight were enclosed in the part touching the rope.

This was because, having searched very carefully for the true ideas of other things, and believing that I knew them all in general, I found nothing in them that was not entirely different from the idea of my mind. And finally, I was not afraid that I might have been caught off guard or biased by my analysis when, seeing that there are bodies that do not think, or rather, conceiving very clearly that certain bodies can exist without thought, I preferred to say that thought does not belong at all to the nature of body, rather than concluding that it is a **mode** <term>mode; a specific state or quality of a substance, such as "shape" is a mode of "matter."</term> of it, simply because I saw others (namely, humans) who think; for, to tell the truth, I have never seen or understood that human bodies have thoughts, but rather that it is the same individuals who think and who have bodies. And I recognized that this occurs through the composition and joining together of the **thinking substance** with the **corporeal substance**; for, considering the nature of the thinking substance separately, I noticed nothing in it that could belong to the body, and I found nothing in the nature of the body, considered entirely on its own, that could belong to thought. But, on the contrary, examining all the modes of both the body and the mind, I did not notice a single one whose concept did not depend entirely on the concept of the very thing of which it is a mode. Furthermore, from the fact that we often see two things joined together, one cannot infer that they are but one and the same thing; but from the fact that we sometimes see one of these things without the other, one can very well conclude that they are diverse. And we must not let the **power of God** <note>Descartes is responding to an objection that God’s omnipotence could theoretically make a body think; he argues that even God cannot make a contradiction, such as making two fundamentally different things truly one and the same in essence.</note> prevent us from drawing this conclusion: for there is no less a contradiction in thinking that things we conceive clearly and distinctly as two diverse things could be made into one single thing in essence and without any composition, than in thinking that one could separate what is in no way distinct. Consequently, if God has placed the faculty of thinking in certain bodies (as indeed He has placed it in those of men), He can, whenever He wishes, separate it from them, and thus it does not cease to be really distinct from those bodies. And I am not surprised to have formerly understood very well—even before I had freed myself from the **prejudices of my senses** <note>Descartes often refers to "prejudices" as the unexamined beliefs we pick up in childhood, such as the idea that our senses show us the world exactly as it is.</note>—that two and three joined together make the number five, and that *when equal things are taken from equal things, the remainders are equal*, and several similar things; even though I did not then consider that the soul of man was distinct from his body; for I see very well that the reason I did not make false judgments in my childhood regarding these propositions, which are generally accepted by everyone, was because they were not yet of any use to me at that time, and because children do not learn to...

<summary>Descartes argues for the "real distinction" between mind and body, asserting that because we can clearly conceive of them as separate, they are distinct substances, even when joined in humans. He maintains that even divine power cannot merge two distinct essences into one without them remaining separate in nature.</summary>

# REPLIES TO THE SIXTH OBJECTIONS

...to join two with three without being able to judge if they make the number five, and so on. Quite the contrary, from my earliest youth I conceived of the **mind** and the **body** (of which I saw confusedly that I was composed) as one and the same thing; and it is the almost universal vice of all **imperfect knowledge** <note>Descartes refers here to our childhood prejudices and sensory experiences before we apply his method of doubt.</note> to join several things into one and take them all for the same thing. This is why it is later necessary to take the trouble to separate them and, through a more exact examination, distinguish them from one another.

But I am greatly astonished that very learned persons, accustomed for thirty years to **metaphysical speculations** <term>metaphysical speculations; abstract philosophical reasoning about the nature of reality beyond physical science.</term>, having read my *Meditations* more than seven times, should persuade themselves that if I were to reread them with the same spirit as if they had been proposed to me by an enemy, I would not value or have such a favorable opinion of the reasons they contain as to believe that everyone should yield to the force and weight of their truths and connections—especially given that they themselves show no fault in all my reasoning.

And certainly, they attribute much more to me than they should, and more than one should think of any man, if they believe that I use such an **analysis** <term>analysis; Descartes' method of breaking down complex problems into their simplest parts to find absolute certainty.</term> that I could use it to overturn true demonstrations, or give such a color to false ones that no one could ever discover their falsity. On the contrary, I openly profess that I have never sought any other method than that by which one could ensure the certainty of true reasons and discover the vice of false and **deceptive** <note>original: "captieuses"</note> ones.

Therefore, I am not as surprised to see very learned people not yet agreeing with my conclusions as I am joyful to see that, after such a serious and frequent reading of my arguments, they do not blame me for having advanced anything inappropriately, or for having drawn any conclusion outside of **proper logical form** <note>original: "dans les formes"; referring to the syllogistic or mathematical rules of logic.</note>. For the difficulty they have in accepting my conclusions can easily be attributed to the **long-standing habit** <note>original: "coutume invétérée"</note> they have of judging differently what these conclusions contain. This is much like what has been observed of **astronomers**, who cannot imagine that the sun is larger than the earth, although they have very certain reasons that demonstrate it. But I do not see that there could be any other reason why neither these gentlemen, nor anyone else I know, has been able to find anything to criticize in my reasoning so far, except that they are entirely true and **indubitable** <term>indubitable; something so certain that it is impossible to doubt.</term>. This is especially true since the principles upon which they are based are neither obscure nor unknown, having all been drawn from the most certain and evident notions...

<summary>Descartes argues that our initial confusion of mind and body is a result of childhood habit, which must be corrected through rigorous analysis. He defends the logical integrity of his work, noting that even his critics have failed to find a formal error in his arguments.</summary>

# REPLIES TO THE SIXTH OBJECTIONS

...which present themselves to a mind that a general doubt regarding all things has already freed from all kinds of **prejudices** <term>prejudices; in Cartesian philosophy, these are the unexamined beliefs and "common sense" assumptions we gather during childhood that cloud clear reasoning.</term>; for it necessarily follows from this that there can be no **errors** that any person of even moderate intelligence could not have easily noticed. ### SEVENTH SET OF OBJECTIONS
->OR THE DISSERTATION BY THE REVEREND FATHER * <note>The asterisk refers to Pierre Bourdin (1595–1653), a Jesuit professor who was one of Descartes' most persistent and biting critics.</note> CONCERNING<-

->SIR,<-

The requests you make of me regarding your new method of searching for truth in the sciences are numerous and important; and although, to extract a response from me, you do not use simple prayers but very pressing entreaties, I shall nonetheless remain silent and not satisfy your desire at all, unless you first promise me that throughout this entire discourse we will not have regard in any way for any of those who have previously written or taught anything concerning this matter, and that you will regulate your requests such that one cannot believe you have the intention of knowing what they thought about it, and with what success they wrote; but as if no one before you had ever thought, nor said, nor written anything on this subject, that you will only propose to me the difficulties that might be encountered in the search you are making for a new method of philosophizing, so that by this means, we might not only seek the truth, but seek it also in such a way that we do not offend the laws of friendship and the respect that must be kept between scholars. Since you agree to this and promise it to me, I also promise to answer all your requests.

### SEVENTH SET OF OBJECTIONS

...know of ever having asked him for his opinion concerning the method I use to search for truth. On the contrary, having seen for a year and a half the skirmish <note>original: "vélitation"; a term for a preliminary verbal attack or minor academic debate</note> he had written against me, in which I saw that he was straying from the truth by attributing to me several things that I have never written or thought, I do not hide the fact that from then on I judged that everything which might come from him alone would not be worth the trouble of losing much time in responding to it. 

But because it concerns the body of a society <note>Refers to the Society of Jesus, the Jesuits, who were the preeminent educators of the time.</note> very famous for its piety and for its doctrine, and of which all the members are usually so well united that it rarely happens that anything is done by one of them that is not approved by all the others, I admit that not only have I requested, but I have even very urgently pressed some of them to please take the trouble to examine my writings, and if they found anything in them contrary to the truth, to have the kindness to inform me. To which I even added several reasons that made me hope they would not refuse me this favor; and in this hope, I ventured to write to one of them that henceforth I would place great value on everything that would come, both from this author and from any other of the company, and that I would not doubt that what would be sent to me thus on their behalf would be the censure, the examination, and the correction—not only of that individual whose name the writing might bear, but of several of the most learned and wisest of the society. 

Consequently, I expected that it would contain no quibbling <term>quibbling (cavillations); petty or trivial objections designed to evade the main point of an argument.</term>, no fallacies <term>fallacies (sophismes); arguments that seem plausible but are logically unsound.</term>, no insults, nor any useless discourse, but only good and solid reasons, and that no arguments which could reasonably be alleged against me would be omitted. Thus, I would have reason to hope to be entirely delivered from all my errors by this single writing, and if it happened that there were anything in my works which escaped its censure, I would believe that it could be refuted by no one, and therefore that it would be very certain and very true. 

This is why I would now judge the same thing of this dissertation, and I would believe that it had been written by the advice of the whole society, if I were certain that it contained no quibbling, no fallacies, nor any useless discourse; but if it is true that this writing is full of them, I would believe I was committing a crime to suspect that so great a number of pious persons had had a hand in it. And because in this I do not wish to trust my own judgment, I will say candidly and frankly what it seems to me, not so that the reader adds faith to my words, but only to give him occasion to examine the truth more closely.

He notes that if the response lacks logical rigor, it likely does not represent the wisdom of the entire Society of Jesus.</summary>

AND RESPONSES

"I shall remain silent, however, etc." <note>Descartes is quoting the opening of Bourdin’s latest response.</note> Here our author <note>Pierre Bourdin, the Jesuit priest and critic of Descartes.</note> promises not to attack anyone’s opinions, but only to respond to the questions I have asked him—even though I am not aware of ever having asked him any, and indeed have never seen him nor spoken with him about anything. However, since the questions he pretends I am proposing to him are mostly composed of words found in my *Meditations* <note>original: "Méditations"; referring to Descartes’ 1641 work *Meditations on First Philosophy*, the foundation of his system.</note>, one would have to be blind not to see that it is these very works he intends to attack with this writing. Perhaps the reasons that compel him to feign the contrary are pious and honorable; but for my part, I can suspect no others than that he believed this would allow him more freedom to impose upon me whatever he pleased. He likely felt he could not be proven wrong by my writings if he declared from the start that he intended no harm to anyone. Furthermore, he may wish to avoid giving readers the occasion to examine my *Meditations*, which they might do if he had only mentioned them. It seems he prefers to make me pass for unskilled and ignorant in order to dissuade them from ever reading anything that might come from me. And so, having fashioned a mask out of a few poorly stitched pieces of my *Meditations*, he tries not to hide, but to disfigure my face. This is why I here lift the mask and show myself openly, both because I am not accustomed to playing such characters and because it seems to me unbecoming to use such tactics when dealing with a religious person <note>In this context, "religious" refers to Bourdin’s status as a member of a Catholic religious order (the Jesuits).</note> on a subject so serious and important.

### FIRST QUESTION.

->*Whether doubtful things should be considered false,*<-
->*and in what way.*<-

You ask, in the first place, if this is a good rule for searching for truth: *everything that has the slightest appearance of doubt must be held as false*. But so that I may respond to you on this matter, I have a few questions of my own to ask you beforehand. First, what do you mean by these words: *that which has the slightest appearance of doubt*? Second, what do they mean: *must be held as false*? Third: how should one hold a thing to be false? As for the first, which concerns the doubt one may have about something, here is how you answer it, and in few words.

SEVENTH OBJECTIONS

## § I.
### *What it is to have the slightest appearance of doubt.*

A thing can be said to have some appearance of doubt if I can doubt whether it exists, or if it is as I say it is, not because of some light and ill-founded suspicions, but for good and solid reasons. Furthermore, a thing can be said to have some appearance of doubt which, though it seems clear to me, can nevertheless be subject to the deceptions of some evil genius <note>original: "mauvais génie"; also translated as "evil demon," a hypothetical being Descartes uses to test the absolute limits of doubt.</note> who takes pleasure in employing all his industry to ensure that what is false in effect appears to me nevertheless clear and certain. 

What is doubtful in the first sense has much appearance of doubt: for example, that there is an earth, colors, that you have a head, eyes, a body, and a mind; what is so in the second sense has less, but still has enough to be considered doubtful, and to be so in effect: for example, that two and three make five, that the whole is greater than its part and similar things. This is very well answered. But if it is so, what is there, I ask you, that does not have some appearance of doubt? What will there be that is exempt from the ruses of this evil genius? 

Nothing, you say, nothing at all, until we are assured, by the unshakable principles of metaphysics, that there is a God, and that he cannot be a deceiver; so that one can say that before we know if there is a God, and assuming there is one, if he can be a deceiver, we can never be quite certain or assured of anything. And, to give you here my thought in its entirety, if I do not know that there is a God, and a true God, who prevents this evil genius from deceiving me, I could and even should always apprehend that he might seduce me by his artifices, and that, under the appearance of truth, he might make me see what is false as clear and assured; but when I am entirely and certainly assured that there is a God, and that he can be neither deceived nor a deceiver, and that thus he necessarily prevents this evil genius from abusing me in the things that I have clearly and distinctly <note>term: "clearly and distinctly"; Descartes’ technical standard for truth—information that is present and accessible to the mind (clear) and distinguished from all other things (distinct).</note> conceived, it will be then that if such things are met with—that is, if I happen to have clearly and distinctly conceived some of them—I shall hold them for true and for certain. 

So that I may then with assurance establish as a rule of truth and certainty that everything we conceive *clearly* and *distinctly* is true. I wish for nothing more on this article. I come now to my second question.

<summary>Descartes explores the levels of doubt, distinguishing between sensory uncertainty and the more radical doubt posed by the "evil genius" hypothesis, eventually concluding that certainty requires a non-deceiving God.</summary>
<keywords>René Descartes, Pierre Bourdin, evil genius, radical doubt, clear and distinct perception, existence of God, metaphysics, mathematical certainty</keywords>

AND RESPONSES

## § II.
### *What does this mean: to hold a thing as false?*

Since, according to you, it is a matter of doubt whether you have eyes, a head, or a body, and since you say you must even hold this to be false, I ask you then to tell me: what does it mean to hold a thing as false? Would it not be to believe and to say: "It is false that I have eyes, a head, or a body"? Or rather, to believe and to say, through a determination entirely opposed to our doubt: "I have no eyes, no head, nor a body"? In a word, would it not be to believe, say, and affirm the opposite of the thing one doubts? 

"That is exactly it," you say; "that is well and good." 

But I ask you to tell me your thoughts on this further: if it is not a certain thing that two and three make five, must I then believe and affirm that two and three do not make five? 

"Yes," you say, "that is how one must believe and affirm it." 

I ask you again: if it is not certain whether, while I am saying these things, I am awake or if I sleep, must I then believe and say: "Yes, while I am saying these things, I am not awake, but I am sleeping"? 

"That," you say, "is how it must be believed and said." 

I will ask you only one more thing, so as not to weary you: if it is not certain that what appears clear and assured to someone who doubts whether they are awake or asleep is actually clear and assured, must I then believe and say: "What appears clear and assured to one who doubts whether they sleep or wake is not clear and assured, but is false and obscure"? Why do you hesitate at this point? You could never grant too much to your mistrust <note>The critic is pushing Descartes' method to its extreme: if we cannot be 100% sure of something, should we logically conclude that the opposite is true?</note>. Has it never happened to you, as it has to many others, that the very same things which seemed clear and certain while sleeping later appeared false and doubtful? Without a doubt, prudence dictates that we should never entirely trust those who have once deceived us. 

But, you say, it is quite different for things that are completely certain, for they are such that even to those who sleep, or who are mad, they can never appear doubtful. Is it then in all seriousness, I ask you, that you say that completely certain things are such that they cannot even appear doubtful to those who sleep or are mad? But honestly, where will you find these things? And why—if it is true that to those who sleep or are troubled in mind <note>original: "l'esprit troublé," referring to those suffering from insanity or delirium.</note>, things that are ridiculous and absurd nonetheless sometimes appear not only true, but also very certain—why then would those things which are the most assured not appear to them false and <unclear>doubtful</unclear>?

<summary>This page critiques Descartes' method of radical doubt, questioning whether doubting a proposition requires one to actively affirm its opposite. It challenges the reliability of "certainty" by pointing out that the dreaming and the insane often feel absolute certainty about absurdities.</summary>

# SEVENTH OBJECTIONS

...shameful? And as proof of this, I knew a person who, one day, as they were dozing off, having heard the clock strike four, began to count the strikes like this: one, one, one, one. At that moment, the absurdity they conceived in their mind made them cry out: "I think this clock is mad; it has struck one o'clock four times!" And indeed, is there anything so absurd and so contrary to reason that it cannot enter the mind of a madman or a man who sleeps? Is there anything that a dreamer does not approve of and believe, and about which they do not flatter themselves as if it were a very fine thing they had discovered and invented? 

Finally, to conclude everything in a word, I say that you will never be able to establish the certainty of this axiom—namely, that everything that seems true to one who doubts whether they sleep or wake is certain, and so certain that it can be taken as the foundation of a very true and very exact metaphysics <note>Metaphysics: The branch of philosophy that deals with the first principles of things, including abstract concepts such as being, knowing, substance, cause, identity, time, and space.</note>—well enough that I would hold it as certain as this one: "two and three make five." Nor could you make it so certain that no one could in any way doubt it, nor be deceived in it by some evil genius <note>original: "mauvais génie." In Descartes' *Meditations*, the "evil genius" is a hypothetical, powerful, and clever demon who uses all his energy to deceive the philosopher, making him doubt even the most basic mathematical truths.</note>.

And yet, I do not fear being considered stubborn, even though I persist in this thought. This is why I will either conclude here according to your own rule: "it is not certain that what appears certain to one who doubts whether they wake or sleep is certain, therefore what appears certain to one who doubts whether they wake or sleep can and must be considered false." Or else, if you have some particular rule, you will take the trouble to communicate it to me. I come now to my third question, which concerns the way in which one must hold a thing to be false.

## § III.
### *How one should hold a thing to be false.*

I ask you—since I am not assured that two and three make five, and since by the previous rule I must believe and say that two and three do not make five—whether I should not immediately believe it so strongly that I persuade myself that the thing cannot be otherwise, and therefore that it is certain that two and three do not make five. You are surprised that I ask you this; but I am not surprised, since it also surprised me. Nevertheless, it is necessary that you answer it if you also want me to answer you. Do you want me then to hold it for certain that two and three do not make five? I see well that you want it, and even that you want everyone...

# AND ANSWERS

...believes it and holds it to be so certain that it cannot be made doubtful by the tricks of this evil genius <note>original: "mauvais génie." In Descartes’ philosophy, this is a hypothetical, powerful deceiver who might manipulate our every perception.</note>.
You are mocking me, you say; can such a thing enter the mind of a wise man?

What then! Would this be as doubtful and uncertain as this: two and three make five? If it is so, if it is a doubtful thing that two and three do not make five, I will believe nothing of it, and I will say according to your rule that it is false, and therefore I will admit the contrary, and so I will say: two and three make five, and I will do the same everywhere else. And because it does not seem certain that there is any body <term>body: In 17th-century philosophy, "body" refers to any physical, material substance that occupies space, as opposed to the "mind" or "soul."</term> in the world, I will say that there are none at all. But also, because it is not a certain thing that there is no body in the world, I will say by opposition that there is some body in the world, and thus at the same time there will be some body in the world and there will be none.

It is true, you say, this is how one must act, and this is properly what is called doubting—to come and go upon one's steps, to advance and retreat, to affirm this and that and immediately deny it, to stop at one thing and then depart from it.

Nothing could be better; but, to make use of the things that will be doubtful, what shall I do? For example, what shall I do with this one: two and three make five? And with this other: is there some body? Shall I assert it? Or shall I deny it?

You will neither assert it, you say, nor deny it; you will use neither one nor the other, but you will hold both to be false, and you will expect nothing but wavering, doubtful, and uncertain things from those things which are thus wavering and uncertain.

Since I have nothing left to ask you, I am going to answer all your questions one after another as soon as I have made here a brief recapitulation of your entire doctrine. 1. We cannot doubt all things, and especially material things, as long as we have no other foundations in the sciences than those we have had until now. 2. To hold something as false is to refuse one's approval to that thing as if it were manifestly false, or even to feign that one has the same opinion of it as of a false and imaginary thing. 3. That which is doubtful must be so thoroughly held as false that its opposite is also doubtful and held as false.

# SEVENTH OBJECTIONS

...things that I do not recognize at all as my own, although they are expressed here almost entirely in my own words. This is why I only ask the reader to remember what I wrote in my first Meditation and at the beginning of the second and third, as well as what I said in their synopsis; for they will recognize that most of the things reported here have indeed been taken from them, but that they are presented here in such a disorder, and so corrupted and misinterpreted, that although in the places where they were originally situated they contain nothing but what is very reasonable, here they nevertheless appear for the most part quite absurd.

**For good and solid reasons.** I said, toward the end of the first Meditation, that *very strong and maturely considered* reasons could oblige us to doubt all the things that we had never yet clearly enough conceived. This was because in that place I was dealing only with that general and universal doubt which I have often myself called hyperbolic <note>original: "hyperbolique." From the Greek for "excessive," this refers to a doubt pushed to the furthest possible extreme for the sake of finding an absolute truth.</note> and metaphysical, and of which I said one must not make use for matters regarding the conduct of life. And, consequently, that in its regard, anything that could give rise to the slightest suspicion of uncertainty should be taken as a valid enough reason for doubting. But here this "officious and sincere man" <note>Descartes is using heavy irony here to describe his opponent, Pierre Bourdin, who he feels is being neither helpful (officious) nor honest (sincere).</note> brings forward as examples things of which I said one could doubt for good and solid reasons—namely, whether there is an earth, whether I have a body, and similar things—so that readers who have no knowledge of this metaphysical doubt, applying it instead to the usage and conduct of life, will take me for a man who has lost his senses.

*Nothing, you say, nothing at all.* I have sufficiently explained in various places in what sense this must be understood. That is to say, while we are attentive to some truth that we conceive very clearly, we cannot then in any way doubt it; but when we are not so attentive, and we do not think of the reasons that prove it (as often happens), even though we remember having clearly conceived several such truths, there is nonetheless none of them that we cannot reasonably doubt if we are ignorant of the fact that all the things we conceive very clearly and very distinctly <term>clearly and distinctly: In Cartesian philosophy, a "clear" perception is present and accessible to the mind, while a "distinct" one is so precise that it is distinguished from all other objects.</term> are all true. But here this "very exact man" interprets that word, *nothing*, in such a way that from what I said once in my first Meditation—where I supposed I perceived nothing clearly and distinctly, and that there was nothing I was not permitted to doubt—he concludes that I can also know nothing certain in the following Meditations.

He clarifies that certain knowledge is possible when the mind focuses "clearly and distinctly" on a truth, provided one accepts the foundational rule of his system.</summary>

But because it belongs only to wise persons to distinguish between what is clearly conceived and what only seems and appears to be so, I am not surprised that this "good man" takes one for the other here.

->Responses.<-

**Response 1.** If, in the search we make for the truth, this rule—namely, that everything that has the slightest appearance of doubt must be held as false—is understood in this way: when we search for what is certain, we must in no way rely on what is not certain, or on what has some appearance of doubt, I say that it is a good rule, that it is in use, and commonly accepted by all philosophers.

**Response 2.** If this rule of which we speak is understood in this way: when we search for what is certain, we must so thoroughly reject all things that are not certain, or that are in some way doubtful, that we do not make use of them at all; or even that we must no longer consider them any more than if they did not exist; or rather that we must not consider them at all, but must turn our thought entirely away from them; I say also that it is legitimate, assured, and even familiar to the lowest <term>apprentices</term> <note>Descartes refers here to students or beginners in the study of logic and philosophy.</note>, and that it has so much relation and affinity with the preceding rule that one can hardly distinguish it from the other.

**Response 3.** But if this rule is understood in this way: when we search for what is certain, we must so thoroughly reject all things that are doubtful that we suppose that they do not exist in fact, or that their opposite truly exists, and that we use this supposition as an assured foundation—that is to say, that we use these things that are not, and that we rely on their nonexistence; I say that it is not legitimate, but false and contrary to true philosophy, because it supposes something doubtful and uncertain in order to search for what is true and certain; or because it supposes as certain what can be sometimes one way, and sometimes another—for example, that doubtful things do not exist in fact, even though it may be possible that they do exist.

**Response 4.** If someone, understanding this rule in the sense explained above, wanted to use it to seek what is true and certain, he would undoubtedly waste his time and effort; he would work without fruit or success, seeing as he would no sooner prove what he seeks than its opposite. For example, let us suppose that someone seeks and examines whether he has a <term>body</term> <note>original: "corps." In Cartesian philosophy, the body is the "extended thing" (res extensa), distinct from the mind or "thinking thing."</note>, or if he can be corporeal, and that, to clarify this truth, he argues thus: it is not certain that any body exists; therefore, following our rule, I will assert and say the contrary—namely, that no body exists. Then he will resume his argument: no body exists; yet I know very well, on the other hand, that I am and that I exist; therefore, I cannot be a body. In truth, this is very well concluded; but you see how, by the same reasoning, he can also prove the contrary. It is not certain, he says, that any body exists; therefore, following our rule, I will assert and say: no body exists. But is this proposition—*no body exists*—not itself doubtful? Undoubtedly it is, and who could show me the contrary? If that is so, I have what I ask for. It is certain that no body exists <note>Bourdin is mocking Descartes here by deliberately misapplying the rule of doubt to create a logical loop.</note>. Therefore, following our rule, I will say: some body exists; now, as it is that I am and that I exist, I can therefore be a body if nothing else prevents it. You see then that I can be a body, and that I can not be a body. Are you satisfied? I fear that you are too much so, as far as I can conjecture from what follows. This is why I come to your second question.

### SECOND QUESTION.

->*Whether it is a good method of philosophizing to make a general renunciation of all the things that can be doubted.*<-

You ask me, in the second place, if it is a good method of philosophizing to make a renunciation of all the things of which one can in some way doubt; but you must not expect any answer from me if you do not explain at greater length what this method is, and here is how you do so.

To philosophize, you say, and to search for whether there is something certain and very certain, and to know what that thing is, here is how I go about it: Since all the things I formerly believed and that I have known until now are doubtful and uncertain, I hold them all to be false, and there is not one that I do not reject; and thus I persuade myself that there is no earth, nor heaven, nor any of the things I formerly believed to be in the world, and even also that there is no world, no bodies, no minds, and in a word that there is nothing at all. This is Descartes’ famous thought experiment where he imagines a powerful deceiver to test the absolute certainty of his knowledge.</note> who employed all his strength and all his industry to make me fall into error. # SEVENTH OBJECTIONS

...sometimes we dream; there are sometimes certain madmen who think they see what they do not see, and what perhaps is not and will never be.

Are these all your reasons? When you promised strong and maturely considered ones, I also expected that they would be certain and free from any kind of doubt, such as your rule demands—that rule we are using now, which is so exact that it does not admit even the slightest shadow of doubt. But these reasons you have just brought forward—namely, that our senses deceive us sometimes, that sometimes we dream, and that there are madmen—are they certain and free from doubts? Or rather, are they not simply pure doubts and suspicions? Who taught you that they are certain and beyond all doubt, and in conformity with that rule you always have at hand, namely: *that one must be very careful to admit nothing as true that we cannot prove to be such*? Has there ever been a time when you could say: "Certainly and indubitably <note>original: "indubitablement"</note> my senses are deceiving me right now, I know it very well. Now I am dreaming; a little while ago I was dreaming; this man is mad, and thinks he sees what he does not see, and he is not lying"? 

If you say yes, be careful how you prove it; indeed, even take care that this evil genius <note>original: "mauvais génie" — the malicious deceiver Descartes imagines to justify his radical doubt.</note> of whom you speak has not perhaps deceived you. For it is much to be feared that at the very moment you offer this as a very strong and maturely considered reason for doubt—*the senses sometimes deceive us*—this cunning genius is pointing his finger and mocking you for having allowed yourself to be so misled. If you say no, why do you say so confidently that we sometimes dream? Why, following your first rule, do you not rather say this: "It is not entirely certain that the senses have sometimes deceived us, that we have sometimes dreamed, or that there have sometimes been madmen; therefore I will say this, and establish it as a principle, that our senses never deceive us, that we never dream, and that there are no madmen."

But, you say, I have some suspicion of it. And I tell you that this is what causes my hesitation <note>original: "scrupule" — used here to mean a point of doubt or a difficulty that stops one's progress.</note>; for, when I thought to move my foot forward, I felt these "strong reasons" give way beneath me and vanish like shadows and suspicions, which made me afraid to press down upon them. Yet I have some suspicion of it just as you do.

You have some suspicion of it, you say? It is enough that you suspect it; it is enough that you say: "I do not know if I am sleeping or if I am awake; I do not know if my senses deceive me or do not deceive me."

<summary>Pierre Bourdin critiques Descartes' method by pointing out a logical paradox: if Descartes requires absolute certainty for any truth, he cannot "certainly" know that his senses deceive him or that he is dreaming. Bourdin argues that Descartes' reasons for doubting are themselves merely "suspicions" and thus fail his own test of certainty.</summary>

## AND ANSWERS

But forgive me if I say that this is not enough for me, and that I am not satisfied by it; for I do not see clearly how you can infer from this: *I do not know if I am awake or if I sleep, therefore I sleep sometimes.* For if you never slept, if you always slept, if you were not even able to sleep, and if this genius <note>original: "génie" — referring to the "evil genius" or malicious deceiver (*malin génie*) Descartes uses as a thought experiment to justify doubting everything.</note> mocked you by having the power to persuade you that you sleep sometimes, and that sometimes you are mistaken—even though that were not the case—believe me, since you introduced this genius, and since you reduced your strongest and most solid reasons to a *perhaps*, you have spoiled everything, and can draw nothing good from it. How do you know if this cunning genius does not propose all things to you as doubtful and uncertain, despite the fact that they are certain and assured, so that after having rejected them all, he may throw you naked into the pit you have dug for yourself? Would you not do better if, before making such a <term>general abdication</term><note>The total renunciation of all previously held beliefs and knowledge.</note> of all things, you established for yourself a certain rule by which you could recognize if all the things you reject are rightly or wrongly rejected? And, if you will take my word for it, I advise you to once again call your thoughts to judgment, to deliberate upon them maturely and seriously, and to rush nothing in this matter.

That is not necessary, you say; I could not grant too much to my distrust here, and I know that there can be no peril or error in this.

AND RESPONSES

I follow you. In all honesty, I find it easy for you to go first like this without any reluctance.

### *Remarks of Mr. Descartes.*

"Since all the things I have known until now are doubtful." He has written here "I have known" instead of "I believed I knew": for there is a contradiction between these terms—"I have known" and "are doubtful"—which he undoubtedly did not notice. However, one should not attribute this to <term>malice</term><note>In 17th-century philosophical debate, 'malice' refers to a deliberate, bad-faith attempt to misrepresent an opponent's argument to make it look foolish.</note> for that reason; for otherwise, he would not have touched upon it as lightly as he did. On the contrary, if he were pretending that the error had come from me, he would have used many words to labor the point against me.

"I say no mind, no body." He says this in order to have the opportunity later to <term>quibble</term><note>The original French 'pointiller' suggests a pedantic focus on trivial points to avoid the substance of the argument.</note> for a long time over the fact that at the beginning—supposing that the nature of the mind was not yet sufficiently known to me—I placed it among the doubtful things. He then notes that afterward, recognizing that a thing that thinks could not fail to exist, and calling this thinking thing by the name "mind," I said that a mind existed. He acts as if I had forgotten that I had previously denied it when I took the "mind" for something unknown to me. It is as if he believed that things I denied at one time because they appeared uncertain must always be denied, and that it were impossible for them to later become evident and certain. It is worth noting that throughout his critique, he considers doubt and certainty not as relations between our knowledge and the objects, but as properties of the objects themselves which remain always attached to them; as if things we have once recognized as doubtful can never be made certain. This should be attributed to simplicity rather than to malice.

"What, all things?" He quibbles here on this word "all," just as he did before on the word "nothing," but uselessly and in vain.

"You admit it, being forced." He has done the same with this term "forced," but as uselessly as with the previous ones; for it is certain that those reasons are strong enough to oblige us to doubt—reasons which are themselves doubtful and uncertain, and which for that reason must not be retained but rejected, as was noted above. They are, I say, strong enough as long as we have no others which, while dispelling doubt, bring certainty at the same time. And because I found no such certainties in the first <term>Meditation</term><note>Descartes refers to his 'Meditations on First Philosophy' (1641), specifically the first chapter where he employs "radical doubt" to strip away all uncertain beliefs.</note>, although I looked in every direction and meditated constantly, I said for that reason that...

the reasons I had for doubting were strong and maturely considered. But this exceeds the grasp of our author, for he adds: *when you promised good and strong reasons, I also expected they would be certain, such as your rule demands*, as if this rule he imagines could be applied to the things I said in the first Meditation; and a little later he says: *was there ever a time when you could say certainly and indubitably: my senses are deceiving me right now; I know this very well;* where he falls into a contradiction similar to the previous one, not perceiving that holding a thing to be indubitable, and at the same time doubting that same thing, are two things that <term>contradict</term><note>Descartes is pointing out that Bourdin is confusing the *act* of doubting with a *claim* of certain knowledge about deception.</note> each other. Doubtless, this <term>general abdication</term><note>The process of "stripping away" or renouncing all previous beliefs to restart philosophy from a blank slate.</note> of all our past knowledge is a matter of the greatest importance. I gave sufficient warning of this at the end of my response to the fourth Objections, and in the preface to these Meditations, which I proposed for reading only to the most robust minds. I also gave warning of the same thing very expressly in my *Discourse on the Method*, where, having described two different types of minds for whom this general abdication is not suited—if perhaps our author finds himself included under one or the other type, he should not for that reason attribute his errors to me.

# AND REPLIES

What do you mean, "I know"? When I said that I knew there could be no danger in this <term>general abdication</term><note>French: *abdication générale*. This refers to Descartes’ method of temporarily setting aside all previous beliefs to find a stable foundation for knowledge.</note>, I added: because at that time I was not considering things in order to act, but only in order to know them. This shows so clearly that I was speaking in that place only of a <term>moral way of knowing</term><note>A level of certainty sufficient for the practical conduct of daily life, but which may not meet the absolute requirements of logic or science.</note> which suffices for the conduct of life. I have often said this is very different from the <term>metaphysical</term> way which is the subject here—so different, in fact, that it seems only our author alone could have been ignorant of it.

And yet they want me to retain this way of knowing, which is filled with doubts and difficulties; I could not grant too much to my own <term>distrust</term><note>French: *défiance*. In this context, it refers to the cautious, methodical skepticism Descartes employs to avoid error.</note>. Here again, there is a contradiction in his words: for everyone knows that he who distrusts—while he is distrusting, and consequently neither affirming nor denying anything—cannot be led into error by any <term>genius</term><note>Refers to the "evil genius" or "cunning demon" hypothesis from the *Meditations*.</note>, however cunning he may be. This cannot be said of one who adds two and three together, as is proven by the example he himself brought up above regarding the man who counted an hour four times over.

It is not without a great fear of appearing too distrustful that I reject these ancient maxims. Although he uses many words here to try to persuade me that one must not be too distrustful, it is nevertheless a thing worthy of note that he does not bring the slightest reason to prove it, except only this: that he "fears" or "distrusts" that one should not distrust so much. Here there is even more <term>repugnance</term><note>In 17th-century logic, "repugnance" often meant a formal contradiction or inconsistency.</note>; for from the very fact that he fears, and that he does not know for certain that he should not distrust, it follows that he *ought* to distrust.

Do you reject without scruple, as something false, this ancient proposition: *I have within me the clear and distinct idea of God*; or this one: *Everything that I conceive very clearly and very distinctly is true*? He calls these things "ancient" because he fears people might take them for new, and that I might have the glory of being the first to notice them—but I care very little about that. He also seems to want to slip in some doubt regarding the idea we have of God, but only in passing; perhaps for fear that those who know with what care I have excepted from this "abdication" all things regarding <term>piety</term> and morals in general, might take him for a slanderer.

Finally, he does not see that this abdication only concerns one who does not yet conceive something clearly and distinctly—such as, for example, the <term>Skeptics</term><note>A school of philosophy that argues that true knowledge is impossible. Descartes uses their tools of doubt but rejects their final conclusion.</note>, to whom this abdication is familiar. Insofar as they are Skeptics, they have never conceived anything clearly; for, from the moment they had conceived something clearly, they would have ceased...

### § II.

->*Preparing the way that grants entry to this Method.*<-

When I have thus performed an abdication of all my past knowledge, I begin to philosophize in this way: *I am, I think; I am while I think.* This proposition, *I exist*, is necessarily true every time I pronounce it or conceive it in my mind.

<meta>This page continues the "Seventh Set of Objections" raised by the Jesuit Father Pierre Bourdin against René Descartes' Meditations. # SEVENTH OBJECTIONS

you are learned and experienced. You are a good guide, you know all the detours and all the paths through which we must pass: I shall have good hope.
What is a man, you say? If you want me to respond, allow me first to ask you which man you intend to speak of? Or what is it you seek when you seek to know what a man is? Is it that man I once imagined myself to be, whom I thought I was, and whom—since I have rejected everything—I now suppose I am not at all? ### *Remarks by Monsieur Descartes.*

I begin to philosophize in this manner: *I am, I think, I am while I think.*<note>original French: "Je suis, je pense, je suis pendant que je pense." This is a variation of Descartes' famous "Cogito, ergo sum" (I think, therefore I am). He emphasizes here that existence is certain specifically during the act of thinking.</note> It should be noted here that he admits himself that to begin philosophizing well, or to establish the certainty of any proposition, one must follow the path I have taken, which is to begin with the knowledge of one's own existence; I say this so that it may be known that, in other places where he has pretended that I began with a positive or affirmative <term>abdication</term><note>Meaning a formal renunciation or giving up of beliefs.</note> of all things that are doubtful, he has said the opposite of what he actually thought. I will not add here with what subtlety he introduces me, beginning to philosophize, when he makes me speak in this way: *I am, I think, etc.* For one can easily recognize, even without me speaking of it, the candor he maintains in all things.

Why do you mention the **mind** when you say, "when I conceive it in my mind"; have you not even banished the body and the mind? I have already previously warned that he was looking for an opportunity to <term>quibble</term><note>original: "pointiller." To raise petty or trivial objections.</note> over the word **mind** [esprit]. But here, to "conceive in one's mind" means nothing other than to think, and therefore he wrongly supposes that I mention the mind as being considered as a part of man. Furthermore, even though I previously rejected the body and the mind along with all the rest of my former opinions as doubtful things or things I did not yet clearly conceive, that does not prevent me from being able to take them back afterward, if it happens that I conceive them clearly. But that is beyond the reach of our author, who thinks that **doubt** is something inseparably attached to objects; for he asks a little later: *how can it be that the same things which were previously doubtful are no longer doubtful now?*

<summary>In this passage, Descartes defends his foundational principle—"I think, therefore I am"—against Father Bourdin's mockery, clarifying that rejecting an idea as "doubtful" is a temporary methodological step, not a permanent dismissal of its reality.</summary>

and uncertain? He even wants me to have made a solemn <term>abdication</term><note>A formal renunciation or giving up of beliefs.</note> of them, and he also admires my skill in using what is doubtful to seek what is certain, etc., as if I had taken as the foundation of my philosophy that one must always consider doubtful things to be false.

Do you want me to consult what I formerly believed I was; do you want me to resume this old *dictum*<note>original: "dictum." A formal pronouncement or saying.</note>, etc. I will use a very familiar example here to make him understand the conduct of my process, so that henceforth he will no longer be ignorant of it, or no longer dare to pretend that he does not understand it.

If by chance he had a basket full of apples, and he feared that some were rotten, and he wanted to remove them for fear that they might corrupt the rest, how would he go about doing it? Would he not first begin by emptying his basket; and after that, looking at all those apples one after another, would he not choose only those that he saw were not spoiled, and, leaving the others aside, put them back into his basket? In the same way also, those who have never philosophized well have various opinions in their mind that they began to amass from their early childhood; and, rightly fearing that most of them are not true, they try to separate them from the others, for fear that their mixture will make them all uncertain. And to avoid making a mistake, they could do no better than to reject them all at once, no more and no less than if they were all false and uncertain; then, examining them in order one after another, take back only those that they recognize to be true and indubitable. This is why I did not do poorly at the beginning by rejecting everything; then considering that I knew nothing more certainly nor more evidently than that I, who was thinking, was something, I did not have such a bad reason to establish that as the first foundation of all my knowledge; and finally, I also did not do poorly to ask after that what I had formerly believed I was, not so that I should still believe all the same things about myself, but in order to take back those that I recognized to be true, to reject those that I found to be false, and to set aside for examination at another time those that seemed doubtful to me. This shows that our author is not right to call this an art of drawing certain things from uncertain ones, or as he says hereafter, a "method of dreaming"; and that all he recounts here and in the following two paragraphs about the rooster of Pythagoras<note>original: "coq de Pythagore." A reference to a satirical work by the ancient writer Lucian, where a rooster (the reincarnation of Pythagoras) talks to a cobbler. Bourdin uses this to mock Descartes' internal dialogue and his "dreaming" method.</note>, and the opinions of philosophers concerning

<summary>Descartes explains his method of doubt using the "basket of apples" analogy, clarifying that he rejects all opinions initially only to sort through them and keep those that are certain. He defends this as the necessary foundation for finding the truth of his own existence.</summary>

# SEVENTH OBJECTIONS

...the nature of the body and of the soul are matters entirely useless and beside the point, since, according to the method I had prescribed for myself, I ought not—and indeed did not wish—to involve myself in reporting anything that others have ever thought on the subject. Instead, I only reported what I myself formerly thought of it, and what people are usually accustomed to think when they allow themselves to be led solely by <term>natural light</term><note>In Cartesian philosophy, "natural light" (lux rationis) refers to the innate human capacity for reason and clear, distinct perception, independent of divine revelation or sensory deception.</note>, whether it be true or false; for I did not report it in order to believe it, but only to examine it.

## § III.

### *What the body is.*

"What is the body?" you ask. "What did I formerly understand by the body?"
You will not take it poorly if I look in all directions, as I fear falling into traps everywhere. Therefore, tell me, I pray you, which "body" do you mean? Is it the one I formerly imagined to be composed of certain properties—but which I imagined poorly, according to the laws of our <term>meditation</term><note>Referring to the process of systematic philosophical reflection described in his *Meditations on First Philosophy*.</note>? Or is it some other body, if perhaps such a thing can exist? For what do I know? I doubt whether that is possible or not. 

If it is the first one you mean, I shall have no trouble answering you. By "body," I understood everything that can be bounded by some shape; which can be contained in some place and fill a space in such a way that every other body is excluded from it; which can be perceived by the senses, and moved by something else that touches it and from which it receives an impression. This is how I described the first "body" I conceived, such that I believed I was obliged to give the name "body" to everything I saw to be clothed in all these properties I have just explained. And yet, I did not think because of this that I was immediately obliged to believe there was nothing else but that which was, or could be, called "body"; seeing mainly that it is quite one thing to say: "I conceived of the body as this or that," and another to say: "I conceived of nothing but this or that as being a body."

If it is the second you mean, I will answer you according to the opinion of the most modern philosophers; for you are not so much asking what I think of it as what anyone might think of it. By "body," I mean everything that can be contained in some place, like a stone, or defined by its location, in such a way that it is <note>original: "tout entier dans le tout, et tout entier dans chaque partie"</note> entirely in the whole, and entirely in each part,

<summary>Descartes defines "body" by contrasting his initial sensory-based understanding (extension, shape, and movement) with the more abstract definitions used by scholastic philosophers. He clarifies that his method involves examining these old definitions rather than blindly accepting them.</summary>

## § IV.
### *What the soul is.*

### *Remarks of Monsieur Descartes.*

*That is exactly it, you say to me. Here, and almost everywhere else, he introduces me as answering things that are entirely contrary to my opinion. But it would be too tedious to point out all of his fictions.*

*And even so, since your design is to establish and demonstrate that the human mind is not corporeal, you must by no means assume it to be so. He wrongly feigns here that I assume the very thing I was meant to prove. But to things that are thus feigned without cause, and which cannot be supported or sustained by any reason, one should, it seems to me, answer nothing other than that they are false. I have never in any way disputed what should be called by the name of body, or soul, or mind. Instead, I have only explained two different kinds of things: namely, that which thinks and that which is extended <note>By "extended," Descartes means anything that takes up physical space (length, width, and depth).</note>. I have shown that all other things relate to these two alone, and I have also proved by good reasons that they are two substances truly distinct from one another, one of which I called "mind" and the other "body." But if these names displease him, he may attribute others to them if he sees fit; I shall not prevent him.*

But what am I? Without difficulty, I am one of the things I formerly believed *I was*. <note>Descartes is here quoting the "student's" previous argument to refute it.</note> He attributes this to me, as is his habit, along with an infinite number of similar things, without any appearance of truth.

He attributes to me here again something I never thought. For I have never inferred anything about a thing simply because I renounced it. On the contrary, I expressly warned of the opposite in these terms: *But perhaps it may also be the case that these very things which I suppose to be nothing, because they are unknown to me, are not in fact different from the "me" whom I know,* etc.

Am I then a mind? It is also not true that I examined whether I was a mind, for at that time I had not yet explained what I meant by the name "mind." But I examined whether I had within me any of the things I attributed to the soul as I had just described it; and not finding in myself all the things I had attributed to it, but noticing only thought, for that reason I

I have not said that I was a soul, but only that I was a <term>thinking thing<note>original: "chose qui pense." In Latin, *res cogitans*. This is Descartes' famous definition of the self stripped of all physical attributes.</note></term>, and I gave to this thinking thing the name of mind, or that of understanding, or of reason, intending nothing more by the name of "mind" than by that of a "thinking thing": and therefore I was careful not to cry out, *I have found it, I have found it!* <note>original: "εὕρηκα, εὕρηκα" (eureka). A reference to Archimedes, used here to mock the opponent's claim of a sudden discovery.</note> as he does here quite inappropriately. For on the contrary, I expressly added that I was previously ignorant of the meaning of these words, so that it is impossible for anyone to doubt that by these words I meant precisely the same thing as by "a thinking thing."

I have therefore believed nothing of any value. Quite the contrary, *you exclaim. That is still not true*: for I have never supposed that the things I had believed previously were true, but only I examined whether they were so.

*It matters not, you say, you are a body or a mind. It is also not true that I ever said that.*

*You had wrongly believed in the past, you say, that thought belonged to the body; you ought to have believed on the contrary that it belonged to the mind.* It is false again that I said that, for let him say, if he likes, that a thinking thing is better named by the name of "body" than by the name of "mind," I do not trouble myself over it, and he has nothing to settle with me on that point, but only with the grammarians. But if he pretends that I intended to mean by the name of "mind" something more than a "thinking thing," it is for me to deny it. As a little later, where he says: *if you pose this as the foundation of all your demonstrations—namely, that thinking is something proper to the mind, or to a spiritual and incorporeal thing, etc.—is this not asking for a favor and assuming the very point in question?* I deny that I have supposed in any way that the mind was incorporeal, but I say that I demonstrated it in the <note>Descartes refers to the later part of his book where he finally argues for the distinctness of the mind and body.</note> **Sixth Meditation**.

But I am so weary of correcting him for not telling the truth, that henceforth I shall not pretend to see it, and shall only listen without saying anything to the rest of his mockery until the end. Although, nonetheless, if it were someone other than him, I would believe he wanted to disguise himself to satisfy the unruly desire he had to mock; and that in imitating now the fearful man, now the lazy man, and now the man of little sense, he wanted to imitate, not the <term>Epidicuses or the Parmenos<note>original: "Epidiques... Parmenons." These are clever or bumbling servant characters from the ancient Roman comedies of Plautus and Terence.</note></term> of ancient comedy, but the vilest character of our own, who through his silliness and buffoonery takes pleasure in making others laugh.

<header>AND RESPONSES</header>

->§ VI.<-

### *Attempting the entry once more.*

"I am willing," you say, "provided that you follow me closely."

I obey you, and do not abandon you: begin again.

"I think," you say. And I also. "I am," you add, "while I think." And I likewise am while I think. "But what am I?" you continue. Oh! How right you are to ask! For that is the very thing I seek, and it is what makes me say, quite as willingly as you: but what am I then? You continue. "What did I believe formerly? What thought did I formerly have of myself?" There is no need to multiply your words; I understand them well enough. I only pray you to help me and give me your hand. I do not see where to set my foot amidst such darkness. "Say as I do," you tell me, "just follow me. What did I believe formerly that I was?" Formerly? Was there such a time? Did I believe anything formerly? "You are mistaken," you add. Far from it—it is you yourself, if you please, who are mistaken when you speak of "formerly." I have made a <term>general abdication<note>original: "abdication générale." A legalistic term Descartes uses to describe his method of doubt, where he sets aside all previous beliefs to find a certain foundation.</note></term> of everything that was formerly in my <term>belief<note>original: "créance." This refers to the stock of opinions or "credit" one gives to ideas before they are proven.</note></term>. I no longer know any "formerly," any more than if it had never been and were nothing. But what a good guide and a good leader you are; how aptly you squeeze my hand, how you pull me along. "I think," you say, "I am." That is true: I think, I am. I know that, I know only that, and besides that there is nothing, and nothing has been. "Courage," you say to me, "what did you believe formerly that you were?" I think you want to know if I did not spend fifteen days or a month learning how to rid myself of everything in this way; I only spent about an hour on it, and even then it was with you, but in truth it was with such <term>mental strain<note>original: "contention d'esprit." A state of intense, focused intellectual effort required to maintain the state of pure doubt.</note></term> that it made up for the brevity of the time. This is why I can say that I spent a month on it, or if you like, a year. I think, therefore I am <note>original: "Je pense donc je suis." This is the famous *Cogito*, the foundational certainty Descartes reaches.</note>. I know only that. I have rejected everything.

"But consider it well," you tell me, "try to <term>remember<note>original: "se ressouvenir." Descartes challenges the reliability of memory here, as memory relies on the existence of a past that he has technically doubted away.</note></term>."

What does that mean, to remember? I think, in truth, at this moment that I have formerly thought; but because I think now that I formerly thought, does it follow that I actually *did* think formerly?
