<header>SEVENTH OBJECTIONS</header>

"You are fearful," you tell me, "your shadow frightens you. Begin again: *I think.*"

Ah! how wretched I am! I see less than I did before; and this *I think* that I saw previously so clearly, I do not perceive it now. I <term>dream<note>original: "songe." While often translated as "dream," in this context it also implies "musing" or "imagining," used here to mock the lack of certainty in Descartes's thought process.</note></term> that I think, I do not think.

"Far from it," you tell me, "he who dreams, or who slumbers, thinks."

I understand you now; to dream is to think, and to think is to dream.

"It is not that," you tell me, "thinking has a greater scope than dreaming. He who dreams thinks, but he who thinks does not always dream, and sometimes thinks while awake."

Is that true? But tell me, are you not dreaming, or are you indeed thinking when you tell me this? For if you were dreaming while saying that thinking extends further than dreaming, would it actually extend further for that reason? Certainly, I will imagine, if you wish, that dreaming has more scope than thinking. But who taught you that thinking has more scope? Perhaps you do not think at all, but only dream: for how do you know if it is not true that every time you believed you were thinking while awake, you were not actually thinking, but only dreaming that you were thinking while awake? So that everything you do is nothing but dreaming that sometimes you think while awake, and sometimes you actually dream. What will you answer to that? You say not a word. Will you believe me? Let us try another <term>ford<note>original: "gué." A metaphorical crossing point in a river; Bourdin suggests the current philosophical path is too deep and dangerous to cross.</note></term>; this one is not safe, and I am surprised that, not having surveyed it beforehand, you wanted to make me pass through it. Do not ask me any longer, then, what I formerly thought I was, but ask me what I dream at present that I formerly dreamed I was. If you do so, I will answer you. And so that the poorly-tuned words of a dreamer do not disturb our discourse, I will use those of a man who is awake; only remember that "thinking" shall henceforth signify nothing other than "dreaming," and do not rely any more on your thoughts than a sleeping man does on his reveries. Or else, to remember it better, call your *method* the *method of dreaming*. And hold as your principal maxim *that to reason well, one must dream*. I see that this advice pleases you, since you continue thus:

*What then did I formerly believe that I was?*

Here is the stumbling block where I just now tripped. Here we must be on our guard. That is why you must permit me to ask why you do not first put this forward as a maxim: *I am.*

<summary>In this passage, Bourdin mocks Descartes's method by arguing that if the senses and reason are doubted, there is no way to distinguish thinking from dreaming. He sarcastically proposes that Descartes's philosophy be renamed the "Method of Dreaming."</summary>

Is it one of the things I once believed I was, or am I that very same thing I once believed I was? "That is not necessary," you tell me. Forgive me, but it is very necessary; otherwise, you waste your time when you examine what you think you were in the past. As, for example, suppose it were possible that you are not today what you once believed you were—as is said of **Pythagore** <note>Pythagoras, the Greek philosopher often associated with the doctrine of metempsychosis, or the "transmigration of souls," where a soul moves from one body to another after death.</note>—but that you were something else entirely; would you not then search in vain for what you once believed you were?

But, you tell me, this **maxim** <note>A general truth or rule of conduct.</note> is old, and therefore abolished. I know it well, for we have rejected everything. But what is to be done about that? Either we must stop here and go no further, or we must make use of it. "Not at all," you tell me, "we must strive once more and try to move forward, but by another path." Here it is: *I am either a body or a spirit.* Would I then not be a body?

Do not go further. Who taught you this: *I am a body or a spirit*, since you have rejected both? And what do you know if, instead of being a body or a spirit, you are not a soul or some other thing? For what do I know of it? Nothing; that is what we are searching for; and if I knew it, I would not give myself so much trouble. For do not think that I have come into this **country of abdication** <note>A metaphorical reference to Descartes's state of "universal doubt," where he has abdicated or renounced all his previous certainties and beliefs.</note>, where everything is to be feared and filled with darkness, merely for the purpose of taking a walk and diverting myself; the sole hope of encountering the **truth** there has brought and drawn me here.

"Let us resume then," you tell me: *I am a body or something that is not a body, or else something that is not corporeal.*

Here is another path, and quite new, which you are entering; but is it certain? "It is very certain," you tell me, "and necessary."

Why then did you discard it? Was I not right to fear that you should not have rejected everything, and that it might be that you granted too much to your mistrust? But let us pass on; I am willing for that to be certain. What follows from it? You pursue: *Am I not a body? Is there not in me any of the things that I once believed belonged to the body?*

Here is another **stumbling block**. We will stumble there without a doubt, if you do not take this maxim as a guide: *I thought rightly in the past concerning what belongs to the body*; or else: *nothing belongs to the body except what I once believed belonged to it.*

# SEVENTH OBJECTIONS

Why is that? you ask me.
It is because if you have forgotten something in the past, or if you have thought incorrectly (and I believe that being a man as you are, you will not deny that you could have failed), all the trouble you are taking will be useless; and you have great reason to fear that the same thing might happen to you as happened recently to a poor peasant.

This rustic and simple man, having one day seen a wolf from afar, spoke thus to his master—an affable and well-born young man whom he was accompanying: "What do I see? Without a doubt it is an animal, for it moves and walks. But what animal is it? It must be one of those I know. What are these animals? An ox, a horse, a goat, a donkey? Is it then not an ox? No, it has no horns. Is it not a horse? It is not one; its tail is too short. Is it not a goat? It is not a goat, for a goat has a beard, and this one has none. It is therefore a donkey, since it is neither an ox, nor a horse, nor a goat." You smile? Wait for the end of the fable. His master, seeing the stupidity or the simplicity of his servant, said to him: "You could just as easily have said it was a horse as a donkey." "How so?" asked his servant. "Here is how," replied his master. "This animal you see—is it not an ox? 'No,' you said, 'it has no horns.' Is it not a goat? 'No, it has no beard.' Is it then not a donkey? 'Not at all, for I see no ears on it.' Is it then a horse?" This good fellow, surprised by this new **analysis** <term>A method of inquiry that breaks a complex topic into smaller parts to better understand it.</term>, cries out immediately: "I was mistaken; it is not an animal, for I only know these animals: the ox, the horse, the goat, and the donkey. Now, since it is neither an ox, nor a goat, nor a donkey, it follows," he says, all joyful and triumphant, "that it is not an animal. Therefore, it is something that is not an animal." He was surely a good philosopher for a peasant, but not for a man who had graduated from the **Lycée** <note>Original: "lycée." A reference to the Lyceum, the ancient school of Aristotle. Do not be clever; milk is not more like milk than this **reasoning** <term>The logical process of drawing a conclusion from premises.</term> is like yours. You do not say everything you think about it. Is it not exactly the same when you say: "I know everything that belongs or can belong to the body"; or even: "nothing belongs to the body..."

### § VII.

->*The entrance is attempted for the third time.*<-

"I think," you say. I deny it; you dream that you think. "That," you tell me, "is what I call thinking." You are wrong. Each thing must be called by its name. You are dreaming, and that is all. Continue.

"I am," you say, "while I think." Let that pass; since you wish to speak in such a manner, I will not quibble over it. "This is certain and evident," you add. I deny it. You are only dreaming that this appears certain and evident to you. You insist: "Therefore, at the very least, is this certain and evident to a man who dreams or slumbers?" Meanwhile, consider a little within yourself if you might not henceforth better draw this conclusion from your antecedent: "And therefore, if I am, as it is certain that I am, I am nothing." For either your antecedent was poorly established, or, if it was well established, it is destroyed by the conditional proposition.

which follows, namely, whether I am. That is why I deny this antecedent <note>In logic, the "antecedent" is the first part of a conditional "if-then" statement. Here, the antecedent is Descartes's claim that "nothing exists."</note>; since I have made a general renunciation of all things, there is no longer any body, no longer any soul, no longer any mind, there is nothing left. And it is not without reason that I deny it; for either you are wrong to make this general renunciation, or it is not true that you are making it; indeed, you could not even do so, since you, who make it, necessarily exist. And to answer you in formal terms, when you say: *there is no longer anything, no body, no soul, no mind, etc.*, either you do not include yourself in this proposition, *there is no longer anything*, and you mean only, *there is nothing left, except me*; which you must necessarily do so that your proposition may be true and stand, as in those other logical propositions: *every proposition written in this book is false*. I am not telling the truth. <note>This is a version of the "Liar’s Paradox," where a statement undermines its own validity.</note> And a thousand others which exclude themselves from what they say. Or else you do include and shut yourself within it, so that you mean to reject yourself when you reject everything, and not to be when you say, *there is no longer anything, etc.* If the first is true, then this proposition—namely: *since I have made a general renunciation, there is nothing left, etc.*—is not true. For you exist, and you are something; and by necessity you are either a body, or a soul, or a mind, or some other thing; and therefore something necessarily exists, whether it be a body or a mind, etc. If the second is true, you are mistaken, and even doubly so: both because you want something impossible, by saying that you are not while you are, and also because you yourself destroy your own proposition in the consequent <note>The "consequent" is the "then" part of the "if-then" statement; here, the conclusion that "I am not a body."</note>, by saying: *therefore if I am, as it is certain, etc.* For how can it be that you are if there is nothing? And while you suppose that there is nothing, how can you say that you are? And if you say that you are, do you not destroy what you had put forward before, namely, *there is nothing, etc.*? Consequently the antecedent is false, and the consequent also. But you do not stop there, and you renew the combat thus:

When, you say, I say: *there is nothing, I am not certain whether I am a body, or a soul, or a mind, or some other thing. I do not even know if there is any other body, or any other soul, or any other mind.* And therefore, following our rule <note>Descartes’s rule of Methodical Doubt, which dictates that one should treat anything even slightly uncertain as if it were absolutely false.</note>, which requires us to hold as false everything that is doubtful, I will say: *there is no body, no soul, no mind, no other thing.* And therefore, if I am, as it is certain, I am not a body.

That is all very well; but allow me, I pray you,

Nothing which is such that I can doubt whether it exists, exists in fact.

No spirit exists in fact.

Therefore, nothing that exists in fact is a spirit.

Nothing that exists in fact is a spirit.

Now, it is the case that I (who am a thinking substance) exist in fact.

Therefore I (who am a thinking substance) am not a spirit.

As for me, I never denied that a thinking thing was a body because I supposed that I had formerly thought well concerning the nature of the body, but because—not using the name "body" except to signify a thing that was well known to me, namely, to signify an <term>extended substance</term> <note>In Cartesian philosophy, "extension" is the defining attribute of matter; it refers to anything that takes up physical space (length, breadth, and depth).</note>—I recognized that the <term>thinking substance</term> <note>The "res cogitans" or mind, which Descartes argues is fundamentally different from physical matter because it does not occupy space.</note> is different from that which is extended.

These subtle and witty <note>The original French "galantes" here suggests a polished, clever, or even mocking style of banter used in social circles, rather than anything romantic.</note> ways of speaking which are repeated here several times—namely: *I think, you say; I deny it; you are dreaming. And since he would not dare receive upon his shield the blows of such a powerful adversary, he evades them as much as he can; he distinguishes, and finally by means of these words, *determinately* and *indeterminately*, as if by so many small winding paths, he flees and escapes. Truly, the spectacle is quite agreeable, especially when one knows the subject of the quarrel. It arises because he happened to read in my writings that to begin to <term>philosophize</term><note>To seek basic truths about the nature of reality and knowledge.</note> well, one must resolve once in their life to rid themselves of all the opinions they previously held in their belief. This is because, even though there may be several among them that are true, they are mixed with many others that are mostly false or doubtful. There is no better way to separate the true from the false than to reject them all from the beginning, without retaining any, so that afterwards one may more easily recognize those that are true, discover new ones, and admit only those that are certain and <term>indubitable</term><note>Impossible to doubt; absolutely certain.</note>.

This is the same thing as if I had said that, to ensure that in a **basket full of apples** there are none that are rotten, one must empty them all out from the start, leaving not a single one, and then only put back those that have been recognized as being perfectly sound, and put back no others. But our author, not understanding, or rather feigning not to understand a reasoning of such sublime speculation, was principally astonished that it was said there was nothing that should not be rejected; and passing over this for a long time and often...

When he asks, therefore, that I show him this clear and distinct notion so that he may be "refreshed by the sight of it," he is merely playing games—just as he does when he introduces me as showing it to him in these terms: *I know certainly that I am, that I think, that I am a thinking substance,* etc. And when he wishes to refute these "games" of his own mind with this example: *You know just as certainly that there is no mountain without a valley; therefore, you have a clear and distinct concept of a mountain without a valley,* he deceives himself with a <term>sophism<note>A clever but false argument, often intended to deceive.</note></term>. Furthermore, the <term>maxim<note>A concise statement of a general truth or rule of logic.</note></term> he brings forward—*from knowing to being, the consequence is not valid* <note>original: "du connaître à l'être la conséquence n'est pas bonne" (Latin: *a nosse ad esse non valet consequentia*). This is because it is impossible for us to know a thing if it is not, in effect, exactly as we know it to be: namely, existing, if we conceive that it exists; or possessing a certain nature, if only its nature is known to us.

It is also false—or at least it has not been proven—that there is any <term>thinking substance<note>Descartes’ term for the mind or soul, which he defines as an immaterial thing that doubts, understands, and wills.</note></term> that is divisible into several parts, as he sets out in the table where he proposes the various kinds of thinking substance, as if it had been proclaimed by an oracle. I cannot help but say that this opinion—the divisibility of the thinking substance—seems to me very dangerous and quite contrary to the Christian religion. They are nothing more than subtleties by which our author seems to want to persuade his disciples that even when he has nothing to say to them, he is still thinking of something worthwhile.

For if by the word *too much* he understands, not simply something more than what was asked, but something false, then this <term>maxim<note>A concise statement of a general rule or principle.</note></term> is true. But the Reverend Father will forgive me if I say that he is mistaken when he attributes something similar to me. For when I reasoned in this manner: *the knowledge of things whose existence is known to me does not depend on that of things whose existence is not yet known to me. Now, it is the case that I know that a thinking thing exists, and I do not yet know if any body exists; therefore, the knowledge of a thinking thing does not depend on the knowledge of the body;* I have concluded nothing "too much" there, nor anything that was not well concluded. 

But when he says: *I know that a thinking thing exists, and I do not yet know if any mind exists, indeed even that none exists, there is nothing, all is rejected*, he says something entirely false and frivolous. For I cannot affirm or deny anything about the <term>mind<note>original: "esprit". In Cartesian philosophy, this refers to the "res cogitans" or thinking substance.</note></term> if I do not first know what is to be understood by the name "mind"; and I cannot conceive of a single thing that one is accustomed to understand by this name where **thought** is not included, so much so that it is a contradiction <note>original: "il répugne". In 17th-century logic, this indicates a logical impossibility or contradiction.</note> that one could know that a thinking thing exists without knowing at the same time that a mind—or a thing that one understands by the name "mind"—exists. And what he adds a little later: *Indeed even that no mind exists, there is nothing, all is rejected*, is so absurd that it does not deserve a response; for when, after this renunciation, one has recognized the existence of a thinking thing, one has at the same time recognized the existence of a mind (at least insofar as by the name "mind" one understands a thinking thing) and therefore the existence of a mind could not then have been rejected.

Finally, when, having to make use of a <term>formal argument<note>Referring to a syllogism, a structured logical argument consisting of a major premise, a minor premise, and a conclusion.</note></term>, he exalts it against the true method of conducting one's reason, which he opposes to mine, he seems to want to insinuate that I do not approve of the forms of **syllogisms**, and therefore that I use a method very far removed from reason; but my writings justify me enough on this point, where every time it has been necessary, I have not failed to use them.

He proposes here a syllogism composed of false <term>premises<note>The starting statements of a logical argument upon which a conclusion is based.</note></term>, which he says is mine; but as for me, I deny and renounce it; for as for this <term>major premise<note>The first part of a syllogism, usually a general statement.</note></term>, *nothing which is such that I can doubt if it exists, exists in effect*, it is so absurd that I do not fear he can ever persuade anyone that it comes from me, unless at the same time he persuades them that I have lost my senses. And I cannot wonder enough with what purpose, with what fidelity, under what hope and with what confidence he has...

For in the First Meditation, where the goal was not yet to establish any truth, but only to rid myself of my old **prejudices** <note>In Cartesian philosophy, 'prejudices' refer to the preconceived notions and unexamined beliefs we acquire from childhood.</note>, after having shown that all the opinions I had accepted into my belief since my youth could be called into doubt, and consequently, that I should no less carefully suspend my judgment regarding them than regarding those that are manifestly false—for fear they might prevent me from seeking the truth as I should—I expressly added these words: *But it is not enough to have made these remarks; I must also take care to remember them, for these old and ordinary opinions still return frequently to my thoughts, the long and familiar usage they have had with me giving them the right to occupy my mind against my will, and to make themselves almost mistresses of my belief. And I will never lose the habit of deferring to them and placing confidence in them, as long as I consider them as they are in fact—namely, in some way doubtful, as I have just shown, and yet highly probable; such that one has much more reason to believe them than to deny them.* 

This is why I think I will not do wrong if, deliberately taking a contrary view, I deceive myself, and if I **feign** for some time that all these opinions are entirely false and imaginary, until at last, having equally balanced my old and my new prejudices, my judgment is no longer mastered by bad habits and turned away from the right path that can lead it to the knowledge of truth. 

Among these words, our author <note>Referring to the Jesuit Father Pierre Bourdin, who authored the 'Seventh Objections'.</note> has chosen these and left out the others: *deliberately taking a contrary view, I will feign that the opinions which are in some way doubtful are entirely false and imaginary.* And furthermore, in place of the word *feign*, he puts these: *I will say, I will believe, and will even believe in such a way that I will assert as true the contrary of what is doubtful*, and intended that this should serve as my maxim or certain rule—not to deliver me from my prejudices, but to lay the foundations of a <term>metaphysics<note>The study of the fundamental nature of reality, including the relationship between mind and matter, and between potentiality and actuality.</note></term> that is altogether certain and accomplished. 

It is true, nonetheless, that he first proposed this somewhat ambiguously, and as if hesitating, in the second and third paragraphs of the first question; and even in this third paragraph, after having supposed that following this rule he must believe that two and three did not make five, he asks if he must immediately believe it so much that he persuades himself that it cannot be otherwise. From this, it is manifest that he knew very well that I did not hold the contrary of what is doubtful to be true, and that no one, in my view, could use it as the **major premise** <note>In a syllogism—a three-part logical argument—the major premise is the broad, general statement (e.g., "All men are mortal").</note> of a **syllogism** <term>syllogism: a form of reasoning where a conclusion is drawn from two given or assumed propositions.</term> from which a certain conclusion was expected; for there is a contradiction between not asserting, not denying, and using neither, and asserting one of the two contraries as true and making use of it. 

But subsequently, having imperceptibly lost the memory of what he had reported as being my opinion, he not only asserted the contrary, but he even repeated and instilled it so often that he rebukes almost nothing else in his entire dissertation. He also composes solely from this those twelve faults that he attributes to me throughout the rest of his treatise. From this it follows, it seems to me, very clearly that not only here, where he attributes to me this major premise: *nothing that is such that one can doubt whether it exists, exists in fact*, but also in all the other places where he attributes similar things to me, he speaks against his own feeling and against the truth. And although it is with regret that I make this reproach, nevertheless the defense of the truth I have undertaken obliges me not to be more reserved toward a person who has had no more respect for it. And as in his entire dissertation he has, it seems to me, almost no other design than to persuade and instill in the minds of his readers this false maxim that he has disguised in a hundred ways, I see no other way to excuse him than to say that he has spoken of it so often that, in the end, he persuaded himself of it and no longer recognized its falsehood.

As for what now concerns the **minor premise** <note>The second part of a logical argument that applies the general rule to a specific case (e.g., "Socrates is a man").</note>, namely: *now it is a fact that every body is such that I can doubt whether it exists*, or else: *now it is a fact that every mind is such that I can doubt whether it exists*, if one understands it indefinitely for all kinds of time—as it must be understood to serve as proof for the conclusion drawn from it—it is also false, and I deny that it is mine. For a little after the beginning of the *Second Meditation*, where I certainly recognized that a thinking thing existed (which, following ordinary usage, is called by the name **mind**), I could no longer doubt that a mind existed. Similarly, after the *Sixth Meditation*, in which I recognized the existence of the body, I could also no longer doubt its existence. Admire, meanwhile, the excellence of our author’s wit, to have had the skill to so ingeniously invent two false premises so that, by employing them in proper form in a syllogism, a false conclusion followed! <header>AND REPLIES</header>

...why he does not wish me to have cause for laughter here; for in his entire dissertation I find only reasons for joy—not a very great joy, to be sure, but a true and solid one nonetheless. This is because, by criticizing several things that are not mine, but which he has merely attributed to me, he makes it clear that he has done his absolute best to find something worthy of censure in my writings, without ever having been able to succeed.

And indeed, it is quite apparent that he did not laugh from the heart, given the serious reprimand with which he concludes this entire section. This is made even clearer by the responses that follow, in which he appears not only somber and severe, but even resentful and cruel. For, having no reason to wish me ill, and having found nothing in my writings deserving of his censure—except for that false maxim which he himself invented and could not legitimately attribute to me—he nevertheless behaves as though he has entirely persuaded his readers. He has done this not through the strength of his arguments, for he has none, but first, through that remarkable confidence with which he spoke (a confidence one does not suspect of being false in a man of his standing <note>Father Bourdin was a well-respected Jesuit professor, and Descartes is suggesting that Bourdin relies on his social and religious authority rather than logic.</note>), and further, by the frequent and constant repetition of that same maxim. It often happens that by dint of hearing the same thing, we acquire the habit of accepting as true what we know to be false; these two methods are usually more powerful than any reasoning for persuading the common people and those who do not examine matters closely. 

Consequently, he insults the "defeated" party with great arrogance. Like a solemn pedagogue <term>pedagogue: a teacher, often used here in a derogatory sense to imply someone who is pedantic, condescending, or overly strict.</term> treating me like one of his little schoolboys, he scolds me bitterly. In the twelve responses that follow, he finds me guilty of more sins than there are commandments in the Decalogue <note>The Decalogue refers to the Ten Commandments.</note>. I am willing, however, to excuse the Reverend Father because he seems not to be quite himself. Although those who have drunk a little more than they should usually see no more than two things for every one, the zeal that carries him away disturbs him so much that in this single thing he has himself invented, he finds twelve faults in me to correct. I could call these insults and slanders if I wished to speak plainly and without any disguise of words, but I prefer to call them blunders and wanderings, so that I may laugh in my turn, as he has done. And meanwhile, I beg the reader to remember that in all that follows, he has not uttered a single word against me in which he has not been mistaken and deceived.

<meta>This page transitions from Descartes’ introductory remarks to the specific text of the "Seventh Objections" authored by the Jesuit Pierre Bourdin. Bourdin here begins his formal critique of Descartes’ method of systematic doubt, arguing that discarding all previous knowledge is both dangerous and illogical.</meta>

# SEVENTH OBJECTIONS

->*Responses to the second Question, namely whether it is a good*
->*method of philosophizing to make a general renunciation*
->*of all things that can be doubted.*<-

Answer I. This method is flawed in its principles, for it has none at all, and yet has an infinite number. In all other methods, to discover the truth and derive certainty from the certain, one uses clear, evident principles, known to everyone and natural to the human mind. For example, "the whole is greater than its part," or "from nothing, nothing is made" <note>original: "De rien, rien ne se fait," a translation of the Latin philosophical axiom *ex nihilo nihil fit*.</note>, and a thousand other similar ones by means of which one gradually raises one’s knowledge and advances surely in the search for truth. 

But this method, quite the contrary, in order to make something—not out of something else, but out of nothing—cuts away, rejects, and abjures all the old principles without retaining a single one. By deliberately adopting contrary sentiments, for fear it might seem that all means are cut off from it and that it lacks wings, it feigns new principles directly opposed to the old ones. By this means, it strips itself of its old prejudices only to clothe itself in others that are entirely new. It leaves the certain to embrace the uncertain; it puts on wings, but wings of wax <note>A reference to the myth of Icarus, whose wax wings melted when he flew too close to the sun, leading to his fall.</note>. It rises very high, but only to fall; finally, out of nothing it wants to make something, but in effect it makes nothing.

Answer II. This method is flawed in its means, for it has none, since it cuts off the old ones and proposes no new ones. Other disciplines have forms of logic, syllogisms <term>syllogism: a form of logical argument where a conclusion is drawn from two premises (e.g., All men are mortal; Socrates is a man; therefore Socrates is mortal).</term>, and ways of arguing that are entirely certain. By these means and under their guidance—no more and no less than by Ariadne’s thread <note>In Greek mythology, Ariadne gave Theseus a ball of thread to navigate the Labyrinth; here it represents a logical guide through complex problems.</note>—they easily emerge from their labyrinths and resolve the most tangled questions with safety and ease. 

This method, on the contrary, corrupts and spoils the entire ancient form when it pales with fear at the mere thought of that evil genius <term>evil genius: (French: *mauvais génie*) Descartes’ famous thought experiment of a powerful deceiver who makes us doubt even mathematical truths.</term> it has imagined, when it fears it is always dreaming, and when it does not know if it is in its right mind. Propose a syllogism to it: it will be terrified by the major premise, whatever it may be. Perhaps it will say, "This evil genius is deceiving me." What will it do at the minor premise? It will tremble; it will say it is uncertain, that it does not know if it is not sleeping, and that things which seemed clearest and most certain while sleeping have a hundred times been found false after waking. What will it do finally at the conclusion? It will flee them all as so many nets spread out to trap it. "Does one not see," it will say, "that fools, children, and..."

Bourdin mocks the Cartesian fear of the 'evil genius' and 'dreams,' claiming such doubt makes traditional logical reasoning (syllogisms) impossible.</summary>

This convenience is fine, no doubt; but is it not like someone who would tear off a child's nose for fear that he might get a runny nose? Do other mothers not do better by simply wiping their children's noses? That is why, all things considered, I have only one thing to say to you: namely, that once all form is removed, nothing can remain but the formless.

Answer III. This method fails in its purpose, being unable to conclude anything, nor teach us anything certain. But how could it, since it blocks all the paths that could lead it to the truth? You have seen it yourself and experienced it with me in these detours, or rather these errors similar to those of Ulysses <note>Bourdin compares Descartes' philosophical journey to the long, wandering, and often mistaken voyage of Ulysses (Odysseus) after the Trojan War.</note>, which you made me take, and which have greatly exhausted us both. You maintained that you were a spirit, or that you had a mind; but you have never been able to prove it, and you remained stuck on the path, embarrassed by a thousand difficulties, and this so many times that I have trouble remembering them. And nevertheless, it will be good to remember them now, so that the answer I have to give you loses none of its force. Here then are the main points of this method by which it cuts its own nerves and deprives itself of all hope of ever being able to reach knowledge of the truth. 1. ...that I find primarily to fault in this method. It posits or establishes poor foundations, and leans upon them in such a way that, once these foundations are destroyed or withdrawn, the method itself is destroyed or no longer appears.

Response IV. This method sins by excess—that is to say, it does more than the laws of prudence require and more than anyone has ever desired. I admit, in truth, that there are men who wish for the existence of God and the immortality of the soul to be demonstrated to them; but until now, no one has been found who was not satisfied with knowing that there is a God who governs all things, and that the human soul is spiritual and immortal, with as much certainty as they know that two and three make five, or that men have bodies; so that it is entirely useless and superfluous to seek a greater certainty in these matters. Furthermore, just as in things regarding the practical conduct of life there are certain limits of certainty that suffice for us to act surely and prudently, so too in speculative <note>Speculative matters refer to theoretical or philosophical knowledge, as opposed to "practical" knowledge used in daily life.</note> matters there are limits which, once reached, provide security; so much so that without regarding everything one might wish to attempt or seek beyond those limits, one can prudently and safely stay where one is, for fear of going too far and doing too much. But, you will tell me, it is no small praise to go further than others and to cross a ford <note>Original: *gué* — a shallow crossing in a river.</note> that has never been attempted by anyone. I admit, the praise is great, provided that one can cross it without the danger of shipwreck. Therefore,

As for the Vth response, I say that this method sins by deficiency—that is to say, wishing to embrace more things than it can, it holds nothing. I seek no one but you as witness and judge. What have you accomplished so far with all this magnificent apparatus? What has this abdication <note>Bourdin uses "abdication" to refer to Descartes' decision to strip away all his previous beliefs through doubt.</note> produced for you—an abdication so solemn, and even so general and generous that you did not spare even yourself, reserving for yourself only this common notion: **I think, I am, I am a thinking thing**? This notion is so common, I say, and so familiar to the humblest of men, that there has never been anyone, since the world began, who has doubted it in the slightest, or who has ever seriously asked for proof that he is, that he exists, that he thinks, that he is a thinking thing; so much so that you should not expect to receive great thanks from anyone, unless perhaps from someone who, moved like me by a singular affection for you, thanks you for the goodwill you have toward all of mankind...

Response VI. This method sins and falls into the very fault it criticizes in others. For it is amazed that all men, without exception, believe and say with such confidence: "I have a body, a head, eyes, etc."; yet it is not amazed at itself when it says with equal confidence: "I have no body, no head, no eyes, etc." <note>Bourdin is mocking Descartes' "Methodical Doubt," where Descartes temporarily pretends his physical body doesn't exist to see what remains certain.</note>

Response VII. This method sins and commits a fault unique to itself; for while the rest of mankind holds certain things to be somewhat certain—and even sufficiently certain—for example, that I have a head, that there are bodies, spirits, etc., this method, by a design peculiar to itself, calls them into doubt. It then treats their opposites as certain—namely, that I have no head, that there are no bodies, no spirits—and holds this to be so certain that it claims it can serve as the foundation for a very exact and accomplished metaphysics. Indeed, it leans upon this idea in such a way that, if you take away this support, the method will fall flat on its face. <note>Original: *donnera du nez en terre* — literally "will hit its nose on the ground."</note>

Response VIII. This method sins through imprudence, for it does not realize that a two-edged sword is to be feared everywhere; thinking to avoid one edge, it finds itself wounded by the other. For example, it does not know if there is a body that truly exists in the world; and because it doubts this, it rejects the idea and admits its opposite: "there is no body in the world." By taking this opposite—which is at the very least as doubtful as its contrary—as a very certain thing, and leaning upon it without any consideration, it sins and causes itself harm.

Response IX. This method sins knowingly; for, knowing and willing it, and after being warned, it blinds itself. By making a voluntary abdication of all the things necessary to discover the truth, it allows itself to be deceived by its own analysis, proving not only what it claims to prove, but also exactly what it fears most. <note>Bourdin suggests that by stripping away all common-sense certainties, Descartes' method accidentally proves that knowledge is impossible.</note>

Response X. This method sins by commission <note>In a legal or theological sense, a "sin of commission" is an active wrong act, whereas a "sin of omission" is a failure to do what is right.</note> when, contrary to what it had expressly and solemnly forbidden, it returns to its old opinions; and against the laws of its own abdication, it takes back what it had rejected. I believe you remember this well enough.

Response XI. This method sins by omission, for after having established as one of its principal foundations *that we must take very careful heed not to admit anything as true that we cannot prove to be so*, it often forgets itself, incautiously admitting as true and...

taking all this as quite certain without proving it: The senses deceive us sometimes, we all dream, there are madmen, and a hundred other things of this nature.

**Response XII.** This method is flawed in that it contains nothing good, or nothing new, and contains much that is superfluous.

For, firstly, if by this <term>abdication</term><note>Here meaning the formal rejection or setting aside of beliefs.</note> of everything that is doubtful one understands only a <term>metaphysical abstraction</term><note>A mental process where one focuses on one aspect of a thing while ignoring others, without necessarily denying the existence of those other parts.</note>, which causes us to consider doubtful things only *as* doubtful, and which therefore obliges us to turn our minds away from them when we wish to seek something certain—without attaching ourselves to them any more than to things that are entirely false; if that is the case, I say, it says something good, but it says nothing new: and this abstraction would have nothing peculiar to it that is not common to all philosophers, without exception.

Secondly, if by this abdication the method intends that we reject doubtful things to such an extent that we suppose and hold them to be false, and that on this basis the method uses them as false things, or uses their opposites as true things, it will indeed say something new, but it will say nothing good, and this abdication will indeed be new, but it will not be legitimate.

Thirdly, if the method says that by the force and weight of its reasons it proves certainly and evidently this: "I am a thinking thing, and as such I am neither a spirit, nor a soul, nor a body, but a thing so separated from all that, that I can be conceived without anything of them being conceived"; in the same way that one conceives of an "animal" or "a thing that feels" without yet conceiving of "that which whinnies" or "that which roars," etc.—it will say something good, but it will say nothing new. For the chairs of the philosophers <note>A metaphor for university professors or the established academic tradition.</note> sing of nothing else, and this is taught by as many men as there are those who believe that beasts think, or even (assuming that thought also encompasses sensation, so that a thing thinks which feels, sees, or hears) by as many as believe that beasts feel—that is to say, in a word, by all men.

Fourthly, if it is said that it has been proven by good and maturely considered reasons that he who thinks exists in effect, and that he is a thing or a <term>substance</term><note>In 17th-century philosophy, a substance is something that can exist by itself, rather than a property of something else.</note> that thinks, and that while he exists it does not follow from this that there is either spirit, or body, or soul truly existing in the world, one will say something new, but one will say nothing good; neither more nor less than if one...

<summary>Bourdin critiques Descartes' method of doubt, arguing that if it is merely a mental exercise, it is unoriginal; if it treats the doubtful as false, it is logically unsound.</summary>

said that an animal exists, and yet there is neither lion, nor fox, nor any other animal that exists.

Fifthly, if he who uses this method says that he thinks—that is to say, that he understands, wills, imagines, and feels; and that he thinks in such a way that by a reflective action he envisions and considers that thought, which makes it so that he thinks, or rather that he knows and considers that he thinks (which is properly called <term>perceiving</term><note>In this context, Bourdin refers to "apperception," or the mind's conscious awareness of its own operations.</note>, or having an internal knowledge), and if he says that this is the property of a faculty, or of a thing which is above matter, which is spiritual, and therefore that he is a spirit, he will say what he has not yet said, what he ought to have said, what I expected he would say, and what I have even often wished to suggest to him when I saw him striving in vain to tell us what he was; he will say, I say, something good, but he will say nothing new, there being no one who has not formerly learned it from his tutors, and they from their masters, even back to Adam.

Certainly, if he says that, how many superfluous things are in this method! How many exorbitant ones! What <term>battology</term><note>A rhetorical term for needless repetition or wearisome talk; wordiness.</note>! How many machines that serve only for show, or to deceive us! To what end should we be presented with the deceptions of the senses, the illusions of those who sleep, and the extravagances of the mad? What is the purpose of this <term>abdication</term><note>Meaning the formal rejection or setting aside of all previous beliefs and sensory information.</note> so austere that it leaves us with nothing but the void? Why such long travels, lasting so long in foreign lands where the senses do not approach, among shadows and ghosts? Of what use are all these things for the conviction and proof of the existence of God, as if it could not be proved unless everything is overturned? But to what end is this mixing and this change of so many opinions? Why sometimes reject the old ones to clothe oneself in the new, and sometimes reject these new ones to take up the old again? Could it not be, perhaps, that just as in ancient times each god had his particular ceremonies, so too these new mysteries require new ceremonies? But why, without amusing himself with so much trouble, did he not rather, clearly, plainly, and briefly set forth the truth: "I think, I have knowledge of my thought, therefore I am a spirit."

Finally, if he says that understanding, willing, imagining, and feeling—that is, thinking—are so much the property of the spirit that no animal except man thinks, imagines, feels, sees, etc., he will say something new, but he will say nothing good: and furthermore, he will say it without proof and without confession, unless perhaps he is keeping and attaching something (which is the only refuge left to him) to show us...

## FINAL REPLY.

You fear here, no doubt (and I forgive you for it), for your method, which you cherish, and which you caress and embrace as your own offspring. You are afraid that, having found it guilty of so many sins, and seeing it now leaking everywhere, I might condemn it to the scrap heap. Do not fear, however; I am more a friend to you than you think. I will surpass your expectations, or at least I will deceive them. I will remain silent and have patience. I know who you are, and I know the strength and vivacity of your spirit. When you have taken sufficient time to meditate, and especially when you have consulted your <term>analysis</term><note>Descartes’ mathematical method of breaking down complex problems into their simplest parts.</note> in secret, which never fails you, you will shake off all the dust from your method, you will wash away all its stains, and you will then show us a method that is very clean and very clear, and free from every defect. Meanwhile, be content with this, and continue to give me your attention while I continue to satisfy your requests. I have included many things in few words, so as not to be long, and have touched upon most of them only lightly, such as those regarding the spirit, and those concerning <term>clear and distinct conception</term><note>A fundamental Cartesian principle: that anything the mind perceives with total clarity and distinctness must be true.</note>, the true and the false, and other similar things; but you will know well how to pick up what we have dropped on purpose. This is why I come to your third question.

The author of this judgment holds such a rank in the world that it would be difficult to persuade anyone that he lacked wit or any of the other qualities required of a good judge. However, for fear that the great authority of his office might prejudice the truth, I beg the readers here to remember that before he came to the twelve responses he has just made, he attacked nothing of what I actually said. Instead, he employed only vain and useless <term>cavillations</term><note>Frivolous or sophistical objections intended to confuse an argument rather than address its substance.</note> to create an opportunity to attribute to me opinions so unbelievable they did not even deserve to be refuted. Now, in these twelve responses, instead of proving anything against me, he contents himself with vainly assuming that he has already proven the things he attributed to me. To make the fairness of his judgment appear greater, he claims he was only playing when he reported the causes of his accusations; but here, where it is a question of judging, he acts the part of the grave, serious, and severe man. In the first eleven responses, he boldly and definitively pronounces a sentence of condemnation against me; and finally, in the twelfth, he begins to deliberate and distinguish in this manner: *if he means this, he says nothing new; if that, he says nothing good, etc.*, even though it is actually a matter of one and the same thing considered in different ways—namely, his own fiction, the absurdity of which I wish to show you here through this comparison.

I have declared in several places in my writings that I tried everywhere to imitate architects. To raise great buildings in places where the rock, clay, and <term>firm ground</term><note>Original: "terre ferme." This refers to the "bedrock" of certainty Descartes sought to find through his process of methodical doubt.</note> are covered by sand and gravel, architects first dig deep trenches and throw out not only the gravel, but everything that rests upon it, or is mixed or confused with it, so that they may afterwards place their foundations on the rock and firm ground. In the same way, I first rejected as sand and gravel everything I recognized as being doubtful and uncertain. After that, having considered that one could not doubt that the substance which thus doubts everything, or which thinks, exists while it is doubting, I used that as the firm ground upon which I placed the foundations of my philosophy.

Now, our author is like a certain mason who, to appear more skillful than he was and jealous of the reputation of a master architect building a chapel in his town, sought with great care every opportunity to criticize his art and his manner of building. 2. He replied: *This manner of architecture fails in its means, for it has none, since it cuts away the old ones without proposing new ones. Other methods have a square, a rule, a plumb line, by the guidance of which—no less than by an Ariadne's thread <note>A reference to the Greek myth where Ariadne gave Theseus a ball of thread to find his way out of the Minotaur's labyrinth; here, it signifies a logical guide through complexity.</note>—they easily emerge from their labyrinths and arrange even the most shapeless stones with accuracy and ease. But this one, on the contrary, corrupts and spoils the entire ancient form, as it pales with fear at the mere thought of goblins and werewolves <note>These "goblins" and "werewolves" are Bourdin's mocking terms for the "evil demon" and other skeptical scenarios Descartes uses to test the certainty of knowledge.</note>; when it fears that the earth will fail it and sink; when it apprehends that the sand will slip away and be carried off. Suggest that it raise a column, and it will grow pale with fear at the mere positioning of the base, whatever its form may be: perhaps, it will say, the goblins will topple it. But what will it do when it comes time to erect its shaft? It will tremble and say that it is too weak; that it is perhaps only plaster and not marble; and that often we have seen those we believed to be very hard and firm which experience has shown to be very fragile. Finally, what do you hope it will do when it is a question of placing the capital <note>The "capital" is the decorative topmost part of a column.</note> upon this column? It will distrust everything as if they were irons one wished to put on its feet. Has one not seen, it will say, bad architects who have erected many which they thought very firm and which nonetheless fell on their own? How do I know if the same thing will not happen to this one, and if the goblins will not shake the earth? They are wicked; and I do not yet know if the base is so well supported that these evil spirits can do nothing against it. What will you say to that? I cannot guess for what purpose he feigns this, unless perhaps to show that all the things I have proposed as true and certain are entirely inconsistent with that general renunciation of everything doubtful, which he wants to pass off as my only method for seeking truth; this is completely inconsistent, and is no less puerile and inept than the impertinent thought of that mason who made the whole art of architecture consist in digging foundations, and who criticized everything the architect did afterward as being contrary to that.

...that you made me take, and which have greatly fatigued us both. You maintained that you were an architect, or that you knew the art of it, but you never knew how to prove it and you stopped halfway, entangled in a thousand difficulties, and this so many times that I have trouble remembering them all. And nevertheless, it will be good to remember them now, so that the response I have to give you loses none of its force. Here then are the principal points <note>original: "chefs"; meaning the main headings or principles of the argument.</note> of this new manner of architecture, by which it sabotages its own strength and strips itself of all hope of ever being able to advance anything in this art.

First, you do not know if, beneath the surface of the earth, you will find rock: and consequently, you must no more trust this rock or this stone (if indeed you can ever lean upon the rock) than sand itself. From this it follows that everything is uncertain and wavering, and that nothing firm can be built. I will not provide you with any example of this; think of it yourself and search all the storehouses of your memory, and see if you find anything there that is not infected by this stain; you would do me a pleasure to show me even one.

**2.** Before I have found firm ground, beneath which I know there is no sand nor any evil spirits <note>original: "esprits malins"; a mocking reference to Descartes’s "malicious demon" or "evil genius" thought experiment used in his Meditations to doubt the senses.</note> who could shake it, I must reject all things and hold every kind of matter as suspect. Or at the very least, according to the common and ancient way of building, I must before all things define whether there can be any material that one ought not to reject, and what that material is, and warn the excavators at the same time to keep it in their pit. From which it follows, as before, that there is nothing firm, but that everything is too weak, and therefore useless for the construction of an edifice.

**3.** If there is anything that can be shaken even the slightest bit, consider it certain and assume that it is already overturned; think only of digging, and use this empty pit as a foundation. And do not tell me that one will not dig forever, that it is only for a time, and down to a certain depth, according to whether there is more or less sand. Since he does not do this, and indeed since he cannot do it, it must be confessed that he cannot be excused for having been greatly mistaken. 

And I never thought of proving that I (that is to say, a thing that thinks) was a spirit, any more than the other thought to prove that he was an architect. But, to tell the truth, our author, with all the trouble he has given himself here, has proved nothing else except that if he had any wit, he did not have much. And even though, by pushing his *metaphysical doubt* to the limit, one reaches the point of supposing that one does not know if one is sleeping or waking, it does not follow any more from this that one can find nothing certain and assured than it follows from the fact that an architect—who begins to dig his foundations and does not know if he will find stone, clay, or something else under the sand—that he will never, I say, be able to encounter firm ground in that place, or that, having found it, he should not trust in it. 

And it follows just as little that all things are useless for the search for truth simply because, before knowing that there is a God, everyone has occasion to doubt all things—namely, all those of which one does not have a clear perception present to the mind, as I have said several times. Just as, because that architect had commanded that all things be cast out of the pit he was making to dig his foundations until he had found firm ground, it did not follow that there had been neither **rubble** <note>original: "moellon"; rough, unhewn stones used for filling in foundations.</note> nor stone in that pit that he could afterwards employ to build and raise his foundations. ...claim that rock is for supporting great towers. But it is not the same when it comes to establishing the foundations of philosophy; for one cannot say that there are certain limits to doubting below the greatest certainty, beyond which it is useless to pass, and upon which we can even reasonably and confidently rely; for truth, consisting in something indivisible <note>Descartes means that truth does not admit of degrees; a statement is either perfectly certain or it must be treated as potentially false for the purpose of his method.</note>, it may happen that what we do not see to be entirely certain, however probable it may appear to us, is nevertheless absolutely false; and undoubtedly he would philosophize very poorly who had no other foundations for his philosophy than things he recognized could be false. 

But what will he reply to the skeptics <note>Followers of Pyrrhonism who argued that certain knowledge is impossible.</note> who go beyond all limits of doubting? How will he refute them? Undoubtedly he will place them among the desperate and the incurable. That is all well and good; but meanwhile, in what rank do you think those people will place him? And do not tell me that this sect is now abolished; it is as much in force as it ever was; and most of those who think they have a bit more wit than others, finding nothing in ordinary philosophy <note>original: "philosophie ordinaire"; referring to Scholasticism, the Aristotelian system taught in 17th-century universities.</note> that satisfies them, and seeing nothing better, immediately throw themselves into that of the skeptics; and these are primarily those who want the existence of God and the immortality of their soul demonstrated to them. 

So it is that what is said here by our author sounds bad and is a very poor example, especially since he is regarded as a clever man; for it shows that he believes the errors of skeptics who are atheists cannot be refuted; and thus he supports and confirms them as much as he can. For all those who are skeptics today do not doubt, as far as practice is concerned, that they have a head, or that two plus three makes five, and similar things; but they say only that they use them as true things because they seem so to them; but they do not believe them to be **certainly** true, because they are not fully persuaded and convinced of them by certain and invincible reasons. And since it does not seem the same to them regarding the existence of God and the immortality of their soul, it follows that they do not consider that they ought to use them as true things, even regarding practice, unless these two things are first proven to them by reasons more certain than any of those that lead them to embrace what merely appears true to them. 

Now, having así proven both in my *Meditations*, which no one that I know of before me had done, it seems to me that one could devise nothing more unreasonable than to impute to me, as [he] does...

our author, in a hundred places in his dissertation, attributes to me an excessive affectation of doubting, which is the unique error in which the entire sect of the skeptics <note>The Skeptics, or Pyrrhonists, argued that nothing could be known for certain. And certainly, he is quite liberal in enumerating my faults; for, although in that passage he says that it is no small praise to go further than others, and to cross *a ford that has never been attempted by anyone, and that he has no reason to believe I have not done so regarding the subject in question, as I will show shortly*, nevertheless he places this among my faults. This is because, he says, the praise is only great when one can cross it without being in danger of perishing; here he seems to want to persuade readers that I have suffered shipwreck, and that I have committed some signal fault. And yet, he does not believe it himself, nor does he have any reason to suspect it; for if he could have found even the slightest error to show that I had strayed from the right path in the whole course I took to lead our mind from the knowledge of its own existence to that of the existence of God, and of the distinction of itself from the body, there is no doubt he would not have omitted it in a dissertation so long, so full of words and so empty of reasons. He would undoubtedly have much preferred to produce such an error rather than constantly changing the question as he has done whenever the subject required him to speak of it, and introducing me disputing foolishly whether the thinking thing is a spirit <note>original: "esprit"; here meaning an immaterial substance or soul.</note>. He has therefore had no reason to believe, nor even to suspect, that I have committed the least fault in all that I have said and advanced, and by which I was the first to overthrew this enormous doubt of the skeptics; he confesses that this is worthy of great praise; and yet he does not hesitate to reproach me as if I were guilty of this fault, and to attribute to me this doubt of the skeptics, which could with more justice be attributed to anyone else but me.

## AND REPLIES

that man <note>Descartes refers here to an imaginary critic in a parable used by Bourdin.</note> reproached the architect for having done nothing else while digging than uncovering the rock, pretending not to know that it was upon this very rock that he had built his chapel. In the same way, our author <note>Pierre Bourdin (1595–1653), the Jesuit priest who wrote the "Seventh Objections."</note> seems to reproach me, claiming that in rejecting everything that is doubtful, I have done nothing more than uncover the truth of that old dictum, *I think, therefore I am* <note>original: "je pense, donc je suis." This is the famous *Cogito, ergo sum*.</note>. This is perhaps because he counts for nothing the fact that, by this means, I have proven the existence of God and several other things demonstrated in my *Meditations*. He even has the audacity to take me as his sole witness to the liberty he grants himself to say whatever he pleases; just as in other places, regarding subjects just as unbelievable, he does not hesitate to say that *everyone believes it just as he says it; that the school desks sing nothing else; that we have all learned the same thing from our masters, from the most recent all the way back to Adam, etc.* One should place no more faith in this than in the oaths of certain people who are all the more prone to swearing as the things they try to persuade others of are less believable and further from the truth.

6. He responded: *This architect, by his manner of building, falls into the very fault he criticizes in others; for he is astonished to see that all men without exception unanimously say and believe that the sand or the dust that supports us is firm enough, that the earth upon which we stand does not shake, etc. And yet he is not at all astonished to see that, with a similar or even greater assurance, he boldly says that we must reject the sand and everything mixed with it, etc.*

This was just as unreasonable as everything else our author says on similar occasions.

7. He responded: *This art <note>Bourdin uses "art" to refer to Descartes's philosophical method.</note> fails and throws us into a fault peculiar to it. For what the rest of men hold to be somewhat firm—namely, the earth where we are, the sand, the stones—this art, through a design peculiar to itself, takes the exact opposite view. That is to say, it takes the trench from which one has pulled and rejected the sand, the stones, and everything found within, not only as something firm, but even as something so firm that one can found and build a very solid chapel upon it, and leans upon it in such a way that if you take away this support, he will fall flat on his face.*

In this, this poor mason <note>Descartes mockingly refers to Bourdin using the metaphor of a simple builder who does not understand the structural necessity of a foundation.</note> is no less mistaken than our author, when he fails to remember those words he had said a little earlier, namely: *you shall neither affirm it nor deny it, etc.*

In this, the mason was no less mistaken than our author; the former applying to the act of digging, and the latter to the <term>renunciation</term> <note>original: "abdiation," likely a typographical error in the original text for 'abdication' or 'abnegation,' meaning the setting aside of doubts.</note> of doubts, what properly belongs only to the <term>construction</term> <note>original: "contruction."</note> of both buildings and philosophy: for it is very certain that we must admit nothing as true that we cannot prove to be so when it comes to affirming or establishing what is true; but when it is only a matter of digging or rejecting, the slightest suspicion of instability or doubt is enough for that.

<meta>This page continues the "Seventh Objections" leveled against René Descartes by the Jesuit Father Pierre Bourdin. Bourdin uses a mocking architectural metaphor—comparing Descartes's philosophical method of doubt to a mason digging a foundation—to argue that Descartes's "new" method is either common knowledge or logically unsound. The "sand" mentioned here represents the sensory information and uncertain opinions that Descartes rejects to find the "bedrock" of certainty.</meta>

### SEVENTH OBJECTIONS

12. He responded: *This art <note>The "art" refers to Descartes’s philosophical method.</note> fails in that it contains nothing good or nothing new, and much that is superfluous. For, first:*

*1° If, by the discarding and rejection he makes of the sand, he means only that excavation used by all other architects—who reject sand only insofar as it is not firm enough to support the weight of a great building—he will say something good, but he will say nothing new; and this way of digging will not be new, but very ancient and common to all architects, without exception.*

*2° If, by this way of digging, he wants us to reject the sand so completely that we remove it entirely, retaining nothing of it, and making use of its nothingness—that is, the emptiness of the place it previously filled—as if it were something firm and solid, he will say something new, but he will say nothing good; and this way of digging will indeed be new, but it will not be legitimate.*

*3° If he says that by the force and weight of his reasons, he proves certainly and evidently that he is experienced in architecture, and that he practices it, and that nevertheless, as such, he is neither an architect, nor a mason, nor a laborer, but that he is of a condition so different or separate from theirs that one can conceive what he is without having knowledge of the others—just as one can conceive of an animal or a sensing thing without yet conceiving of one that neighs or roars, etc.; <note>Bourdin is mocking Descartes’s argument that the mind (a "thinking thing") can be understood as existing independently of the body or its sensory functions.</note> he will say something good, but he will say nothing new, since nothing else is sung everywhere in the streets, and it is taught by as many men as there are who are even slightly versed in architecture, or even (granting that architecture also encompasses the construction of walls, so that those are said to be versed in architecture who mix sand with lime, who cut stones, or who carry mortar) by as many men as there are who believe that what I have just said is the trade of artisans and laborers—that is, in a word, by all men.*

*4° If he says he has proved by good and maturely considered reasons that he truly exists, and that he is versed in the art of architecture, and that while he exists it does not follow from this that there is any architect, mason, or laborer who truly exists, <note>This targets Descartes’s "Cogito," where he proves his own existence as a thinking thing while still doubting the existence of the external world and other people.</note> he will say something new, but he will say nothing good; no more nor less than if he said that an animal exists, and yet there is neither lion, nor fox, nor any other animal that exists.*

*5° If he says that he builds—that is, that he employs the art of architecture in the construction of his buildings—and that he builds in such a way that by a reflective action <term>reflective action: a conscious act of the mind turning back upon itself to examine its own operations</term> he envisions and considers what he does, and that he thus knows and sees that he builds what*

(which is properly called having knowledge and perceiving what one is doing), and if he says that this is the specific property of architecture, or of that art of building which stands above the practical experience of masons and laborers, and consequently that he is truly an architect, he will be saying what he has not yet said—what he should have said, what I expected him to say, and what I even often wished to suggest to him when I saw him struggling in vain to tell us what he was. He will be saying, I say, something good, but he will say nothing new; for there is no one who did not long ago learn this from their tutors, and those tutors from their masters, all the way back to Adam.

Certainly, if he says this, how many superfluous things will there be in this art! How many exorbitant things! What <term>battology</term> <note>Original: "battologie." A rhetorical term for wearisome and excessive repetition, or "babbling." Bourdin is accusing Descartes of being unnecessarily wordy.</note>! How many machines that serve only for show, or to deceive us? What is the point of making us afraid of the earth’s instability, of earthquakes, of <term>goblins</term> <note>Original: "lutins." Bourdin uses this whimsical term to mock Descartes’s "evil demon" (malin génie) hypothesis, which Descartes used to justify his radical doubt.</note>, and other empty fears? What is the purpose of a pit so deep that it seems to leave us with nothing but the void? Why such long <term>peregrinations</term> <note>Original: "pérégrinations," meaning long journeys or wanderings. This refers to the intellectual journey Descartes takes through his Meditations.</note>, and of such duration, in foreign lands where the senses do not reach, among shadows and specters? Of what use are all these things for the construction of a chapel, as if one could not build one without turning everything upside down? But what is the point of this mixing and changing of so many different materials; why sometimes reject the old and employ the new, and at other times reject the new to resume the old? Might it not be perhaps that—just as we must behave differently in a temple, or in the presence of persons of merit, than in an inn or a tavern—these new mysteries require new ceremonies? But why, instead of amusing himself with so much trouble, did he not rather set forth the truth thus clearly, cleanly, and briefly: *I build, I have knowledge of the building I make, therefore I am an architect.* <note>Bourdin is here parodying Descartes’s famous "I think, therefore I am" (Cogito, ergo sum).</note>

6° Finally, if he says that building houses, arranging and ordering their rooms, studies, porticos, doors, windows, columns, and other ornaments, and commanding all the workers who put their hand to it—such as carpenters, stone-cutters, masons, roofers, laborers, and others—and conducting all their works, is so much the specific property of an architect that no other artisan or worker can do it, he will say something new, but he will say nothing good. Furthermore, he will say it without proof and without acknowledgment, unless perhaps he is keeping and hiding something from us (which is the only refuge remaining to him) to show it to us with astonishment and admiration in its own time;

Lastly, he would answer: You fear here, no doubt (and I forgive you), for your art and manner of building, which you cherish, and which you caress and embrace as your own production. You are afraid that, having rendered it guilty of so many sins, and seeing it now leaking everywhere <note>Original: "faisant eau partout." A nautical and architectural metaphor for a structure or argument that is failing and unable to keep out the elements.</note>, I might condemn it to the scrap heap. I know who you are, and I know the strength and liveliness of your spirit. In the meantime, be content with this, and continue to lend me your attention while I continue to satisfy your demands. I have committed many things in few words so as not to be long, and have only touched on most of them lightly, such as those concerning vaults, the opening of windows, columns, porticos, and other such things. But here is the design for a **new comedy** <note>Bourdin implies that Descartes’s philosophical process is more like a staged play or a farce than a serious scientific inquiry.</note>.

### Whether one can invent a new architecture.

You ask, in the third place, whether one can invent, etc. As he was asking this, some of his friends, seeing that his extreme **jealousy** and the **hatred** by which he was carried away had turned into a **sickness**, did not allow him to declaim further in the public squares, but immediately had him taken to the **doctor**.

For my part, I would not dare, in truth, to suspect anything of the kind from our author; but I will only continue to show here with what care he seems to have tried to imitate him in all things. He behaves entirely like him, acting as a very severe judge who takes careful and scrupulously care not to pronounce anything rashly; for, after having condemned me eleven times for the sole reason that I rejected everything doubtful in order to found and establish what is certain—just as if I had dug deep to lay the foundations of some great edifice—finally, at the twelfth time, he begins to examine the matter and says: 1. <meta>This page continues René Descartes’s rebuttal to Father Pierre Bourdin (the "mason") in the Seventh Objections. Descartes is refuting Bourdin’s claim that a "thinking thing" requires a "reflective act"—thinking about thinking—to be considered spiritual or distinct from matter. Descartes argues that the simple act of thinking is enough to define a substance as incorporeal.</meta>

### SEVENTH OBJECTIONS

that a thing must be a <term>thinking substance</term><note>Descartes’s famous "res cogitans," the idea that the essence of the mind is thought.</note> in order to be entirely spiritual and above matter (which alone he wishes to be properly called by the name of "spirit"). He claims that beyond this, it is required that by a **reflective act** upon its own thought, it thinks that it thinks, or that it has an **internal knowledge** of its thought. He is mistaken in this, just as that mason is when he says that a man experienced in **architecture** must, by a reflective act, consider that he has that experience before he can be an architect. For although there is no architect who has not often considered, or at least who could not have often considered, that he knows the art of building, it is nonetheless a manifest truth that this consideration is not necessary to truly be an architect. A similar consideration or reflection is just as little required for a thinking substance to be above matter. 

For the first thought, whatever it may be, by which we perceive something, does not differ more from the second—by which we perceive that we have already perceived it—than that second thought differs from the third, by which we perceive that we have already perceived having perceived that thing before. And one could not provide the slightest reason why the second of these thoughts would not come from a **corporeal subject** <note>A physical body or material substance.</note> if one grants that the first can come from one. This is why our author errs in this much more dangerously than that mason: for by removing the true and very intelligible difference between **corporeal** and **incorporeal** things—namely, that the latter think and the others do not—and by substituting another in its place which cannot have the character of an essential difference—namely, that the former consider that they think and the others do not consider it—he hinders, as much as he can, the understanding of the **real distinction** between the <term>soul</term> and the body.

6. And he is even less excusable for favoring the side of **brute beasts** <note>In the 17th century, the question of whether animals had souls or could "think" was a major point of contention between Descartes and his critics.</note> by granting them thought as well as to men, than is this mason for wanting to attribute to himself and his fellows the knowledge of architecture as well as to architects.

And finally, it appears quite clearly that both have had no regard for what was true, or even plausible, but only for what might be most suitable to disparage his adversary and make him pass for a man of little sense to those who did not know him, and who would not take much trouble to know him. And for that reason, the one who reported this whole story noted very well, to express the furious envy and jealousy

<summary>Descartes argues that the essence of the soul is simply "thinking" and does not require a secondary "reflection on thinking," while criticizing his opponent for attributing thought to animals.</summary>

## AND REPLIES

[...of] this mason, that he had praised as a magnificent **display** the trench that this architect had dug; but that, regarding the rock discovered by that means, and the chapel built upon it, he had neglected and disparaged it as a thing of little importance; and that nevertheless, to satisfy the friendship he felt for him and the goodwill he had toward him, he did not fail to give thanks and thank him, etc. Just as in the conclusion he introduces him with these fine acclamations in his mouth:

> *Finally, if he says that, how many superfluous things will there be, how many exorbitant ones! What <term>battology</term>!<note>From the Greek "battologia," meaning vain repetition or senseless babbling.</note> How many machines that serve only for show or to deceive us! And a little later (and I forgive you) for your art and manner of building, which you cherish, and which you caress and embrace as your own production, etc.*

Do not fear, however, I am your friend more than you think, etc. For all this represents so <term>naively</term><note>In the 17th-century sense of "naturally" or "artlessly."</note> the illness of this mason that I doubt any poet could have depicted it better. But I am surprised that our author has imitated him so well in all things that he seems not to notice what he is doing, and to have forgotten to use that **reflective act of thought**, which he said just a moment ago makes the difference between man and beast. 

For certainly he would not say that there is too great a display of words in my writings if he considered that the one he used—I will not say to <term>impugn</term><note>To challenge or call into question.</note>, for he provides no reason for doing so, but to **bark** (let me be permitted here to use this somewhat harsh word, for I know of none more fitting to express the thing) after this single metaphysical doubt of which I spoke in my first Meditation, is much greater than that which I used to propose it. And he would have easily refrained from accusing my discourse of <term>battology</term> if he had noticed what long, superfluous, and useless loquacity he has used in his entire dissertation, at the end of which he nonetheless asserts that he did not wish to be long. 

But because in that very place he says he is my friend, to treat him as amicably as I possibly can—just as that mason was taken by his friends to the physician—I will likewise take care to recommend him to his <term>superior</term>.<note>A reference to Father Bourdin's religious superior in the Jesuit order.</note>
